title: Bulk optical scattering as a depth-of-interaction design parameter in monolithic PET…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper is a draft from November twenty twenty-six.
reels.words: this paper is a draft from november twenty twenty-six. it studies a monolithic pet detector. one block of crystal turns a gamma ray into a flash of light. the pool of light on the photodetector array gives the position of the flash. this paper asks whether the crystal can carry more information about depth. the change it studies is bulk scattering. simulations usually treat scattering as a loss. in a loaded nanocomposite, the scattering grows with the particle loading, so it can be set by design.

reels.name: Detector
reels.cap: The reference detector is a slab of L S O.
reels.words: the reference detector is a slab of l s o. it measures fifty millimetres by fifty millimetres and ten millimetres thick. black paint covers five of its faces. the sixth face carries an eight by eight array of s i p m detectors. each one is five point eight millimetres wide on a six millimetre pitch. a gamma ray deposits its energy at one point. the crystal emits light in every direction. light can leave only inside a cone around the face normal. the half angle of the cone is fifty-five point five degrees. light outside the cone reflects back inside until the black paint absorbs it.

reels.name: Scatter
reels.cap: Now the crystal scatters light.
reels.words: now the crystal scatters light. a photon that would have reached the black paint turns at a scattering point instead. many of those photons now arrive inside the exit cone. the array detects eight hundred and sixty-eight photons per event in the clear crystal and one thousand five hundred and eighty-five at a scattering length of two millimetres. the amount of light also depends on the depth of the flash. in the clear crystal it is nearly the same at every depth. with scattering, a flash near the readout face has little crystal to cross, so most of its light arrives. a flash near the entrance face loses more to the black paint. so the detected light rises toward the readout face.

reels.name: Bound
reels.cap: The paper measures depth information with the Cramer Rao bound.
reels.words: the paper measures depth information with the cramer rao bound. it is the smallest error that any unbiased estimator can reach. take two flashes that differ only a little in depth. each s i p m catches a slightly different mean count from the two. the counts are poisson, so each one has noise of about its square root. the fisher information adds up how far each mean moves compared with its noise. the bound is one over the square root of that sum. each design point is simulated once in gate. the mean count of every s i p m is fitted as a smooth function of position, and the slope of that fit gives the fisher information. a maximum likelihood estimator then checks that the bound can be reached.

reels.name: Sweep
reels.cap: The paper simulates nine scattering lengths, from none to sixty-four millimetres.
reels.words: the paper simulates nine scattering lengths, from none to sixty-four millimetres. the left panel shows the depth bound over the whole crystal. it is lowest at two millimetres, at zero point one seven one millimetres, against zero point two two four for the clear crystal. that is twenty-four per cent lower. the interior is more than ten millimetres from the side faces. there the bound keeps falling as the scattering gets stronger. at half a millimetre it reaches zero point zero eight four millimetres. that is half of the clear crystal's zero point one six five. the estimator's error falls by forty-two per cent, from zero point two five zero to zero point one four six.

reels.name: Counts
reels.cap: The Fisher information splits exactly into two terms.
reels.words: the fisher information splits exactly into two terms. the count term follows how the total number of detected photons changes with position. the pattern term follows how the light is shared among the s i p m channels. in the clear crystal the total barely changes with depth, so the count term carries three per cent of the depth information. with scattering lengths up to four millimetres it carries forty-nine to sixty per cent. the gain that scattering adds is therefore carried by the total light. at the clear crystal's photon count, the interior gain at two millimetres shrinks to three point five per cent.

reels.name: Ambiguity
reels.cap: The total light only gives the depth if each event's light yield is known.
reels.words: the total light only gives the depth if each event's light yield is known. two different flashes can send the same total to the array. one is bright and near the entrance face. the other is dim and near the readout face. a real crystal adds a spread to the yield, a factor common to every s i p m. that spread moves the total up and down at a fixed depth, so one total fits a wide range of depths.

reels.name: Spread
reels.cap: The paper weights the count term by one over one plus the total times the spread squared.
reels.words: the paper weights the count term by one over one plus the total times the spread squared. at two millimetres, the weight halves at a spread of two point five per cent, and the gain in the interior vanishes at about three point five per cent. the measured energy resolution of l s o limits its own spread to three point one per cent at most. with the yield unknown, every scattering crystal has a larger depth bound than the clear crystal.

reels.name: Energy
reels.cap: The same total light also measures the energy of the gamma ray.
reels.words: the same total light also measures the energy of the gamma ray. so depth and energy compete for it. with the position known, scattering lowers the median energy bound in the interior from three point two to two point one per cent. with the position estimated jointly, it rises to four point one per cent.

reels.name: Rim
reels.cap: Over the whole crystal, the bound has a minimum at two millimetres.
reels.words: over the whole crystal, the bound has a minimum at two millimetres. the maps across the face show where it comes from. in the interior, the bound falls everywhere as scattering strengthens. along the side walls, a band two to three millimetres wide rises instead. without that band, the curve falls all the way to the shortest length. the optimum is where the interior gain and the rim penalty balance. the optimum sits at about one fifth of the thickness. it lies at one, two and four millimetres for crystals five, ten and twenty millimetres thick.

reels.name: Index
reels.cap: The gain also grows with the refractive index of the crystal.
reels.words: the gain also grows with the refractive index of the crystal. a higher index narrows the escape cone. at index two point one five the half angle is forty-four point two degrees, and fifteen per cent of all directions are trapped for good. scattering frees that light. the optimum then lowers the whole-crystal bound by forty-nine per cent against the clear crystal. at index one point six, it gives no gain.

reels.name: Rivals
reels.cap: Could a surface layer give the same gain?
reels.words: could a surface layer give the same gain? the paper tests four, each with a clear bulk. one has a ground exit face. three have a diffusing sheet, in the grease, at the readout face and at the entrance face. every one has a higher interior depth bound than the clear crystal's zero point one six five millimetres. bulk scattering at two millimetres reaches zero point one one eight. at equal photon counts the bulk stays below the clear value and every layer stays above it.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: The bounds compare designs.
reels.words: the bounds compare designs. they do not predict resolutions. they assume a light yield known for every event and gamma rays at normal incidence. loaded nanocomposites have an index of about one point five to one point seven, where the gain is zero to ten per cent. the timing is not bounded. at the optimum the photon paths turn diffusive over about fifty millimetres, which should lengthen the arrival times.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: This paper asks what bulk scattering does for depth in a monolithic PET crystal.
reels.words: this paper asks what bulk scattering does for depth in a monolithic pet crystal. it computes the cramer rao bound from simulated light and checks it with an estimator. scattering returns light the black wrap would absorb. it makes the detected total depend on depth. in the interior the depth bound halves at the shortest scattering length. the gain lives in the total light, so the light yield must be known to within about three point five per cent. it also costs energy resolution. over the whole crystal the optimum sits near a fifth of the thickness, and surface layers do not reproduce it. the next step is to build a crystal with scatterers mixed into it and measure it.

title: Machine learning enables experimental access to photon-by-photon arrival times in…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Onishi and colleagues at Hamamatsu Photonics wrote this paper.
reels.words: onishi and colleagues at hamamatsu photonics wrote this paper. it reports a way to read the arrival time of every single photon in a scintillation detector, using only the detector's ordinary waveform. a gamma ray enters a scintillation crystal. the crystal turns its energy into many photons, which travel to a silicon photomultiplier, or s i p m. the s i p m answers with one smooth pulse, and the pulse hides when each photon arrived. the method recovers those arrival times from the pulse alone.

reels.name: Response
reels.cap: The method first needs to know what one photon looks like at the output.
reels.words: the method first needs to know what one photon looks like at the output. so the authors fired a laser pulse sixty picoseconds wide at the s i p m and attenuated it until a flash carried about one photon. each flash gives one recorded waveform, and the heights of those waveforms form a histogram with separate peaks. the waveforms in the first peak are single photons, and their average is the single-photon response.

reels.name: Product
reels.cap: A detector pulse is a sum with one single-photon response for every detected photon, each placed at that photon's arrival time.
reels.words: a detector pulse is a sum with one single-photon response for every detected photon, each placed at that photon's arrival time. the authors write the sum as a matrix. each column of the matrix s holds the response, shifted by one more time bin. a vector of zeros and ones marks the bins where photons arrived, and multiplying s by the vector adds up the shifted responses that the ones select. the product is the waveform. going the other way is the hard direction. many sets of arrival times can fit the noisy waveform equally well, so something has to decide which set to keep.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: For every single event, a fresh neural network is trained from scratch.
reels.words: for every single event, a fresh neural network is trained from scratch. its input is a constant vector, and it has four layers with one hundred nodes in each hidden layer. its output has one number for every picosecond time bin. the matrix s turns that output into a reconstructed waveform, and a loss measures the difference from the measured waveform. the loss also penalizes the number of photons, and early time bins cost twice as much as late ones. eight hundred iterations of the optimizer then move the output until the reconstructed waveform matches the measurement. the final output is the list of photon timestamps. no true timestamp is ever used, so the network needs no labels.

reels.name: Binary
reels.cap: The output must hold zeros and ones, because a photon either arrived in a time bin or did not.
reels.words: the output must hold zeros and ones, because a photon either arrived in a time bin or did not. each output node first produces a value between zero and one with a sigmoid. on the forward pass, a threshold of zero point five turns that value into a zero or a one. a threshold has no useful gradient, so the backward pass treats it as the identity and lets the gradient through unchanged. this straight-through estimator lets the optimizer train a network with binary outputs.

reels.name: Simulation
reels.cap: The authors first tested the method on a Geant4 simulation, where the true photon times are known.
reels.words: the authors first tested the method on a geant4 simulation, where the true photon times are known. gamma rays of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts strike an l y s o crystal that measures three by three by ten millimetres. the simulation tracks every optical photon and turns the true arrival times into a noisy s i p m waveform. the network sees only the waveform. its estimated timestamps land close to the true ones, and its reconstructed waveform follows the true waveform. the timing bias stays within about ten picoseconds. the spread falls to about thirty-five picoseconds for later photons, but it is larger for the earliest photons, which overlap the noisy rising edge. the estimated photon count has a standard deviation of three photons from the true count, which is one point three percent.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: Next the authors measured timing with two L Y S O detectors face to face, and a sodium twenty-two source between them.
reels.words: next the authors measured timing with two l y s o detectors face to face, and a sodium twenty-two source between them. the difference between the two arrival times forms a histogram, and its full width at half maximum is the coincidence timing resolution. read straight from the waveform at the best threshold and sixty-six volts, it is one hundred and sixteen point three picoseconds. the network turns each waveform into photon timestamps. one timestamp alone is clearly worse than several combined. a plain average of many timestamps degrades, because late photons carry little timing information. a maximum likelihood estimate weights the early photons most, and reaches one hundred and nine point seven picoseconds. a virtual test checked the position information. shifting one waveform digitally imitates a source ten millimetres off centre, which should move the histogram's peak by sixty-six point seven picoseconds. the peak moved by sixty-six point two.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: The next test used a three by three by twenty millimetre L Y S O crystal with the sensor on one end.
reels.words: the next test used a three by three by twenty millimetre l y s o crystal with the sensor on one end. a lead collimator selected gamma rays that interact near the top, far from the sensor, or near the bottom, beside it. for the first photon, bottom events arrive earlier, because their path is shorter. for later photons the order reverses, since bottom events include photons on the longest, most reflected paths. their arrival times therefore spread wider, and top events end up with the better timing resolution.

reels.name: Cherenkov
reels.cap: Bismuth germanate, or B G O, emits prompt Cherenkov light and delayed scintillation light.
reels.words: bismuth germanate, or b g o, emits prompt cherenkov light and delayed scintillation light. against an l y s o reference, its time differences form a histogram with a long tail. a gaussian fits the prompt cherenkov events, and an exponentially modified gaussian fits the scintillation tail. the authors then took the fast events and the slow events and compared their photon timestamps. the second photon follows the first after the same delay in both groups. later photons trail the first photon by more in the slow events, so the gap between the twentieth and the first photon sorts the events. a threshold of one hundred and forty-one picoseconds on that gap narrows the full width at half maximum by sixteen percent and the full width at tenth maximum by eighteen percent, but it removes most fast events. a threshold of four hundred and twenty-three picoseconds narrows them by five and six percent, and keeps about sixty percent of the fast events, with about sixty percent accuracy.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: Digital S i P M detectors would give photon times directly, but none has been built yet for radiation detection.
reels.words: digital s i p m detectors would give photon times directly, but none has been built yet for radiation detection. this method lets an ordinary analog s i p m act as a virtually digital one. matching a ten percent timing gain with hardware alone would take about twenty-three percent more photon detection efficiency. the method has limits. its errors are largest for the earliest photons, which matter most for timing. the s i p m's own single photon time resolution sets a floor, and every event needs its own optimization on digitized waveforms.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: This paper recovers the arrival time of every detected photon from one S i P M waveform.
reels.words: this paper recovers the arrival time of every detected photon from one s i p m waveform. the waveform is one measured single-photon response for each photon, which a matrix s writes as a product with a vector of arrival times. a network with binary outputs is trained again for each event until that product matches the waveform, and it needs no labels. in simulation, its timestamps land close to the true ones. in l y s o, they improve the timing resolution from one hundred and sixteen to one hundred and ten picoseconds, show how arrival times depend on depth, and separate cherenkov events from scintillation events in b g o. its limits are the earliest photons, the jitter of the s i p m, and the cost of optimizing every event.

title: Plenoptic imaging of particle interactions in scintillation detectors

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Dai and colleagues at U C San Diego wrote this paper.
reels.words: dai and colleagues at u c san diego wrote this paper. it is a preprint from july twenty twenty-six. it asks where a particle interacted inside a scintillator, in three dimensions, to about one millimetre. an ionizing particle deposits energy in a five centimetre cube of crystal. the crystal answers with a flash that spreads in every direction. the sensor on one face catches only about one hundred photons of it. with so few photons, locating the flash is hard.

reels.name: Masks
reels.cap: Two earlier methods locate an event in a single block of crystal.
reels.words: two earlier methods locate an event in a single block of crystal. centroiding reads the light pattern on a face of the crystal. its depth signal is weak, so the depth resolution stays near a centimetre. coded aperture puts a mask in front of the sensor. the mask blocks a share of the photons, so the signal gets weaker. a lens array bends every photon instead of absorbing it. this paper builds on lenses.

reels.name: Lens
reels.cap: A single lens forms a sharp image of a point only when the point sits at one distance.
reels.words: a single lens forms a sharp image of a point only when the point sits at one distance. closer or farther, the image blurs into a disc. so the size of the disc tells the depth of the point. collecting many photons needs a small f-number, which means a large lens. a large lens must sit far from the source, so the detector stops being compact. the paper therefore drops the main lens. many small lenslets sit five millimetres from the crystal, with the sensor eighteen point five millimetres behind them.

reels.name: Multifocal
reels.cap: An array of lenslets with one focal length has a problem.
reels.words: an array of lenslets with one focal length has a problem. every lenslet blurs the same amount at a given depth, so the whole pattern sharpens at one depth only. away from that depth, the pattern is out of focus. the paper gives the lenslets seven different focal lengths, from three to fifteen millimetres. all lenslets keep the same diameter of three millimetres. the prototype arranges forty-two of them in a hexagonal pattern. now the source moves through depth. at each depth, a different lenslet focuses sharply and the others blur by different amounts. the seven spot sizes form a pattern that changes with depth, and that pattern is what the sensor reads.

reels.name: Bound
reels.cap: The paper scores each design with the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
reels.words: the paper scores each design with the cramér–rao lower bound. it states the best precision that any unbiased estimator can reach. the bound comes from the fisher information, which measures how much the sensor pattern changes when the source moves by a small step. a pattern that barely changes carries little information. a pattern that changes strongly pins the depth down tightly. each pixel adds its squared change divided by its expected count, so photon noise is part of the sum.

reels.name: Design
reels.cap: The paper simulates a source at depths from zero to fifty millimetres.
reels.words: the paper simulates a source at depths from zero to fifty millimetres. it compares the multifocal array with a unifocal array and a single lens, at three focal lengths. each unifocal design is precise only near its own focal depth. the multifocal design stays low across the whole range. at three point five millimetres depth, its bound is thirty-five times lower than the fifteen millimetre design. the photon count changes with depth too, from sixty photons to five hundred, because a closer source fills a larger solid angle of the array.

reels.name: Build
reels.cap: The lenslets sit in a three-D printed holder that couples to a camera.
reels.words: the lenslets sit in a three-d printed holder that couples to a camera. two by two binning gives an effective pixel size of six point nine micrometres. the array covers about two by three centimetres of the scintillator face. a scintillation event cannot be made at a known position inside a crystal. so the team calibrates with an led on a motorised stage. the led emits at five hundred and seventy nanometres, close to the scintillator's emission. the stage moves it to each position, and the camera records the pattern.

reels.name: Dictionary
reels.cap: Small sideways shifts of the source only translate the pattern.
reels.words: small sideways shifts of the source only translate the pattern. so the calibration samples ten depth planes, five millimetres apart. each plane holds an eleven by eleven grid, again with five millimetre spacing. that gives one thousand two hundred and ten patterns in the dictionary. each pattern is a high dynamic range image. the camera records seven exposure times at every position. bright pixels use the short exposures and faint pixels use the long ones. averaging the valid ones keeps the sharp spots and the faint blur together.

reels.name: Clicks
reels.cap: A real scintillation event gives only about one hundred photons.
reels.words: a real scintillation event gives only about one hundred photons. the test images therefore sample photons from the calibrated pattern. the assumed sensor records one bit per pixel. a pixel fires if at least one photon arrives during a short gate. the chance that a pixel fires is one minus e to the minus lambda. lambda is the expected count times the pixel's share of the pattern. most clicks land inside the bright spots, and a few land on the faint blur.

reels.name: Reconstruct
reels.cap: The reconstruction compares the clicks with every pattern in the dictionary.
reels.words: the reconstruction compares the clicks with every pattern in the dictionary. it scores each pattern with the negative log likelihood. the best match gives a coarse position on the five millimetre grid. the true source usually sits between grid points. so the algorithm shifts the chosen pattern sideways until it fits the clicks. for depth, the loss varies smoothly along the z axis, so a parabola through three planes finds the minimum.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: The test uses single events with one hundred expected photons.
reels.words: the test uses single events with one hundred expected photons. five events at different places in the volume come back close to their true positions. across the field of view, the three dimensional error stays near one millimetre. the error stays flat along depth, as the bound predicted. it grows near the edge, because the lens array covers three by four centimetres and the crystal face is five by five. fewer photons make the error larger. at fifty expected photons, a few trials fail badly because the clicks are too sparse to sample the pattern. beyond one hundred expected photons, more light does not help, because the system limits the error.

reels.name: Double
reels.cap: A second vertex makes the problem harder.
reels.words: a second vertex makes the problem harder. the algorithm now runs twice, adding one source each time. each source also gets a photon weight, fitted with newton's method. the test places both sources at the same lateral position, so only depth separates them. each vertex emits one hundred and twenty-five expected photons. when the vertices are close in depth, their patterns overlap and look almost the same. then the errors in position and in photon weight grow. as the depth gap grows, the two patterns separate and both errors fall.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The paper asks where a scintillation event happened, using about one hundred photons.
reels.words: the paper asks where a scintillation event happened, using about one hundred photons. a lens array bends every photon onto the sensor instead of blocking some. seven focal lengths make the spot pattern change with depth. the cramér–rao bound chose that design, and it stays low through the whole volume. a calibration of one thousand two hundred and ten patterns turns the camera into a forward model. a sparse search recovers one event to about one millimetre, and two events with larger errors when they are close in depth. the limits are that the calibration used an led in air, not a real scintillator, and the double-event test used equal weights at one lateral position.

title: Development of a Preclinical PET Scanner With DOI Capabilities Using Semi-Monolithic…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Cucarella and colleagues wrote this paper.
reels.words: cucarella and colleagues wrote this paper. it appeared in i e e e transactions on radiation and plasma medical sciences in twenty twenty-six. it reports a small-animal p e t ring built from semi-monolithic crystals that measure the depth of interaction. the authors test the finished ring against the n e m a n u four standard. that test measures spatial resolution, sensitivity, count rate and image quality.

reels.name: Parallax
reels.cap: A preclinical scanner has a very small field of view, and its ring has an inner diameter of just one hundred and six millimetres.
reels.words: a preclinical scanner has a very small field of view, and its ring has an inner diameter of just one hundred and six millimetres. photons from an off-centre source reach the crystals at a slant. a photon travels some way into a crystal before it interacts. a detector that knows only which crystal fired places the hit on the entrance face. the line between the two placed hits misses the true line, and this parallax error blurs the image towards the edge. a measurement of the depth of interaction moves each hit back to where it happened. then the red lines agree with the true line again.

reels.name: Block
reels.cap: Each module is a block of twenty-two L Y S O slabs.
reels.words: each module is a block of twenty-two l y s o slabs. one slab measures zero point nine seven by twenty-five point six by twelve millimetres. reflective film isolates each slab from its neighbours, so the light of a gamma stays inside one slab. a retroreflector covers the entrance face. an eight by eight array of s i p ms is glued to the opposite face. each s i p m has a three millimetre active area on a three point two millimetre pitch.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: Fourteen blocks form one ring.
reels.words: fourteen blocks form one ring. two rings sit side by side with a gap of one point two six millimetres between them. the inner diameter is one hundred and six millimetres and the axial length is fifty-two millimetres. that makes twenty-eight modules, six hundred and sixteen slabs and one thousand seven hundred and ninety-two channels.

reels.name: Readout
reels.cap: One T O F P E T two chip serves each module, so twenty-eight chips read the whole scanner.
reels.words: one t o f p e t two chip serves each module, so twenty-eight chips read the whole scanner. every channel passes its pulse through three discriminators. the first fires at a very low level. the second sits higher and discards dark counts. the third is an energy threshold that discards small signals. for every gamma, the software records the charge, the channel and the timestamp of each s i p m that fired. two gammas form a coincidence when they arrive within ten nanoseconds.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: When a gamma interacts, light spreads out from that point across the S i P M array.
reels.words: when a gamma interacts, light spreads out from that point across the s i p m array. the depth of the interaction along the twelve millimetres of the slab decides how wide that spread is. a deep interaction lies close to the s i p ms and gives a narrow, bright pattern. a shallow one lets the light fan out wide. the paper reads this with the ratio of the total energy to the largest single s i p m signal. for a wide spread the ratio is large, and for a narrow one it is small. uniform irradiation fills a distribution of this ratio with a lower and an upper edge. those edges are set to the entrance face and the back face, and that turns the ratio into millimetres.

reels.name: Position
reels.cap: The impact position needs three coordinates, and each comes from its own calculation.
reels.words: the impact position needs three coordinates, and each comes from its own calculation. across the slabs, the centre of gravity of the s i p m charges picks the slab through a lookup table. along the slab, a small neural network turns the eight summed signals into a position. it was trained on one module while a slit collimator stepped along the slab in half millimetre steps. the same network then serves all twenty-eight modules. the slab thickness limits the first coordinate to zero point nine seven millimetres. the network gives one point seven millimetres along the slab, and the depth estimator three point zero eight millimetres.

reels.name: Calibrate
reels.cap: Before the positions and energies are trusted, the gains are equalised in three steps.
reels.words: before the positions and energies are trusted, the gains are equalised in three steps. the first step sets the photopeak of each of the sixty-four channels of a module to the mean. the second step gives each of the twenty-two slabs a factor, its photopeak divided by the mean over all slabs. the third step divides the flood map into sixty-four voronoi regions and corrects each one. it also calibrates the energy in kilo electron volts. after all three corrections the energy resolution is sixteen point four percent for the whole detector, thirteen point five percent in the centre of a slab, and fifteen point eight percent at its edge.

reels.name: Resolution
reels.cap: To measure spatial resolution, a small sodium twenty-two source steps outwards from the centre of the field of view.
reels.words: to measure spatial resolution, a small sodium twenty-two source steps outwards from the centre of the field of view. at a quarter of the axial field of view, the radial resolution with depth of interaction rises from zero point seven millimetres at the axis to only one point three four millimetres at twenty-five millimetres off axis. without depth of interaction, the same measurement reaches about two point four millimetres. the gap between the two curves opens towards the edge, where the parallax error is largest.

reels.name: Axial
reels.cap: At the centre of the axial field of view, the source sits in the gap of one point two six millimetres between the two rings.
reels.words: at the centre of the axial field of view, the source sits in the gap of one point two six millimetres between the two rings. the mean resolution there is one point six one millimetres, and the axial direction is the worst at two point seven. at a quarter of the axial field of view, the source sits in front of one ring, and the mean resolution is one millimetre.

reels.name: Sensitivity
reels.cap: For sensitivity, a small sodium twenty-two source moves along the axis in five millimetre steps.
reels.words: for sensitivity, a small sodium twenty-two source moves along the axis in five millimetre steps. at each step the scanner counts the share of the emitted gammas that it detects. at the centre, the thirty percent window from three hundred fifty-eight to six hundred sixty-four kilo electron volts gives three point five percent. the fifty percent window gives four point five percent, and the twenty percent window gives two point seven.

reels.name: Rates
reels.cap: For count rate, a mouse-sized phantom starts at twenty-one mega becquerel.
reels.words: for count rate, a mouse-sized phantom starts at twenty-one mega becquerel. it is measured for thirty seconds every twenty minutes while it decays. at higher activity, more of the coincidences inside the ten nanosecond window are random. the curves show trues, random plus scatter, and the noise equivalent count rate. the noise equivalent count rate peaks at one hundred six point nine kilo counts per second at eleven point seven mega becquerel. that is for the thirty percent window. two points do not seem to have been measured properly, and the authors do not know why. the system saturates at rather low activities.

reels.name: Images
reels.cap: The image quality phantom has five hot rods, one to five millimetres wide.
reels.words: the image quality phantom has five hot rods, one to five millimetres wide. in the reconstruction the one and two millimetre rods are clearly resolved. the recovery coefficient climbs with rod size, from zero point two at one millimetre to zero point eight five at five millimetres. the spill-over ratio is zero point one in the air-filled cylinder and zero point two three in the water-filled one. a micro-derenzo phantom has rods from zero point seven to one point five millimetres. for each rod size, the valley between neighbouring spots is divided by the peak. the rayleigh criterion calls two spots resolved when this ratio stays below zero point seven three five. the one point five, one point two and one millimetre rods pass, and the zero point nine millimetre rods do not.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: This paper asks how a small-animal ring can keep its resolution towards the edge.
reels.words: this paper asks how a small-animal ring can keep its resolution towards the edge. its answer is a block of twenty-two l y s o slabs on an eight by eight s i p m array, where the spread of the light gives the depth. a network, a centre of gravity and a depth estimator then place every hit in three dimensions. with that depth, the radial resolution stays at or below one point three four millimetres out to twenty-five millimetres. the mean resolution at the centre is one point six one millimetres. the scanner reaches three point five percent sensitivity and a noise equivalent count rate of one hundred six point nine kilo counts per second. it resolves one millimetre rods. the ring saturates at low activities, the gap degrades its axial resolution, and some blur remains far from the centre. the next steps are a time skew correction and a compton p e t built with a scatter detector.

title: A full Monte Carlo reconstruction algorithm for improved precision via dual-photopeak…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper by Lucas Polson and colleagues appeared in E J N M M I Physics in twenty twenty-six.
reels.words: this paper by lucas polson and colleagues appeared in e j n m m i physics in twenty twenty-six. it reconstructs lutetium one hundred and seventy-seven s p e c t images from both of the isotope's photopeaks at once. in a phantom, the method matches the standard reconstruction's precision in thirty-seven percent of the scan time. a standard scan needs some time to reach a given precision. the new reconstruction reaches it in thirty-seven percent of that time. that is a speed-up factor of two point seven three in the phantom, and three point two five in a patient.

reels.name: Spectrum
reels.cap: A gamma camera sorts every detected photon by its energy.
reels.words: a gamma camera sorts every detected photon by its energy. lutetium one hundred and seventy-seven produces two peaks, one at one hundred and thirteen kilo electron volts and one at two hundred and eight. each peak gets a window twenty percent wide. standard reconstruction keeps the two hundred and eight window and discards the other. scattered photons have lost energy, so they fill the valleys under both peaks. the triple energy window method estimates that scatter from a narrow window just below the peak and another just above it. a straight line joins the two heights, and the area under it is the estimate. each narrow window holds few counts, so the estimate changes from scan to scan.

reels.name: Detect
reels.cap: A patient holds the activity, and a lead collimator stands between the patient and the crystal.
reels.words: a patient holds the activity, and a lead collimator stands between the patient and the crystal. its holes pass only photons that travel straight along them. a two hundred and eight kilo electron volt gamma ray leaves the body untouched, passes through a hole, and deposits all its energy in the crystal. the camera counts it in the two hundred and eight window. another gamma ray scatters inside the patient. each scatter turns it and takes away part of its energy. it reaches the crystal with less energy than it started with, so the camera may count it in the one hundred and thirteen window. that window then holds scattered photons along with the emitted ones.

reels.name: Counts
reels.cap: Here are the two windows of the phantom scan as stacked bars.
reels.words: here are the two windows of the phantom scan as stacked bars. the one hundred and thirteen window collects one point three five five times the counts of the two hundred and eight window. fifty-five point two percent of them are scatter, against thirty point nine percent in the other window. after subtracting the scatter, it holds only zero point eight seven eight times the primary counts of the other. that is why it is rarely used alone.

reels.name: Joint
reels.cap: Reconstruction starts from a guess of the activity image.
reels.words: reconstruction starts from a guess of the activity image. the system matrix h turns that guess into the counts the camera would record, and the algorithm compares them with the measured counts. the ratio is carried back into the image through the transpose of h, which scales every voxel. to use both photopeaks, the measured counts of the two windows are stacked into one vector. the system matrix is stacked the same way, one block per window. both windows then correct the same image, and each voxel receives the sum of the two corrections.

reels.name: Transport
reels.cap: The analytical model projects activity along straight lines and adds the scatter estimate afterwards.
reels.words: the analytical model projects activity along straight lines and adds the scatter estimate afterwards. the monte carlo model follows photons through the patient's c t image instead. a history starts in a voxel and flies off in a random direction. at each scatter it turns and loses energy. it ends in a pixel of the detector. each voxel and pixel pair gets a weight from the histories that join them. the energy a photon carries on arrival decides which window counts it. a two hundred and eight photon that scattered down into the lower window is counted there by the same history. so both windows come from one model, with no scatter estimate and no scanner measurement.

reels.name: Adjoint
reels.cap: In the hybrid method, the Monte Carlo model computes only the forward projection.
reels.words: in the hybrid method, the monte carlo model computes only the forward projection. the back projection and the sensitivity image stay analytical. the full method uses monte carlo for all three. a forward projection sends its histories to about ten thousand detector bins. a back projection must spread the same histories over about one million voxels. each voxel gets far fewer, so a sampled back projection is noisy, and that noise multiplies the image at every iteration. the paper instead computes the system matrix once per acquisition, from the c t. it then applies the matrix as a fixed operator that adds no new noise.

reels.name: Design
reels.cap: The paper compares six reconstructions, one for each pairing of system model and photopeak content.
reels.words: the paper compares six reconstructions, one for each pairing of system model and photopeak content. the top row uses the analytical model with t e w scatter correction. the bottom row uses monte carlo. the columns use the one hundred and thirteen window, the two hundred and eight window, or both. the grain improves along the columns, and the two rows look alike. the test object is a n e m a phantom with six spheres, from thirty-seven to ten millimetres across. it was scanned fifty-two times for twelve minutes each, so every reconstruction type is repeated fifty-two times.

reels.name: Metric
reels.cap: Counting is random, so each scan of the same phantom gives a slightly different sphere mean.
reels.words: counting is random, so each scan of the same phantom gives a slightly different sphere mean. here are fifty-two of them. their spread divided by their mean is the coefficient of variation, or c o v. c o v falls as one over the square root of the scan time. so halving the c o v takes four times the scan time. the speed-up factor is the baseline's c o v over the method's, squared. it equals the ratio of scan times that reach the same c o v. the baseline is the standard two hundred and eight kilo electron volt reconstruction.

reels.name: Phantom
reels.cap: The one hundred and thirteen window alone does worse than the standard, with speed-ups of zero point six three analytical and zero point nine three Monte Carlo.
reels.words: the one hundred and thirteen window alone does worse than the standard, with speed-ups of zero point six three analytical and zero point nine three monte carlo. joint analytical reconstruction reaches one point eight seven. monte carlo on the two hundred and eight window alone reaches one point three eight. joint monte carlo reaches two point seven three, and that is the largest in every sphere. the two gains multiply. the second photopeak scales the speed-up by one point eight seven analytically, and the monte carlo model adds a factor of one point four seven. the product lands close to the measured two point seven three.

reels.name: Patient
reels.cap: The patient received seven thousand four hundred mega becquerel of lutetium and was scanned forty-eight hours later.
reels.words: the patient received seven thousand four hundred mega becquerel of lutetium and was scanned forty-eight hours later. to imitate a smaller dose, each recorded count was kept or dropped at random, so five hundred of every seven thousand four hundred remained. that allows fourteen independent realizations that share no counts. joint monte carlo reaches a mean speed-up of three point two five over seven regions. it ranges from one point four in the l five vertebra to five point two six in the liver. monte carlo images also read five point seven to nine point five percent higher in activity.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: A standard lutetium reconstruction keeps one photopeak and estimates scatter from two noisy windows.
reels.words: a standard lutetium reconstruction keeps one photopeak and estimates scatter from two noisy windows. this paper reconstructs both photopeaks as one stacked problem, and replaces the scatter estimate with a monte carlo model of the patient and the camera. together these give a speed-up of two point seven three in the phantom and three point two five in the patient. the price is computing time. a phantom reconstruction takes seventy minutes on one g p u, against six for the hybrid method and at most one for the analytical ones. accuracy differs by a few percent between methods.

title: Validation of Celeritas GPU optical photon transport for monolithic scintillation…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This preprint by Daniel Chahine tests Celeritas, which transports optical photons on the G P U for Geant four.
reels.words: this preprint by daniel chahine tests celeritas, which transports optical photons on the g p u for geant four. it asks whether celeritas gets the light of a scintillation detector right. when a gamma ray stops in a crystal, it makes a burst of optical photons. each one is followed as it reflects and scatters inside the slab, until it lands on one of the s i p m tiles. the light each tile counts is what the detector measures. celeritas does this on the g p u, but no one had yet checked its optics against gate.

reels.name: Slab
reels.cap: The detector is a monolithic L S O slab that measures fifty by fifty by ten millimetres.
reels.words: the detector is a monolithic l s o slab that measures fifty by fifty by ten millimetres. a black wrap covers five faces, and the sixth is coupled through one millimetre of epoxy to an eight by eight array of s i p m tiles. each tile is five point eight millimetres wide, and the tiles sit at a six millimetre pitch. the paper tests six designs. each one changes a single optical feature of the slab. in the clear design, nothing scatters a photon in the bulk. two designs add rayleigh scattering, each at its own length. a third adds mie scattering, and every scatter kinks the photon's path. in the ground design, a rough exit face scatters the photon again as it leaves. the last design replaces the l s o with a b g o crystal.

reels.name: Lattice
reels.cap: To compare the two codes, the paper builds an optical lattice.
reels.words: to compare the two codes, the paper builds an optical lattice. photons leave uniform random points of the crystal in every direction, and each is binned by its one millimetre origin cell and by the tile it enters. the light response is the fraction of photons from one cell that each tile counts. each lattice holds two hundred and fifty million photons, and gate and celeritas each make one.

reels.name: Compare
reels.cap: Each cell and tile has two counts, one from each code.
reels.words: each cell and tile has two counts, one from each code. their standardised difference z is the gap between them, divided by the noise expected from counting statistics. if the codes sample the same response, z follows a bell of width one, so its mean square is one. across every cell and tile, the histogram of z between celeritas and gate lies on the null bell. the mean square sits between zero point nine nine seven seven and one point zero zero two nine, and each value lies within three standard errors of one.

reels.name: Unit
reels.cap: Before the full detector, each process is tested alone against its analytic expectation.
reels.words: before the full detector, each process is tested alone against its analytic expectation. photons hit a flat interface from index one point eight two into one point five, and the reflected fraction follows the s and p fresnel curves. the p curve dips to zero at the brewster angle, and both reach total reflection at the critical angle. scattering angles follow the rayleigh and henyey greenstein densities, and absorption follows its integral. all seven checks give chi squared per degree of freedom between zero point seven one and one point two four.

reels.name: Arrival
reels.cap: Arrival time is compared too.
reels.words: arrival time is compared too. every photon of a smaller lattice starts at time zero, and its arrival time is how long it takes to enter a tile. each tile's times fill a histogram in ten picosecond bins up to five nanoseconds. the curves from celeritas and gate coincide over four decades, and chi squared per degree of freedom stays between zero point nine six nine and one point zero seven zero.

reels.name: Events
reels.cap: In a gamma event, Geant four tracks the gamma and its electrons on the C P U.
reels.words: in a gamma event, geant four tracks the gamma and its electrons on the c p u. a step that emits light does not make its photons on the c p u. it hands the photon count and endpoints to celeritas, which creates and tracks the photons on the g p u. the test sends one hundred thousand gammas of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts into the face opposite the tiles. no light statistic of celeritas differs from gate by more than two point seven standard errors, and in every depth layer the light per event stays within about one percent.

reels.name: Speed
reels.cap: Celeritas is also faster.
reels.words: celeritas is also faster. on the lattice it runs nine point seven to thirty six times faster than gate running on twenty four c p u threads. with the photons offloaded, gamma events run three to six times faster than geant four on the c p u. that holds in every design but the clear one. there the offloaded run takes one thousand one hundred and eighteen seconds, while the c p u run takes one hundred and thirty five.

reels.name: Trapped
reels.cap: Why is the clear design slow?
reels.words: why is the clear design slow? above three point one electron volts the index of l s o is high enough that a photon travelling near a diagonal of the polished cuboid is totally reflected at all six faces, so it bounces until bulk absorption removes it. on the g p u, each event waits for its last photon, so thousands of nearly empty iterations pass for a few trapped ones. limiting each photon to one thousand steps cuts the run to one hundred and ninety two seconds.

reels.name: Problems
reels.cap: Building the comparison turned up six problems, and the paper gives the status of each.
reels.words: building the comparison turned up six problems, and the paper gives the status of each. in the mie sampler, the scattered direction was never rotated into the photon's frame. one fresnel transmission coefficient was wrong. in the offload, a neutral particle's photons were spread along the step instead of placed at its end. two cherenkov faults either aborted the run or silently dropped the light. in single precision, a photon could be scored in an invalid volume and abort the run. three were corrected in the offload application, so another application inherits them unless it does the same.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The question was whether Celeritas reproduces the light of a monolithic L S O detector.
reels.words: the question was whether celeritas reproduces the light of a monolithic l s o detector. the light response matches gate, with a mean squared standardised difference of one, and the arrival times agree too. in gamma events with offloaded photons, no light statistic moves by more than two point seven standard errors. the offloaded runs are three to six times faster than geant four. the clear design is the exception, because its trapped photons need a step limit. in single precision, the mie lattice collects too little light. reflector wraps were not tested. and another offload application must repeat the three fixes itself.

title: A New Concept of Liquid Xenon Time Projection Chamber for Medical Imaging

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper, from Baron Li and colleagues at U C San Diego, asks whether a tank of liquid xenon can do the job of the crystals in a PET scanner.
reels.words: this paper, from baron li and colleagues at u c san diego, asks whether a tank of liquid xenon can do the job of the crystals in a pet scanner. in pet, the scanner is a ring of detectors around the patient. an annihilation at the centre sends two five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt photons out back to back, and the two modules that catch them define a line. here every module is one block of liquid xenon, not a grid of crystals.

reels.name: Crystal
reels.cap: A scanner built from L Y S O crystals only knows which crystal fired.
reels.words: a scanner built from l y s o crystals only knows which crystal fired. a gamma ray arrives at an angle, and may stop near the front of the crystal or near the back. the scanner draws the same line, to the crystal's centre, either way. standard crystals are nineteen millimetres long and four millimetres square, and that sets the reconstructed resolution at about four millimetres. a liquid xenon block has to find where the gamma stopped, in all three directions.

reels.name: Module
reels.cap: Each module is one block of liquid xenon, with a cathode below and a photosensor array above.
reels.words: each module is one block of liquid xenon, with a cathode below and a photosensor array above. when a gamma ray interacts in it, the xenon gives off prompt scintillation light that spreads in every direction and reaches the photosensors almost at once. the interaction also frees ionization electrons. an electric field drives them upward, and in the thin electroluminescence layer near the anode each electron gives out a burst of light. that second flash reaches the photosensors later than the first. all of it happens in the liquid, so no liquid gas surface is needed.

reels.name: Position
reels.cap: The wait between the two flashes tells the depth.
reels.words: the wait between the two flashes tells the depth. an interaction near the photosensors gives a short wait. one near the cathode gives a long wait, because its electrons have farther to drift. the pattern of the second flash across the photosensors gives the other two coordinates. and the total light gives the energy, where the scintillation and electroluminescence signals trade against each other, so combining them sharpens the energy resolution. the paper assumes one millimetre in depth, and two by two millimetres across.

reels.name: Stopping
reels.cap: The paper simulated the scanner in OpenGATE, built on Geant4.
reels.words: the paper simulated the scanner in opengate, built on geant4. the ring has an inner radius of three hundred and fifty-four millimetres. the detector thickness was varied from twenty to one hundred and forty millimetres, and the ring is about one hundred and sixty-four millimetres long. lyso is denser and has a higher atomic number, so at every thickness it records more true full-energy events. at a hundred and forty millimetres, lyso reaches about eight percent of the simulated gammas, and xenon about five.

reels.name: Window
reels.cap: An event only counts if its energy lands in a window of two sigma either side of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts.
reels.words: an event only counts if its energy lands in a window of two sigma either side of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts. for liquid xenon, sigma is four point six kilo electron volts, a resolution of two point one percent. for lyso it is twenty-four point three, eleven point two percent. a narrow window leaves little room for events that kept only part of their energy, and they pile up just below the peak. in lyso the wide window reaches down into them. multiple scatters in xenon are rejected too, because a compton scatter at five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts travels more than a centimetre, so the block sees the deposits apart. so of the true five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt events, xenon keeps about ninety-five to ninety-eight and a half percent at every thickness, and lyso about ninety-three to ninety-five.

reels.name: Image
reels.cap: To see what position resolution is worth, the paper simulated a point source at the centre of the ring and reconstructed it with list mode O S E M.
reels.words: to see what position resolution is worth, the paper simulated a point source at the centre of the ring and reconstructed it with list mode o s e m. lyso crystals are nineteen millimetres long and four by four millimetres across. the xenon block is assumed to find each interaction to one millimetre in depth and two by two millimetres across. that turns one block into many small pseudo detectors. every coincidence is a line of response through the source. with coarse cells the lines are snapped to wide steps and cross in a broad patch. with fine cells they cross in a tight spot. in the reconstructed images, the lyso point is about four millimetres wide at half maximum, and the xenon point about one millimetre. only one axial slice at the centre was reconstructed.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: So the paper asks whether liquid xenon can replace crystals in a PET ring.
reels.words: so the paper asks whether liquid xenon can replace crystals in a pet ring. each module records a prompt flash and a delayed one, and the gap gives the depth, while the pattern and size of the light give the position and the energy. lyso still stops more gamma rays. but xenon keeps more true events in its narrow window, and reconstructs a point source at about one millimetre, against four. the study leaves out time of flight. lyso systems reach one hundred and eighty to two hundred picoseconds, and the paper sees about one hundred as a realistic target for xenon. next come experimental tests of the modules and the full system.

title: Investigating the Timing Behavior of Compton Scattering in BGO for Time-of-Flight PET

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper, from Minseok Yi and colleagues at Seoul National University and U C Davis, asks what happens to the timing of a bismuth germanate detector when a gamma ray scatters from one crystal into the next.
reels.words: this paper, from minseok yi and colleagues at seoul national university and u c davis, asks what happens to the timing of a bismuth germanate detector when a gamma ray scatters from one crystal into the next. in a pixelated array this happens all the time. a five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma ray enters one crystal and compton scatters. the scattered photon deposits the rest of its energy in the neighbouring crystal, so both crystals report an energy and a time. which time is the event's?

reels.name: Bench
reels.cap: Two bismuth germanate crystals, each two point five by two point eight by fifteen millimetres, are wrapped in reflective film and stand side by side.
reels.words: two bismuth germanate crystals, each two point five by two point eight by fifteen millimetres, are wrapped in reflective film and stand side by side. an eight-channel s i p m module reads them out, with two channels under each crystal. a tungsten collimator sends five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma rays from a sodium twenty-two source into the centre of crystal 1. a fast l y s o reference detector catches the partner gamma, so every event carries a time. an oscilloscope records two energy signals and four timing signals.

reels.name: Race
reels.cap: Bismuth germanate scintillates slowly, so on its own it cannot give a sharp time.
reels.words: bismuth germanate scintillates slowly, so on its own it cannot give a sharp time. but the recoil electron of the interaction moves faster than light does in the crystal, and it throws out cherenkov light at once. about seventeen cherenkov photons appear for every five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, and they reach the s i p m within tens of picoseconds. only a handful are detected, and the first one stamps the time. the threshold is only about sixty-three kilo electron volts, so even a backscattered photon that keeps one hundred and seventy kilo electron volts still makes light.

reels.name: Classes
reels.cap: In a photoelectric event, the gamma gives all its energy at one point.
reels.words: in a photoelectric event, the gamma gives all its energy at one point. in an intra-crystal scatter, it leaves energy at two points inside the same crystal. in an inter-crystal scatter, the second deposit lands in the neighbouring crystal. and in a penetration event, the gamma crosses crystal 1 and is absorbed in crystal 2. the experiment cannot see points, only the two energies. it forms the position, e two minus e one over e two plus e one, and drops each event on that axis. events near crystal 1 are full-energy deposits, ninety point eight percent of them. events in the middle are inter-crystal scatters, four percent. events near crystal 2 are penetrations, five point two percent.

reels.name: Hidden
reels.cap: Gate simulations with the same geometry check the sorting.
reels.words: gate simulations with the same geometry check the sorting. they also show something the experiment cannot. nearly a quarter of the events that look like full-energy deposits are really intra-crystal scatters. these events are slower. for photoelectric events the first detected photon arrives after a mean of one hundred and eleven picoseconds, with a standard deviation of thirty-six. for intra-crystal scatter it arrives after one hundred and thirty-nine, with a standard deviation of one hundred and seven. splitting energy inside a single crystal already costs timing.

reels.name: Earlier
reels.cap: In an inter-crystal event, both crystals produce a timestamp.
reels.words: in an inter-crystal event, both crystals produce a timestamp. their difference, t one minus t two, is spread symmetrically around zero, over about plus or minus three nanoseconds. neither crystal systematically leads. the simplest rule takes the earlier of the two. a margin k generalises it: take t one only if it is earlier than t two plus k. sweeping k, the best resolution comes at k equal to zero, the strictly earlier timestamp. there, inter-crystal events reach two hundred and twenty-one picoseconds full width at half maximum, against one hundred and eighty-four for full-energy events.

reels.name: Energy
reels.cap: Detectors made of L Y S O choose the crystal with the larger energy.
reels.words: detectors made of l y s o choose the crystal with the larger energy. there the bigger deposit tends to lie deeper, nearer the s i p m, so its light is faster. in bismuth germanate the rule is tested, and it does worse, two hundred and forty-nine picoseconds against two hundred and twenty-one. the reason is in the quadrants. when the crystal 1 deposit is larger and crystal 1 fires first, the rule is right. that holds for thirty-three percent of events, and for twenty-eight point nine percent when crystal 2 wins both. in the other two quadrants, thirty-eight percent of events in all, the larger deposit is not the first to fire. both sites exceed the cherenkov threshold, and a few photons decide the race by chance.

reels.name: Starved
reels.cap: Why does splitting hurt?
reels.words: why does splitting hurt? cherenkov yield is roughly proportional to the deposited energy, so each half of a split event makes fewer prompt photons. integrating the first nanosecond of the waveform counts them. full-energy events average five point seven six detected photons, inter-crystal events four point seven three, and penetration events five point three three. one photon fewer sounds small, but the timestamp is set by the very first of only a handful. the resolution is worst when the energy is split almost equally, and best when one crystal takes most of it.

reels.name: Design
reels.cap: The paper also asks how crystal shape matters.
reels.words: the paper also asks how crystal shape matters. a simulation widens the pixel pitch from one to fifteen millimetres, at a fixed length of fifteen millimetres. the fraction of events with several deposits inside one crystal climbs from fifteen point five percent to forty-seven point five percent. a wider crystal sends more cherenkov light straight to the s i p m, but it makes more intra-crystal scatter. since energy does not predict which crystal fires first, independent timing for each pixel lets the readout keep the earliest photon, while a multiplexed readout that favours the largest energy may miss it.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The question was which timestamp to trust when a gamma ray scatters between two bismuth germanate crystals.
reels.words: the question was which timestamp to trust when a gamma ray scatters between two bismuth germanate crystals. sorting events by energy position separated full-energy, inter-crystal and penetration events, and the simulation showed that a quarter of the full-energy events hide an intra-crystal scatter. splitting energy leaves fewer prompt photons, about one fewer on average. choosing the earlier timestamp beats choosing the larger energy, two hundred and twenty-one picoseconds against two hundred and forty-nine, yet it still falls short of the one hundred and eighty-four reached by full-energy events. all this was measured on only two pixels, so wider arrays and per-pixel readouts remain to be tested.

title: Radar Ranging Using Rydberg Atomic Homodyne Receiver

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper, by Minze Chen and colleagues, replaces a radar's antenna and mixer with a small cell of caesium vapour.
reels.words: this paper, by minze chen and colleagues, replaces a radar's antenna and mixer with a small cell of caesium vapour. a radar separates two targets only when its bandwidth is wide enough. the atoms respond over less than ten megahertz. that allows only about fifteen metres of resolution, far too coarse to split two plates thirty centimetres apart. the paper hops the atoms across the s-band, from two point six to three point six gigahertz, and the resolution cell shrinks to about fifteen centimetres.

reels.name: Bench
reels.cap: A horn antenna transmits a microwave signal toward an aluminium plate, four hundred millimetres across, that a stage slides between one point six and one point nine metres.
reels.words: a horn antenna transmits a microwave signal toward an aluminium plate, four hundred millimetres across, that a stage slides between one point six and one point nine metres. the echo returns to a vapour cell five centimetres long, where a second horn adds a reference field, the local oscillator. two lasers cross the cell from opposite ends, a probe at eight hundred and fifty-two nanometres and a coupling beam at five hundred and nine. the probe's brightness on a photodetector is the receiver's output, recorded by an oscilloscope at one hundred million samples a second. everything sits inside an anechoic chamber.

reels.name: Atoms
reels.cap: Inside the cell, a caesium atom starts in its ground state.
reels.words: inside the cell, a caesium atom starts in its ground state. the probe laser lifts it to an intermediate state, and the coupling laser lifts it on to a rydberg state, where one electron orbits far from the nucleus. together they open a narrow window of transparency in the probe's absorption. a microwave field that couples the rydberg state to its neighbour splits that window in two. the window is called e i t, and the split is the autler townes effect. the gap grows in step with the field strength, so the transmission at the centre falls as the field grows. that centre height is the receiver's reading.

reels.name: Mixer
reels.cap: The echo from the target is a microwave field whose phase depends on the round trip.
reels.words: the echo from the target is a microwave field whose phase depends on the round trip. the local oscillator has the same frequency and a fixed phase. inside the atoms the two fields add, and the probe transmission follows the size of the sum. as the target moves, the echo's phase turns, and the sum swells and shrinks like a cosine. a second reference path, shifted by ninety degrees, gives the sine. together they trace the echo's phase with no electronic mixer. stepping the phase by pi over six, the output lands on a cosine with r squared of ninety-nine point eight nine percent.

reels.name: Hop
reels.cap: One atomic line is far too narrow to give range resolution, so the receiver steps through eight frequencies across the S-band.
reels.words: one atomic line is far too narrow to give range resolution, so the receiver steps through eight frequencies across the s-band. each coarse jump retunes the coupling laser to another rydberg state, from sixty-four d at two point six four gigahertz to fifty-eight d at three point five eight four. those jumps leave gaps. a strong field at two gigahertz, far from resonance, shifts the energy levels by the a c stark effect, and slides the line smoothly across a gap to three point four nine nine gigahertz. the widest step between neighbours is one hundred seventy-three megahertz, which caps the unambiguous range at about zero point eight seven metres.

reels.name: Profile
reels.cap: Each of the eight frequencies returns the echo with its own phase.
reels.words: each of the eight frequencies returns the echo with its own phase. the phase turns faster at higher frequency, in proportion to the target's range. to find the range, the processor tries a guess, and unwinds every phase by that guess. when the guess is right, all eight arrows line up, and their sum is large. sliding the guess along the axis draws the range profile. it peaks where the arrows agree. the peak's width is the speed of light over twice the bandwidth, about sixteen centimetres here, and with only eight frequencies, false peaks remain.

reels.name: Curve
reels.cap: The atoms do not respond linearly.
reels.words: the atoms do not respond linearly. plotted against field strength, the probe transmission is a curve that flattens as the atoms saturate. its slope is the receiver's gain, and the gain peaks at one field, the best bias for the local oscillator. an echo adds to the bias, and walks the output up the curve, where the slope falls, so the response bends away from a straight line. predistortion applies the inverse of the calibrated curve, and the output straightens. the linear range grows from thirty-one point one to thirty-nine point three decibels, and the cancelling case gains more than seven decibels as well.

reels.name: Clean
reels.cap: The raw samples at each frequency are noisy, with sharp spikes.
reels.words: the raw samples at each frequency are noisy, with sharp spikes. a median filter of length fifty removes the spikes, and averaging beats down what remains. predistortion then linearises each in-phase and quadrature pair, and the pair is scaled to unit length, so only its phase, which carries the range, is kept. the last step is compressive sensing. instead of a fourier sum, it searches for the fewest range bins that explain the eight phases, with a huber penalty that tolerates non-gaussian noise. the result is a profile of sparse spikes in place of the fourier sprawl.

reels.name: Accuracy
reels.cap: With a plate at about one point eight metres, the profile peaks at one point seven one nine.
reels.words: with a plate at about one point eight metres, the profile peaks at one point seven one nine. the paper blames the plate's size and path errors for that offset. so the system is calibrated once, at one point nine metres. then the plate moves from one point six to one point eight five metres in five centimetre steps, and the peak follows, five runs at each position. the root mean square error is one point zero four centimetres. no single point strays by more than two point three. and the mean error is almost zero, so there is no systematic bias.

reels.name: Resolve
reels.cap: To test resolution, two plates share the beam, one fixed at one point nine metres.
reels.words: to test resolution, two plates share the beam, one fixed at one point nine metres. the other approaches from one point six. at thirty, twenty-five and twenty centimetres apart, two peaks stand clear. at fifteen they still separate, but at ten and five centimetres the echoes merge into one. the paper reports a resolution of fifteen centimetres, close to the sixteen that the bandwidth predicts. it credits compressive sensing for telling sparse scatterers apart, though many false peaks remain, from multipath and sparse frequencies.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The question was how atoms that respond over less than ten megahertz could measure range finely.
reels.words: the question was how atoms that respond over less than ten megahertz could measure range finely. the answer was to hop them across eight frequencies from two point six to three point six gigahertz, mixing each echo with a reference inside the vapour. predistortion straightened the response and widened the linear range by more than seven decibels, and compressive sensing cleaned the profiles. the receiver followed a plate to one point zero four centimetres root mean square error, and separated two plates fifteen centimetres apart. it remains a laboratory demonstration. every range was calibrated against one plate position, retuning the laser takes ten to a hundred milliseconds, and false peaks from multipath remain.

title: Evolution of PET Detectors and Event Positioning Algorithms Using Monolithic…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This is the twenty twenty-one review of monolithic PET detectors, by Gonzalez-Montoro and colleagues.
reels.words: this is the twenty twenty-one review of monolithic pet detectors, by gonzalez-montoro and colleagues. its subject is a single block of scintillator that replaces a whole array of tiny pixels. an array tells you which pixel lit. only that one pixel counts the light. a monolithic block has no pixels, so the position has to be worked out from the shape of the light itself. i will follow one gamma ray: its light, the counts it leaves, the methods that read them, and what they cost.

reels.name: Parallax
reels.cap: An annihilation sends two photons in opposite directions, and each enters its detector at an angle.
reels.words: an annihilation sends two photons in opposite directions, and each enters its detector at an angle. it can stop anywhere along its depth, and a pixel cannot say where. so the line of response is drawn through the wrong points, and it misses the source. that is the parallax error. a block reads the depth from its light, so the line is redrawn through the true points. and it has no gaps between pixels, so it also catches more photons.

reels.name: Light
reels.cap: A five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt photon is absorbed at one point inside a fifty by fifty by fifteen millimetre block.
reels.words: a five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt photon is absorbed at one point inside a fifty by fifty by fifteen millimetre block. the scintillation light leaves that point in every direction. the flux on each photodetector falls with the square of the distance and with the cosine of the angle. silicon photomultipliers under the block count it, and the counts form a bump, the light distribution. move the hit sideways, and the bump follows it. move it away from the photodetectors, and the bump spreads and flattens, because the light has farther to travel before it lands. that is why a thicker block resolves worse. the position resolution is zero point six eight millimetres at ten millimetres thick, zero point nine at fifteen, and one point two nine at twenty.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: Add up every channel's count, and call the total E.
reels.words: add up every channel's count, and call the total e. take the brightest channel and call it i. their ratio grows as the hit moves away from the photodetectors. it grows in proportion to that distance under the inverse square law, and as its square under the scrimger and baker model. so e over i, read straight from the counts, gives the depth of interaction. it holds for crystals thinner than twenty millimetres, with a depth resolution below three millimetres.

reels.name: Centroid
reels.cap: The simplest way to position a hit is the centre of gravity.
reels.words: the simplest way to position a hit is the centre of gravity. weight each channel's position by its count, and divide by the total. for a hit in the middle, the answer lands on the hit. near a wall, part of the bump is cut off, so the answer is dragged inwards, towards the middle of the block. raising each count to a power first, called r t p, shrinks the small counts that do the dragging, and the answer moves back towards the hit. the power is a trade between linearity and the pull to the centre.

reels.name: Library
reels.cap: Statistical methods begin with a reference set.
reels.words: statistical methods begin with a reference set. a beam is stepped across the block on a grid of positions, and the light distribution at each one is recorded. a new event is compared against all of them. least squares sums the squared residuals, channel by channel. the position with the smallest sum is the answer. chi square divides each residual by that channel's own fluctuation, so noisy channels count for less. maximum likelihood goes further, and has reached positioning errors as small as zero point six millimetres. on a source near the block's edge, the centre of gravity squeezes the events inwards. least squares spreads them back out to the wall.

reels.name: Learn
reels.cap: A neural network learns that mapping directly.
reels.words: a neural network learns that mapping directly. it takes the row and column counts as its inputs, and returns the position and the depth. it is trained once, on calibration data, and needs retraining only when the hardware changes. one deep learning method runs four hundred times faster than an exhaustive search, with errors below one millimetre. gradient tree boosting needs less than an hour of calibration per block, and stays uniform across the whole volume.

reels.name: Walls
reels.cap: The walls decide what the light distribution looks like.
reels.words: the walls decide what the light distribution looks like. black paint absorbs every photon that reaches the side, so the shape is kept, but much of the light is lost. white paint reflects it in every direction, so more light arrives, but the shape is smeared. a specular reflector bounces it like a mirror. a retroreflector, made of corner cubes, sends each photon back the way it came, so it keeps both the shape and the light.

reels.name: Calibrate
reels.cap: A reference set is only as good as the calibration that makes it, and collecting it is the cost.
reels.words: a reference set is only as good as the calibration that makes it, and collecting it is the cost. the traditional way steps a collimated beam across the whole front face, one position after another, with the crystal and the source moved together. every block needs long acquisitions. a faster way lets an uncollimated source flood the block, and recovers each event's position from the data. the lutetium inside the crystal does it unaided, and fills a flood map in minutes. how to calibrate more than a thousand blocks, and keep them calibrated, is still open.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: A time of flight scanner needs each photon's arrival time, and its figure of merit is the coincidence time resolution.
