reels.words: a time of flight scanner needs each photon's arrival time, and its figure of merit is the coincidence time resolution. in a pixel, one channel collects most of the light and fires early and cleanly. in a monolithic block the light is spread over many channels, each catching only a few photons, so each timestamp is noisy. averaging the timestamps, weighted by their energy, partly recovers the loss. with analog s i p m detectors read by an a s i c, a fifty by fifty by fifteen millimetre block reached five hundred and fifty picoseconds over the whole volume, and four hundred and forty at the centre. digital s i p m detectors, cooled to minus twenty degrees, went below two hundred. the best commercial pixelated systems manage two hundred and fourteen.

reels.name: Beyond
reels.cap: Every monolithic design fights the same enemy, the edge.
reels.words: every monolithic design fights the same enemy, the edge. laser etching can write optical barriers inside the block to steer the light. slats remove two of the four edges. a single annulus removes them all, but its crystal is limited by the boule, at eighty-five to a hundred and twenty millimetres across.

reels.name: Systems
reels.cap: Real scanners already use monolithic blocks.
reels.words: real scanners already use monolithic blocks. the albira preclinical scanner resolves better than one millimetre across its whole field of view. the mammi breast scanner reaches one point eight millimetres. and the caremibrain brain scanner reads only sixteen signals per block, to give a three-dimensional position.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The review asks how one block of scintillator can replace a grid of pixels.
reels.words: the review asks how one block of scintillator can replace a grid of pixels. a gamma ray is absorbed at one point, and its light spreads into a bump on the s i p m array. the bump's centre gives the position across the block, and the ratio of total to peak gives the depth. centre of gravity and r t p read the bump simply. least squares, maximum likelihood and neural networks read it against a reference set. the walls decide how much of the bump survives. the price is calibration, and timestamps spread over many channels: five hundred and fifty picoseconds against two hundred and fourteen for pixels. what remains is the edge, calibrating a thousand blocks, and the second interaction a single position cannot hold.

title: The PICO-40L detector

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This is the Pico collaboration's paper on Pico forty L, a bubble chamber at Snow lab that searches for dark matter.
reels.words: this is the pico collaboration's paper on pico forty l, a bubble chamber at snow lab that searches for dark matter. it reports how the chamber is built, how its events are read, and how well it tells them apart. i will follow one nuclear recoil through it, from the liquid, to a bubble, to a picture and a sound.

reels.name: Superheat
reels.cap: The target is liquid octafluoropropane, at about thirteen degrees.
reels.words: the target is liquid octafluoropropane, at about thirteen degrees. squeezed to twelve hundred and twenty kilopascals, it is calm. then the pressure drops to one hundred and eighty-nine point six, far below its vapour pressure of six hundred and twenty to seven hundred and fifty-eight. the liquid is superheated: it wants to boil, but has nowhere to start. now a dark matter particle strikes a nucleus. the nucleus recoils with a few kilo electron volts, and stops within a tiny distance, so its energy sits in one place. that is enough to make a bubble, while a gamma ray's electron spreads its energy along a long track and makes none. at these settings the threshold is three point three kilo electron volts.

reels.name: Cycle
reels.cap: Between events, the chamber sits compressed at twelve hundred and twenty kilopascals.
reels.words: between events, the chamber sits compressed at twelve hundred and twenty kilopascals. to listen, oil is let into a low pressure accumulator and the pressure falls to the setpoint. now the chamber waits, sensitive, for minutes. when a bubble is seen, a trigger fires. three fast piston accumulators open, and the chamber is compressed within about a hundred milliseconds, before the bubble can grow far. it is then held above the vapour pressure for at least sixty seconds, so every bubble collapses.

reels.name: Inverted
reels.cap: In earlier chambers, the target sat in one quartz jar, with a buffer fluid floating on top of it and a bellows above that.
reels.words: in earlier chambers, the target sat in one quartz jar, with a buffer fluid floating on top of it and a bellows above that. particles shed by the bellows, and the surface where the two fluids meet, were sources of unwanted bubbles. pico forty l turns the design over. it has two nested quartz vessels, an outer one three hundred millimetres wide and one thousand and one millimetres long, and an inner one, joined to a bellows below. mineral oil outside pushes the bellows, and the pressure passes straight to the target, with no buffer fluid. the liquid between the vessels is forty-one point seven litres of active volume.

reels.name: Zones
reels.cap: Turning it over brings a problem.
reels.words: turning it over brings a problem. the bellows, seals and steel below are where bubbles like to start. so the lower zone is cooled to minus twenty-two degrees, where the liquid is not superheated at all. a layer of polyethylene insulates it from the upper zone, where a heating plate holds thirteen degrees. only the liquid above is superheated, and only there can a bubble begin. every bubble therefore forms in view of the cameras.

reels.name: Eye
reels.cap: Four cameras watch the liquid, each ringed by forty-eight red L E Ds.
reels.words: four cameras watch the liquid, each ringed by forty-eight red l e ds. every new frame is subtracted from the one before it. when a bubble appears, the difference holds new information, and its entropy leaps. if it crosses a threshold in any camera, the recompression trigger fires.

reels.name: Locate
reels.cap: To place a bubble, the first frame where the entropy crosses its threshold is the genesis frame.
reels.words: to place a bubble, the first frame where the entropy crosses its threshold is the genesis frame. subtracting a bubble-free frame leaves the bubble alone, and its centre in each camera gives a ray. rays traced through the glass and liquid meet at the bubble in three dimensions. how good is that? a bubble on the wall has a known radius, one hundred and forty-five millimetres. its reconstructed radius spreads with a standard deviation of two point seven millimetres.

reels.name: Ears
reels.cap: Twelve piezoelectric transducers press against the base of the outer vessel, in three rings of four, each ring turned thirty degrees from the last.
reels.words: twelve piezoelectric transducers press against the base of the outer vessel, in three rings of four, each ring turned thirty degrees from the last. when a bubble nucleates, its sound spreads through the liquid and the glass, and each transducer records it at one megahertz. the time of nucleation, t zero, is where the signal first leaps ten standard deviations above its noise baseline.

reels.name: Alpha
reels.cap: The sound's frequencies are summed into one number per event, the acoustic parameter.
reels.words: the sound's frequencies are summed into one number per event, the acoustic parameter. its distribution has three peaks. the leftmost holds events from a californium two fifty-two neutron source, which make nuclear recoils like those a dark matter particle would, the central pair is radon two twenty-two and polonium two eighteen, and the rightmost is polonium two fourteen. so a nuclear recoil is told from an alpha decay by where it falls on this axis.

reels.name: Count
reels.cap: A fast pressure sensor in the oil feels the gas that bubbles make.
reels.words: a fast pressure sensor in the oil feels the gas that bubbles make. fitting the rise gives a number that peaks near one point seven for a single bubble, near three for two bubbles, and higher for many bubbles or a bubble on the wall. cutting on it keeps the single bubbles in the bulk.

reels.name: Shield
reels.cap: A dark matter signal is rare, so everything else must be rarer.
reels.words: a dark matter signal is rare, so everything else must be rarer. the chamber sits two thousand and seventy-two metres underground, which cuts the cosmic muon flux to zero point two seven per square metre per day. it stands in twenty tonnes of ultrapure water, and its pressure vessel is filled with mineral oil. each layer stops neutrons that are heading for the liquid.

reels.name: Budget
reels.cap: What background is left?
reels.words: what background is left? neutrinos from the sun scatter off nuclei, one point four events per live-year. neutrons from radioactivity in the components give zero point five eight, gamma rays give zero point zero five, and cosmic neutrons less than zero point one. combined by monte carlo, the total is two point two three single-bubble events per live-year.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: Pico forty L asks whether a bubble chamber can be turned over.
reels.words: pico forty l asks whether a bubble chamber can be turned over. its liquid is superheated by dropping the pressure, and crushed again after every bubble. right side up, two quartz vessels and a bellows below remove the buffer fluid, and a cold zone keeps bubbles where cameras can see them. four cameras trigger on entropy and place the bubble to two point seven millimetres. twelve transducers time it, and tell alphas from nuclear recoils. about two background events a year are expected. the chamber is still being commissioned, and a small population of events, probably alphas, still reaches the dark matter region.

title: Multigap RPC for PET: development and optimisation of the detector design

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This is a twenty twelve paper from Georgiev and colleagues at Sofia University.
reels.words: this is a twenty twelve paper from georgiev and colleagues at sofia university. it asks whether resistive plate chambers, a workhorse of particle physics, can serve as the gamma detectors of a p e t scanner. it answers by following one photon through the whole chain, from the annihilation to the electrons in the gas. the authors simulate photon conversion in geant four, for different converter materials and geometries. those results justify a sandwich of gas, insulator and converter, with bismuth or lead. the rest of the paper shows why.

reels.name: Idea
reels.cap: A P E T scanner inside an M R I magnet cannot use photomultiplier tubes, because magnetic fields upset them.
reels.words: a p e t scanner inside an m r i magnet cannot use photomultiplier tubes, because magnetic fields upset them. a resistive plate chamber has no such weakness. it is two plates around a thin gas gap, and a charged particle crossing the gap sets off a pulse. its timing has been reported at twenty picoseconds. to detect a gamma, one plate is made a converter. a photon knocks an electron out of it, the electron enters the gas, and an avalanche follows.

reels.name: Yield
reels.cap: A photon from the body enters the converter and sometimes interacts, by Compton scattering or the photo effect.
reels.words: a photon from the body enters the converter and sometimes interacts, by compton scattering or the photo effect. each interaction ejects an electron. but only an electron that reaches the gas counts, and an electron has a short range in the metal. the paper writes that balance as one equation. electrons are created at a rate k times the photon number, and lost at a rate b times the electron number. for a thin converter, the yield rises and then saturates. for a thick one, the photon beam is attenuated, so the yield peaks and falls. the best design weighs the two.

reels.name: Direct
reels.cap: The obvious design puts the converter in direct contact with the gas, behind a two millimetre glass plate and a three hundred micrometre gap.
reels.words: the obvious design puts the converter in direct contact with the gas, behind a two millimetre glass plate and a three hundred micrometre gap. the authors tried five metals, with atomic numbers from seventy-four to eighty-three: tungsten, platinum, gold, lead and bismuth. in every one the yield saturates near forty micrometres, at most about point three eight percent, for bismuth and lead. but the picture changes with photon energy. lower energy photons give a higher yield than five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts. that is backwards, because the lower energy photons are the scattered ones. the paper says this clearly disproves the intuitive design.

reels.name: Sandwich
reels.cap: So the authors put a glass plate between the converter and the gas.
reels.words: so the authors put a glass plate between the converter and the gas. a bismuth converter now sits between two glass plates, and forms the cathode. glass is smooth and highly resistive, which prevents discharges, and its ageing is well studied. the glass also soaks up the weaker signals from scattered photons, and the drop is large once the glass is thicker than fifty micrometres. for two hundred micrometres of glass, the yield at five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts is point two two eight percent, forty percent below the first design. at three hundred and seven kilo electron volts it is point zero four five percent, ninety percent below. so scattered photons are suppressed without measuring any energy. the best glass and bismuth are each fifty micrometres thick.

reels.name: Stack
reels.cap: A single sandwich loses efficiency to its glass, so the authors repeat it.
reels.words: a single sandwich loses efficiency to its glass, so the authors repeat it. the multigap design stacks many units of glass, bismuth and glass, each with its own gas gap. each gap sees fewer photons than the one below, because the beam is attenuated on the way up. so the photons reaching gap i fall off as e to the minus i minus one, x over c. the yield of the stack is the sum over all the gaps. the paper simulated one hundred gaps, each fifty micrometres of glass, fifty of bismuth and fifty of glass. the yield is twenty-three point eight percent, comparable to crystal detectors. it is highest for five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, and at three hundred and seven it is half as large.

reels.name: Body
reels.cap: To test it, the authors simulated a human body as a block of tissue forty by forty by one hundred and fifty centimetres, with photons starting at its centre.
reels.words: to test it, the authors simulated a human body as a block of tissue forty by forty by one hundred and fifty centimetres, with photons starting at its centre. most leave at five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, but a long tail has lost energy by scattering. multiply that spectrum by the detector's response, and the tail is cut down while the full energy peak stays tall. about eighty-six percent of the registered photons are above three hundred and eighty kilo electron volts. those are fit for reconstruction. above to below that line, the ratio is better than six to one.

reels.name: Build
reels.cap: The basic module is a six gap glass chamber, with copper readout strips on both sides.
reels.words: the basic module is a six gap glass chamber, with copper readout strips on both sides. fishing line holds the gaps apart, and graphite paint forms the high voltage electrodes on the outer glass. twenty such modules, stacked on top of one another, form a supermodule of one hundred and twenty gas gaps. the small prototype is one hundred and twenty by seventy millimetres, and the full scale one is three hundred and fifty by seventy.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: The design aims at a time resolution of thirty five picoseconds.
reels.words: the design aims at a time resolution of thirty five picoseconds. the two photons of one annihilation reach their detectors at slightly different times, so the difference places the annihilation along the line of response. thirty five picoseconds narrows it to an eleven millimetre stretch. that sharper placement improves the image and lowers the patient's dose.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The question was whether a resistive plate chamber can be a P E T detector that works inside an M R I.
reels.words: the question was whether a resistive plate chamber can be a p e t detector that works inside an m r i. the idea is a converter plate that turns a photon into an electron, and the trade between thick enough to convert and thin enough to escape. putting the converter against the gas fails, because it favours scattered photons. putting glass in between suppresses them. stacking a hundred gaps recovers an efficiency of twenty-four percent, with eighty-six percent of the registered photons above three hundred and eighty kilo electron volts. two limits remain. the avalanche in the gas was not simulated, and the prototypes' test results come in a separate publication.

title: Photon quantum entanglement in the MeV regime and its application in PET imaging

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper appeared in Nature Communications in twenty twenty-one, from Watts and colleagues at the University of York.
reels.words: this paper appeared in nature communications in twenty twenty-one, from watts and colleagues at the university of york. it asks what pet can gain from the fact that its two annihilation photons are quantum entangled. and it does three things. it adds entanglement to a geant four simulation. it checks that simulation against a cadmium zinc telluride detector. and it uses the simulation to pick true events out from scatter and random backgrounds in a simulated scanner.

reels.name: Pair
reels.cap: When a positron meets an electron, they annihilate into two photons of point five one one mega electron volts, flying off in opposite directions.
reels.words: when a positron meets an electron, they annihilate into two photons of point five one one mega electron volts, flying off in opposite directions. each photon has a linear polarisation, and the two are always at right angles. but which way each one points is left open: the two share a single entangled state. measure one as horizontal, and the other is vertical, however far apart they are.

reels.name: Planes
reels.cap: A Compton scatter is the tool that reveals polarisation.
reels.words: a compton scatter is the tool that reveals polarisation. a photon is likelier to scatter at right angles to its polarisation, so the plane of its scatter records which way it pointed. seen down the line of flight, the angle between the two scatter planes is delta phi. when the planes are parallel, that pair is at its least likely. turn one plane through ninety degrees, and the pair becomes most likely. the rate follows a cosine of twice delta phi.

reels.name: Witness
reels.cap: The ratio of the likeliest scatter to the least likely is called R.
reels.words: the ratio of the likeliest scatter to the least likely is called r. for unpolarised photons it is exactly one, a flat line. photons that are merely perpendicular, with no entanglement, can reach at most one point six three. entanglement predicts up to two point eight five, at scatter angles of eighty-one point seven degrees. so a measurement above one point six three is a witness of entanglement. earlier experiments found two point four seven and two point three three, with photons up to two and a half metres apart, wider than a clinical scanner.

reels.name: Sim
reels.cap: The authors added this to the Geant four simulation, and call the result Q E Geant four.
reels.words: the authors added this to the geant four simulation, and call the result q e geant four. it tracks the first photon until it is destroyed, storing the direction of its first compton scatter. the second photon's first scatter is then drawn from the entangled rate, using that stored scatter. after that first scatter, both photons are treated as independent, because the entangled state is assumed to collapse completely.

reels.name: Rig
reels.cap: The test bench was a PET demonstrator from Kromek, built from two cadmium zinc telluride cubes, ten millimetres on a side, eighty-seven millimetres apart.
reels.words: the test bench was a pet demonstrator from kromek, built from two cadmium zinc telluride cubes, ten millimetres on a side, eighty-seven millimetres apart. a one millimetre bead of sodium twenty-two, one hundred and seventy kilobecquerels, sits midway. each cube's anode is split into one hundred and twenty-one pixels, each point eight millimetres square. when a photon scatters in a cube and is then absorbed, two clusters of pixels fire. seen down the axis, the line through the two clusters gives that photon's scatter plane, and delta phi is the angle between the two cubes' lines.

reels.name: Result
reels.cap: In the measurements, the black dots are the coincidence rate against delta phi.
reels.words: in the measurements, the black dots are the coincidence rate against delta phi. the entangled simulation, in blue, follows them closely, with a chi squared per degree of freedom of one point eight seven. the rate dips near zero and one hundred and eighty degrees and peaks near ninety. the enhancement ratio is one point eight five plus or minus zero point zero four, and one point nine five plus or minus zero point zero seven for tighter polar angles. the red line, perpendicular photons without entanglement, peaks well below the data. the green line, unpolarised photons, is flat.

reels.name: Loss
reels.cap: What happens when one photon scatters before it reaches the detector?
reels.words: what happens when one photon scatters before it reaches the detector? the authors put a nylon block in the path of one photon, and turned that cube through thirty-three degrees. the scattered photon arrived with about four hundred and forty kilo electron volts. the simulation assumes that the first scatter, in nylon or in the crystal, breaks the entanglement completely. the measured correlation is clearly smaller than for back-to-back photons, and the simulation agrees. taking that data needed over a month.

reels.name: Idea
reels.cap: Pairs that travel straight to the detectors stay entangled.
reels.words: pairs that travel straight to the detectors stay entangled. scatter pairs and random pairs do not, so they show far less correlation. now sort the events by delta phi. between eighty and a hundred degrees, true events are at their most likely. between zero and twenty degrees, they are at their least likely. the backgrounds hardly notice the difference. so the difference between the two bins is made of true events, and scale factors from the simulation turn it into the true profile and the background.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: To test the method, the authors simulated a preclinical scanner.
reels.words: to test the method, the authors simulated a preclinical scanner. it has four rings of the same ten millimetre cadmium zinc telluride crystals, with their front faces forty-nine point one millimetres from the centre. in the middle sits a standard n e m a n u four mouse phantom, a plastic cylinder holding five capillaries, one to five millimetres wide, filled with a positron source. the run covered ten to the twelve annihilations, about as many as a patient's scan accumulates.

reels.name: Extract
reels.cap: The filtered back projection image shows all five capillaries, with a scatter background.
reels.words: the filtered back projection image shows all five capillaries, with a scatter background. the authors cut a profile through the two lowest capillaries, once for pairs with delta phi near ninety degrees and once for pairs near zero. the ninety-degree profile has much taller peaks. a scaled subtraction gives the true profile, in red, and it matches the actual true profile, known only from the simulation. the same subtraction recovers the scatter background, though noisily, from artefacts of the reconstruction. and figure seven shows the same for random backgrounds.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: The extraction works on average.
reels.words: the extraction works on average. delta phi cannot say which single event was true. this proof of principle used two bins of delta phi, only a fraction of the data. the mouse phantom's scatter fraction is fifteen per cent, while human scans reach up to sixty-seven per cent, so the method should suit them better. the next steps are to use the information within iterative reconstruction such as m l e m, and to repeat the prior-scatter measurement with more data.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: The two annihilation photons are born entangled, with perpendicular polarisations.
reels.words: the two annihilation photons are born entangled, with perpendicular polarisations. that shows up as a cosine in the angle between their scatter planes, with a ratio above one point six three that a non-entangled pair cannot reach. the authors put that into geant four, and a cadmium zinc telluride detector measured one point eight five. after a prior scatter the correlation shrinks. so events near ninety degrees and near zero differ in their true content, and subtracting them recovered the true, scatter and random profiles in a simulated scanner. that is a first step, not yet a clinical method.

title: Characterization in Geant4 of different PET configurations

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper comes from the Autonomous University of Puebla, in Mexico, by López Toxquia and colleagues.
reels.words: this paper comes from the autonomous university of puebla, in mexico, by lópez toxquia and colleagues. it builds three small-animal pet scanners in geant4 and asks which one performs best. it judges them on coincidence time resolution, spatial resolution and acceptance, and finds that two flat modules do worst, while the first of two rings does marginally best. but look at the timings it reports. they come out in picoseconds, while real scanners are quoted in nanoseconds. working out why is the key to reading every number in the paper.

reels.name: Scanners
reels.cap: Here are the three scanners, drawn to scale and seen down the bore.
reels.words: here are the three scanners, drawn to scale and seen down the bore. ring-pet is four rings of lyso crystals, twelve centimetres across. each ring holds twenty-four crystals, ninety-six in all. ring-pet2 keeps the same rings but cuts each crystal to a third of the width. a ring now holds seventy-two, two hundred and eighty-eight in all, and the four rings together are a third as long. the third scanner drops the ring. two flat modules face each other ten point two centimetres apart, each a twenty by twenty grid of crystals, eight hundred in all. in the middle of every scanner sits the same water sphere, six centimetres across.

reels.name: Pair
reels.cap: Every crystal is a block of LYSO, a lutetium-based scintillator, ten millimetres deep.
reels.words: every crystal is a block of lyso, a lutetium-based scintillator, ten millimetres deep. its face is fifteen millimetres square in ring-pet, five in ring-pet2, and two in the modules. behind each block, where a silicon photomultiplier would sit, the authors put a scorer. geant4 does not simulate electronics, so the scorer stands in for the whole sensor, with one hundred percent efficiency. for each gamma it records two things. a gamma flies in, and the scorer notes where it first struck the crystal, and its flight time, measured from the moment it was made. every timing in this paper is built from those flight times alone.

reels.name: Source
reels.cap: Every event starts at the same place, with a positron released at the centre of the water sphere.
reels.words: every event starts at the same place, with a positron released at the centre of the water sphere. it wanders, losing energy to the water, and where it finally stops, it annihilates into two gammas of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, flying apart. how far it wanders depends on the radionuclide, and the paper models four, each with its own spectrum of positron energies. fluorine eighteen reaches at most six hundred and thirty-five kilo electron volts. oxygen fifteen reaches one thousand seven hundred and twenty, and its positrons travel at least twice as far before stopping. carbon eleven and nitrogen thirteen fall in between. for each scanner, the paper models three hundred and fifty-six thousand events across the four radionuclides.

reels.name: Gap
reels.cap: Now follow one annihilation out to the crystals.
reels.words: now follow one annihilation out to the crystals. its two gammas fly to opposite crystals of the ring, and each scorer stamps an arrival time. had the annihilation sat exactly at the centre, the two stamps would agree. move it one millimetre towards the right-hand crystal. the right gamma now arrives earlier, by the time light takes to cross a millimetre, and the left one later by the same. the stamps differ by six point seven picoseconds, computed here from the speed of light. repeat that for every event, and the differences pile into a histogram. a gaussian fitted to it has a width, sigma, and that sigma is what the paper calls the coincidence time resolution. so a timing of a few picoseconds says where the positrons stopped, not how fast a detector is.

reels.name: Position
reels.cap: The same difference also gives a position.
reels.words: the same difference also gives a position. half of it, times the speed of light, is how far from the centre the annihilation sat along the line. done for every event in ring-pet, the points form a cloud around the centre, small for fluorine and wide for oxygen. project the cloud onto the x axis and histogram it. its full width at half maximum and its full width at a tenth of maximum are what the paper reports as spatial resolution. for oxygen in ring-pet they are zero point four five four and four point one three four millimetres. the peak is sharp and the tails are long, which is why the two widths differ ninefold.

reels.name: Ctrs
reels.cap: Here are the coincidence time resolutions, redrawn from the paper's table.
reels.words: here are the coincidence time resolutions, redrawn from the paper's table. ring-pet's sigma grows from one point two seven picoseconds for fluorine to eight point three one for oxygen, because a longer positron range spreads the stopping points further. ring-pet2 runs alongside it, from one point two two to seven point seven five, and the two rings are not significantly different, with p at zero point zero seven six. the modules sit far above, at four point nine five picoseconds for fluorine and fourteen point eight six for oxygen, significantly worse than either ring. the paper does not say what in the flat geometry adds those picoseconds.

reels.name: Widths
reels.cap: Spatial resolution tells a different story.
reels.words: spatial resolution tells a different story. for fluorine, all three scanners give the same full width at half maximum, zero point zero nine six millimetres, against zero point one zero two in the literature, levin and hoffman's calculation of positron range. for oxygen they spread a little, zero point four five four for ring-pet to zero point five zero nine for the modules, around a literature value of zero point five zero one. no difference between the scanners is significant. that is what to expect. with exact impact points and flight times, the width is set by how far positrons travel in water, not by the scanner around them. so matching the literature, eight point nine percent apart on average, checks geant4's positron physics, which the authors call a partial validation.

reels.name: Acceptance
reels.cap: Acceptance takes every annihilation produced and asks what fraction was recorded as a true coincidence.
reels.words: acceptance takes every annihilation produced and asks what fraction was recorded as a true coincidence. both gammas of a pair have to be caught, and most pairs are not. ring-pet keeps the most, seventeen point four one percent for fluorine. ring-pet2 keeps fourteen point five four, and the modules fourteen point four nine, falling to twelve point nine seven for oxygen. ring-pet's lead is significant, with p at zero point zero zero one, while ring-pet2 and the modules cannot be told apart.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: How far should someone building a scanner trust these numbers?
reels.words: how far should someone building a scanner trust these numbers? start with timing. a typical time to digital converter resolves twenty picoseconds, coarser than every ring value here. only a new pico t d c card, at two point two picoseconds, could measure them. real coincidence timing sits in nanoseconds, because the scintillation light, the sensor and the electronics, none of which enter these flight times, dominate it. then acceptance, which the paper ties to detector area. ring-pet's crystal faces add up to twenty-one thousand six hundred square millimetres, ring-pet2's to seven thousand two hundred, and the modules' to three thousand two hundred. that is a nearly sevenfold range, against acceptances within a fifth of each other, so area alone cannot explain them.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: So here is the paper in one pass.
reels.words: so here is the paper in one pass. it asked which of three small-animal pet geometries works best, a ring of large crystals, a ring of small ones, or two flat modules. each was built in geant4 with a perfect scorer in place of the sensor, and fed positrons from four radionuclides at the centre of a water sphere. timing and position both came from the gap between two flight times, so both measure positron range, in picoseconds and in fractions of a millimetre. the modules came out worst in timing, and the large-crystal ring best in acceptance. what the study leaves out is the detector itself, the light, the sensor and the clock that set these numbers in a real scanner.

title: The user's own tutorial

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This is a crystal of L S O, ten millimetres thick, and this is a gamma of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, fired straight at it.
reels.words: this is a crystal of l s o, ten millimetres thick, and this is a gamma of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, fired straight at it. the first gamma passes through and leaves nothing. so does the second. the third stops in the crystal and leaves all of its energy. a program printed these lines, one for each gamma. the program is one file of one hundred and one lines. it is written against geant four, a c plus plus library that follows particles through matter, one step at a time. there is no geant four program to run. you write your own program, compile it yourself, and link it against that library. this video shows what files such a program is made of, what calls what inside it, which tools build it, and how this one file grows, change by change, into a simulation of a scintillator slab read by sixty four sensor tiles.

reels.name: One file
reels.cap: The file, main dot c c, holds five small classes of yours and a main function.
reels.words: the file, main dot c c, holds five small classes of yours and a main function. each class inherits from a geant four base class and overrides one or two methods. the first is the detector. its method, construct, builds the geometry and returns the world volume. the second is the physics list, which registers one module of electromagnetic physics. the third is the gun. its method, generate primaries, puts one gamma into each event. the last two do the scoring, because geant four records nothing by itself. the stepping action is called after every step, and adds up the energy that step left in the crystal. the event action zeroes that total before each event and prints it afterwards. none of these methods is ever called by your own code.

reels.name: Volume
reels.cap: Inside Construct, every volume is three objects.
reels.words: inside construct, every volume is three objects. a solid is the shape alone, here a box. geant four's box takes half lengths, so a crystal fifty millimetres wide is written as twenty five. a logical volume is that shape filled with a material. a placement puts the logical volume at a position inside a mother volume. the crystal's mother is the world, a box of air, and the world itself has no mother. the last argument of a placement asks geant four to check for overlaps, and it is worth leaving on.

reels.name: Main
reels.cap: The main function is where your five objects meet Geant four.
reels.words: the main function is where your five objects meet geant four. its first line creates the run manager, which is the kernel's front door. the next lines hand over the detector and the physics list with set user initialization, and the gun, the event action and the stepping action with set user action. at this point nothing has been built. the run manager has only stored five pointers. then come two calls. initialize builds the geometry and the physics tables. beam on, with the number ten, runs ten events. main has no loop in it at all.

reels.name: Calls
reels.cap: So who calls your methods?
reels.words: so who calls your methods? follow one run from the top. main calls initialize, and initialize calls your detector's construct, once. the world volume it returns goes to the navigator. initialize also has the physics list build its particles and processes, once, which fills the cross section tables. then main calls beam on, and the loop over events belongs to the kernel. for each event it calls the gun's generate primaries, which puts one gamma on the stack. it calls the event action's begin of event. then, for each track on the stack and for each step of that track, it calls your stepping action. when the stack is empty it calls end of event, which prints the total. then the next event starts, ten times over. your code is called by the kernel, and control never starts in it.

reels.name: Tools
reels.cap: To turn that file into a program you need five things on the machine.
reels.words: to turn that file into a program you need five things on the machine. a c plus plus compiler turns your source into machine code, and geant four eleven needs the c plus plus seventeen standard. c make reads a file called c make lists dot t x t, finds geant four, and writes the build instructions. ninja runs those instructions. then there is geant four itself, which is three things. it is headers, compiled libraries, and a small file, geant four config dot c make, that tells c make where the other two are. last come the data sets of cross sections, each found through an environment variable. here one more tool, pixi, installs all five from a single file, pixi dot toml, and runs every command inside that environment. that takes a download. building geant four from source instead takes an hour or so.

reels.name: Build
reels.cap: Every example in this video is built with the same two commands.
reels.words: every example in this video is built with the same two commands. the first is the configure step. c make, given a source folder and a build folder, reads c make lists dot t x t, finds geant four, and writes ninja's instructions into the build folder. you run it once, and again only when c make lists changes. the second command is the build step. it compiles each dot c c file to an object file, then links the objects with the geant four libraries into one executable. you run it after every edit, and only the changed files are recompiled. everything generated lives in the build folder, so the source folder stays clean and the build folder can be deleted at any time. here, configuring took about twenty six seconds, compiling a few seconds, and the run itself about one second.

reels.name: C make
reels.cap: The C make lists file for the one file example is a few statements, and four of them carry the meaning.
reels.words: the c make lists file for the one file example is a few statements, and four of them carry the meaning. project names the program, mini, and says its language is c plus plus. find package looks for geant four's config file, and stops if it is not found. add executable names the program again and lists its source files. headers are not listed. target link libraries links geant four in, and with it come the include paths and the compiler flags that geant four itself was built with. when a second source file is added later, the add executable line is the one that changes.

reels.name: Split
reels.cap: The second version of the program does the same physics, and what changes is its shape.
reels.words: the second version of the program does the same physics, and what changes is its shape. the one file is split into one class per file. main moves to mini dot c c and holds nothing else. the detector becomes a pair of files. a header, dot h h, declares the class so that other files can use it, and a dot c c file defines its methods. the physics list is one line of code, so it stays in a header alone. the gun and the actions share a third pair. c make lists now names three source files, and a header is never listed, because it is compiled into whichever dot c c file includes it. one new file is not code at all. it is a macro, run dot mac, which holds the settings of the run. this is already the shape of the full slab application.

reels.name: Threads
reels.cap: The split version also runs on several threads, and that changes what main hands over.
reels.words: the split version also runs on several threads, and that changes what main hands over. geant four parallelises over events. each worker thread runs its own event loop. all of them share one geometry and one set of physics tables, which are read only once they are built. the actions are different, because they hold the state of the event in progress. so every thread needs a gun, an event action and a stepping action of its own. main therefore registers three objects, not five. the third is a factory, a class called actions. the kernel calls its build method once on each worker, and build creates that worker's own set. on the master thread, which simulates nothing, it calls build for master, which creates only a run action.

reels.name: Rows
reels.cap: With several threads, the energy total can no longer be a global variable.
reels.words: with several threads, the energy total can no longer be a global variable. it moves into the event action, and each stepping action is given a pointer to its own thread's event. each worker finishes its events in its own order. at the end of an event, a worker appends one row to a list shared by all threads, and it holds a lock while it does. at the end of the run, the run action on the master sorts the rows by event number and writes them to a file, e dep dot t x t. two thousand gammas gave one thousand one hundred and fifteen events that left energy, and eight hundred and seventy five of those left all of it.

reels.name: Macro
reels.cap: In the split version, main no longer calls Initialize or Beam on.
reels.words: in the split version, main no longer calls initialize or beam on. it executes a macro, a text file of geant four commands, and here the file has four lines. the first sets the number of threads to four. the second, run initialize, is the same initialize call as before. the third sets the gun's energy, and it exists because the program has a particle gun. the fourth, run beam on, is beam on with two thousand events. the order matters. the thread count must come before initialize, and the gun command after it. the point of a macro is that the event count, the energy and the thread count all change without recompiling.

reels.name: Light files
reels.cap: The third version adds scintillation light, and it changes only the detector file, the physics header and the actions pair.
reels.words: the third version adds scintillation light, and it changes only the detector file, the physics header and the actions pair. main, the macro and c make lists are untouched, which is the reason for splitting the program up. in the physics header, one more module is registered, g four optical physics. it adds the optical photon as a particle, the scintillation and cherenkov processes that make photons, and the processes that carry them. in the detector file, the crystal's material gets a table of optical properties, and a thin glass sensor is placed against one face. in the actions, the stepping action now counts each photon that enters the sensor, and notes when the first one arrived.

reels.name: Light
reels.cap: Registering the physics is not enough to get light.
reels.words: registering the physics is not enough to get light. scintillation reads its yield from the material's table, here twenty five thousand photons per m e v, so a gamma that leaves all its energy makes about twelve thousand eight hundred. a photon can only travel in a material that has a refractive index. the crystal is given one point eight and the glass sensor one point five. the air is deliberately given none, so a photon that reaches air is killed at the surface, and the five bare faces behave as black walls. only the face with the sensor counts light, about five thousand two hundred photons on average. the same rule is a trap. forget one material's refractive index, and light is lost in silence.

reels.name: Slab
reels.cap: The slab application is the third version with one idea added.
reels.words: the slab application is the third version with one idea added. nothing about the detector is written in c plus plus. every box, every material, every optical table, the source and the run are read from one file, spec dot jason, and that file is written by python. the detector no longer names l s o or a sensor. construct is a loop over the boxes listed in the spec. the sixty four sensor tiles are one logical volume placed sixty four times, each with its own copy number, and the stepping action reads that copy number as the channel. the spec replaces the macro as well, so main reads the thread count and the event count from it, and calls initialize and beam on itself. python converts every number to geant four's internal units first, so the c plus plus multiplies by no unit at all.

reels.name: Slab calls
reels.cap: Here is one slab run from end to end.
reels.words: here is one slab run from end to end. you type one command, pixi run python, with a run folder and the design keys you want to change. the python package fills in the full design, builds the spec from it, and writes spec dot jason into the run folder. then it starts the compiled program, build slash slab, as a subprocess, and hands it the spec and the folder. inside, it is the call tree you already know. main creates the run manager, registers detector, physics and actions, calls initialize, then beam on. when the run ends, the master writes binary num pie tables. python packs those into one file, events dot n p z. the build is one command as well, pixi run build, which is the same two c make commands with their flags.

reels.name: Wrong
reels.cap: When a first application fails, it usually fails in one of a few known places.
reels.words: when a first application fails, it usually fails in one of a few known places. at the configure step, c make says it could not find a package configuration file provided by geant four. c make was not told where geant four is, so run it inside pixi run. at start up, the program aborts because a data variable is not set. the binary was run outside the environment. in the geometry, a volume comes out twice the size intended, because a box takes half lengths. an energy is off by a power of ten when a number was written without its unit. in a macro, command not found for the gun means the command came before run initialize. and if light is made but none arrives, a material on the way has no refractive index.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: To sum up, Geant four is a library, and a simulation is your own C plus plus program linked against it.
reels.words: to sum up, geant four is a library, and a simulation is your own c plus plus program linked against it. the program is five small classes and a main. they are a detector, a physics list, a gun, and two actions that score. main hands them to the run manager, and from then on the kernel calls them, construct once and the actions for every event and every step. building it needs a compiler, c make, ninja, and geant four with its data, and takes two commands, configure once and build after every edit. as the program grows, each class gets its own file. with threads, a factory builds one set of actions per worker, rows are gathered under a lock, and a macro holds the settings of the run. light costs one more physics module, an optical table on each material, and a sensor. the slab moves every number out of the c plus plus into a spec written by python. to start your own, copy the third example, change the detector file first, and run ten events, reading the start up output for overlaps before anything else.

title: Geant4: how a simulation is built

reels.name: Hook
reels.cap: Fire a single five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma into a slab of L S O.
reels.words: fire a single five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma into a slab of l s o. it crosses the wrap, stops in the crystal, and a flash of scintillation light spreads out to an eight by eight array of silicon photomultipliers. geant four can simulate all of that, but it will not hand you the result. geant four records nothing by default, and it has no executable that simulates a detector. you write a small application, and the kernel calls your code at the moments it chooses. so this video is about those moments. it asks which function is called on every step, how the program knows that a photon has reached a surface, how you get the coordinates of a deposit or the arrival time of a photon out, and what happens when two gammas share one event. the running example is the slab application from the tutorial this video follows, fifty by fifty by ten millimetres of l s o read out by sixty four sensor tiles.

reels.name: Moves
reels.cap: Geant four has no configuration file that describes a simulation.
reels.words: geant four has no configuration file that describes a simulation. everything you customise is done in three moves. first, you derive. the kernel is written against abstract base classes. it knows that a detector construction has a method called construct, which returns the world volume, and it knows nothing else about yours. so you write a class, here called detector, that inherits from that base class and overrides construct. second, you register. in main, you create one object of your class and hand it to the run manager with set user initialization. the run manager keeps the pointer. third, you are called. from then on the kernel owns the control flow. it calls construct through the base class pointer, at a moment it has fixed, and uses what comes back. you never write the simulation loop. you fill in the places where the loop stops to ask.

reels.name: Pieces
reels.cap: Three objects are mandatory, and they are three different kinds of answer, asked at three different times.
reels.words: three objects are mandatory, and they are three different kinds of answer, asked at three different times. the slab's main registers them in three lines, which are a detector, a physics list, and an actions object that makes the primary generator. then it calls initialize, and the kernel asks the first two. it calls construct once, and gets back the world volume with every other volume placed inside it. on that tree the kernel builds its navigator, which every later step will ask which volume a point is in and how far away the next boundary is. it calls construct process once, and gets, for each kind of particle, the list of processes attached to it. from those lists it builds cross section tables, and every later step will ask each process on the list how far the particle goes before it acts. so geometry and physics are data. the kernel is given them once and then only reads them. the third piece is different. the primary generator is code, and the kernel runs it at the start of every event. its method, generate primaries, adds one or more vertices to the event. the kernel converts them to tracks and pushes them on a stack, and that is what starts the event.

reels.name: Loops
reels.cap: The loop that does the asking is four loops, one inside the other.
reels.words: the loop that does the asking is four loops, one inside the other. a run is one call to beam on, with a fixed geometry and fixed physics for some number of events. an event starts from its primaries and holds everything that follows from them. a track is one particle, a primary or any secondary. a step is one straight segment of a track, from a pre step point to a post step point. each level has a place where the kernel stops for you. a run action is called at the start and the end of the run. an event action is called at the start and the end of each event. the generator is called once per event, and a stepping action is called after every single step. these actions are made in one method, build, which the run manager calls once on every worker thread, because each thread needs its own copies.

reels.name: Stack
reels.cap: Inside one event, tracks are not followed in parallel.
reels.words: inside one event, tracks are not followed in parallel. the kernel keeps a stack. it starts with the primaries, pops one track, follows it, pushes the secondaries it made, and pops the next. the stack is last in, first out, and the event ends when it is empty. the general rule is that a track is followed to its end. take a gamma that compton scatters twice. it is followed through both scatters and out of the world before either recoil electron is touched. the secondaries are held until their parent has finished, and only then pushed. and because the last one pushed is the first one popped, the electron made last is followed first.

reels.name: Suspend
reels.cap: Scintillation breaks that rule, on purpose.
reels.words: scintillation breaks that rule, on purpose. a process may set the status of its track to f suspend. the kernel then stops the track where it is, pushes it back on the stack, and pushes its secondaries on top of it. g four scintillation does this after every step in which it makes photons, and the option that tells it to is on by default. so in the slab, the gamma is followed to its absorption and the photoelectron is pushed. the electron takes one step, makes photons, and is suspended. every photon of that step is followed to its end, one at a time. only then does the electron resume, take its second step, and wait again. the reason is memory. one event here makes about twelve thousand eight hundred optical photons, and every track waiting on the stack costs memory. following the photons of each step before the next step is taken keeps only one step's worth waiting at a time.

reels.name: Ask
reels.cap: Now go inside a single step.
reels.words: now go inside a single step. one function runs once per step, g four stepping manager stepping, and the first thing it does is define the physical step length. here is a gamma inside the crystal. its particle type has five processes attached, which are photoelectric, compton, rayleigh, conversion and transportation. the stepping manager goes down that list and calls post step g p i l on each one. g p i l stands for get physical interaction length, and it is how a process says how far the particle may go before that process wants to act. each one returns a distance. then it goes down the list again with along step g p i l, and this is where transportation answers, with the distance to the next volume boundary. the stepping manager keeps the smallest length returned and remembers which process returned it. so yes, a function is called for every process, on every step. the shortest proposal wins, and it alone decides how long the step is.

reels.name: Act
reels.cap: With the length decided, the step is carried out in the same fixed order.
reels.words: with the length decided, the step is carried out in the same fixed order. first, along step do it is called for every continuous process. transportation's moves the particle to the new point, and for an electron, ionisation's takes away the energy lost on the way. then post step do it is called for the process that won. if photoelectric won, the gamma is absorbed there and a photoelectron is made. a do it does not touch the track itself. it fills in a particle change, which holds the new energy, the new direction, the new status and the list of secondaries, and hands it back. the stepping manager applies it. that is why a process can be written without knowing what any other process did on the same step. the secondaries are collected, and last of all the stepping manager calls your code. if the volume has a sensitive detector, its hit method is called, and then user stepping action receives the finished step.

reels.name: Budget
reels.cap: How does a process such as Compton scattering choose the distance it proposes?
reels.words: how does a process such as compton scattering choose the distance it proposes? it does not draw a new random distance on every step. at the start of a track it draws a number of mean free paths, once, as minus the logarithm of a uniform random number. on each step it asks for the mean free path in the current material at the current energy, which comes from the cross section tables, and returns the product of the two. after a step in which it did not act, it subtracts the fraction of a mean free path that the step used. the number carries across volume boundaries. only the mean free path changes there, which is how a gamma can cross wrap, crystal and grease on a single draw. and when the process finally does act, its post step do it clears the number, so the next step draws a fresh one.

reels.name: Limit
reels.cap: Transportation is a process like the others, and its proposal comes from the geometry.
reels.words: transportation is a process like the others, and its proposal comes from the geometry. take an optical photon inside the crystal. in its along step g p i l, transportation calls compute step on the navigator, with the position and direction of the photon. the navigator returns the distance, along that direction, to the surface of the current volume or of a daughter inside it. say that is three point one millimetres to the crystal face, while rayleigh scattering proposed four point seven millimetres. transportation's is shorter, so it has limited the step. its along step do it then marks the post step point with a status, f geom boundary. that flag is the only thing that says the step ended on a surface. everything that needs to know reads it from the step.

reels.name: Forced
reels.cap: So how does the optical boundary process know that the photon is at an interface?
reels.words: so how does the optical boundary process know that the photon is at an interface? it never competes for the step length. when it is asked, it returns infinity, and it marks itself forced. a forced process has its post step do it called at the end of every step, whoever won. so the boundary process runs after every single step an optical photon takes, and its first act is to read the flag that transportation set. if the step ended in the bulk, say because rayleigh scattering won, the status is not f geom boundary, and the process returns at once, having done nothing. if the step ended on a surface, it carries on. nothing in this is special to optics. a boundary is detected by transportation, flagged on the step, and acted on by whichever process chooses to look.

reels.name: Interface
reels.cap: Once it knows it is on a surface, the boundary process works out what the surface is.
reels.words: once it knows it is on a surface, the boundary process works out what the surface is. the pre step point is in the volume being left, and the post step point is in the volume being entered. it reads the refractive index, r index, from the properties table of each material. if the material being entered has none, the photon is absorbed there. next it looks for a surface you defined, first a border surface registered for exactly this ordered pair of volumes, then a skin surface on either one. if there is neither, the interface is a perfect polished boundary between the two indices. it asks the navigator for the surface normal at the crossing point. then it applies snell's law. if the sine of the outgoing angle comes out at one or more, the photon is totally internally reflected. otherwise it computes the fresnel transmission coefficient and draws one random number. the photon is transmitted with that probability and reflected otherwise. the new direction goes into the particle change, and a reflected photon simply starts its next step from the surface, heading back.

reels.name: Deposit
reels.cap: Now to getting data out.
reels.words: now to getting data out. after every step, geant four hands your stepping action a pointer to the finished step, and it stores nothing itself. recording is three decisions, which are where you look, what you read off the step, and where you keep it. here is how the slab records the coordinates of an energy deposit. the first line is the filter. a stepping action sees every step of every track in every volume, so it keeps only steps that begin in the crystal and deposit more than a threshold. the second line takes the post step point, and the third reads its position. the last line pushes five numbers onto a list that belongs to the event. they are x, y and z, then the global time, which is the time since the event began, and the energy deposited on this step. that is one deposit with its coordinates, and it took four lines.

reels.name: Arrival
reels.cap: The arrival time of a photon at a silicon photomultiplier is read the same way, with one trick.
reels.words: the arrival time of a photon at a silicon photomultiplier is read the same way, with one trick. a step whose pre step point sits on a boundary has just entered its volume. so a photon is arriving when three things are true. the track is an optical photon. the volume at its pre step point is the sensor tile. and the status of its pre step point is f geom boundary. when all three hold, the slab calls count with two values read off that point. the global time is the arrival time. the copy number of the touchable says which of the sixty four placements of the tile this is, so it is the channel. then it sets the status of the track to f stop and kill, so the photon is counted once and never followed again. the slab only counts. pushing that time into a list for the channel, at this same line, is all it takes to keep every arrival time.

reels.name: Keep
reels.cap: The third decision is where you keep it, and the answer is an object of your own that lives exactly as long as the thing you are summarising.
reels.words: the third decision is where you keep it, and the answer is an object of your own that lives exactly as long as the thing you are summarising. in the slab, the stepping action holds a pointer to the event object of its thread and appends to it on every step. begin of event action clears that object. end of event action reduces it to one row, which is sixty four channel counts plus the true interaction position. at the end of the run, the run action on the master thread sorts the rows by event number and writes them to disk. and if you would rather not filter every step yourself, attach a sensitive detector to one logical volume, and it is called only for steps that start in that volume.

reels.name: Pair
reels.cap: What if you want two gammas in the slab at the same time?
reels.words: what if you want two gammas in the slab at the same time? start with what geant four will not do. tracks do not interact. it transports one particle at a time through matter that does not change. no process takes a second track as its input, and a track leaves nothing behind in the material for a later one to meet. so two gammas in one event give exactly what they would give in two separate events, added together. putting them in one event is still useful, because an event has one clock. generate primaries may add as many vertices as it likes, each with its own position and its own start time. the generator of the slab loops over a batch, sets a position, sets the time to k times a fixed spacing, and adds the vertex. all of them go on the stack before tracking begins. they are followed one after another, but each track carries its own global time, so the recorded times come out as if the gammas had been simultaneous.

reels.name: Readout
reels.cap: Where two gammas really do interact is in the readout, not in the transport.
reels.words: where two gammas really do interact is in the readout, not in the transport. a microcell that has just fired cannot fire again. pulses overlap. an electronics channel has dead time. none of that is in the tracking. it is modelled afterwards, on the recorded arrival times and counts, in a step called digitisation, which is your own code at the end of the event or offline in python. simulating both gammas in one event is what gives that step the photons from both on one time axis. what you cannot get this way is the deposit of one particle changing the physics of another, such as a light yield that drops where the ionisation is already dense. birks quenching is applied to each step on its own. an effect like that needs a process of your own, or a correction applied to the recorded deposits.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: So here is the whole of it.
reels.words: so here is the whole of it. a geant four application is three objects that you derive, register and leave for the kernel to call. geometry and physics are data it is given once, which become the navigator and the process lists. the primary generator is code it runs at the start of every event, and it feeds the stack. the stack is last in, first out, and a track is followed to its end unless a process such as scintillation suspends it. on every step, every process of the particle is asked for a distance. the shortest wins, the continuous processes act along the step, the winner acts at its end, and then your stepping action is called. a discrete process spends one random draw of mean free paths across steps and across volumes. transportation gets its distance from the navigator, and leaves a flag on the step when the geometry cut it short. the optical boundary process is forced, so it runs after every step, and it reads that flag. you record by reading the step, its two points, its time and its copy number, into objects you own. and tracks never interact. two gammas in one event share a clock and nothing else, so pile up and dead time are yours to model afterwards.

title: Geant4: how a simulation is built

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: Here is one event in a detector you already know.
reels.words: here is one event in a detector you already know. a gamma ray of five hundred and eleven k e v enters a slab of l s o, fifty millimetres wide and ten thick. it is absorbed, the crystal flashes, and light spreads to an eight by eight array of silicon photomultipliers on the far face. what comes out is one row of sixty four counts. geant four made that row, by following every particle step by step and sampling what happens to it at random. each history is one random sample, and answers come from averaging many. how is such a simulation built, and what would you have to write to build your own?

reels.name: Toolkit
reels.cap: Geant four is not a program.
reels.words: geant four is not a program. there is no executable that you point at a detector. it is a toolkit, and its core is a kernel that knows how to move particles through matter, and knows nothing about your experiment. you write a small application around it. but your code does not call geant four in a loop. you hand the kernel a few objects, and the kernel calls them, whenever it reaches a question only you can answer. what is the world made of? which physics applies? what starts an event? that reversal is the idea to hold on to. the kernel owns the loop, and your code is the set of answers.

reels.name: Loops
reels.cap: Watch the kernel work and you see four nested loops.
reels.words: watch the kernel work and you see four nested loops. start at the smallest. a step is one straight segment of a particle's path, from a pre-step point to a post-step point. a track is one particle, followed step after step. when the gamma scatters off an electron, it is still the same track afterwards, and the recoil electron is a new one. an event is everything that follows from one primary particle, so the gamma, its electrons and every scintillation photon belong to one event, and events never interact. a run is many events with the same detector and the same physics, here one hundred thousand of them. run, event, track, step. every hook, every output and every question about speed belongs to one of these levels.

reels.name: Stack
reels.cap: Inside one event, the tracks are not followed side by side.
reels.words: inside one event, the tracks are not followed side by side. the kernel keeps a stack. it starts with the primary gamma. the kernel takes the top particle and tracks it all the way to its end, and any secondary made along the way is pushed onto the stack. then it pops the next one. the electron is next, but scintillation is an exception. after a step that makes light, the electron is paused and put back on the stack, with that step's photons on top of it, so they are followed first, one at a time. only when they are gone does the electron take its next step and make the next batch. step by step, that comes to about twelve thousand eight hundred photons, which is why they dominate the run time. when the stack is empty, the event is over. a stacking action of your own can also kill or delay a new track before any time is spent on it.

reels.name: Provide
reels.cap: So what do you have to write?
reels.words: so what do you have to write? the kernel insists on three things, and you hand each one to its run manager. the first is a detector construction, which answers what the world is made of and where everything sits. each volume is a shape, then a shape with a material, then a placement. the slab's sensor tile is defined once and placed sixty four times, and the copy number becomes the channel. the kernel asks for all of this once, before the run. after that, every step asks the finished tree which volume it is in, and how far away the next boundary is. the second is a physics list, which says which particles exist and which processes act on each one. you almost never build it from scratch. the slab registers two ready-made blocks, one for electromagnetic physics and one for optical, because at this energy nothing hadronic happens. it is read once as well, and then every step asks each of a particle's processes how far it will go. the third sets up your actions, and one of them is mandatory. the primary generator is different in kind, because it is code the kernel runs again at the start of every event, here a particle gun firing one gamma at the crystal face. so two of the three are descriptions the kernel reads once, and the third is code it keeps calling.

reels.name: Hooks
reels.cap: The other actions are optional, and they are how anything gets out, because Geant four records nothing by default.
reels.words: the other actions are optional, and they are how anything gets out, because geant four records nothing by default. each one hangs on a level of the nested loops. a run action is called when a run begins and when it ends, which is where files are opened and written. an event action brackets every event, a tracking action every track, and a stepping action is called after every single step. a stepping action sees everything, the particle, the volume, the energy deposited, and it can count, record or kill. the slab uses just these, a run action, an event action and a stepping action, and its whole measurement is made of them.

reels.name: Race
reels.cap: Now the heart of the kernel, which is how one step is decided.
reels.words: now the heart of the kernel, which is how one step is decided. take an optical photon somewhere in the crystal. the kernel asks each of its processes the same question. how far can this particle go before you act? rayleigh scattering samples a distance from its mean free path and proposes four point seven millimetres. absorption proposes about fifty metres. transportation is a process too, and it answers with the distance to the next boundary, three point one millimetres. the shortest proposal wins, and that is the step. transportation moves the photon that far, and the winner acts at the end point, here on the crystal face, where the photon reflects or refracts. then your stepping action is called, and if the track is still alive the race is run again.

reels.name: Sample
reels.cap: Where does a proposal come from?
reels.words: where does a proposal come from? a discrete process has a mean free path in each material, and distances between interactions follow an exponential. so the kernel draws one random number and turns it into a distance. a short mean free path means short proposals, and that process wins often. the losers of a race are not forgotten. their distances are simply shortened by the step just taken, which for an exponential is the same as sampling afresh.

reels.name: Gamma
reels.cap: Put the pieces together and follow one event in the slab.
reels.words: put the pieces together and follow one event in the slab. the event action clears its counts. the gun places one gamma just outside the entrance face and pushes it onto the stack. on each step the gamma's processes race. photoelectric absorption, compton scattering and the rest sample their distances, and transportation offers the next boundary. the gamma crosses the wrap, enters the crystal, and after a few millimetres photoelectric absorption wins. the gamma is gone and a photoelectron takes its place on the stack. for the electron, ionisation is a continuous process. it drains energy along the whole step and keeps the steps down to tens of micrometres, so the electron stops within a few tenths of a millimetre, and every one of those steps deposits energy.

reels.name: Light
reels.cap: Every step that deposits energy makes light.
reels.words: every step that deposits energy makes light. the scintillation process samples a number of photons, twenty five thousand for each m e v in l s o, so about twelve thousand eight hundred in this event, sent in all directions and spread over the forty nanosecond decay. each step's photons go onto the stack above the paused electron, and are followed before it steps again. then each photon is tracked in turn. rayleigh scattering turns it in the bulk. at a polished face it reflects totally beyond the critical angle, and otherwise it refracts out, into the black wrap where it dies, or through the grease toward the sensors. a photon whose step begins on the boundary of a sensor tile has just entered it. the stepping action adds one count to that tile's channel and kills the photon. thousands of photons later, the stack is empty.

reels.name: Row
reels.cap: When the stack is empty the event ends, and the event action stores one row, with sixty four channel counts and the true position of the interaction.
reels.words: when the stack is empty the event ends, and the event action stores one row, with sixty four channel counts and the true position of the interaction. events run on parallel worker threads. each worker has its own event, its own stack and its own copy of your actions, while the geometry and the physics tables are built once and shared. so events finish out of order. after one hundred thousand of them, the run action sorts the rows by event number and writes them to disk. that table is the simulation's whole output, and you chose every column of it.

reels.name: Recap
reels.cap: So here is the whole of it.
reels.words: so here is the whole of it. geant four is a toolkit whose kernel owns the loop, and your application is the set of answers it calls for. the kernel runs four nested loops, run, event, track and step, and inside an event it works through a stack, one particle at a time. you provide three things, a detector, a physics list and your actions, with a primary generator to start each event. every step is a race between processes, in which the shortest proposed distance wins and the winner acts. nothing is recorded unless your actions record it. one gamma in the slab became an electron, thousands of photons, and one row of sixty four counts. every geant four project follows this pattern, and only the geometry, the physics, the primaries and the observable change. if you have used gate, you have already run one. its volumes, sources, actors and physics list are these same four pieces, written for you.

title: Axial localization and tracking of self-interference nanoparticles by lateral point…

reels.name: Open
reels.cap: In twenty twenty-one, Liu and colleagues published this paper in Nature Communications.
reels.words: in twenty twenty-one, liu and colleagues published this paper in nature communications. it reads how high a nanoparticle sits above a mirror from the shape of its image. here are single nanoparticles lying on plain glass, seen through an ordinary microscope. each one is a bright spot. the same kind of particle, held one hundred and fifty-four point nine nanometres above a mirror, shows up as a ring. what the ring looks like depends on that distance, and the paper reads the distance back to within two point eight nanometres, from a single camera frame.

reels.name: Blob
reels.cap: A microscope cannot draw a point.
reels.words: a microscope cannot draw a point. light from one tiny emitter spreads through the lens and lands on the camera as a blurred spot hundreds of nanometres wide, however small the emitter is. that spot is called the point spread function. slide the emitter sideways and the spot slides with it, so its centre can be found far more finely than its width. raise the emitter by a few tens of nanometres, though, and the spot hardly changes, so height is the hard direction. pet physicists know one way out from monolithic crystals, where the width of the light spread tells the depth of interaction. this paper gets its change of shape from a mirror.

reels.name: Crystal
reels.cap: The emitter used here is an upconversion nanoparticle, a crystal thirty-three nanometres across that holds more than ten thousand lanthanide ions.
reels.words: the emitter used here is an upconversion nanoparticle, a crystal thirty-three nanometres across that holds more than ten thousand lanthanide ions. near-infrared laser light at nine hundred and eighty nanometres is absorbed by ytterbium ions. they hand the energy on to thulium ions, and a thulium ion that has collected several of those packets emits one blue photon near four hundred and fifty-five nanometres. three properties matter for what follows. each emission line is narrow. the hundreds of emitters point in random directions and radiate independently. and the crystal is far smaller than the wavelength, so all of its emitters sit at nearly the same height.

reels.name: Mirror
reels.cap: Now stand the particle on a thin layer of glass over a silver mirror.
