reels.words: now stand the particle on a thin layer of glass over a silver mirror. each emitter sends light up towards the camera and down towards the mirror, and the downward light bounces back up beside the direct light. the emitter is interfering with its own reflection. the reflected wave has travelled twice the spacing further, so it lags by a phase set by the spacing, plus a fixed shift from the reflection and a small one from the tight focus, called the gwee phase. at seventy-one point six nanometres the paper puts the total at one point nine pi, and the two waves add. at one hundred and fifty-four point nine nanometres it is three point one pi, and straight up they cancel.

reels.name: Dipoles
reels.cap: Which directions cancel depends on how an emitter points, so the authors simulate it.
reels.words: which directions cancel depends on how an emitter points, so the authors simulate it. they replace the crystal's random emitters by three dipoles at one point, along x, y and z. each one faces its own mirror image. a finite element code solves maxwell's equations for each, and the three intensities are added with equal weight, because independent emitters do not interfere with one another. at the cancelling spacing, the two horizontal dipoles go dark along the axis above the particle. the vertical dipole never radiates along that axis, so the mirror has nothing to cancel there. summed, the light forms a hollow shell, and a slice across it is a ring.

reels.name: Shapes
reels.cap: Here is what the camera records.
reels.words: here is what the camera records. the spacing is set by the thickness of the glass layer, and these are real images at six spacings. at seventy-one point six nanometres each particle is a spot. by one hundred and thirty-three point six it has opened into a ring, and at one hundred and fifty-four point nine the ring is at its clearest. at two hundred and fourteen point seven it has closed to a spot again, because the phase has gone round once more. at three hundred and twenty-seven it is a wide ring, and by four hundred and eighty-four it is a spot inside a ring, like an archery target. the simulation gives the same sequence. spacing has been written into shape.

reels.name: Features
reels.cap: To turn a shape into a number, cut a line through the image and plot the brightness along it.
reels.words: to turn a shape into a number, cut a line through the image and plot the brightness along it. a ring gives two humps with a dip between them. the paper measures four things on that profile. the first is the full width at half maximum of the whole pattern. the second is the width of the inner dip. the third is the area under the curve, and the fourth is the depth of the dip as a fraction of the peak. measured at many known spacings, each of the four traces out a calibration curve. where a curve is steep, a small change in height makes a large change in the feature, and the paper estimates better than five nanometres over three ranges of spacing.

reels.name: Stairs
reels.cap: The test is a staircase.
reels.words: the test is a staircase. three steps of glass were laid on the mirror, and an atomic force microscope, which feels a surface with a sharp tip, measured their heights. adding the particle's radius puts the particles at one hundred and four point seven, one hundred and twenty-one point nine and one hundred and thirty-one point nine nanometres above the mirror. one camera frame of twenty milliseconds then gives every particle's shape, and the calibration turns the shapes into one hundred and three point seven, one hundred and twenty-four point seven and one hundred and thirty point eight nanometres. the largest disagreement is two point eight nanometres. a single feature can miss by more. the dip depth alone puts the middle step at one hundred and twenty-nine point six.

reels.name: Track
reels.cap: Because one frame is enough, a moving particle can be followed.
reels.words: because one frame is enough, a moving particle can be followed. the authors let a particle wander in glycerol above the mirror and filmed it for thirteen seconds at ten frames a second. in every frame, the centre of the pattern gives the position sideways and its shape gives the height. this is the measured track in three dimensions. its mean square displacement grows in step with the time lag, as free diffusion should. the fitted diffusion coefficient gives a viscosity of three hundred and forty-seven point seven centipoise, which matches the glycerol. the authors also swept the focus through two hundred nanometres while recording. the pattern keeps its shape, so the height survives a drifting focus.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: So here is the whole paper in one picture.
reels.words: so here is the whole paper in one picture. a microscope reads the height of a tiny emitter badly, because when it rises, its blurred image hardly changes. the authors take an upconversion nanoparticle and stand it over a silver mirror, so that its light interferes with its own reflection. now, as the particle rises, the phase goes round, and its image opens from a spot into a ring and closes again. four features of that shape, calibrated against known heights, turn one camera frame into a height. on a glass staircase the answer agreed with an atomic force microscope to two point eight nanometres, and the same reading followed a particle drifting through glycerol in three dimensions. the method works between about thirty and five hundred nanometres above the mirror, it needs that mirror under the sample, and how the four features are combined is in a supplement this video has not seen.

title: Geant4: a Game Changer in High Energy Physics and Related Applicative Fields

reels.name: Open
reels.cap: This is a preprint from twenty twenty-four by Tullio Basaglia and colleagues.
reels.doc: Page one, then the thing the paper is about: one particle showering through a layered detector, and the paper's own two renderings of where the same code ended up.
reels.words: this is a preprint from twenty twenty-four by tullio basaglia and colleagues. it looks back on twenty-five years of geant four, the toolkit that simulates particles passing through matter. the same code follows radiation out of a therapy source a few centimetres across, and through a model of the international space station. the paper asks why software built for collider detectors is used so far from them. its answer is design decisions taken in nineteen ninety-four.

reels.name: Cited
reels.cap: The first evidence is a count of citations.
reels.doc: The paper's own chart, then the same paper at the top of five piles of papers.
reels.words: the first evidence is a count of citations. among eleven monte carlo transport codes, the bar for geant four towers over the rest. its reference paper has collected more than sixteen thousand citations. it is the most cited publication in five web of science categories, from particle physics and nuclear physics to nuclear technology, instrumentation and astronomy. together those categories hold more than two million papers.

reels.name: Spread
reels.cap: The citations also spread.
reels.doc: Fig. 7: how many research areas cite Geant4; then Fig. 8: how evenly, against two other works.
reels.words: the citations also spread. in two thousand and three, the papers citing geant four came from a handful of research areas. twenty years later they come from more than thirty. the authors also borrow a diversity index from ecology. on that index, the citations of geant four are far more varied than those of the higgs boson discovery paper, or of pythia, an event generator from the same field. so how did detector software end up everywhere?

reels.name: Toolkit
reels.cap: Start with what a user actually does.
reels.doc: One application: the kernel with three sockets, the classes the user plugs in, and the levels they can watch.
reels.words: start with what a user actually does. geant four cannot be run. it is a toolkit, and the user writes an application around its kernel. the application creates a run manager, and hands it three things. one class describes the geometry and materials. one selects the physics processes. one generates the primary particles. optional action classes let the user look in at every run, event, track and step. gate is an application tool built on geant four in this way, and its own reference paper has more than sixteen hundred citations.

reels.name: Fortran
reels.cap: The reason for that shape is the code Geant four replaced.
reels.doc: GEANT 3 as a wall of Fortran subroutines, what tangled it, and where its physics was weak.
reels.words: the reason for that shape is the code geant four replaced. the old geant three was written in fortran. its last version, from early nineteen ninety-four, ran to about sixty-three thousand lines. its procedures were tangled together. to add one new geometrical shape, nearly sixty subroutines had to be modified. its hadronic physics came from external packages that cern did not control. and its electromagnetic models were weakest below ten kilo electron volts and above one hundred giga electron volts.

reels.name: Blind
reels.cap: Geant four turned that inside out.
reels.doc: Tracking talks to every process through one socket; any card with the right tab fits.
reels.words: geant four turned that inside out. its tracking code handles every physics process blindly, through one abstract base class. tracking never learns which process it is talking to. ionisation and bremsstrahlung present the same interface, and so does a process written years later by a user. a new process plugs in, and tracking is left unchanged. the authors call this the key to extending the physics. the energy range grew with it, from about one hundred electron volts up to the peta electron volt scale.

reels.name: Layers
reels.cap: The whole toolkit is organised the same way, as packages that depend only on the ones beneath them.
reels.doc: Fig. 3 redrawn as seven rows of packages, each depending only on the rows below it.
reels.words: the whole toolkit is organised the same way, as packages that depend only on the ones beneath them. at the bottom sit units, constants and random numbers, then materials, geometry and particles. above them come tracks, processes and tracking. events and runs control the simulation, and visualisation and storage attach at the top through abstract interfaces. this architecture has not changed in twenty-five years. meanwhile the code grew from two hundred and eighty-three thousand lines to more than eight hundred and seventy-two thousand.

reels.name: Voxels
reels.cap: In the nineteen nineties, many physicists believed C plus plus was too slow for this work.
reels.doc: One geometry of twelve volumes: a benchmark of two lanes, then the question tracking asks at each step.
reels.words: in the nineteen nineties, many physicists believed c plus plus was too slow for this work. early benchmarks showed geant four running faster than geant three point two one. one reason is in the geometry. at every step, tracking must find which volume the particle meets next. testing every volume is wasteful. geant four slices space into smart voxels, each listing only the volumes inside it. tracking then tests a few candidates instead of all of them.

reels.name: Cuts
reels.cap: A second reason is how Geant four decides which secondary electrons to create.
reels.doc: One volume with a thin sensitive layer behind it and a charged track crossing: which secondaries to make.
reels.words: a second reason is how geant four decides which secondary electrons to create. other codes use an energy cut. geant four sets its threshold as a range, a distance. a secondary electron whose range is longer than the threshold is produced and tracked, because it could cross a boundary and be seen in the next volume. one with a shorter range would stop close by, so it is never created. its energy is deposited on the spot. that saves time without giving up accuracy where it matters.

reels.name: Threads
reels.cap: A third reason came later.
reels.doc: A queue of independent events dealt out to four threads that share one copy of the geometry and tables.
reels.words: a third reason came later. in geant four, every event is independent of every other, and that was designed in from the start. so when multi-core processors arrived, version ten in twenty thirteen gave each thread its own events to simulate. the geometry and the physics tables never change during a run, so all the threads share one copy.

reels.name: Language
reels.cap: Two decisions looked risky at the time.
reels.doc: Two decisions that looked risky in 1994: a language nobody in the field used, and an open source.
reels.words: two decisions looked risky at the time. in nineteen ninety-four, particle physics ran on fortran. eighty percent of cern's program library was written in it. the team chose c plus plus anyway, because industry used it, tools existed for it, and it was expected to last. the second decision was to open the source. a simulation shapes the result of an experiment, so others must be able to read the code. that is still not universal. fluka is not publicly distributed, and m c n p is under export control.

reels.name: Team
reels.cap: The project itself was called R D forty-four, and it was built differently too.
reels.doc: RD44: many institutes writing to one repository, held together by version control, tests and a daily release.
reels.words: the project itself was called r d forty-four, and it was built differently too. earlier transport codes came from small teams at one laboratory. r d forty-four spread its physicists, computer scientists and engineers across institutes worldwide. to hold that together it used version control, incremental testing, and a release cycle of twenty-four hours, which was almost unknown in physics software. approved in november nineteen ninety-four, it delivered the first release on the fifteenth of december nineteen ninety-eight, on time.

reels.name: Telescope
reels.cap: Here is what that flexibility bought.
reels.doc: An X-ray telescope in cross-section: the rays it was built for, then the protons nobody built it for.
reels.words: here is what that flexibility bought. in nineteen ninety-nine nasa launched the chandra x-ray telescope, and soon after launch its detectors degraded. the european telescope x m m was about to follow. a geant four simulation of x m m found the cause. protons of about one hundred kilo electron volts were scattering along the mirror shells, and the mirrors were funnelling them onto the detectors. the european space agency took countermeasures before launch, and x m m kept its designed performance in orbit.

reels.name: Pyramid
reels.cap: The same toolkit reached archaeology.
reels.doc: Khufu's pyramid in cross-section: muons from the sky, a detector under the stone, a prediction and a surprise.
reels.words: the same toolkit reached archaeology. cosmic muons pass through khufu's pyramid at giza, and the stone absorbs some of them. a geant four simulation predicted how many muons should arrive from each direction. detectors measured more than expected from one direction. less stone was in the way. that excess revealed a large void above the grand gallery.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: So the paper's case is this.
reels.doc: The kernel again, and the four decisions made on it; then what industry did with it, and what is next.
reels.words: so the paper's case is this. geant four lasted because its source is open, because its objects let users extend it, because its language endured, and because its team was broad. industry noticed as well, with more than two hundred united states patents and more than six hundred european ones. the work is not finished. the high luminosity l h c is planned for twenty thirty to twenty forty-one, and it needs more throughput, so parts of the kernel are being ported to graphics processors.

title: A Path to Verifiable Recovery for Non-Invasive Brain-Computer Interfaces Using…

reels.name: Unreliable
reels.cap: Page five shows the problem is real.
reels.doc: Page 5: how rarely evaluation is clean, a 99.8 that was 53, and the dials behind any one published number.
reels.words: page five shows the problem is real. one review of clinical deep learning found seventeen of sixty-three papers clearly kept training and test data apart. one of those studies reported ninety-nine point eight percent accuracy. re-run with the subjects split properly, it scored fifty-three. labs differ in how many electrodes they use, where they put them, how fast they sample, and how long a window they call the task. turn any one of those dials and the number at the end moves.

reels.name: Modes
reels.cap: The idea starts on page eleven.
reels.doc: Pages 11 and 12: the head as a sphere, the patterns that describe it, and the sixteen the report keeps.
reels.words: the idea starts on page eleven. a head is roughly a sphere, and there is a standard set of patterns for anything painted on a sphere. they are the spherical harmonics. page twelve draws seven of them. they are ordered by how finely they cut the sphere up. the first has no dividing line at all. the next few split it into halves and quarters, and further along the patches shrink. the report keeps only the patterns up to a degree it calls l. stopping at degree three leaves sixteen, and those sixteen are the vocabulary.

reels.name: Fit
reels.cap: Page thirteen puts the electrodes onto that sphere.
reels.doc: Page 13: the electrodes sit on the sphere, each one reads the sixteen patterns, and the sixteen weights rebuild the field.
reels.words: page thirteen puts the electrodes onto that sphere. each one sits at its own angle on the head, so it picks one value out of each of the sixteen patterns. one number is computed per electrode from a one-second window, and those twenty-two numbers are the field to match. finding the sixteen weights that add up closest to it is a small least squares problem. the smooth colour is the rebuild, and the rings are the electrodes carrying their own values on top. the weights multiply back out into electrode space, so every window is compressed and recovered by arithmetic alone.

reels.name: Sources
reels.cap: Pages eighteen and nineteen pick the sources.
reels.doc: Page 18: four public datasets, four electrode caps, and the degree each pair of them can afford.
reels.words: pages eighteen and nineteen pick the sources. four public datasets, two of people imagining movement, two of people imagining speech. they agree on nothing. the smallest cap carries nineteen electrodes and the largest a hundred and twenty-eight. they sample from two hundred up to one thousand and twenty-four times a second. a basis needs at least as many electrodes as patterns, so the motor pair is held to degree three and sixteen weights, and the speech pair gets degree nine and a hundred.

reels.name: Ladder
reels.cap: Page twenty-four does something unusual with the labels.
reels.doc: Page 24: the targets, ordered from the vague state of the person down to the thirty-nine concepts.
reels.words: page twenty-four does something unusual with the labels. instead of one target per dataset, the same recordings are labelled at several levels of specificity. at the top is only the state of the person. idle, engaged, or doing the task. below that, whether the task was done out loud or only imagined. below that, which part of the body moved. then which side. then which of five fingers. at the bottom, which of thirty-nine concepts a sentence carried. each step down is a harder claim about the same second of recording.

reels.name: Separation
reels.cap: Page twenty-seven says how an answer is scored, and it is not accuracy.
reels.doc: Page 27: separation drawn as the gap between the mean probability on true and on false labels, and chance.
reels.words: page twenty-seven says how an answer is scored, and it is not accuracy. a decoder gives every label a probability. average that probability where the label was true, average it again where the label was false, and the score is the gap between them. it is called separation, and an output ignoring its input scores zero at any class balance. it still needs something to beat. the labels are shuffled a hundred times over, and the best score the shuffling reaches is chance.

reels.name: Fidelity
reels.cap: Page thirty-five holds the first result, and it is about the input.
reels.doc: Page 35: the first result, the input's unexplained variance on test subjects against the shuffled control.
reels.words: page thirty-five holds the first result, and it is about the input. this table is the unexplained variance of every source. for the motor dataset it is three point eight five percent on test subjects. with the values shuffled between electrodes, they leave thirty-four point three percent unexplained. that gap is the claim. the basis is reading real spatial structure, and it holds on subjects it was never fitted to. it does not say that the structure has anything to do with what the person was thinking.

reels.name: Confounds
reels.cap: Pages thirty-eight and thirty-nine take most of that back.
reels.doc: Pages 38 and 39: a trial's own clock scores as well as the decoder, and a session layout the target could read.
reels.words: pages thirty-eight and thirty-nine take most of that back. a trial's events always run in the same order, so where a window ends is a clue. so the report scores a predictor that sees only the timing. on one speech decoder the clock alone scores zero point three against the decoder's zero point one one. on the other, zero point three five against zero point one two. page thirty-nine finds a second one. a body-part target looked like it read the body, but its sessions came in two kinds, and inside one kind its score drops from zero point four two to zero point one three. it was telling sessions apart.

reels.name: Subjects
reels.cap: Page forty-two asks what survives a new person.
reels.doc: Pages 42 and 43: each target as a pair of bars, held-out sessions against new people, then the confidence dial.
reels.words: page forty-two asks what survives a new person. the movement decoders hold, barely moving from held-out sessions to new subjects. the speech decoders do not. one target falls from zero point five five to zero point two five, and another from zero point five nine to zero point one eight. they had learned the people. page forty-three asks whether the system noticed. every target carries a small network that reports its own confidence. on the subject it does worst on, that confidence reads zero point nine, which is what it reads on the ones it does best on.

reels.name: Map
reels.cap: Page forty-six is the conclusion, and it is careful.
reels.doc: Page 46, then the report as a grid of its pages, and the chain from the opening handed back changed.
reels.words: page forty-six is the conclusion, and it is careful. a path, it says, not an arrival. here is the whole report as a map. the problem is laid out in the first chapter, the basis is built through chapter two, the datasets and the targets come next, the results run from page thirty-five, and a summary of every target closes on page forty-four. it delivers a pipeline where the input is accountable before the output. every window's compression loss is known, and the confounded targets are marked rather than quietly reported. the recovery is weak, and this report says so.

title: Why Monte Carlo simulation still sits outside PET and SPECT image reconstruction, and…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper is a roadmap, not a result.
reels.doc: Page one, then the thing the paper is about: a ring of detectors round a patient, the counts it collects, and the two rules -- one analytic, one simulated -- that try to predict them.
reels.words: this paper is a roadmap, not a result. seventeen authors ask one question. why is monte carlo simulation still outside image reconstruction in p e t and s p e c t, and what would it take to bring it inside. a scan is a counting experiment. a tracer decays inside the patient, photons leave the body, and a ring of detectors counts them. reconstruction asks which picture of the tracer would have produced those counts. to answer that it needs a forward model, a rule that turns a picture into expected counts. today that rule is analytic. it describes emission, transport and detection with deliberate simplifications. monte carlo is the most complete rule we have. it follows one photon at a time, through the patient and into the crystal, with almost no approximations. and it sits outside the loop, as a reference the loop never sees.

reels.name: Loop
reels.cap: Inside a reconstruction the picture is improved over and over.
reels.doc: One pass of a reconstruction, on the cycle of figure 2.2: the estimate goes forward into expected counts, the measured counts come alongside, and the mismatch is carried back into the image.
reels.words: inside a reconstruction the picture is improved over and over. each pass projects the current estimate forward into expected counts, compares those with the measured counts, and carries the mismatch back into the image. the comparison is a ratio, measured over expected. the step back is the adjoint, which spreads that ratio along every line it could have come from. together they give the gradient, the direction the picture moves. so the loop asks the forward model for two things, and neither of them is a picture of a scan. it asks for the expectation of the counts in each bin that recorded something, and for a way back from the detector into the image.

reels.name: Mismatch
reels.cap: Monte Carlo offers neither directly.
reels.words: monte carlo offers neither directly. one run is a realisation, a single noisy draw of what the scanner might have recorded, and the loop needs the average of every draw it could have made. averaging more runs brings the noise down, but only as the square root of the number of photons simulated, while the cost grows in proportion. four times the precision costs sixteen times the work. and the noise does not simply average away, because the simulated counts sit underneath the measured ones. a fluctuation downward matters more than the matching fluctuation up, so what comes back is biased, and the emptier the bin the worse it gets. time of flight and long scanners spread the same counts over far more bins. exactly where the field is going, the bins are emptiest and this bias is largest.

reels.name: Faster
reels.cap: Speed is the part that has been solved.
reels.words: speed is the part that has been solved. a three minute bed position at a normal injected dose means tracking about forty five billion decays, which is days of computing. graphics cards cut that by seventy to a hundred times. forced detection aims every photon straight at the detector and carries the probability of that flight as a weight, instead of waiting for the rare one that would arrive on its own. replacing the collimator and the crystal with a learned response table saves twenty to a hundred and eighty times more, and a generative model that skips the tracking altogether saves more than a hundred. that was the easy part. the roadmap is blunt about it. faster simulators are necessary and they are not sufficient.

reels.name: Scatter
reels.cap: So where does more faithful physics actually pay.
reels.words: so where does more faithful physics actually pay. the first answer is scatter. a photon that scatters in the patient arrives with less energy and from the wrong direction, and the line it is assigned to is wrong. analytic models follow a photon that scatters once and approximate everything after that. monte carlo follows every order at no extra cost, because it never evaluates the series. it samples it. in s p e c t that difference reaches the patient. monte carlo based reconstruction raised striatal uptake ratios by up to twenty five percent, lifted lesion detection in liver imaging from thirty one to fifty percent, and improved contrast recovery in yttrium ninety imaging by up to forty two percent.

reels.name: Range
reels.cap: The second answer is positron range.
reels.words: the second answer is positron range. a positron does not annihilate where it was emitted. it scatters away first, and the two photons mark the end of that walk rather than the start. how far it walks depends on the isotope. in water, fluorine eighteen blurs the image by a tenth of a millimetre at half maximum, oxygen fifteen by half a millimetre, and both have tails five to ten times wider than their peaks. it also depends on the tissue. the same tracer spreads further in lung than in muscle, and activity shines through into the airways. a blur that is fixed across the image cannot do that. a simulation that walks the positron through the real density can.

reels.name: Signal
reels.cap: The third use turns the first one around.
reels.words: the third use turns the first one around. scattered photons are subtracted as a nuisance. but what a photon scattered off is the attenuation, so those events carry information about it. when the attenuation map is wrong, and from a magnetic resonance scan or a truncated c t it often is, the error spreads into the activity everywhere. estimating both at once from the emission data alone leaves an ambiguity, which time of flight very nearly removes. very nearly. the roadmap argues the scattered events could close what is left, if the scatter model is right in absolute terms and its gradient with respect to attenuation is available. that asks for a simulator you can differentiate.

reels.name: Inside
reels.cap: Now the hard part.
reels.words: now the hard part. putting the simulation inside the loop means the forward model is different every iteration, because every iteration draws new photons. reconstruction becomes a stochastic problem. what comes back is the true direction, plus a bias, plus a fluctuation. the fluctuation falls as one over the square root of the photon budget. the bias falls as one over the budget. convergence needs both held down. which suggests spending little early, while the picture is rough and a rough direction will do, and more as it settles. then there is the way back. simulators are built to run photons forwards. running them backwards means starting at the detector pair, launching two photons inward, with time running in reverse and energy climbing at every scatter. almost nobody does this. the back step is done analytically instead, and that mismatch is a bias no photon budget can remove.

reels.name: Hardware
reels.cap: All of this has to run on real machines.
reels.words: all of this has to run on real machines. the number of detector pixels in a p e t scanner has doubled every five years. the system matrix has doubled every eighteen months. arithmetic has kept pace. memory has not. peak compute has doubled every one point three years, memory bandwidth every three. and monte carlo is memory bound. a photon's path is random, so each step reaches into a different corner of memory, the cache misses, and the processor waits. the projection is ten to fifty times per node over the next decade, and most of that comes from moving the arithmetic into the memory rather than from making the processor faster.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: So where does that leave the four questions the roadmap opened with.
reels.words: so where does that leave the four questions the roadmap opened with. how much of the physics should be simulated. use simulation where the analytic models fail and keep them where they work. almost every practical answer will be a hybrid. how precise does it have to be. not uniformly precise. little early, more near the end, and stricter than the measured noise would suggest wherever the bins are sparse. is scatter a nuisance or a signal. a nuisance when only the activity is wanted, a signal when the attenuation is. within reach already are monte carlo system models in s p e c t, scatter estimates that are right in absolute terms, and using simulation to check the fast analytic models everything else relies on. further off are stochastic reconstruction with controlled noise, a real adjoint, and simulating a whole acquisition inside the loop. faster simulators are necessary. the roadmap's point is that the algorithms have to be built for them at the same time.

title: COMET, a transformer that predicts the efficacy of a whole lipid nanoparticle recipe

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This paper is in Nature Nanotechnology, from Alvin Chan and colleagues at M I T.
reels.words: this paper is in nature nanotechnology, from alvin chan and colleagues at m i t. its abstract promises a way to design lipid nanoparticles with a neural network. a lipid nanoparticle is the fatty bubble that carries messenger r n a through the body. when it reaches a cell and unloads, the cell reads the message and makes the protein. how well that works depends on which fatty molecules are in the bubble and how much of each. finding a good mixture normally means making them in the lab, one at a time. instead, a transformer called comet learns from three thousand measured recipes. it then scores fifty million it has never seen, and the ones it likes best get made.

reels.name: Recipe
reels.cap: Four classes of lipid go into the shell.
reels.words: four classes of lipid go into the shell. an ionizable lipid, which grabs the r n a. a sterol, which stiffens the wall. a helper lipid, and a p e g lipid that keeps particles apart. picking one molecule from each class gives eighty four combinations. but a recipe also fixes how much of each goes in, as a percentage of all the lipid. and two more knobs sit outside the lipids. how much nitrogen in the lipid there is per phosphate in the r n a, and the ratio of the water phase to the alcohol phase when the two are mixed. earlier models scored the ionizable lipid on its own and ignored the rest. this paper asks a model to read the whole recipe at once.

reels.name: Lance
reels.cap: To train anything, they first had to measure.
reels.words: to train anything, they first had to measure. lipids dissolved in alcohol and messenger r n a in buffer are pushed together, and a particle forms as the two streams meet. each recipe gets its own well of cells. the r n a codes for a firefly enzyme, so a well that took the message glows. the brightness becomes a number between zero and one. the sweep runs in four parts. nine hundred and seventy five recipes vary which molecule fills each class. six hundred and thirty seven put two ionizable lipids in together. others turn the two mixing knobs, and four hundred and ninety two sweep the percentages. altogether three thousand and twenty eight distinct recipes were made and measured, each one in two different mouse cell lines. they call this dataset lance.

reels.name: Reads
reels.cap: Here is the whole first part at once.
reels.words: here is the whole first part at once. every square is one recipe, darker where more of the message got through. the stack of bars down the left side is each row's molar ratio. the block for the clinical lipid m c three is pale almost everywhere. the block for c k k e twelve is dark almost everywhere. so the ionizable lipid matters. but no single ratio of the four wins inside every block. putting two ionizable lipids in one particle is stranger still. a strong lipid can carry a weak partner, and the pair beats either one alone. and a recipe that works in one cell line need not work in the other. each dot here is one recipe, placed by how well it did in each. seven hundred and seventy two land high in both, while whole groups are good in one and poor in the other.

reels.name: Tokens
reels.cap: COMET has to read all of that.
reels.words: comet has to read all of that. take one lipid. a pretrained chemistry model reads its three dimensional structure and turns it into five hundred and twelve numbers. its molar percentage becomes a second short vector, and which of the four classes it is becomes a third. the three are joined into one token that stands for this lipid in this recipe. every lipid in the recipe gets a token the same way, and the two mixing knobs get tokens of their own. a recipe is now a short list of vectors, and a recipe with five lipids simply makes one more.

reels.name: Attention
reels.cap: The tokens go in as a list, with no order to them.
reels.words: the tokens go in as a list, with no order to them. one extra token is added that stands for no ingredient at all. its job is to look at every other token and gather them up. that gathering is repeated through a stack of attention blocks, so the ingredients are weighed against each other rather than scored apart. a small network then turns the summary token into one predicted efficacy. each cell line gets its own summary token and its own head, while the blocks in the middle are shared. so what the model learns about recipes from one cell line helps it in the other.

reels.name: Ranking
reels.cap: Training does not ask COMET for the brightness of a well.
reels.words: training does not ask comet for the brightness of a well. it shows the model two recipes at a time and asks only which of the two did better. a margin term adds the rest of what the measurement knows. when one recipe beat the other by a long way, the two predicted scores are pushed further apart than when it barely won. because the robot that mixes the lipids is not perfect, the percentages are jittered by a tenth of their value during training. where the two cell lines pull the weights in different directions, the updates are steered into a direction that suits both. and five separately trained models are averaged.

reels.name: Scores
reels.cap: Hold out a random fifth of the measured recipes, train on the rest, and ask COMET to put the held-out ones in order.
reels.words: hold out a random fifth of the measured recipes, train on the rest, and ask comet to put the held-out ones in order. its order agrees with the measured order at zero point eight seven three. a fairer test holds out the best tenth of all recipes, so the model has never seen a winner. agreement drops to zero point seven two five, and it still places four out of five of those unseen winners in the top half of its ranking. training on both cell lines at once lifts the harder test again. stripping the training pieces out one at a time separates two of them from the rest. averaging five models sits at the top, and training on one cell line alone sits well below everything else. the pieces in between are hard to tell apart. held out by chemistry instead, with three ionizable lipids and a sterol removed from training altogether, agreement is zero point seven seven six in the first cell line and only zero point five zero nine in the second.

reels.name: Learned
reels.cap: A model can score well by learning a shortcut, so the authors tried to break it.
reels.words: a model can score well by learning a shortcut, so the authors tried to break it. they scrambled which lipid sat in which slot of the training recipes. the more they scrambled, the further performance fell, with no cliff and no plateau. corrupting the mixing knobs as well pushed it lower again. a model leaning on a shortcut would not decay so smoothly. they also checked what the score tracks. it follows the particle's physical size only loosely, at zero point six five, but follows the measured delivery above zero point nine five. so comet is predicting the thing itself, not a stand-in for it.

reels.name: Screen
reels.cap: Now the model is pointed at recipes nobody has made.
reels.words: now the model is pointed at recipes nobody has made. the space is every lipid choice, crossed with every molar percentage, crossed with the mixing knobs. enumerated, it holds about fifty million recipes. recipes sitting close to a known winner are thrown out first, so what is left is genuinely new. comet then scores everything that remains. the top tenth of a percent is kept. recipes the five models disagree about are dropped, and from what survives a chemically spread-out handful is chosen to be made. a second search works the other way, staying close to a recipe that already works and nudging its percentages, then its molecules, then the ratio of lipid to r n a.

reels.name: Bench
reels.cap: Ten of the new recipes were made and put on cells.
reels.words: ten of the new recipes were made and put on cells. every one of them gave more light than the three lipid nanoparticles already approved for use in people. the other search, the one that stays near a recipe that already works, improved two of three parent recipes in the first cell line and all three of them in the second, which is the harder of the two. four of the picks were then given to mice, under the skin. each bright spot is a mouse making the protein from the delivered message. totalled over a day, the picks gave more than forty times the light of the older clinical lipid and more than five times the light of the one in the vaccines.

reels.name: Reach
reels.cap: Because a recipe is just a list of tokens, parts of it can be swapped out.
reels.words: because a recipe is just a list of tokens, parts of it can be swapped out. replace a lipid with a branched polymer and comet still ranks, after four hundred and fifty four of them. point it at a human gut cell line with two hundred and ninety five. change the cargo to a different message and ninety eight are enough. ask instead whether a recipe survives being freeze dried, and a hundred and sixty eight are enough for that. those small sets would be hopeless alone. trained on the freeze-drying data by itself, agreement is zero point four nine two. carrying lance alongside lifts it to zero point seven zero five, and averaging five models reaches zero point seven eight eight.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Laying ten thousand virtual recipes out by how the model represents them gives a map.
reels.words: laying ten thousand virtual recipes out by how the model represents them gives a map. high scoring recipes gather in their own regions, and the two cell lines put their good regions in different places. asking what the prediction leans on, which molecules are in the recipe dominates, with the nitrogen to phosphate ratio and the percentages behind it. two limits also fall out, that too much ionizable lipid and too little sterol both hurt. the caveats are real. against a random forest the gain is modest on a dataset this small, and when a parent recipe was already excellent, the model could not improve on it. cells are also a weak guide to a whole animal, so not every pick that shines in a well will shine in a mouse. still, the shape of the idea is the lasting part. write a formulation down as a list of its ingredients with their amounts, and a transformer can be asked to judge the mixture rather than its parts.

title: In vitro and in vivo evaluation of xenogeneic bone putty with the carrier of hydrogel…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from the journal Cell and Tissue Banking, published in twenty eighteen.
reels.doc: Page 1: which paper, who wrote it, and its question drawn as the thing it is about: a putty of bone grains held in a glue, here a glue made of bone too, tested on cells in a dish and in holes in rat skulls.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from the journal cell and tissue banking, published in twenty eighteen. its title asks how well a bone putty made from cow bone works, with a gel made from bone as its carrier. it is by naili zhang and colleagues at binzhou medical university in china. the abstract begins with bone putty, a classic bone graft. it is made of grains of bone held together by a sticky carrier. the carrier changes how well the putty heals, so the authors made the carrier out of bone as well. they tested it on bone forming cells in a dish, and in holes cut in the skulls of rats.

reels.name: Problem
reels.cap: The introduction starts with holes in bone too large to heal on their own.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: holes too big to heal, why a patient's own bone is limited, what demineralised bone matrix is (a grain with its mineral washed out, leaving fibres and growth factors), the two ways it helps bone grow, and why loose grains need a carrier.
reels.words: the introduction starts with holes in bone too large to heal on their own. bone grows in from the two ends, but cannot bridge the gap. the gold standard is to move bone from elsewhere in the same patient, but there is only so much of it, and the second wound can hurt, bleed or get infected. demineralised bone matrix is bone with its mineral washed out. here is a grain of bone, opened up, with its hard mineral crystals. acid dissolves the crystals, and leaves the soft collagen fibres with growth signals called bone morphogenetic proteins, or b m ps, still bound to them. it helps bone grow in two ways. the fibres are a scaffold that bone cells crawl along, and the b m ps tell nearby stem cells to turn into cells that make bone. loose grains are hard to use. put into a hole, they are washed out by blood and rinsing. so they are mixed with a sticky carrier into a putty that can be pressed into a hole of any shape. many carriers have been tried, from glycerol to hyaluronic acid to collagen, and the choice changes how much bone grows.

reels.name: Idea
reels.cap: The idea is a gel made from the bone matrix itself.
reels.doc: Pages 2 and 3: the gel made by dissolving the matrix itself, so grains and glue are both bone; why pepsin in the cold rather than strong acid and heat (the growth factors survive); why cow bone; and the plan of tests.
reels.words: the idea is a gel made from the bone matrix itself. its collagen is cut into pieces small enough to dissolve, and the liquid sets into a gel that still holds the growth factors. then both the grains and their glue are bone. older recipes dissolved the matrix with strong acid at forty to fifty degrees, which can wreck the growth factors. pepsin, a digestive enzyme, does it gently in the cold, and is easy to switch off and wash out afterwards. the bone came from cows rather than human donors, because donated human bone is in short supply, while cow bone is plentiful and built much like ours.

reels.name: Recipe
reels.cap: The methods start with four thigh bones from young cattle, frozen, cleaned of muscle, and smashed into grains.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: the gel recipe as one grain changing in place (sieved to 0.5 to 1 mm, fat out with lipase over 4 h, mineral out in acid over 48 h, digested by pepsin in the cold, spun, the pepsin switched off, freeze dried, sterilised), then Figure 1's three photographs of the digest, the gel and the dried sheet.
reels.words: the methods start with four thigh bones from young cattle, frozen, cleaned of muscle, and smashed into grains. grains half a millimetre to one millimetre across were sieved out. here is one of them, opened up. an enzyme that digests fat, lipase, took out the fat over four hours. hydrochloric acid then dissolved the mineral over forty eight hours. pepsin in weak acetic acid, kept cold, digested the grains until no pieces were left. spinning it for twenty minutes sent anything undissolved to the bottom, and the clear liquid on top was kept. a salt bath then switched the pepsin off. freeze drying left a white sheet, which was sterilised with twenty kilograys of gamma rays and stored in the freezer. figure one, on page four, shows the three stages. the cloudy digest, the gel after spinning, and the dried white sheet.

reels.name: Cells
reels.cap: First, how much B M P is in the gel.
reels.doc: Pages 3, 4 and 6: the B M P measured in the gel, three kinds of well (collagen, gel, B M P 2) seeded with cells that can become bone cells, A L P lighting up in them, then Figure 2: A L P at 3 and 7 days and the red calcium nodules at 14 days.
reels.words: first, how much b m p is in the gel. an antibody test found about three billionths of a gram in every gram of gel, two point nine five nanograms. next, mouse cells that can become bone making cells were grown in wells. some wells held collagen, which carries no signal, some held the gel, and some held pure b m p two, a strong signal, for comparison. at three and seven days they measured alkaline phosphatase, or a l p, an enzyme cells make early on as they turn into bone cells. the more cells that turn, the more a l p. figure two on page six has the results. at seven days the gel wells made far more a l p than collagen, but only about half as much as b m p two. after fourteen days, a red dye that stains calcium showed hard mineral nodules forming with the gel, and a large one with b m p two, but none with collagen.

reels.name: Putty
reels.cap: To make the putty, the dried gel was dissolved again, and one millilitre of it was mixed with four hundred and fifty milligrams of grains, each a quarter to half a millimetre across.
reels.doc: Pages 4 to 6: the putty recipe drawn as its ingredients (1 ml of gel, 450 mg of grains of 250 to 500 um), the collagen putty made the same way, the loosening test (a 1 cm ball in warm salt water, grains drifting off, the cloud's width measured), and Figure 3's photographs and widths.
reels.words: to make the putty, the dried gel was dissolved again, and one millilitre of it was mixed with four hundred and fifty milligrams of grains, each a quarter to half a millimetre across. a second putty used plain collagen gel instead, made the same way. to see whether it holds together, a ball one centimetre across was put in warm salt water. as it loosens, grains drift off, and the width of the spreading cloud was measured over a day. figure three shows the ball whole after half an hour, starting to fall apart at two hours, half of the balls broken up by eight hours, and only a third still whole at twelve hours. the cloud widened from one point three six centimetres at half an hour to three point two centimetres after a day. only the gel putty went through this test, so it does not tell us whether the collagen putty held together any better or worse.

reels.name: Rats
reels.cap: Twenty four rats were split into three groups.
reels.doc: Pages 4, 5 and 7: twenty four rats in three groups, a 6 mm square hole in each skull filled with gel putty, collagen putty or nothing; micro C T at 12 weeks; Figure 4's scans; then our three skulls whose holes fill with new bone, from the rim in the empty one and around the grains in the putties, to the paper's percentages.
reels.words: twenty four rats were split into three groups. each had a square hole six millimetres wide cut in the top of its skull, filled with the gel putty, the collagen putty, or left empty. a hole this big in a rat's skull does not heal by itself. after twelve weeks the skulls were scanned with micro c t, an x ray scanner for small samples that builds a three dimensional picture, and the new bone inside each hole was measured. figure four on page seven shows the scans. in the gel putty hole, new bone fills most of the hole. the collagen putty hole is patchier, with more open space between the pieces, and the empty one is still a hole. back on our three skulls, in the empty hole a little bone crept in from the rim, but the middle stayed open. with either putty, bone also formed in the middle, around the grains. the new bone came to twenty seven point three cubic millimetres with the gel putty, twenty point four with collagen putty, and twelve point six with nothing. as a share of the bone an uninjured skull has there, that is fifty eight, forty two and twenty eight percent, which is how much of each hole is filled here. the gel putty beat both the collagen putty and the empty hole, and both differences were statistically significant.

reels.name: Slices
reels.cap: The skulls were then softened in acid, cut into slices through the middle of the hole, each seen edge on, with old bone at both ends and the filled hole between, four micrometres thick, and stained.
reels.doc: Pages 5 and 8: where the slices come from (a cut through the middle of the hole, seen edge on: host bone at both ends, the filled gap between), what the two stains colour, then Figure 5 at low and high magnification.
reels.words: the skulls were then softened in acid, cut into slices through the middle of the hole, each seen edge on, with old bone at both ends and the filled hole between, four micrometres thick, and stained. the h and e stain colours tissue pink and purple. masson's trichrome colours mature bone red, and new bone that has not yet hardened blue. in figure five, the top row is the whole hole at low magnification. with the gel putty it is packed with grains and new bone, with the collagen putty there is less, and the empty hole is a thin strip of loose tissue. closer in, the grains, marked with hashes, are being reworked, with new bone growing around them. in the masson stain, the gel putty shows more red, mature bone, while the collagen putty shows more blue, bone that has not yet hardened. the empty hole holds only loose connective tissue.

reels.name: Trust
reels.cap: In the dish, the gel was a weaker signal than pure B M P two, though clearly stronger than collagen.
reels.doc: Pages 9 and 10: the gel a weaker signal than pure B M P 2 in the dish; the gap the authors name (no test in muscle, where bone does not grow on its own); and the limits of the design (twenty four rats, one time point).
reels.words: in the dish, the gel was a weaker signal than pure b m p two, though clearly stronger than collagen. the authors name one gap. they did not put the putty in muscle, where no bone grows, which is the standard test of whether a material makes bone all by itself. there are other limits they do not dwell on. twenty four rats in three groups is a small study. the skulls were looked at once, at twelve weeks, so we do not see how fast the bone came in. and the putty was not compared with putties already on sale.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map, with the references on page eleven.
reels.doc: Pages 1 to 10 as a map of where things are (page 11 is references), then the running picture once more: the three skulls with their holes filled to the paper's percentages.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map, with the references on page eleven. why putty, and the idea, are on pages one to three, the gel recipe on three and four, the cell tests on three to six, the putty on four to six, the rats and their scans on four, five and seven, the slices on five to eight, and the discussion on eight to ten. the takeaway is a putty made only of bone, grains of cow bone in a gel made from the same bone. it was easy to handle, and in rat skulls it filled more of the hole with bone than the same grains in collagen. whether it makes bone on its own, and how it compares with putties already in use, are still to be tested.

title: Voxel-Level Brain States Prediction Using Swin Transformer

reels.name: Front
reels.cap: This paper came out in twenty twenty five, in the I triple E Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics.
reels.doc: Page 1 of the paper (src/Sun2025.pdf via tools/front_page.sh), so the viewer recognises it (DESIGN, front page).
reels.words: this paper came out in twenty twenty five, in the i triple e journal of biomedical and health informatics. its first author is yifei sun. it predicts brain activity with a swin transformer.

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: Can a neural network watch the resting brain for twenty three seconds, and predict what it does next, voxel by voxel?
reels.words: can a neural network watch the resting brain for twenty three seconds, and predict what it does next, voxel by voxel? that's the question of this paper.

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Functional M R I measures the BOLD signal, a blood oxygen proxy for neural activity, as a three D volume of voxels, here every zero point seven two seconds.
reels.words: functional m r i measures the bold signal, a blood oxygen proxy for neural activity, as a three d volume of voxels, here every zero point seven two seconds. the paper calls each volume a brain state. the model sees the last thirty two states, about twenty three seconds, and predicts the next ten, seven point two seconds into the future, at full voxel detail. why bother? to understand how brain states unfold, to shorten scans for patients who can't stay in the scanner, and one day for brain computer interfaces.

reels.name: Data
reels.cap: The data are resting state scans of one hundred unrelated young adults from the Human Connectome Project, two scans each, twelve hundred time points, two millimetre voxels.
reels.words: the data are resting state scans of one hundred unrelated young adults from the human connectome project, two scans each, twelve hundred time points, two millimetre voxels. they are smoothed, band pass filtered and z scored. each volume, ninety one by one oh nine by ninety one voxels, is halved in each dimension, then cropped or padded to a forty eight voxel cube. only voxels inside the brain count. a sliding window cuts each scan into samples of thirty two inputs and ten targets. eighty subjects train the model, and twenty unseen subjects test it.

reels.name: Model
reels.cap: A voxel-level brain is huge.
reels.words: a voxel-level brain is huge. ordinary self attention compares every token with every other, which is far too expensive here. the authors' earlier model worked on three hundred and seventy nine brain regions instead. the swin transformer only attends within small local windows. in the next layer the windows are shifted, so information flows across window borders. and patch merging builds a hierarchy, from fine detail to the whole brain. the encoder is swift, a four d swin transformer for f m r i. it cuts the input into patches of three by three by three voxels by four time points, embeds them, and runs three stages of window attention, shrinking space down to a four voxel cube with a hundred and forty four channels. the decoder folds time into channels, so one pass outputs all ten future states, and climbs back up with three transposed convolutions. skip connections, as in a u net, pass fine detail across. the output is ten full brain volumes. because only past states go in, there's no information leak from the future.

reels.name: Loss
reels.cap: Training compares the prediction with the real future using mean squared error, counted only inside the brain.
reels.words: training compares the prediction with the real future using mean squared error, counted only inside the brain. but a blurry prediction that hugs the average can also score a low error. so the loss adds structural similarity, s s i m, extended to three d, which compares local means, contrasts and correlations. the final loss is the masked m s e plus two times one minus s s i m. the model trained with adam on an a one hundred, and converged in twenty four epochs.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: On twenty unseen subjects, the average masked error is zero point zero three five, and the structural similarity is zero point nine five four, close to a perfect one.
reels.words: on twenty unseen subjects, the average masked error is zero point zero three five, and the structural similarity is zero point nine five four, close to a perfect one. two controls. shuffle the order of the input states, and the error explodes to four thousand eight hundred and ninety: the model really uses the temporal sequence. and compare each prediction with the previous real state instead: the error doubles, to zero point zero seven six. so the model isn't just copying the last frame forward. how does accuracy hold up further into the future? the error stays below zero point zero one for the first five steps, about three and a half seconds, then climbs, to zero point one four four at the tenth. the error maps show no spatial bias, the error just grows evenly with time. and side by side with the real brain states, the predictions keep the same contrast patterns, step after step.

reels.name: Regions
reels.cap: Breaking the error down over one hundred cortical regions of the Yeo atlas, the spread is narrow, with no outliers.
reels.words: breaking the error down over one hundred cortical regions of the yeo atlas, the spread is narrow, with no outliers. the best predicted are the superior and inferior parietal lobules, of the dorsal attention and control networks: well connected hubs with strong, stable signals. the worst are limbic: orbitofrontal cortex and the temporal pole. these areas suffer signal loss and artefacts in f m r i, and vary more at rest. even so, the worst region's error is only about forty percent above the best.

reels.name: Outro
reels.cap: In context: BrainLM reported errors around zero point five, though with different preprocessing.
reels.words: in context: brainlm reported errors around zero point five, though with different preprocessing. the authors' regional model was better on the very first step, but its error passed zero point one five after five seconds, while this voxel model stays accurate in the short term. next steps are longer input windows with a loss that weights the far future, full resolution data, and task f m r i, not just rest. the takeaway: a swin transformer can learn how the resting brain evolves, voxel by voxel, well enough to predict its next seven seconds.

title: Position estimation using neural networks in semi-monolithic PET detectors

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Physics in Medicine and Biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture that grows from block to answer.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from physics in medicine and biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page. the title is position estimation using neural networks in semi-monolithic pet detectors. it comes from marta freire and colleagues at the i3m institute in valencia. the abstract sets out the work. a semi-monolithic block is eight thin slabs of lyso crystal side by side, on an eight by eight grid of silicon photomultipliers. each slab is twenty five point eight millimetres long, three point one millimetres across, and twenty millimetres from top to bottom. when a gamma ray stops in a slab, its light spreads along that slab, but the mirror film between slabs keeps it in that one row. summing the light down each column gives eight numbers. one small network turns them into the position along the slab, a second turns them into the depth, and the event lands back in the slab. the paper compares three coatings for the faces and two sipm models. the best places events to one point one millimetres along the slab and one point seven millimetres in depth, with an energy resolution from eleven to sixteen percent.

reels.name: Why
reels.cap: The introduction starts with sensitivity.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: why total-body scanners need new detectors, and the middle way between pixels and one block.
reels.words: the introduction starts with sensitivity. most clinical scanners see only twenty to thirty centimetres of the body, about one eighth of it, so most of the gamma rays a patient gives off are never caught. a scanner long enough to cover the whole body fixes that, and several total-body scanners have now been built. page two shows the one this group is building, a ring of detector blocks, each block a stack of eight slabs. such a scanner asks three things of its detectors, good timing, the place of each hit in all three directions, and an accurate reading of its energy. most detectors today are pixelated, a grid of small crystals, each on its own sipm. all of a crystal's light lands on one sipm, which is good for timing, but nothing tells how deep the gamma ray went, and the walls between crystals cost some area. a monolithic block is one solid crystal. its light spreads over many sipms, and the spread's shape gives the depth, but each sipm then sees few photons, which slows the timing. the semi-monolithic block sits in between, a block along the slabs and pixels across them.

reels.name: Before
reels.cap: Semi-monolithic blocks have been tried before.
reels.doc: Pages 2 and 3: the semi-monolithic blocks tried before, drawn as how thick they were.
reels.words: semi-monolithic blocks have been tried before. chung and colleagues simulated one in two thousand and eight and measured a single slab in twenty ten. zhang and colleagues measured blocks in twenty seventeen and twenty nineteen. all of them were ten millimetres thick. zhang also found that black outer faces improve the position but hurt the energy and the timing. mueller and colleagues, in twenty twenty two, used nineteen millimetre slabs and a machine learning method called gradient tree boosting. this paper's slabs are twenty millimetres thick, which suits a clinical scanner.

reels.name: Coatings
reels.cap: The aim, near the top of page three, is to compare coatings on the crystal's faces and two SiPM models, mainly for the position in three dimensions, and also for the energy.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: the aim, the parts, what each coating does to the light, and the five detectors.
reels.words: the aim, near the top of page three, is to compare coatings on the crystal's faces and two sipm models, mainly for the position in three dimensions, and also for the energy. timing is left for a follow-up paper. section two names the parts. the eight slabs are polished, with a mirror film called e s r between them. the faces that differ are the top and the two ends of each slab. black paint absorbs the light that reaches it. the e s r film reflects it, like a mirror. a retroreflector sends it straight back the way it came, so the light stays centred under the hit. figure two, on page four, shows the five detectors tested. one has black ends with a retroreflector on top, one has e s r ends with a retroreflector, and one is e s r everywhere. the older s13 sipms were tried with two of them, the newer s14 with all three. table one adds that the s14 detects about fifty percent of the photons, against forty percent for the s13.

reels.name: Bench
reels.cap: Figure three shows the bench.
reels.doc: Pages 3 to 5: the source, the pinhole and the stages, and the grid of beam positions they scan.
reels.words: figure three shows the bench. a sodium twenty two source, one millimetre across, sits behind a tungsten pinhole, with a two millimetre hole, with a small reference detector behind it to catch the partner gamma ray. two motor stages move the block, so the narrow beam enters the side of the slabs at one spot after another. page five gives the scan. the block moved in one millimetre steps, along the slab and up it, five minutes at each spot. that makes a grid of twenty five by nineteen, four hundred and seventy five beam positions on the third slab.

reels.name: Signals
reels.cap: Each event gives sixty four signals, but the paper adds them up along the rows and along the columns, leaving eight plus eight.
reels.doc: Page 5: the 64 signals made into 8 + 8, the depth from a ratio, the filters and the split.
reels.words: each event gives sixty four signals, but the paper adds them up along the rows and along the columns, leaving eight plus eight. the row sums say which slab was hit, the column sums say where along the slab, and everything added together is the energy. for depth, they use a simple ratio, the total energy divided by the brightest signal. a near hit makes a narrow, tall spot, so the ratio is small. a far hit makes a wide, flat spot, and the ratio grows. three filters then clean the events. only those within fifteen percent of the photopeak are kept, only those in the third slab, and only those near the centre of their beam position's cloud, which drops gamma rays that scattered before stopping. the events are then split, half for training, five percent for checking during training, and forty five percent for the final test.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: Section two point three gives the networks.
reels.doc: Pages 5 and 6: the two small networks, how they learn from the scan, and the three numbers that grade them.
reels.words: section two point three gives the networks. one small network estimates the position along the slab, a second estimates the depth. each takes the eight column sums, passes them through two hidden layers of sixty four nodes, and gives out one number. figure three c, back on page four, draws the same pair, though it labels them with sixteen inputs, where the text says eight. to train them, the scan supplies the answer for every event, the beam position the block was moved to. training shrinks the root mean squared error between the true position and the predicted one, equation one, and the checking set stops the training before the networks just memorise the data. three numbers then grade the answers at each beam position. the bias is how far the average answer sits from the true position. the mean absolute error is how far, on average, each answer misses. the full width at half maximum measures how wide the cloud of answers is. the beam itself is two millimetres wide, and the paper leaves that in.

reels.name: Energy
reels.cap: The results start on page six.
reels.doc: Pages 6 and 7: the slabs pulled apart, the first position estimate squeezed by mirrors, and the energy.
reels.words: the results start on page six. figure four a, on page seven, shows the eight slabs come out cleanly apart. fewer events reach the far slabs, because the beam enters through the first, and the attenuation length of lyso at five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts is one point two centimetres. the third slab is the one studied. figure four b shows the first, simple estimate of the position, the centre of gravity of the light. with e s r on every face, the estimates bunch toward the middle of the slab, because the mirrors fold light from the ends back inward. figure four c gives the energy resolution. with black ends it is sixteen percent for both sipms. with e s r everywhere it is eleven percent for the s13 and thirteen for the s14, and e s r ends with a retroreflector give fifteen. black paint absorbs light, so fewer photons reach the sipms, and the energy is measured less precisely.

reels.name: Maps
reels.cap: Figure five maps the error along the slab at all four hundred and seventy five beam positions, for all five detectors.
reels.doc: Pages 7 and 8: the error at every beam position, worst at the ends and the top, and why.
reels.words: figure five maps the error along the slab at all four hundred and seventy five beam positions, for all five detectors. it is worst near the two ends of the slab, where the light is cut off by black paint or folded back by a mirror. black ends shrink that edge effect, and two matching patches appear in the middle of every map. figure six, on page eight, does the same for the second network. depth is hardest near the top of the slab, far from the sipms, where the light has fanned out the most before it lands. black ends with a retroreflector on top keep the light's shape, and shrink those errors.

reels.name: Averages
reels.cap: Figure seven averages over every beam position.
reels.doc: Page 8: Figure 7, the errors averaged over every beam position.
reels.words: figure seven averages over every beam position. the sipm model makes almost no difference, so it comes down to the coating. along the slab, the error is one point one millimetres with black ends, and one point three with either e s r version. in depth it is one point seven millimetres with black ends, two point zero with e s r ends and a retroreflector, and two point two with e s r everywhere. the widths of the clouds run from two point five to three millimetres along the slab, and in depth from three point two to three point nine.

reels.name: Discussion
reels.cap: The discussion, at the bottom of page eight, first explains the energy.
reels.doc: Pages 8 to 10: the energy check, the networks' speed, a faster calibration, and the other blocks compared.
reels.words: the discussion, at the bottom of page eight, first explains the energy. the values were taken without any energy calibration, but the two peaks of the sodium spectrum sit where they should, five hundred and eleven and twelve hundred and seventy five kilo electron volts, a ratio of zero point four, so they are fair estimates. the networks are fast. written carefully, they place four and a half million events per second on ordinary processors, and almost twice as many on a graphics card. calibration is the slow part. four hundred and seventy five beam positions at five minutes each is about forty hours for one detector. the group plans to swap the pinhole for a fan beam, a thin sheet of gamma rays. twenty five sheets from the top would give the position along the slab, then, with the block turned by ninety degrees, nineteen more for the depth, forty four positions in all. table two, printed sideways on page ten, compares semi-monolithic detectors. zhang's blocks were ten millimetres thick. mueller's were nineteen millimetres, and this one is twenty, with an error along the slab as small as the thin ones, which the authors put down to the networks. last, back on page nine, the best coating also has to suit the timing, which the group measured separately.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: The conclusion, on page eleven, repeats the result.
reels.doc: Pages 11 and 12: the conclusion drawn on the slab, and the references worth knowing.
reels.words: the conclusion, on page eleven, repeats the result. a semi-monolithic block twenty millimetres thick, read by two small networks, places events to one point one millimetres along the slab and one point seven millimetres in depth, with black ends and a retroreflector on top, while the best energy resolution, eleven percent, comes with e s r on every face. among the references, cucarella and colleagues, in twenty twenty one, measured the timing of this kind of block. hetzel and colleagues, in twenty twenty, describe the fan beam collimator. and on page twelve, mueller and colleagues, in twenty twenty two, is the gradient tree boosting study, on nineteen millimetre slabs.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All twelve pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. the case for long scanners and semi-monolithic blocks is on pages one and two, earlier blocks and the aim on two and three, the coatings and the five detectors on three and four, the bench and the signals on four and five, the networks and how they are graded on five and six, slabs and energy on six and seven, the maps of the error on seven and eight, the averages on eight, the discussion on eight and nine, the comparison table on ten, and the conclusion and references on eleven and twelve. the takeaway is that eight thin slabs keep the light in one row and let it run along that row, and two small networks read it to one point one millimetres along the slab and one point seven millimetres deep, in a block twenty millimetres thick.

title: Nanocrystalline Lead Halide Perovskites to Boost Time-of-Flight Performance of Medical…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Advanced Materials Interfaces, published in twenty twenty four, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract's four steps drawn as a strip.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from advanced materials interfaces, published in twenty twenty four, page by page. the title says that nanocrystals of lead halide perovskite can help medical imaging detectors time their signals better. the first author is fiammetta pagano at cern, working with a group in prague. the abstract in the grey box lays out the work in four steps. thin films of these nanocrystals are laid on top of crystal scintillators. under soft x-rays of about ten kilo electron volts, the film improves the timing by up to ten times. the idea is then tried with the five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma rays of pet, where the timing improves from two hundred and seventy two to one hundred and eighteen picoseconds.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: The right column starts with how good timing already is.
reels.doc: Page 1 right column and page 2 top: timing today, why low energy is hard, why CT wants it anyway.
reels.words: the right column starts with how good timing already is. detectors in particle physics reach below thirty picoseconds, and the best pet scanners about two hundred. the field has set itself a challenge of ten picoseconds for pet. then comes the catch. the timing spread grows as one over the square root of the energy left in the detector. a ten kilo electron volt x-ray leaves about fifty times less energy than a pet gamma ray, so its timing is about seven times worse. so why chase timing at low energy? the bottom of the page answers with c t, where x-rays cross the body to a detector. some scatter on the way, take a longer path and arrive late, so a detector that times well enough can throw them out. page two puts numbers on it. a simulation found that one hundred picoseconds would remove three quarters of the scattered x-rays. but the best crystal today, lyso, manages only about seven hundred picoseconds at fifteen kilo electron volts.

reels.name: Problem
reels.cap: Further down page two the nanocrystals come in.
reels.doc: Page 2 left column: the nanocrystals are fast, but thin, and swallow their own light; the heterostructure.
reels.words: further down page two the nanocrystals come in. lead halide perovskites glow fast and bright. their weakness is stopping power, because a film of them lets most gamma rays pass, and a useful detector would have to be centimetres deep. and making them thicker does not help. their light sits at the edge of the colours they absorb, which is called a small stokes shift, so light made deep inside is swallowed again on its way out. in the group's earlier work, a film one hundred micrometres thick with ten percent nanocrystals was already cloudy. the way out is at the bottom of the column, a heterostructure. a thin film of nanocrystals goes on top of a dense crystal. the crystal gives the stopping power, and the film gives the fast light. the next column names the three crystals tried, b g o, lyso and gagg.

reels.name: Decay
reels.cap: Figure one, top right, measures the film alone, on glass.
reels.doc: Figure 1 (page 2): the film alone, a spike and three decays; 45% of the photons in the first nanosecond.
reels.words: figure one, top right, measures the film alone, on glass. it counts photons against time after an x-ray pulse, on a log scale. the spike at the start is an almost instant flash, and the box lists three slower decays, the fastest about zero point six nanoseconds. section two point one, below it, sums this up. about forty five percent of the photons come out within the first nanosecond, and that early crowd of photons is exactly what good timing needs.

reels.name: X ray
reels.cap: Page three tests the films on the crystals.
reels.doc: Page 3, Figure 2: the X-ray set-up, the timing with and without the film, the thickness scan, Equation 1.
