reels.words: page three tests the films on the crystals. x-rays come from above. the film of nanocrystals, about fifty micrometres deep, faces them, the crystal sits under it, and a silicon photomultiplier under that reads the light. figure two a shows the spread of arrival times for each crystal, dotted without the film and solid with it. the solid curves are far narrower. panel b's table gives the widths. b g o goes from two thousand eight hundred and seventy five picoseconds to two hundred and thirty six, gagg from two thousand three hundred and sixty five to two hundred and twenty nine, and lyso from five hundred and ninety to two hundred and fifty. the film alone gives one hundred and ninety six. panels c and d vary the film on gagg. with no film the spread is two thousand three hundred and sixty five picoseconds. one micrometre of film brings it to four hundred and fourteen, eight micrometres to two hundred and seventy three, and twenty to two hundred and fifty eight. the full fifty micrometres gave two hundred and twenty nine. equation one explains the gain. the spread grows with the square root of the decay time and shrinks with the square root of the light output, so a fast flash helps even when it is faint. thicker films also stop more of the x-rays, about five percent at one micrometre and ninety two percent at fifty, so more fast light is made.

reels.name: Light
reels.cap: Page four checks the light.
reels.doc: Page 4 left column, Figure 3: no light is lost, some is even bounced back; the X-ray verdict, 6x and 10x.
reels.words: page four checks the light. figure three plots how much light each event gives, and with the film on top no light is lost. for b g o and gagg the solid curves even reach further right, so there is more. the likely reason is in the text. light from the crystal that heads up, away from the photodetector, bounces off the nanocrystals and comes back down. the column ends with the x-ray verdict. on gagg, one micrometre of film made the timing six times better, and about ten micrometres made it ten times better.

reels.name: Gamma
reels.cap: Section two point three moves to PET's gamma rays of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts.
reels.doc: Page 4 right column and page 5, Figure 4: the film under GAGG, shared events, sorting pulses, 272 vs 118 ps.
reels.words: section two point three moves to pet's gamma rays of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts. now the film goes under the gagg plate, between it and the photodetector. the gagg stops the gamma ray, the electron it knocks out can cross into the film, and there it makes fast light. events that leave energy in both are called shared events. telling these events apart is the trick. gagg gives a slow pulse, the film a fast one. so a pulse's height against its total charge sorts the events, and so does how quickly it rises. page five shows this in figure four. panel a draws the three kinds of event. panel b plots pulse height against charge, with a band of gagg events, a band of film events, and the shared events in between. panel c sorts by rise time instead, and the fast events sit in the lower red box. panel d is the result. gagg's own events time at two hundred and seventy two picoseconds, the shared and film events at one hundred and eighteen, better than twice as good.

reels.name: Conclusion
reels.cap: The conclusion starts below the figure.
reels.doc: Page 5 text: about 240 ps everywhere, the extrapolation to 60 keV (under 100 ps), and the next step.
reels.words: the conclusion starts below the figure. every crystal reached about two hundred and forty picoseconds with the film, and even the thinnest film, one micrometre, took gagg from two point four nanoseconds to about four hundred picoseconds. the right column extrapolates. two hundred and forty picoseconds at ten kilo electron volts, scaled by the square root of ten over sixty, becomes about ninety eight picoseconds at sixty kilo electron volts, under the hundred picoseconds that c t needs. next, the authors want the nanocrystals set in a solid such as glass, so that many thin layers can be stacked to stop harder radiation, up to pet's gamma rays.

reels.name: Methods
reels.cap: The experimental section starts at the bottom of page five, where the nanocrystals are made by hot injection.
reels.doc: Pages 5 to 7: the recipe, the two layouts, the attenuation estimate, and what is measured on each pulse.
reels.words: the experimental section starts at the bottom of page five, where the nanocrystals are made by hot injection. on page six the recipe continues. cesium oleate is injected into a lead bromide solution at one hundred and seventy degrees celsius, and ten seconds later the flask goes into an ice bath. the film is then built on the crystal one microlitre drop at a time. figure five, on the right of page six, shows the two layouts, the film facing the x-rays, and the film under the crystal for gamma rays. below it, the stopping numbers are worked out. the x-rays' mass attenuation, one hundred and four point nine square centimetres per gram, times the density, four point eight three grams per cubic centimetre, gives about five hundred and seven per centimetre. across fifty micrometres that stops ninety two percent. the authors call these rough, since a film of nanocrystals is less dense than a solid crystal. page seven, figure six, shows what is measured on each pulse. the rise time is how long the signal takes between two thresholds, the amplitude is its height, and the charge is its area. each sample is timed against a reference crystal of sixty one picoseconds, and the formula at the bottom of the column takes that reference out, to leave the sample's own timing.

reels.name: References
reels.cap: The right column of page seven says who did what, and the references begin.
reels.doc: Page 7 right column and page 8: the set-up paper, the group's earlier film and the heterostructure idea.
reels.words: the right column of page seven says who did what, and the references begin. reference eleven describes the x-ray timing set-up. page eight finishes the list. reference sixteen is the group's earlier film, the cloudy one from page two, and reference twenty two is where the heterostructure idea comes from.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the whole paper as a map.
reels.doc: All eight pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the whole paper as a map. the motivation and the idea are on pages one and two. the x-ray results are on pages three and four, the gamma ray test runs from page four into five, the methods fill pages five to seven, and the references close it. the takeaway is that a thin film of perovskite nanocrystals on a dense crystal adds fast light without losing any, improving the timing up to ten times under x-rays, and more than twice for gamma rays of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts. setting the nanocrystals in a solid is the next step.

title: A neural network-based algorithm for simultaneous event positioning and timestamping in…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Physics in Medicine and Biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture that grows from block to answer.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from physics in medicine and biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page. the title is a neural network-based algorithm for simultaneous event positioning and timestamping in monolithic scintillators. it comes from pietro carra and colleagues at the university of pisa and the italian national institute for nuclear physics. the abstract sets out the problem. a monolithic detector is one solid block of crystal, here lyso, twenty five point six by twenty five point six by eight millimetres. a gamma ray's light lands on sixty four silicon photomultipliers underneath, and each reports two numbers, how much light it caught and when its light arrived. one network turns the light pattern into a position, a second turns the arrival times into a time stamp, and a small layer joins the two, so the event's place and time come out together. tested on a real block, it reaches zero point seven eight millimetres across the face, one point two millimetres in depth, and one hundred and fifty six picoseconds in timing, on a low-cost chip that keeps up with a million events per second.

reels.name: Clock
reels.cap: Timing is at the heart of this paper.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: coincidence timing, pixels against a block, why a block's timing lags, the aim and the setup.
reels.words: timing is at the heart of this paper. a pet scanner catches both gamma rays from each annihilation, and the difference in their arrival times says where along the line it happened. over many events those differences scatter, and the width of their spread, the coincidence time resolution, is called the c t r. one hundred and fifty six picoseconds is about two point three centimetres along the line. page one goes on to today's clinical detectors. they are pixelated, each crystal three millimetres across and twenty long, on its own sensor, and their c t r runs from two hundred to five hundred picoseconds. page two weighs the two designs. a pixel can be made longer to stop more gamma rays, but then its timing smears as the light bounces around, and it cannot tell how deep the hit was. a monolithic block places hits to about a millimetre and tells how deep they were, but its timing has lagged, under two hundred picoseconds only with digital sensors and a heavy maximum likelihood method. the authors' guess is that a block shares its light among many sensors, so each gets a small signal that crosses the trigger level late and unevenly, while a pixel puts all of its light on one. the best methods so far cannot run inside a detector, and they need long calibration scans over a fine grid of beam positions. so the aim is set near the bottom of the page, one million events per second, handled inside the detector itself, on a block twenty five point six millimetres across and eight from top to bottom, read by sixty four sipms, three millimetres each.

reels.name: Simulation
reels.cap: Page three builds the simulation.
reels.doc: Page 3: the optical and SiPM simulation, the three coatings, the beam grid, and the joint idea.
reels.words: page three builds the simulation. geant4 follows the gamma ray and every optical photon it makes, twenty nine thousand photons per mega electron volt, so about fourteen thousand eight hundred for each gamma ray, at zero point five one one mega electron volts. a second simulation turns the photons reaching each sipm into its electrical signal, noise included. three coatings are compared. black paint swallows the light that reaches it, a reflector sends it back toward the sensors, and a mixed version has black sides and a reflective top. the authors expect positioning and timing to prefer different coatings. beams are aimed at points one millimetre apart across the face, and the sipms are run from one to fifteen volts above their breakdown voltage, the overvoltage. then comes the paper's key idea. the sipms that fire first sit right under the hit, so timing helps to place it, and knowing where it hit says which sensors give the most reliable times, so position helps the time stamp. so the two should be estimated together.

reels.name: Position
reels.cap: The positioning network is described at the bottom of page three.
reels.doc: Pages 3 to 5: the positioning network, built up from its 8 x 8 input; Table 1; how results are scored.
reels.words: the positioning network is described at the bottom of page three. its input is the light caught by all sixty four sipms, an eight by eight image, scaled so that it adds up to one, and its outputs are the hit's x, y and how deep it was. its weights are stored as sixteen bit numbers, which a programmable chip, an f p g a, handles fast. figure two, on page four, shows the first layer. each neuron looks only at a two by two patch of sipms, and two neurons look at every patch, since neighbouring sipms carry related information. the later layers are fully connected, and two hand-made features join at the last layer, the number of sipms that caught over five percent of the light and how spread out the light is, both clues to how deep the hit was. table one, on page five, gives the chosen network, six layers of one hundred and twenty eight, forty, thirty, fifteen, ten and three neurons, trained for five hundred epochs. depending on how many weights it has, a network like this takes ten to ninety percent of a medium f p g a, leaving room for other logic. the results are scored with two numbers. one is the spread of placed positions, measured as the full width at half maximum. the other is the bias, the average offset between the placed and the true positions.

reels.name: Stamps
reels.cap: Section two point three lists four ways to time stamp an event.
reels.doc: Pages 5 and 6: four ways to time stamp an event, Table 2, and the joint network of Figure 3.
reels.words: section two point three lists four ways to time stamp an event. the simplest, called e w w d, averages the sipm time stamps, weighted by how much light each saw, after correcting each for its distance from the hit. m l i t e is the maximum likelihood method from van dam and colleagues, the best in the literature but too heavy for real time. n n is the new network. each sipm's time stamp is the moment its signal crosses a fixed level, and the network takes all sixty four time stamps and amounts of light as an eight by eight grid of pairs. n n w instead reads every sipm's whole waveform, which a scanner does not normally record, so it shows the best that could be done. table two, on page six, sums up what each needs. only e w w d works without scanning a beam across the crystal, and the two networks also need training. figure three is the joint network. the trained positioning network gives x, y and how deep, the timing network gives the time, and one fully connected layer of twenty neurons takes all four and gives back a refined position and time. training goes in two steps. first the two networks are trained on their own, then they are frozen and only the joining layer learns.

reels.name: Bench
reels.cap: Page seven moves to the real detector.
reels.doc: Page 7: the measured setup, the 45 degree trick that gives a depth to train on, the timing correction.
reels.words: page seven moves to the real detector. figure four shows how its beams are made. a sodium twenty two source sits above the block, and a small reference crystal on the far side only fires for gamma pairs along one line, so each accepted event lies on a known line through the block. knowing how deep each training event was is harder. first the reference sits straight above, and the network learns x and y from those events. then it is tilted to forty five degrees. along that slanted line, every step sideways is an equal step down, so the y position the network finds tells how deep the event was, and that depth becomes the training target. the reference crystal and its own sensor reach about one hundred and thirty picoseconds. four thousand events are taken at each of four hundred points, about one point two millimetres apart. the measured timing mixes the block's error with the reference's, so the reference part is taken away in quadrature, and the result is multiplied by root two to stand for a pair of identical blocks. the training is also repeated with fewer and fewer measured points, from four hundred down to twenty five, with and without simulated events added.

reels.name: Placing
reels.cap: The results begin at the bottom of page seven.
reels.doc: Pages 7 to 9: the positioning results, Figure 5, Table 3, how well spots separate, Table 4.
reels.words: the results begin at the bottom of page seven. a network of eight thousand parameters works best. figure five, on page eight, follows a line from the crystal's centre to its corner. each beam gives a sharp peak, on a flat floor of about three percent misplaced events. the spread and the bias stay low until the last few millimetres before the corner. table three compares six layers with three, at the same eight thousand parameters. at three volts, six layers place hits within zero point four six millimetres across the face on average, three layers within zero point five six. above about eleven volts the sipm noise takes over, and at fifteen volts three layers fall to one point five five. page nine adds a check. beams one millimetre apart give spots on average two point four widths apart, so neighbouring spots overlap by less than one percent. table four changes the coating. in the corners, the black crystal gives zero point six nine millimetres, the fully reflective one zero point nine three, so for positioning, black is best.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: Figure six, also on page nine, plots the timing of the four methods against overvoltage, for a reflective crystal.
reels.doc: Pages 9 and 10: Figure 6 and Table 5, the coatings for timing (Table 6), and the trade-off of Figure 7.
reels.words: figure six, also on page nine, plots the timing of the four methods against overvoltage, for a reflective crystal. all do best near eleven to twelve volts. table five has the best values. e w w d reaches two hundred and seventy two picoseconds, even with the true hit position handed to it, m l i t e one hundred and fifty one, the new network one hundred and twenty nine, and the whole-waveform network eighty four. page ten repeats this for the coatings, in the corners. for the network, black gives two hundred and twenty two picoseconds, reflective one hundred and thirty two, the reverse of the positioning order. figure seven puts both on one plot, the spread of positions against the timing, with black at low voltage and reflective at high voltage at opposite ends.

reels.name: Joint
reels.cap: Table seven, at the bottom of page ten, tests the joint network on timing.
reels.doc: Pages 10 to 12: what joining position and time buys, Tables 7 and 8, the maps of Figure 8.
reels.words: table seven, at the bottom of page ten, tests the joint network on timing. for black crystals at twelve volts, the corners improve from two hundred and twenty to one hundred and seventy nine picoseconds, and for reflective ones from one hundred and thirty one to one hundred and twenty two. table eight, on page eleven, shows gains in position too. for a reflective crystal at three volts, the spread in the corners drops from zero point nine three to zero point seven one millimetres. for black at three volts, the error in how deep drops from one point seven four to one point zero eight, better by over thirty percent. figure eight maps the joint network on a reflective crystal. its timing is best in the corners, probably because there the light falls on fewer sipms. page twelve concludes that the two estimates really do help each other.

reels.name: Real
reels.cap: Table nine, on page twelve, is the real block at twelve volts.
reels.doc: Pages 12 to 15: the measured block, with and without simulated training data (Table 9, Figures 9 to 12).
reels.words: table nine, on page twelve, is the real block at twelve volts. trained on measured events only, it reaches zero point eight eight millimetres across, three point five three in how deep, and one hundred and ninety four picoseconds. adding simulated events to the training brings those to zero point seven eight, one point five five and one hundred and fifty six. figure nine, at the top of the page, shrinks the measured grid. without simulation, the spread grows from about zero point seven five to over one point five millimetres, but with it the result holds down to sixty four measured points. the text gives three reasons why simulation helps. it is cheap, so there are about twenty thousand events per point instead of four thousand, on about two thousand five hundred points instead of four hundred, and the true hit point is known exactly. figure ten shows the training loss jumping when the measured data are brought in, but only tripling, so the two kinds of data are close. figure eleven shows a clean, bell-shaped histogram of time differences, and an energy resolution of eleven percent. figure twelve, on page fourteen, maps the real block at eleven volts. the spread and bias grow toward the corners, as in the simulation, and a uniform source shows events piling up in the centre, where the bias pulls them together. on page fifteen, a hundred random points that were not in the training set give one hundred and fifty five picoseconds and zero point eight millimetres, so the network has not memorised its grid.

reels.name: Discussion
reels.cap: The discussion, on page fifteen, weighs it up.
reels.doc: Pages 15 and 16: the bias, simulation against measurement, what still needs real data, the competition.
reels.words: the discussion, on page fifteen, weighs it up. the joint network's bias is about zero point three millimetres over most of the block, rising to zero point eight in the corners, which could be reduced with a penalty in training or with separate networks for the edges and the centre. real data cost little against simulation, fourteen picoseconds of timing, from one hundred and forty two to one hundred and fifty six. page sixteen says some measured points are still needed, at least sixty four, for what simulation misses, such as how the crystal is coupled to the sipms and differences between them. against other monolithic detectors, the closest, from borghi and colleagues, reached two hundred and fifteen picoseconds, one point seven millimetres across, and four point seven in how deep, without running in real time. the coating and the voltage also let one detector be tuned, black at low voltage for zero point six millimetres, or reflective at high voltage for under one hundred and thirty picoseconds.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: The conclusion, on page sixteen, says monolithic crystals with these networks reach under two hundred picoseconds and under one millimetre at once, in hardware a detector can carry.
reels.doc: Pages 16 to 18: the conclusion and its price, the limits, and the references worth knowing.
reels.words: the conclusion, on page sixteen, says monolithic crystals with these networks reach under two hundred picoseconds and under one millimetre at once, in hardware a detector can carry. the price is a calibration scan for every detector, with a fast reference crystal for the timing, which simulation can make much shorter. page seventeen names the limits. the crystal was only eight millimetres from top to bottom, while clinical ones are about twenty, and at very high event rates the signals may pile up. so thicker crystals, b g o and larger sipms come next. among the references, berg and cherry in twenty eighteen timed whole waveforms with a convolutional network, and decuyper and colleagues in twenty twenty one is the positioning network paper, which has a video of its own. on page eighteen, lamprou and colleagues in twenty twenty is the e w w d method, and van dam and colleagues in twenty thirteen is m l i t e.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All eighteen pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. the problem and the aim are on pages one and two, the simulation and the joint idea on three, the positioning network on three to five, the timing methods and the joint network on five and six, the real bench on seven, positioning results on seven to nine, timing on nine and ten, the joint network's gains on ten to twelve, the real block on twelve to fifteen, the discussion on fifteen and sixteen, and the conclusion, limits and references on sixteen to eighteen. the takeaway is that two light networks, joined so that position and time inform each other, give a solid block timing close to pixels, one hundred and fifty six picoseconds with zero point seven eight millimetres on a real detector, fast enough to run on the detector's own chip.

title: Artificial neural networks for positioning of gamma interactions in monolithic PET…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Physics in Medicine and Biology, published in twenty twenty one, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture that grows from block to position.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from physics in medicine and biology, published in twenty twenty one, page by page. the title is artificial neural networks for positioning of gamma interactions in monolithic pet detectors. it comes from milan decuyper and colleagues at ghent university in belgium. the abstract sets the scene. instead of a grid of small crystals, a monolithic detector uses one solid block, here a simulated block of lyso, fifty by fifty by sixteen millimetres. a gamma ray's light lands on an eight by eight array of sensors underneath, whose rows and columns are summed into sixteen numbers. a neural network takes those sixteen numbers and estimates where in the block the gamma ray first interacted. the abstract warns of one pitfall, a network that learns only the calibration grid. the best network places events with a median error of zero point seven seven millimetres in three dimensions, and compton scattering inside the crystal accounts for much of what remains.

reels.name: Monolithic
reels.cap: The introduction starts with today's scanners.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: pixels against one block, depth from the patch's width, the cut-off edges, nearest neighbour.
reels.words: the introduction starts with today's scanners. they cut the detector into small crystals, so a hit can only be placed at the centre of whichever crystal fired, and the crystal size, three to five millimetres, limits the detail. a monolithic detector is one solid block instead. the light from each hit spreads over the sensors underneath, and the paragraph at the bottom points out that its shape also tells the depth. light from a hit far from the sensors arrives spread wide and low, and a narrow, tall patch comes from a hit close to them. page two names the hard parts. near the edges of the block, part of the light patch is cut off, so the position has less to go on. many methods have been tried, from maximum likelihood to nearest neighbour lookups and neural networks. the group's own earlier study used nearest neighbour positioning on the same simulated block. each new event is compared with a large library of reference light patches, and the closest match gives the position. that works well but costs a lot of computing for every event. the aim here is a network that does as well and runs faster.

reels.name: Data
reels.cap: Page three says why a network suits the job.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: why a network, the simulated block and its sixteen sums, the beams, Figures 1 and 2.
reels.words: page three says why a network suits the job. it learns straight from the light patch, without hand-made features, its output is a position anywhere rather than one of the calibration points, and once trained it is fast. the data come from a simulation of the fifty by fifty by sixteen millimetre block. underneath sits an eight by eight array of light sensors, but the rows and the columns are summed, so each event gives just sixteen numbers. to train it, a thin beam of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gamma rays is aimed straight down at chosen points, ten thousand events at each. each event's target is the place of its first interaction. figure one, on page four, shows the layout. the training points form a forty nine by forty nine grid, one millimetre apart, and a second set of ten by ten points in the centre sits half a millimetre off that grid. figure two draws the network. it has sixteen inputs, a few fully connected hidden layers, and two outputs for x and y, with a third added later for how deep the hit was. the text below says they tried two to five hidden layers of sixty four to one thousand and twenty four neurons each.

reels.name: Pitfall
reels.cap: Page five raises the pitfall.
reels.doc: Page 5: a network that memorises the grid, validation on the in-between points, training, depth, scatter.
reels.words: page five raises the pitfall. the network only ever sees events from the grid points. if it memorises them, it snaps every event onto a grid point, and tested on those same points it looks wonderfully sharp. for a beam in between, though, it is always wrong. so the authors validate on the second set, the in-between points, and keep the network from the epoch that places those points best. training uses the adam optimiser and an l1 loss, and stops after forty epochs without improvement. section two point four adds a third output, how deep the hit was. section two point five notes that about sixty percent of the gamma rays scatter at least once inside the crystal before being absorbed, so most of the light comes from somewhere other than the first interaction.

reels.name: Size
reels.cap: The results start on page six.
reels.doc: Pages 6 to 8: network size (Figures 3 and 4), why validation matters (Figure 5, Table 1), training data.
reels.words: the results start on page six. figure three plots the median distance between predicted and true positions against the neurons per layer. on the training grid, the left panel, bigger networks keep getting better. on the in-between points, the right panel, the gain stops at about two hundred and fifty six neurons. figure four shows the same for the width of the spread of predictions, where three layers of two hundred and fifty six neurons reach the lowest, zero point four millimetres. page seven shows why the in-between points matter. figure five maps where a five layer network places events from a uniform source. validated on the grid itself, it piles events into lines through the middle of the block. validated on the in-between points, the map is even. table one puts numbers on it. validated on the grid, that network reaches zero point three seven millimetres on the grid but zero point four five in between. then comes the amount of training data. figure six, on page eight, shows it. going from one hundred to one thousand events per point helps a lot, and beyond that the median distance stays flat, so one thousand events per point is enough.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: Table two scores the chosen network, three layers of two hundred and fifty six neurons trained on one thousand events per point.
reels.doc: Pages 8 and 9: Table II, mean against median, depth, and the maps of Figures 7 and 8.
reels.words: table two scores the chosen network, three layers of two hundred and fifty six neurons trained on one thousand events per point. over the whole block, predictions spread zero point four six millimetres at half height, and zero point four in the centre. the median distance from the true position is zero point five millimetres, but the mean is one point one, a sign of a few events placed far off. adding the depth output barely changes those numbers. in three dimensions the median error is zero point seven seven millimetres, and the depth itself is off by a median of zero point three nine. page nine shows where the errors are. figure seven a plots every predicted position from the grid beams. in panel b, the colour is each point's spread, and the worst are at the edges, where the light patch is cut off. figure eight maps a uniform source, and it comes out evenly spread across the block.

reels.name: Scatter
reels.cap: Page ten has the depth errors.
reels.doc: Pages 10 and 11: the depth errors (Figure 9), Table 5 split by scatter, Figures 10 and 11, the speed.
reels.words: page ten has the depth errors. figure nine is their histogram. it has a sharp peak at zero, with a longer tail on the negative side, for events placed too close to the sensors. table five splits the events in two. for events that did not scatter, the median 3d error is zero point four millimetres. for the scattered ones it is one point five nine, and the width of their depth error grows from zero point seven one to one point eight millimetres. page eleven shows, in figure ten, that the long tail belongs to the scattered events. figure eleven compares the maps, crisp grid points for unscattered events and a blur for scattered ones. speed is no problem. one graphics card places twenty one million events per second.

reels.name: Discussion
reels.cap: The discussion opens on the same page.
reels.doc: Pages 11 to 13: why the grid fools you, the edges, against nearest neighbour, depth, forward scatter.
reels.words: the discussion opens on the same page. judged on the training grid alone, the authors would have picked four or five layers of one thousand and twenty four neurons, a network that memorises the grid. page twelve adds that the l1 loss scores an even spread of predictions the same as one bunched on grid points, and that memorising starts in the centre first, so in-between points are only needed there. at the edges, the network also leans inwards, because it never saw a target beyond twenty four millimetres from the centre. against the earlier nearest neighbour method on the same simulation, the spread in the centre shrinks by seventeen percent, and the map is more even. page thirteen compares how deep hits are placed. the earlier method sorted events into six layers by how deep they were, with a mean error of one point six millimetres in that direction. the network gives a continuous answer, almost forty six percent better. the same page explains the scatter tail. most scattering goes forward, so the light comes from deeper, closer to the sensors, a narrower patch that the network reads as a deeper hit.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: Page fourteen sums up.
reels.doc: Pages 14 and 15: the conclusion and the references worth knowing.
reels.words: page fourteen sums up. networks should not be too complex, in-between points catch a network that memorises the grid, and three layers of two hundred and fifty six neurons trained on one thousand events per point did best, beating nearest neighbour. among the references, bruyndonckx and colleagues in two thousand and four had an early network for monolithic blocks, iborra and colleagues used ensembles of networks, and on page fifteen, stockhoff and colleagues is the nearest neighbour study this one builds on.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All fifteen pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. the idea and the hard parts are on pages one and two, the simulated block and the network on three and four, the grid pitfall on five, network size and training data on six to eight, the maps, depth and scatter on eight to eleven, the discussion on eleven to thirteen, and the conclusion and references on fourteen and fifteen. the takeaway is that a small network reading sixteen light sums can place gamma interactions in a solid crystal to about half a millimetre, better than nearest neighbour lookups and fast, as long as it is tested on points it never trained on.

title: Neural network based classification of energy sharing events in heterostructured…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from I triple E Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences, published in twenty twenty five, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract's four steps drawn as a strip.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from i triple e transactions on radiation and plasma medical sciences, published in twenty twenty five, page by page. the title promises to sort the events in layered scintillators with neural networks, using only the little a scanner's electronics can read. the first author is carsten lowis at cern. the abstract runs in four steps. layers of b g o and a fast plastic called ej232 share each gamma ray's energy. the electronics of a whole scanner read only a few numbers from each pulse. so two neural networks learn from those numbers, one to spot full energy events and one to estimate how the energy was shared. the first gets between ninety one point six and ninety six point eight percent right.

reels.name: Sharing
reels.cap: The introduction starts with time of flight.
reels.doc: Page 1 right column and page 2 top: timing, the trade-off, BGO and EJ232, and why the split matters.
reels.words: the introduction starts with time of flight. the two gamma rays from one annihilation fly apart, and the difference in their arrival times places it on the line between the detectors. a modern scanner such as the biograph vision does this to two hundred and fourteen picoseconds. the catch is a trade-off. dense crystals like b g o stop gamma rays well but glow slowly, while plastics like ej232 glow fast but stop little. the heterostructure layers the two, and since both give about the same amount of light, their signals add up on equal terms. the last lines of the column say why sharing happens. the electron a gamma ray knocks loose in b g o travels about seventy micrometres, so it often crosses into the plastic next door. page two gives the consequence. each flash is a mix of the two materials' flashes, weighted by the energy each one received, so the timing of every event depends on how its energy was split.

reels.name: Readout
reels.cap: Earlier studies sorted the events with two measures of each pulse, its peak height and its total charge.
reels.doc: Page 2 left column: the old method needs height and charge together, scanner chips cannot give both.
reels.words: earlier studies sorted the events with two measures of each pulse, its peak height and its total charge. but the chips that read out a whole scanner cannot measure both at once, so the authors turn to a neural network that can learn from whichever pair of numbers a chip provides. a paragraph further down says why this is harder than in older two-material detectors called phoswiches. there each pulse comes from one material or the other, while here energy sharing blends them into one mixed signal.

reels.name: Measure
reels.cap: The methods start at the bottom of page two.
reels.doc: Page 2 bottom and right, page 3 Figures 2 and 3: the set-up, the stack, the ground truth, time over threshold.
reels.words: the methods start at the bottom of page two. the layered crystal sits on a silicon photomultiplier, facing a small reference crystal with a sodium twenty two source between them. figure one, top right, is a photo of exactly that. the stack is three by three by fifteen millimetres, with plastic layers of two hundred micrometres and b g o layers of one hundred, and no glue between them. next comes the ground truth the networks learn from. figure two a, on page three, plots each pulse's charge against its peak height. pure b g o events fall along one edge, pure plastic events along the other, and the events that kept all the energy, called photoelectric, along the top. panel b turns this into the energy left in each material, and photoelectric events are those totalling between four hundred and forty and six hundred and sixty five kilo electron volts. figure three, below it, adds the measure a scanner chip can always give, time over threshold. it is how long the pulse stays above a set level. the authors use two levels, ten and twenty millivolts, and form three pairs of inputs, height with time over threshold, charge with time over threshold, and the two times over threshold.

reels.name: Networks
reels.cap: The first network is described at the bottom left of page three.
reels.doc: Page 3: the first network (photoelectric or not), its training, Table I, and the second network.
reels.words: the first network is described at the bottom left of page three. it takes the two numbers, scaled between zero and one, passes them through a few layers of sixteen nodes, and ends in one output, rounded to yes or no, photoelectric or not. it learned from seventy percent of four hundred and seventy nine thousand events and was tested on the other thirty. table one, top right, gives the sizes picked after trying from one to thirty two layers and from two to sixty four nodes. the second network, further down the column, has the same shape, but its output is the share of the energy that went into the plastic, learned from the photoelectric events alone, about a hundred and ninety five thousand of them.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: Page four has the results.
reels.doc: Page 4: Figure 4 row by row, Table II's scores, and the share error from Table IV (page 5).
reels.words: page four has the results. figure four has one column per pair of inputs. the top row shades in red the events the network calls photoelectric, in curved regions, because time over threshold does not grow in step with energy. the middle row checks them against the true energies, with the real photoelectric window as a black box. the bottom row plots the predicted share against the true one, and all three hug the diagonal. table two, on the right, scores the first network on the test events. charge with time over threshold is best, at ninety six point eight percent correct. height with time over threshold gets ninety two point six percent, and the two times over threshold ninety one point six. the events the best pair wrongly lets in miss the energy window by only seven point seven kilo electron volts on average, against thirty six point two and forty three point nine for the others. the second network's result closes the page. table four, at the top of page five, gives the error of its predicted share. height with time over threshold is best, at one point eight nine percent, which for a five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt event is about nine point seven kilo electron volts. the other pairs reach two point seven six and two point eight seven percent.

reels.name: Why
reels.cap: The discussion explains the winners.
reels.doc: Page 5: why charge suits the photoelectric test and height the share; the conclusion and FastIC.
reels.words: the discussion explains the winners. b g o and ej232 give about the same light per unit of energy, so a pulse's charge tracks the total energy, which is just what the photoelectric test needs. a pulse's height, though, comes mostly from the fast plastic, so it tracks the energy in ej232, which is what the second network estimates. the right column adds that even the two times over threshold alone manage both jobs. knowing each event's split also lets an image reconstruction blur each event by its own timing, sharp for plastic-rich events and wider for the rest. next, the method moves to fastic, a readout chip that gives height and time over threshold, the best pair for the second network.

reels.name: References
reels.cap: Page six holds the references.
reels.doc: Page 6: the group's earlier heterostructure papers and the perovskite film paper.
reels.words: page six holds the references. reference twelve is the group's overview of heterostructured scintillators, reference thirteen models how the shared flash adds up, and reference fifteen is the perovskite film paper, which has a video of its own.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All six pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. the idea and the readout problem are on pages one and two, the measurement and the networks on pages two and three, the results on four and five, the explanation and the outlook on page five, and the references on six. the takeaway is that two small neural networks can sort the events of a layered scintillator from the few numbers a scanner chip can read, picking out full energy events up to ninety six point eight percent of the time and estimating the energy split to about two percent. trying it on the fastic chip is the next step.

title: Highly Luminous Scintillating Nanocomposites Enable Ultrafast Time Coincidence…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Advanced Functional Materials, published in twenty twenty five, and it goes through the paper page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract's four steps.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from advanced functional materials, published in twenty twenty five, and it goes through the paper page by page. the title promises very bright plastic scintillators that time gamma rays very precisely. the authors are irene villa and angelo monguzzi's group in milano bicocca, with cern and the czech academy of sciences. the abstract in the grey box tells the whole story in four steps. a plastic scintillator is loaded with nanoparticles of hafnium oxide. tuning its parts makes it very bright. thin films of it are stacked with sheets of a dense crystal called b g o. and the stack times gamma rays to one hundred and fifteen picoseconds.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: On the right of the first page the authors explain why timing matters.
reels.doc: Page 1, right column: why the arrival difference matters, and what CTR measures (200 ps -> 3 cm).
reels.words: on the right of the first page the authors explain why timing matters. in pet, two gamma rays fly apart from one point and reach two detectors. the difference between their arrival times says where along the line the point was. real detectors never measure that difference exactly, so many events give a spread of differences. the width of that spread at half its height is the coincidence time resolution, or c t r. the best commercial scanners reach about two hundred picoseconds, which blurs each point over about three centimetres of the line. the paper aims far below that.

reels.name: Strategy
reels.cap: Page two opens with the paper's strategy.
reels.doc: Page 2 text: energy sharing between a dense crystal and a fast plastic, and the plastic's two weaknesses.
reels.words: page two opens with the paper's strategy. a dense crystal such as b g o stops the gamma ray, and the electron it knocks loose carries energy into a neighbouring fast layer, which flashes quickly. the paper calls this energy sharing. the catch is in the next column. plastics are light, about one gram per cubic centimetre, so they lower the stack's stopping power. and they give fewer than twenty thousand photons per mega electron volt, so each event makes little light.

reels.name: Mechanism
reels.cap: The top of page two holds Figure one.
reels.doc: Figure 1 (page 2): the energy diagram, where the energy goes before and after the grains are heated.
reels.words: the top of page two holds figure one. its left half sketches the idea, grains of hafnium oxide scattered through the plastic so that gamma rays hit something heavy. the right half is the more useful map, a diagram of where the energy goes. a gamma ray frees charges in the plastic, and they settle into excited states. that energy hops from molecule to molecule until it reaches the dye, b b q, which gives off the light. but the grains carry defect states just below the dye's level, so some energy drains into them and is lost. the bottom panel is the fix. heating the grains to nine hundred and fifty degrees celsius removes those defects, and energy caught in the grains now flows back into the plastic along the green arrow. the plastic itself is also changed, from polystyrene to polyvinyl toluene.

reels.name: Ingredients
reels.cap: Page three explains each ingredient.
reels.doc: Page 3: the dye, the yields with raw grains, and the energy ladder that explains the fix.
reels.words: page three explains each ingredient. the dye, b b q, turns ninety three percent of its energy into light and decays in zero point seven nanoseconds. in polystyrene it gives three thousand eight hundred photons per mega electron volt. adding the untreated grains makes it worse, down to eighteen hundred at four percent loading. the reason is in the next paragraph. the grains' defects glow at two point nine two electron volts, just below the dye at three point zero two, so the dye's energy slides down into the defects. after heating, the grains hold energy at four point nine six electron volts instead, above the plastic's gap at four point four two, so it flows back into the plastic.

reels.name: Particles
reels.cap: Page four is Figure two, the evidence for those claims.
reels.doc: Page 4, Figure 2: the heated grains under the microscope (43 nm) and the yield against loading.
reels.words: page four is figure two, the evidence for those claims. panel d shows the grains under the electron microscope, before and after heating. the heated grains come out rounder, about forty three nanometres across. panel i plots the light yield against how much of the grains is mixed in. untreated grains only lower it, while heated grains peak at two point five percent, at sixteen thousand five hundred photons per mega electron volt. the text below adds that this beats the old dye, popop, by fifty percent.

reels.name: Brighter
reels.cap: The last paragraph of page four swaps polystyrene for polyvinyl toluene, which glows about ten times more.
reels.doc: Page 4 end and page 5, Figure 3: the new plastic, 63 500 ph/MeV, the yields side by side, the fast flash.
reels.words: the last paragraph of page four swaps polystyrene for polyvinyl toluene, which glows about ten times more. page five shows what that does. figure three b plots the new mix. its yield peaks at the same loading, at sixty three thousand five hundred photons per mega electron volt. put side by side, the steps add up. polystyrene with the dye gave three thousand eight hundred photons per mega electron volt. heated grains raised that to sixteen thousand five hundred. the new plastic reached sixty three thousand five hundred, about six times the ten thousand of the b g o crystal itself. figure three e shows the flash itself, rising in one hundred and twenty three picoseconds and decaying in about two nanoseconds. figure three f shows the price, because the grains scatter light and make the film cloudy.

reels.name: Device
reels.cap: Page six builds the device.
reels.doc: Page 6: the parts, the 3 mm stack of 100 um layers, and Equation 1 read term by term.
reels.words: page six builds the device. figure four a lists the parts, the dye, the plastic, the heated grains and the b g o sheets. films one hundred micrometres thick alternate with b g o sheets just as thin, stacked into a cube three millimetres on a side. the timing is predicted by equation one, at the bottom of the right column. the c t r grows with the rise time of the flash, and with its decay time, and it shrinks with the number of photons that reach the detector. so a brighter scintillator times better, which is why the light yield matters so much.

reels.name: Model
reels.cap: Page seven refines that equation for the stack.
reels.doc: Page 7: Equation 2's factors, the light that escapes (beta 0.05 / 0.65 / 0.38), 71 ps, 28% vs 38%.
reels.words: page seven refines that equation for the stack. equation two splits the photon count into its factors. beta is the share of light that gets out of the scintillator, chi is the detector's efficiency, then comes the light yield, and the energy deposited. the measured beta is the trouble. for the composite alone it is only zero point zero five, against zero point six five for a perfectly clear block and zero point three eight once the scattering is counted. the right column then predicts the best timing these materials allow, seventy one picoseconds. further down, a simulation finds that twenty eight percent of the stack's events are useful, against thirty eight percent for solid b g o.

reels.name: Result
reels.cap: Page eight has the result, Figure five.
reels.doc: Page 8, Figure 5: which events count (>= 50 keV in the plastic) and the timing, 115 ps against 179 ps.
reels.words: page eight has the result, figure five. panel c sorts events by how much energy landed in the b g o and how much in the plastic. only the events between the two red lines count, the ones that left at least fifty kilo electron volts in the plastic. panel d is the timing. solid b g o gives one hundred and seventy nine picoseconds. the stack gives one hundred and fifteen, the same as a cube made only of the composite at one hundred and fourteen. the text below adds that the group's earlier stack managed one hundred and eighty.

reels.name: Roadmap
reels.cap: From that timing the authors work backwards to the share of light that escapes the stack, about zero point two nine.
reels.doc: Page 8 right column and page 9: what the stack's light extraction is (0.29), what would give 81 and 54 ps, and the conclusion (four times the yield, 70% of BGO's stopping power, the aim below 50 ps).
reels.words: from that timing the authors work backwards to the share of light that escapes the stack, about zero point two nine. the right column then looks ahead. a detector twice as efficient, chi of zero point five instead of zero point two five, would reach eighty one picoseconds. getting all the light out would reach fifty four picoseconds. page nine opens with the conclusion. the light yield went up about four times, and the stack keeps about seventy percent of the stopping power of solid b g o while timing at one hundred and fifteen picoseconds. the stated goal is below fifty picoseconds.

reels.name: Methods
reels.cap: The rest of page nine is the recipe.
reels.doc: Pages 9 to 12: the recipe, the timing set-up, the simulation, and the references to the neighbouring papers.
reels.words: the rest of page nine is the recipe. the grains are baked at nine hundred and fifty degrees celsius for two hours. the films are spread with a doctor blade, and the stack is put together by hand, with no glue, in a teflon cube lined with reflector. page ten says how the timing was measured. a sodium twenty two source sends gamma pairs to the sample and to a reference crystal that times at sixty one picoseconds. a simulation code called fluka worked out where in the stack the energy is left. page eleven holds the references. reference four b is the group's earlier stack, which has a video of its own. reference five b, by pagano and colleagues, adds a perovskite film to a crystal, and is covered in another video too. page twelve finishes the list.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the whole paper as a map.
reels.doc: All twelve pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the whole paper as a map. the story and the idea are on pages one and two. the material is built on pages three to five, the device and its model are on six and seven, the result is on page eight, and the recipe and references run from page nine to the end. the takeaway is that heating the hafnium oxide grains made a fast plastic about four times brighter, and that brightness let a stack of b g o and plastic time gamma rays at one hundred and fifteen picoseconds. getting more of the light out is the next step.

title: Simulation study on 3D convolutional neural networks for time-of-flight prediction in…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from Physics in Medicine and Biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture that grows from block to answer.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from physics in medicine and biology, published in twenty twenty two, page by page. the title is simulation study on 3d convolutional neural networks for time-of-flight prediction in monolithic pet detectors using digitized waveforms. it comes from jens maebe and stefaan vandenberghe at ghent university. the abstract sets out the work. a simulated monolithic detector is one solid lyso crystal on an eight by eight grid of silicon photomultipliers. the crystal is fifty millimetres across and sixteen millimetres thick. when a gamma ray stops in it, its light spreads over many sipms. each sipm's signal is sampled ten billion times a second, which stacks the event into a block of numbers, eight by eight by thirty one. a 3d convolutional network squeezes that block, down to one number, the time the gamma ray arrived. two such detectors facing each other time a pair to one hundred and forty one picoseconds, against one hundred and seventy seven for the usual average of the first few time stamps, twenty six percent better.

reels.name: Flight
reels.cap: The introduction starts with time of flight.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: what time of flight buys, and why a solid crystal has been slow at it.
reels.words: the introduction starts with time of flight. in pet, an annihilation sends two gamma rays out in opposite directions, to two detectors facing each other. if they arrive at the same moment, the source sat in the middle. the difference in arrival times says how far it sat from the middle. how precisely that difference is measured is called the coincidence time resolution. today's best clinical scanners manage just over two hundred picoseconds, which pins the source to about three centimetres along the line. small benches with thin pixel crystals have gone below one hundred picoseconds, half that blur. clinical scanners use pixelated detectors, a grid of small crystals, each keeping its light on one sipm. a monolithic detector is one solid crystal, tens of millimetres across. it is cheaper and finds the depth of each hit, but its timing is harder, because the light is spread thinly over many sipms, so each sees fewer photons. on the other hand, the many signals together also say where the light landed, which could help the timing. usually, the arrival time in a monolithic crystal is an average of the first few sipm time stamps. each stamp is the moment an analog signal crosses a low trigger level, and the first few are averaged. that is open to noise from dark counts, though digitizing the signals allows a baseline correction. still, squeezing each waveform into one crossing throws most of it away. berg and cherry showed in twenty eighteen that a convolutional network can read time of flight straight from the waveforms of two pixels. this paper does it for a monolithic block, with 3d kernels that look across the sipm grid and along time at once.

reels.name: Simulation
reels.cap: Section two builds the data.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: the simulated block, the events, the symmetry trick, and the crystal's faces.
reels.words: section two builds the data. the crystal is fifty by fifty millimetres, and sixteen millimetres thick, on an eight by eight grid of sipms, each six point zero seven millimetres square. it copies a real detector that places gamma rays to one point one four millimetres. only gamma rays that leave all their energy in the crystal are kept, ten million of them, six million for training, two million for checking, and two million for testing. the square block looks the same turned or flipped eight ways, so only twelve point five percent is simulated, and the rest are copies turned into place. extra test sets of one million each come in tilted, from ten to fifty degrees, to see whether a network trained on straight beams copes. the gate toolkit tracks each gamma ray and the light it makes. the lyso gives twenty nine thousand photons per mega electron volt, rising in seventy picoseconds and dying away over forty two nanoseconds. on page four, the sides are painted black, the top is polished with a mirror on it, and the bottom is coupled to the sipms.

reels.name: Sipm
reels.cap: Table one lists the SiPM, a SensL J-Series, at two voltages.
reels.doc: Pages 4 and 5: the two SiPM settings, and one SiPM's signal built step by step from its photons.
reels.words: table one lists the sipm, a sensl j-series, at two voltages. at plus six volts it detects fifty percent of the photons, against thirty eight at plus two point five, but it also has three times the dark counts and three times the crosstalk. so the paper asks which voltage times better. the sipm signal is then built from the photons gate delivers. here are the photons reaching one sipm in one event. photons are removed at random to match the detection efficiency, and dark counts are added at random times. each count is shifted by a jitter of fifty picoseconds, and some make crosstalk copies of themselves. equation one then turns every count into a small pulse and adds them up, a fast rise and a slow fall. last, electronic noise is added, a tenth of one photon's pulse.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: Section two point two weighs two ways to train.
reels.doc: Pages 5 and 6: one detector against a reference, the cut-out window, and the network's shapes.
reels.words: section two point two weighs two ways to train. one feeds both detectors of a pair to a network, as berg and cherry did. the other times one detector at a time, and subtracts the two times afterwards, so each detector is calibrated on its own. the true times come from a small, fast pixel detector set as far from the source as the first. the network is given a short window of each event. the sixty four signals are summed to find the onset, and the window runs from five hundred picoseconds before it to two thousand five hundred after. it is sampled every hundred picoseconds, thirty one samples per sipm, and the first five hundred picoseconds set the baseline. each event is now a block of eight by eight by thirty one numbers. table two gives the network. three 3d convolutions slide a small kernel, three by three sipms by five samples, stepping two samples at a time, so the block shrinks to six by six by fourteen, then four by four by five, then two by two by one, while the channels grow from one to sixteen, twenty four and thirty two. two by two by thirty two is the hundred and twenty eight numbers the first dense layer takes, and the last gives out one number, the arrival time. the targets are the true arrival times with a hundred picoseconds of jitter added, as the reference detector would give. the network never needs to know where the gamma ray hit, so a single source position, far enough to light the whole detector, calibrates it. training uses the adam optimiser on the mean squared error, stopping when the checking set stops improving for five rounds.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: For comparison, section two point three runs the usual method, a trigger level and an average of the first few stamps.
reels.doc: Pages 6 to 8: the usual method tuned, how a pair's timing comes from one detector's, and the numbers.
reels.words: for comparison, section two point three runs the usual method, a trigger level and an average of the first few stamps. on page seven, it is tuned over one to ten stamps and trigger levels from a tenth of a photon to five photons, keeping the best. results are reported for a pair of identical detectors. each detector's errors against the true arrival time form a bell curve, and combining that curve with its mirror image gives the pair's curve, a little broader. figure one shows both for the network. at plus six volts the pair reaches one hundred and forty one picoseconds, and one hundred and sixty two at plus two point five. figure two, on page eight, tunes the usual method. at plus six volts its best is an average of the first four stamps at six tenths of a photon, one hundred and seventy seven picoseconds. at plus two point five, three stamps at half a photon give one hundred and eighty seven. so the network is twenty six percent better at plus six volts, and fifteen percent better at plus two point five. figure three adds the single-detector numbers and two more measures, with the network ahead on every one. the rest of the results use plus six volts.

reels.name: Angles
reels.cap: Table three, on page nine, sends the tilted test sets through the network trained only on straight beams.
reels.doc: Pages 8 and 9: tilted gamma rays, a network trained on straight ones.
reels.words: table three, on page nine, sends the tilted test sets through the network trained only on straight beams. straight in, the pair times to one hundred and forty one picoseconds. tilting up to fifty degrees only takes it to one hundred and forty five, three percent worse. so one calibration with straight beams is enough.

reels.name: Uniform
reels.cap: Figure four, on page ten, maps a single detector's timing over the crystal.
reels.doc: Pages 9 and 10: where in the crystal the timing is worse, and how it holds up at slower sampling.
reels.words: figure four, on page ten, maps a single detector's timing over the crystal. the first column is the network, the second the usual average, and both are worse at the edges and corners, the average more so. the last column plots it against how deep the gamma ray stopped, and the average gets steadily worse as the hit moves toward the sipms, while the network stays flat. figure five, on page eleven, lowers the sampling rate. the network always gets thirty one samples, so at ten billion samples a second they cover three nanoseconds, and at one billion they cover thirty. the network still times a pair to under two hundred picoseconds at one billion a second, while the average falls apart, near five hundred. so deep learning could make cheaper digitizers good enough.

reels.name: Why
reels.cap: The discussion explains the gap.
reels.doc: Pages 11 and 12: why the network wins, drawn as a hit near the SiPMs, and the average tuned per depth.
reels.words: the discussion explains the gap. at a low trigger level, each sipm's stamp depends only on its very first photon, and the average ignores where the sipms sit. the network sees a window of early photons and how the light is laid out. take a hit close to the sipms. most of its light falls on the one sipm right underneath, so the others see a few stray photons and fire late and at random, yet the average still mixes their stamps in. the same thing makes the timing worse over the centre of each sipm in the map of figure four. figure six, on page twelve, gives the average its best chance, tuning the number of stamps for each of sixteen layers through the crystal. near the top it averages five stamps, close to the sipms only one, and it is still well behind the network there.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: On the voltage, plus six volts wins for both methods.
reels.doc: Pages 12 and 13: the voltage, the reference detector, and what the simulation leaves out.
reels.words: on the voltage, plus six volts wins for both methods. it catches twelve percent more of the photons, including early ones that would be missed. its extra dark counts are mostly removed by the baseline correction, so one voltage can serve both timing and positioning. the reference detector blurs the training targets, but it does not change the answer. zero mean noise on the targets leaves the mean squared error's best answer where it was, and any fixed offset is the same in every detector, so it cancels in the difference. section four point four lists what the simulation leaves out. the sipm never saturates, since its twenty two thousand two hundred and ninety two microcells far outnumber the few hundred photons each one sees. afterpulsing is left out, at zero point seven five percent and five percent. there is no time skew between sipms, and only events that leave their full energy are kept. real measurements will likely be somewhat worse, but the trends should hold.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: The conclusion, on page fourteen, repeats the result.
reels.doc: Pages 14 to 16: the conclusion, and the references worth knowing.
reels.words: the conclusion, on page fourteen, repeats the result. with signals sampled every hundred picoseconds, a 3d network times a pair of fifty by fifty by sixteen millimetre blocks to one hundred and forty one picoseconds, against one hundred and seventy seven for the usual average. among the references, berg and cherry, in twenty eighteen, first read time of flight from waveforms with a network. on page fifteen, decuyper and colleagues placed gamma rays in monolithic blocks with networks, lamprou and colleagues timed large blocks by averaging the first stamps, and onishi and colleagues trained a timing network from a single source position.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All seventeen pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. time of flight and the usual method are on pages one to three, the simulated block on three and four, the sipm signals on four and five, the network on five and six, the main results on six to eight, tilted beams on eight and nine, the timing across the crystal and the sampling rate on nine to eleven, why the network wins on eleven and twelve, the voltage and the limits on twelve and thirteen, and the conclusion and references on fourteen to seventeen. the takeaway is that a 3d network reading every sipm's waveform at once uses the timing and the light pattern together, and in simulation times a pair of monolithic blocks to one hundred and forty one picoseconds, against one hundred and seventy seven for the usual average, while needing only one source position to calibrate.

title: Implementing an integrated neural network for real-time position reconstruction in…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from I triple E Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences, published in twenty twenty four, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture: the crystal's 64 signals going either through 64 converters into a digital processor, or straight into an analog network chip that gives x and y.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from i triple e transactions on radiation and plasma medical sciences, published in twenty twenty four, page by page. the title is implementing an integrated neural network for real-time position reconstruction in emission tomography with monolithic scintillators. it comes from susanna di giacomo and colleagues at the politecnico di milano, with dennis schaart at delft. the abstract sets out the problem. a monolithic detector is one solid crystal on an eight by eight grid of silicon photomultipliers. a gamma ray's light lands on many of them at once, so all sixty four signals must be read. most machine learning hardware is digital, so each signal first needs its own converter to a number, and then a processor works out the position. this paper puts the network itself in analog circuits, so the sixty four signals go straight in, and two come out, the x and y of the hit. the chip has forty two neurons, with weights of five bits, in a zero point three five micrometre process, on twenty three square millimetres. it computes by moving charge through grids of capacitors. tested in simulation and on measured data, it places hits to better than two millimetres, in a crystal ten millimetres thick. it handles two hundred thousand events a second, and spends thirty eight nanojoules on each answer.

reels.name: Why
reels.cap: The introduction starts from what clinical scanners use.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: why monolithic crystals, what they cost in calibration and in data, and the goal: compute the position at the detector.
reels.words: the introduction starts from what clinical scanners use. most cut the crystal into pixels of about three by three by twenty millimetres, so all the light stays in one pixel, and the scanner resolves three to five millimetres. a solid crystal lets the light spread, and the shape of the spread gives the position to better than two millimetres, and the depth too. page two lists scanners already built this way. albira's blocks are ten thick and forty eight millimetres across, and reach zero point seven millimetres. the beta cube uses twenty five millimetre blocks and reaches zero point eight four. caremibrain and the mindview insert use fifty millimetre blocks, fifteen and twenty thick, and reach one point four and one point six. the price is calibration. the detector's response has to be recorded with a beam at a fine grid of positions, and at the edges the light is cut off and reflected. statistical methods and, more and more, neural networks turn the light pattern into a position. those methods need the whole light pattern for every gamma ray. each coincidence involves two modules, with tens of sipms each, and each sipm gives about four bytes. at, say, ten million coincidences a second, that is several gigabytes a second to move and process. the goal of the work is to move that processing to the front end, next to the sipms, with a chip that takes in the analog signals and gives out the coordinates, removing the converters and the processing that follows.

reels.name: Memory
reels.cap: Figure one, on page three, shows the detection module.
reels.doc: Page 3: Fig. 1, the chip in the detector module, and why computing inside the memory saves time and energy.
reels.words: figure one, on page three, shows the detection module. the crystal sits on the sipm array, a front-end chip shapes the sixty four signals, and the network chip turns them into two, x and y, so only two signals need a converter. section two explains the choice of hardware. in an ordinary computer the processor and the memory are separate, and every weight and every input crosses one bus, the von neumann bottleneck. in-memory computing does the arithmetic where the weights are stored. a grid of cells holds the weights, inputs arrive along the rows, and each column adds up its products, all at once. analog networks go back to the nineteen eighties, with resistors, charge-coupled devices, capacitors and floating gates as the memory. here the memory elements are capacitors and the arithmetic is done with charge, which the authors believe is the first analog network for positioning in pet and spect.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: Every layer of a network multiplies each input by a weight and adds the products up, then passes the sum through a nonlinear function.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: multiply and accumulate with capacitors (Fig. 2), the 64-20-20-2 network (Fig. 3), the clipped activation, the output range, and the signal count falling from 64 to 2.
reels.words: every layer of a network multiplies each input by a weight and adds the products up, then passes the sum through a nonlinear function. here the inputs are voltages, each weight is the size of a capacitor, and a charge integrator adds the charges, with a feedback capacitor that sets the scale. figure two, on page four, puts the two side by side. on the left the network, on the right a grid of programmable capacitors, one column per neuron, each ending in an integrator. the network, in figure three, takes sixty four inputs, the eight by eight sipms laid in a line, has two hidden layers of twenty neurons, and gives two outputs, the x and y coordinates. the nonlinear function comes free. the integrator's output cannot go past its power supplies, so it clips, like a relu with a ceiling. each coordinate runs from minus twenty five to plus twenty five millimetres, given out as a voltage from zero to three point three volts. each layer also gets one fixed extra input, the bias. and since only two signals leave the module instead of sixty four, cables, connectors and converters shrink with them.

reels.name: Neuron
reels.cap: Figure four shows one neuron's input.
reels.doc: Pages 4 and 5: the analog neuron (Fig. 4 and 5): a weight as a bank of binary capacitors, the two phases that multiply and add with charge, the sign bit, and charge sharing that cuts the energy fifteen times.
reels.words: figure four shows one neuron's input. the weight is four capacitors, sized one, two, four and eight, each joined in or left out by a switch, so four bits pick a weight from zero to fifteen. a fifth bit gives the sign. five bits is a compromise. more bits mean more capacitors, and capacitors fill most of the chip. with four bits the positions come out about thirty five percent worse, and with three bits about one hundred and twenty percent worse. figure five shows how the neuron computes in two phases. in phase one, switches connect the weight capacitor to the input, and it charges in proportion to both. in phase two, the capacitor is switched over to the integrator, and its charge moves onto the feedback capacitor, raising the output voltage. for a negative weight the capacitor is flipped, and its charge is taken away instead. on page five, every input adds its share, so the output is the sum of each input voltage times its capacitor over the feedback capacitor. charging capacitors costs energy, so the input is put on the smallest capacitor only, and its charge is then shared across the bank, which cuts the energy fifteen times and puts a fifteen under the feedback capacitor.

reels.name: Simulated
reels.cap: Section three trains the network on a P C, with the weights rounded to five bits during training, then loads them into the chip.
reels.doc: Page 5 and Table I: training with 5-bit weights, the weight count, the simulated detector, and how well the quantised network places hits compared with one at full precision.
reels.words: section three trains the network on a p c, with the weights rounded to five bits during training, then loads them into the chip. each layer has one weight per input, plus the bias, per neuron, which adds up to one thousand seven hundred and sixty two weights, or eight point eight one kilobits of memory. the training data come from a monte carlo simulation. the crystal is fifty one millimetres across and ten thick, on eight by eight sipms of six point two millimetres. only events within five percent of the full energy are kept. one hundred thousand events land all over the crystal, split seventy five percent for training, fifteen for testing and ten for validation. a second check uses a pencil beam at an eleven by eleven grid, with six hundred events at each spot. with five-bit weights, in x, the positions scatter over one point two two millimetres at half height, and one point two one in y, with a mean error of one point six six millimetres. at full precision it is one point two three and one point one four, and one point seven two, so five bits lose almost nothing.

reels.name: Measured
reels.cap: The second dataset was measured, on a detector from earlier work by Borghi and colleagues.
reels.doc: Pages 5 and 6 and Table II: a measured detector, the network against k-nearest neighbours, and why their FWHM differ while their mean errors agree.
