reels.words: the second dataset was measured, on a detector from earlier work by borghi and colleagues. its crystal is thirty two millimetres across and twenty two thick, read by eight by eight digital photon counters. a pencil beam visited a grid of one hundred and twenty eight by one hundred and twenty eight spots, one hundred events each. here half the events train the network, ten percent validate it and forty percent test it. borghi's method, k-nearest neighbours, matches each light pattern to stored ones, and reached a spread of about one point seven millimetres. the five-bit network gives two point seven seven and two point nine four, but its total mean error is two point four six millimetres, against two point four four at full precision and two point four eight for k-nearest neighbours. page six explains the gap. the network's errors spread as a bell curve, while k-nearest neighbours gives a sharp peak with wide tails. a width at half height favours the sharp peak, so the fair comparison is the mean error, where the two are the same. and this crystal is thick, twenty two millimetres, where with depth the light from one spot changes, which makes positioning harder for any method.

reels.name: Circuit
reels.cap: Section four simulates the whole circuit at a ten megahertz clock.
reels.doc: Pages 6 and 7: the full circuit simulated in Cadence (Fig. 6), the circuit's imperfections, and noise in the neurons and at the inputs (Fig. 7 and 8), shown to be small against the target.
reels.words: section four simulates the whole circuit at a ten megahertz clock. figure six, on page seven, gives it one event, a hit at minus ten and plus five millimetres, as sixty four sipm voltages, and the two outputs settle within a microsecond. the answer is zero point eight millimetres from the true spot, in line with the software. real switches inject charge and add stray capacitance, so the stray capacitances were put into training, to match the real circuit. noise from the switches and integrators reaches at most four point seven millivolts. figure seven adds up to five millivolts at every neuron, ten thousand times over, and the outputs wander by about zero point one millimetres, zero point two three five at half height. against a target resolution of one point five millimetres, noise adds in quadrature, giving one point five two, too little to matter. figure eight puts the noise on the sixty four inputs instead. five millivolts there moves the answer by less than zero point zero two millimetres, which is negligible.

reels.name: Chip
reels.cap: Figure nine is the layout of the whole chip.
reels.doc: Pages 7 and 8: the layout (Fig. 9), its area, the clock and the event rate, and the energy per answer.
reels.words: figure nine is the layout of the whole chip. the first layer, sixty five inputs by twenty neurons, takes most of it, the second layer is twenty one by twenty, and the output layer twenty one by two. the integrators sit in a column, beside the registers that time the switches. the chip is made in a zero point three five micrometre process and covers twenty three square millimetres, seven and a half of them capacitors. the smallest capacitor is one hundred femtofarads. the old process is cheap and suits most analog front ends, and a newer one would allow smaller capacitors and lower latency. at a ten megahertz clock, one answer takes four point six microseconds, so the chip handles up to two hundred thousand events a second. it draws seven point six milliwatts, and dividing by the rate gives thirty eight nanojoules for each answer. that is ninety three point five five billion operations per second per watt, or one hundred and thirty five point seven counting the analog parts alone.

reels.name: Compare
reels.cap: The discussion admits the network is small.
reels.doc: Page 8: the network is small next to others, the rate fits preclinical scanners, the efficiency sits among digital accelerators, and the circuit's flaws are not yet in training.
reels.words: the discussion admits the network is small. it has forty two neurons in two layers, and places hits to one point two two millimetres. carra and colleagues used six layers and two hundred and twenty three neurons for zero point seven eight. freire and colleagues used two layers of sixty four for x alone, on slabs, for two point six. decuyper and colleagues used three layers of two hundred and fifty six, and reached zero point five. the size was set by the chip's area and its old process, and they also give depth. two hundred thousand events a second suits preclinical scanners such as insert and hyperion two, while an f p g a running boosted trees has reached two million. on efficiency, ninety three point five sits between google's t p u version two at one hundred and eighty and mit's eyeriss at eighty three point one, though they do different jobs. scanners burn hundreds of watts, mostly in electronics and cooling, so less power at the detector saves twice. one gap remains. training happens offline, so the circuit's own flaws are not yet in the loop.

reels.name: Close
reels.cap: The conclusion sums up.
reels.doc: Pages 8 and 9: the conclusion, and the references worth knowing.
reels.words: the conclusion sums up. the chip computes a network with grids of switched capacitors and five-bit weights, and gives the x and y of each hit as voltages. it computes where the data are stored, and since a detector's signals are analog to begin with, they need no converting before the network. among the references, borghi and colleagues describe the measured detector and its k-nearest neighbour calibration. freire and colleagues, decuyper and colleagues, and carra and colleagues each place hits with networks, and each has a video of its own.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All ten pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. why compute at the detector is on pages one and two, computing in the memory on page three, the network on three and four, the analog neuron on four and five, the simulated and measured results on five and six, the circuit and its noise on six and seven, the chip and its energy on seven and eight, and the comparison, conclusion and references on eight to ten. the takeaway is that a small neural network can be built from capacitors and run on the detector's analog signals directly, turning sixty four signals into a position for thirty eight nanojoules, about as well as a full-precision network in software.

title: Music theory for guitar, built from why rather than memorised

reels.name: Octave
reels.cap: Pluck an open string, and its whole length swings back and forth.
reels.words: pluck an open string, and its whole length swings back and forth. how many swings it makes each second is its pitch: for the low e string, about eighty two. now press it at the twelfth fret, exactly halfway. half the length swings twice as fast, a hundred and sixty five times a second. draw the two vibrations as waves, and every crest of the low one meets a crest of the high one. played together, they blend into one sound, the same note, only higher. that doubling is an octave, which is why both are called e. somewhere over the rainbow opens with this same leap. listen.

reels.name: Twelve
reels.cap: After the octave, the simplest ratio is three to two: a string two thirds as long sounds a fifth higher.
reels.doc: Where twelve notes come from: one octave wrapped around a circle (one turn = x2, so a fifth, x1.5, is log2 1.5 = 0.585 of a turn). Hopping by fifths and marking each landing fills the circle; the twelfth landing is 0.0196 turn (a quarter of a semitone) past the start, so the octave holds twelve spots.
reels.words: after the octave, the simplest ratio is three to two: a string two thirds as long sounds a fifth higher. the fifth is the sweetest sound after the octave. listen. so why is a ratio of one and a half called a fifth? the name counts notes, not the ratio. climb the scale from c, through d, e and f, to g. g is the fifth note, and its frequency is one and a half times c's. now wrap one octave around a circle: going once around doubles the frequency, and brings you back to the same note. a fifth is a bit more than half a turn. keep hopping by fifths, and drop a note wherever you land. the landing spots fill the circle, one by one. after twelve hops you are almost exactly back where you started, just a quarter of a semitone past it. that is why an octave holds twelve notes. in numbers: twelve fifths multiply the frequency by about a hundred and thirty, seven octaves by exactly a hundred and twenty eight. modern tuning shares out that difference, nudging the twelve spots to be perfectly even, so every step, a semitone, multiplies the frequency by the same one point oh six. twelve equal steps that together make one doubling: so each step is the twelfth root of two, one point oh five nine five. multiply by it twelve times, and you land on exactly two. the steps multiply rather than add, so the circle is a logarithmic scale: how far round you are is the log, base two, of the frequency ratio.

reels.name: Helix
reels.cap: Now let those twelve notes climb a spiral as the pitch rises, one full turn for each octave.
reels.doc: The twelve notes up a spiral: angle = position in the octave, height = octave. Seen from above (the height squashed to nothing) every octave falls on one circle of twelve spots.
reels.words: now let those twelve notes climb a spiral as the pitch rises, one full turn for each octave. every note sits straight above its own octave, in the same spot on every turn. as a formula: k semitones up, the frequency is multiplied by two to the power k over twelve, which is k twelfths of a turn round, and k twelfths of an octave up. that also explains the eighty two point four from the start. by agreement, this a is tuned to exactly four hundred and forty. low e sits twenty nine semitones below it, so four forty, times two to the minus twenty nine twelfths, is eighty two point four. look straight down the spiral, and every octave falls onto one circle: twelve spots, and each one needs a name.

reels.name: Letters
reels.cap: Most music uses just seven of the twelve.
reels.doc: The seven lettered notes are seven fifths in a row (F C G D A E B); in pitch order two of their steps are one semitone (E-F, B-C). The other five take a neighbour's name. The piano keyboard lays it out.
reels.words: most music uses just seven of the twelve. take seven hops in a row along the fifths, and you get seven notes that all agree, each a fifth from the next. those seven got the letters a to g, in order of pitch. in that order, two of the steps are only one semitone: e to f, and b to c. the five notes left over take a neighbour's name, a sharp just above it or a flat just below. that is the piano keyboard: white keys for the seven letters, black keys for the five in between, and no black key at the two half steps. so there is no e sharp: it would just be f.

reels.name: Major
reels.cap: Line up the seven letters starting from C, and climb: the steps go whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
reels.doc: The seven letters from C as a ladder of steps (the major scale), then a public-domain melody walked on it, its contour drawn as a piano roll as it plays.
reels.words: line up the seven letters starting from c, and climb: the steps go whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. that ladder of steps is the major scale. listen. melodies are walks on this ladder. here is twinkle, twinkle, little star. its first leap, c up to g, is a fifth, and the shape it traces on the ladder is the tune itself.

reels.name: Neck3 d
reels.cap: A guitar neck is a ruler for these steps.
reels.doc: The neck in 3D, then from above: the frets are a ruler of semitones at their real spacing.
reels.words: a guitar neck is a ruler for these steps. each fret shortens the string just enough to raise it one semitone, and because each step takes a fixed fraction of what is left, the frets crowd closer as they climb. the twelfth fret sits at exactly half the string, the octave, and the seventh a third of the way along, leaving two thirds ringing: the fifth we hopped by. in numbers: each fret leaves the string one over one point oh five nine five as long, about ninety four percent of it, so after n frets, two to the minus n over twelve is left. twelve frets leave two to the minus one, a half. seven leave about two thirds.

reels.name: Tuning
reels.cap: Now the six strings.
reels.words: now the six strings. fret five on the low e string is a, the same note as the next string played open. listen. the same holds all the way across: each string is five semitones, a fourth, above the one below, except g to b, which is only four. why fourths? your hand spans about four frets, so with the strings a fourth apart, you can walk up through every semitone without moving it: each string carries on where the last one stopped. if every gap were a fourth, the top string would be f. shrinking one gap to four semitones pulls it back to e, so both outer strings are e, two octaves apart, and the common chord shapes fit the fingers.

reels.name: Notes
reels.cap: Now name every fret with the letters.
reels.words: now name every fret with the letters. walk up from each open string, two frets for each letter, but only one from e to f and from b to c, where the piano had no black key. every other string works the same way from its own open note, and at the twelfth fret the whole pattern starts again, an octave up. each note turns up in several places. here are all the e's. one octave up is always two strings up and two frets along, or three frets when you cross onto the b string.

reels.name: Intervals
reels.cap: The distance between two notes is an interval, and on the neck it is just a count of frets.
reels.words: the distance between two notes is an interval, and on the neck it is just a count of frets. three frets is a minor third, four a major third, five a fourth, seven a fifth, and twelve an octave. you already know these sounds from famous openings. greensleeves begins with a minor third, when the saints go marching in with a major third, here comes the bride with a fourth, twinkle, twinkle with a fifth, and somewhere over the rainbow with an octave. listen to each. why do these sound smooth? each sits close to a simple ratio of frequencies: six to five, five to four, four to three, three to two and two to one. add up the two waves of a fifth, and the sum repeats every two cycles, a short, steady pattern the ear hears as smooth. six frets, the tritone, is about the square root of two: the opening leap of maria, from west side story. its waves never settle into a short pattern, and it sounds tense. listen to a fifth, then a tritone.

reels.name: Power
reels.cap: Guitarists use the fifth on its own all the time.
reels.doc: The fifth on its own as a movable shape: root, fifth (one string up, two frets along) and octave; no third.
reels.words: guitarists use the fifth on its own all the time. put a finger on a root, add the fifth, one string up and two frets along, and the root again an octave above. that is a power chord. listen. it has no third, so it is neither major nor minor, and its simple three to two stays clean even through heavy distortion. that is why so many rock and punk riffs are built from it, like smells like teen spirit. the shape never changes, so sliding it along the neck plays any root. listen.

reels.name: Maj min
reels.cap: What makes a scale major is mostly one note: the third.
reels.words: what makes a scale major is mostly one note: the third. from c up to e is four semitones, a major third, close to the simple, bright five to four. listen to twinkle, twinkle once more. now lower the third by one fret, to three semitones, and the sixth with it. same tune, same rhythm. listen to the mood change. that darker sound is minor. the full natural minor scale lowers the seventh too, and then its steps match the white keys played from a, so every major key has a minor key hiding inside it.

reels.name: Triads
reels.cap: A chord is several notes at once, and the basic recipe is to stack thirds: take every other note of the scale, C, E and G.
reels.doc: Chords as triangles on the clock of twelve notes: a major triad's sides are 4, 3 and 5 semitones, a minor triad the mirror image (3, 4, 5); turning a triangle around the clock keeps the chord type and changes the root.
reels.words: a chord is several notes at once, and the basic recipe is to stack thirds: take every other note of the scale, c, e and g. on the clock they make a triangle: four semitones, then three, then five back to the start. lower the e to e flat, and the sides swap, three then four: a minor chord, the major triangle flipped as in a mirror. turn a triangle around the clock, and you get the same kind of chord on a new root: here, d minor. two stacked thirds give only four triangles: major, minor, diminished, squeezed small, and augmented, perfectly even. listen to each.

reels.name: Shapes
reels.cap: On the neck, a triangle becomes a hand shape.
reels.words: on the neck, a triangle becomes a hand shape. this is e major, spread over all six strings: three roots, one third, and two fifths. listen. move the third down one fret, and it becomes e minor, the same one note change as before. listen. put the third back, and slide the whole shape up five frets, with one finger barring where the open strings were, and it is a major. intervals don't care where they start, so every shape moves.

reels.name: Key
reels.cap: Now stay inside one key, using only the seven notes of C major.
reels.doc: The triangle walked through the seven notes of C major, using only those notes: its shape (the chord type) changes by itself, giving I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
reels.words: now stay inside one key, using only the seven notes of c major. build a triangle on each note of the scale, and it changes shape by itself as it climbs: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. guitarists call these chords by their number in the scale, so in every key, one, four and five are the major chords, and six is the main minor one. listen to all seven, climbing.

reels.name: Progress
reels.cap: A song is a walk between these numbered chords.
reels.doc: What a guitarist sees: the chords of a key as root positions on the neck (I on the low E string, IV and V on the A string), the same pattern in every key. Progressions named from songs; only chords are played.
reels.words: a song is a walk between these numbered chords. one, four and five alone carry thousands of songs, like twist and shout, la bamba and wild thing. on the neck the pattern never changes: one has its root on the low e string, four sits on the next string at the same fret, and five two frets further along. listen, in the key of a. add six, the minor chord, and you get the most famous loop in pop: one, five, six, four. let it be, with or without you and don't stop believin' all ride it, each in its own key. listen. to change key, guitarists don't relearn anything. slide the whole pattern three frets up, and the same numbers now play in c. listen.

reels.name: Pull
reels.cap: Why does five lead home so strongly?
reels.doc: Why V leads to I: G7 holds the tritone B-F, and each of those notes is a semitone from a note of C major.
reels.words: why does five lead home so strongly? stack one more third on the g chord, and you get g seven: g, b, d and f. b and f are six semitones apart, the tense tritone from before. and each of them is one semitone from home: b rises to c, f falls to e. the tension lets go onto the home chord, c. listen.

reels.name: Scale neck
reels.cap: On the guitar, a key is less a list of letters than a picture.
reels.doc: A key on the guitar is a picture: C major's notes over the whole neck, carved into windows a hand can cover, which overlap and repeat at the twelfth fret; a new key slides the whole picture.
reels.words: on the guitar, a key is less a list of letters than a picture. here is every note of c major from the nut to the fifteenth fret: the natural notes from before, with every c marked as home. nobody reads it all at once. players carve it into positions: a window of about four frets, where every note sits under a finger without moving the hand. listen to two octaves of c inside this one. slide the window and the same notes take a new fingering. a handful of these windows cover the neck, each one overlapping the next, and from the twelfth fret the picture starts over. changing key slides the whole picture. g major is this same pattern, five frets lower. listen to it in the window at the second fret.

reels.name: Modes
reels.cap: Start the same seven notes on each of their seven letters, and you get seven modes, each with its own mood.
reels.words: start the same seven notes on each of their seven letters, and you get seven modes, each with its own mood. here they all share one root, brightest at the top. going down, each mode lowers exactly one note by a semitone. major is second from the top, natural minor is fifth, and at the bottom sits locrian, so dark that even its fifth has dropped. each mode's flavour comes from the note that sets it apart. sweet home alabama is mixolydian: major, with a lowered seventh. oye como va is dorian: minor, with a raised sixth. and the simpsons theme is lydian: major, with a raised fourth.

reels.name: Mode shapes
reels.cap: On the neck, the modes get much simpler.
reels.doc: Modes under the hand, two ways. Parallel: keep A's root and position and move one finger, each step lowering one note a fret (Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian). Relative: each of those is the dots of another major key.
reels.words: on the neck, the modes get much simpler. here is a major in one position, its root on the fifth fret. listen. guitarists also read it the other way round. a mixolydian uses exactly the notes of d major, a dorian those of g major, and a minor those of c. so, dorian over a often just means: play your g major shapes, but make a home.

reels.name: Penta
reels.cap: The major scale has two half steps, and those are where notes clash.
reels.words: the major scale has two half steps, and those are where notes clash. drop the two notes that make them, f and b, and five notes remain with no half steps at all: the pentatonic scale. start those five on a, and you get the minor pentatonic. on the neck it falls under the hand as one box at the fifth fret, with its roots here. soloists think of it as a map: almost nothing in it sounds wrong. the solo of stairway to heaven lives largely inside this box. listen.

reels.name: Boxes
reels.cap: That box is not alone.
reels.doc: The pentatonic over the whole neck: the box is one of five overlapping windows on one pattern, which repeat at the twelfth fret; soloists climb through them; the minor shape slid three frets down is the major pentatonic.
reels.words: that box is not alone. here are the same five notes over the whole neck. the box from stairway is one window on it. slide the window and you get the next box, sharing notes with the last. five boxes in all, and from the twelfth fret they repeat. soloists use that overlap to travel: a phrase in one box, a step into the next. listen to the top string alone walk up the neck through all five. over an a chord, the box at the fifth fret sounds bluesy and dark. listen. for a sweeter, country sound, players slide the whole pattern three frets down. now the same dots spell a major pentatonic, with a sitting where c used to be: the relative minor from before, as a shape. listen to the same box at the second fret.

reels.name: Blues
reels.cap: Add one note to the minor pentatonic, the flat fifth, and you have the blues scale.
reels.words: add one note to the minor pentatonic, the flat fifth, and you have the blues scale. it squeezes between the fourth and the fifth, a passing note full of tension. the other secret is the third. blues plays this minor third over major chords, where it rubs against the chord's own major third, one fret higher. so guitarists bend it part of the way, to a pitch between the two that no fret can give: the blue note. listen. underneath, the band plays dominant seventh chords on one, four and five, in a loop twelve bars long. johnny b. goode is this loop, and so are a thousand other songs. the chords' roots sit right inside the box, so the whole form lives under one hand. listen to all twelve bars.

reels.name: Jam
reels.cap: When musicians play together, they rarely name notes.
reels.doc: Playing with others: 'blues in A' becomes one root on the low E string; the chords' roots and the soloing box hang off it; the box holds the root and seventh of every chord, so a soloist aims for those as the chords change; a new key is a slide, or a capo.
reels.words: when musicians play together, they rarely name notes. someone just calls out: blues in a. the guitarist's first move is to find a on the low e string, at the fifth fret. everything else hangs off that one dot. the chords come from the numbers: four on the next string at the same fret, five two frets on. and the soloing box sits on that same root, so chords and solo share one place on the neck. then, as the chords change, they aim for each chord's own notes. over a seven: a, e and g. over d seven: d, a and c. over e seven: e and d. the box holds the root and the seventh of all three chords, which is why one box can carry a whole blues. listen to a solo that lands on them. and when the singer says, take it up a whole step, nobody relearns a thing: slide everything two frets, and it's blues in b. or clamp a capo at the second fret, and keep playing the same shapes. listen.

reels.name: Map
reels.cap: So, from the start: doubling the frequency gives the octave.
reels.words: so, from the start: doubling the frequency gives the octave. hopping by fifths fills the octave with twelve notes. seven fifths in a row became the lettered notes and the major scale, and its third decides major or minor. stacking thirds makes the chords, and their place in the scale gives the numbers songs are built from. the neck lays it all out as shapes that move. learn why, and there is very little left to memorise.

title: Probabilistic bias correction

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Weather forecasts are now good about two weeks ahead.
reels.words: weather forecasts are now good about two weeks ahead. beyond that, in weeks three to six, their skill falls away, and forecasters call this stretch the predictability desert. this nature paper adds a cheap machine learning step after the forecast. it is called probabilistic bias correction, or p b c. for every grid cell on the globe, it corrects the forecast's probabilities rather than the weather itself. we will see how forecasts for weeks three and four are scored, what the two corrections inside p b c do, and how much skill they add.

reels.name: Score
reels.cap: Take one grid cell and one target, the average temperature in week three.
reels.doc: One cell, one week: 100 climatological observations set the quintiles; the ensemble becomes a staircase F(k); the observation a 0/1 staircase O(k); RPS is the summed squared gap. Synthetic numbers (src/compute.py).
reels.words: take one grid cell and one target, the average temperature in week three. twenty years of observations around this date set four thresholds, called quintiles, which split history into five equally likely bins. the forecast model runs an ensemble of fifty-one members. at each threshold we count the fraction of members that fall below it. these fractions form a staircase, f of k, which gives the chance of ending up below threshold k. then the week happens, and the observation lands here. it makes a staircase too, which is zero below its bin and one from there up. the ranked probability score squares the gap between the two staircases at each threshold, and adds them up to one point five six. climatology always says twenty, forty, sixty and eighty percent, and here it scores zero point six. the skill score, r p s s, is one minus the ratio of the two, taken over many weeks and the whole globe. a positive skill score means the forecast beats climatology.

reels.name: Pipeline
reels.cap: P B C takes in three things.
reels.doc: Fig. 1 redrawn as inputs -> two corrections -> projection -> average -> output.
reels.words: p b c takes in three things. the first is the model's ensemble, the second is the climatological thresholds, and the third is recently observed weather. what comes out is a corrected staircase for every cell, bin and lead time. inside, two light models run side by side. one is called debias plus plus, and the other persistence plus plus. each output is projected onto valid distributions, and then the two are averaged. the whole thing is retrained every day.

reels.name: Debias
reels.cap: Debias plus plus takes in today's staircase, the model's past forecasts, and what the weather actually did on those dates.
reels.doc: Debias++: the mean gap between observed and forecast staircases over a window of dates in each of the past 20 years, added to today's staircase and clipped to [0, 1]. Synthetic warm-running model (src/compute.py).
reels.words: debias plus plus takes in today's staircase, the model's past forecasts, and what the weather actually did on those dates. it gives back a corrected staircase. it looks at a window of dates around today's date, in each of the past twenty years. averaged over that window, the model's staircase sits below the observed one, because this model runs warm. the gap between them is the bias, measured separately in each bin. debias plus plus adds that gap to today's forecast, and clips the result so that it stays between zero and one. the window can be fourteen, twenty-eight or thirty-five days wide, and the width that scored best over the previous three years is used.

reels.name: Persist
reels.cap: Persistence plus plus adds what the model may miss, which is recent weather and the time of year.
reels.doc: Persistence++ for one bin: least-squares weights on [1, climatology, two lagged observed indicators, the model's forecast], fitted on 20 years of synthetic weeks; output clipped to [0, 1] (src/compute.py).
reels.words: persistence plus plus adds what the model may miss, which is recent weather and the time of year. when the forecast is issued, the latest observed week is known, and so is one a lead time earlier. the target week is three weeks ahead. for each cell and bin, it takes in five numbers. the first is a constant, the second is the climatological probability for this date, the next two say whether each observed week fell below the threshold, and the last is the model's own forecast. a least-squares fit on past weeks gives each number a weight. the weighted sum, clipped between zero and one, becomes the new probability. here both observed weeks were cold. the model alone gave a chance of zero point one of falling below the second threshold, and persistence plus plus raises it to zero point five six.

reels.name: Project
reels.cap: Each correction works on one bin at a time, so a staircase can come out stepping down, and no real distribution can do that.
reels.doc: Projection onto valid CDFs, drawn for three thresholds: staircases (F1, F2, F3) with 0 <= F1 <= F2 <= F3 <= 1 fill a tetrahedron whose corners are the four possible observations; RPS is the squared distance to the corner that happened. Isotonic regression is the nearest-point projection, so it moves closer to every corner.
reels.words: each correction works on one bin at a time, so a staircase can come out stepping down, and no real distribution can do that. with three thresholds, each staircase is a point in three dimensions, with one coordinate per threshold. the staircases that never step down fill this tetrahedron. each possible observation sits at one of its four corners. the score is the squared distance from the forecast to the corner that actually happened. isotonic regression moves an invalid point to the nearest point of the tetrahedron, and that brings it closer to the observed corner. because the tetrahedron is convex, the move brings it closer to all four corners at once, so the score improves whatever the weather does. finally, the two corrections are averaged. the midpoint of two points inside the tetrahedron is also inside it.

reels.name: Ecmwf
reels.cap: First comes ECMWF's dynamical ensemble, tested from 2016 to 2024.
reels.doc: Fig. 2a redrawn: global RPSS 2016-2024 for raw, operationally debiased and PBC-corrected ECMWF.
reels.words: first comes ecmwf's dynamical ensemble, tested from 2016 to 2024. its raw temperature and pressure forecasts score below zero, which is worse than climatology. ecmwf's own operational debiasing lifts them above zero. given the same forecasts, p b c beats both baselines for every variable and both weeks. for temperature it adds 26 to 37 percent to the debiased skill, and for pressure it adds 16 to 32 percent. for precipitation, where debiasing leaves almost no skill, p b c reaches zero point zero six to zero point zero seven. it improves precipitation skill in 98 percent of grid cells.

reels.name: Quest
reels.cap: P B C also works on A I models.
reels.doc: AIFS doubled (text), then Fig. 4 redrawn for precipitation: AI Weather Quest, autumn 2025, live RPSS.
reels.words: p b c also works on a i models. applied to ecmwf's a i model, a i f s, it doubled the mean skill of zero point zero three. then came a live test in ecmwf's 2025 a i weather quest, where forecasts are submitted before the weather happens. the authors entered p b c applied to e c m w f and to poet, a hybrid a i model, under the name microduet. in the autumn season it was the best entry for every variable and both weeks. it beat six national forecasting centres, their combined ensemble, three versions of a i f s and thirty-four other teams. precipitation shows the gap most clearly. all six centres' debiased forecasts score below zero. their combined ensemble gets back above zero. microduet scores zero point zero seven in week three and zero point zero six in week four. that is more than twice the combined ensemble in week three, and three times it in week four.

reels.name: Extremes
reels.cap: When it is retrained for the top and bottom five percent, P B C also improves forecasts of extremes.
reels.doc: Fig. 5c redrawn: flood BSS for the top precipitation semidecile, all GDACS floods and severe ones.
reels.words: when it is retrained for the top and bottom five percent, p b c also improves forecasts of extremes. floods are the hardest test. the paper scores two thousand four hundred and thirty-five flood events from 2016 to 2026. each one is judged on the heavy-rain forecast in a twenty degree box around the flood. raw e c m w f scores between zero point zero four and zero point zero six. operational debiasing drives that to nearly zero. p b c raises the raw skill by 76 to 92 percent. for the eighty-eight severe floods, which killed over a hundred people or displaced eighty thousand, it raises the skill by 86 to 150 percent.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: P B C has clear limits.
reels.words: p b c has clear limits. it learns errors that repeat, but it does not learn new physics. it can only sharpen the signal that is already in the model, so it is post-processing rather than a better model. the skill it reaches is still modest. a skill score near zero point one means the forecast's error is about ten percent smaller than climatology's. the truth it is scored against is also the e r a 5 reanalysis on a one and a half degree grid, not station measurements. what it offers is low cost. it is a few small fits, retrained daily on top of any model, and the code is open. that was enough to top the first season of the a i weather quest.

title: Model-Based Deep Learning PET Image Reconstruction Using Forward-Backward Splitting…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a paper from I triple E Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences, published in twenty twenty one, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture: data and the current image go into an EM step and a regularisation step, a fusion joins them; then the abstract's numbers as bars.
reels.words: this video reads a paper from i triple e transactions on radiation and plasma medical sciences, published in twenty twenty one, page by page. its title is model-based deep learning pet image reconstruction using forward backward splitting expectation maximisation. it is by abolfazl mehranian and andrew reader at king's college london. the abstract says the method splits each update of a map reconstruction into three steps. an e m step fits the image to the data through the physics, a regularisation step cleans the current image, and a fusion blends the two, weighted by one number. the regulariser can be a small convolutional network, and the whole algorithm is then unrolled into a recurrent network whose weights, including the regularisation strength, are shared by every update. it is compared with o s e m, an m r guided map e m, and a u-net that denoises images after reconstruction. on simulations, the errors were twenty point seven percent for o s e m and seventeen point seven for map e m, against thirteen point four for the u-net and fourteen point four for f b s e m. on patient scans, the regional errors were seven point eight, five point nine, five point seven and three point nine percent. the authors conclude that the u-net denoiser did about as well as their network.

reels.name: Background
reels.cap: The introduction starts with priors.
reels.doc: Pages 1 and 2: why learn a prior (a handcrafted smoothing prior dims a small lesion, shown on our phantom), the three groups of deep learning for PET reconstruction, the unrolled methods before this one, and what the paper sets out to do.
reels.words: the introduction starts with priors. most come from markov random fields, and charge for differences between neighbouring voxels, on the idea that those differences are noise. but they smooth away real detail as well. on our own phantom, a strong smoothing prior leaves a small lesion fifty four percent too dim. it then sorts deep learning for pet reconstruction into three groups. direct methods learn the whole mapping from sinogram to image. enhancement methods clean up an image after it is reconstructed. and model-based methods unroll an iterative algorithm, so the network works inside the physics. gong and colleagues unrolled an a d m m algorithm with a u-net prior. lim and colleagues unrolled block coordinate descent, with a different denoiser at every iteration. this paper proposes an algorithm that works with any differentiable convex prior, learns every hyperparameter from data, can take an m r image as a second input, and asks whether a reconstruction network beats simply denoising afterwards.

reels.name: Split
reels.cap: Section two starts from the MAP reconstruction.
reels.doc: Page 2 (and 3): the MAP objective, forward-backward splitting into a regularisation step and an EM step, the closed-form fusion, run on our phantom; Algorithm 1; and what gamma does (our run, swept over gamma), down to its two limits, OSEM and De Pierro's MAPEM.
reels.words: section two starts from the map reconstruction. it maximises the poisson log likelihood of the data, minus a penalty r, weighted by beta. forward backward splitting solves this in two moves, a gradient step down the penalty, then a proximal step toward the data. here it is on our own phantom, at the twentieth update. the regularisation step moves the current image a little way down the penalty, which smooths it. the e m step is the ordinary m l e m update, which fits the data through the system matrix. setting a derivative to zero then gives a closed form that fuses the two images, voxel by voxel. the weight is set by delta, one over gamma times the sensitivity. algorithm one lists the steps, with ordered subsets for speed. equation seven regularises, equation eight is the e m update, and equation nine fuses them. gamma decides how much each step counts. with a small gamma, the fused image follows the smoothed one, and in our run the small lesion comes out fifty four percent too dim. in between, it is nineteen percent too dim, with little noise. as gamma grows, the fusion keeps the e m image, and page three notes that in that limit the algorithm becomes o s e m, noise and all. with a quadratic prior over m r chosen neighbours, it becomes de pierro's map e m instead.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: For the regulariser the authors use a convolutional network, and unroll the algorithm into a recurrent network with N states, one per update, sharing their parameters, so the number of weights does not grow with the numb
reels.doc: Page 3: the unrolled network of Fig. 1 (EM update, residual learning unit, ReLU, fusion, optional MR input, the same weights in every state) and the supervised loss, Eq. (12).
reels.words: for the regulariser the authors use a convolutional network, and unroll the algorithm into a recurrent network with n states, one per update, sharing their parameters, so the number of weights does not grow with the number of updates. figure one draws it. each state has an e m update fed by the data y, a residual learning unit of d convolution layers, which adds its output back to the input image and passes the sum through a rectified linear unit, so the image can never go negative, and a fusion block whose only trainable number is gamma. an m r image can be fed in as a second channel. training is supervised. each example is a low-dose sinogram, with an optional m r image, and a high-dose reference image. the weights are chosen to make the squared error between the last state's image and the reference small, averaged over the training set.

reels.name: Data
reels.cap: The simulations start from the M R scans of seventy patients, segmented into tissues.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: the simulated phantoms (uptakes as bars, the dataset count), the high- and low-dose counts, the patients (35 to train, 10 to test, 30 and 2 minute scans), and Fig. 2's reason for a MAPEM reference.
reels.words: the simulations start from the m r scans of seventy patients, segmented into tissues. white matter is given an uptake of thirty two and grey matter ninety six, three to one. four lesions of two to eight millimetres are added, hot ones at one hundred and forty four and cold ones at forty eight. three random rotations of each give two hundred and ten datasets. from each, a high-dose sinogram of one billion counts is simulated, and a low-dose one with ninety to one hundred and twenty million, about ten times fewer. the real data are brain pet m r scans of forty five patients. thirty five are used for training and ten for testing. each thirty minute scan is also cut down to two minutes, fifteen times shorter, to make the low-dose input. figure two shows why the patient reference is not plain o s e m. low-dose o s e m in the simulations is noisy next to the high-dose reference. for patients, longer o s e m runs sharpen the image, but adds ringing at the edges, so an m r guided map e m image of the full scan is used instead.

reels.name: Training
reels.cap: Two versions of each network are trained, one on PET alone and one with the M R image as well.
reels.doc: Pages 4 and 5: the four networks (FBSEM-Net and U-Net, PET only or with MR), the shortcuts that made 3-D training fit (twelve states drawn as blocks), and Table I's weight counts.
reels.words: two versions of each network are trained, one on pet alone and one with the m r image as well. the comparison is a u-net that denoises a reconstructed image, extended to 3-d. the e m step runs on a g p u projector, and only the regulariser and fusion have weights. training a 3-d unrolled network is slow and memory hungry, so the sinograms are trimmed, one example is used at a time, the network starts from an o s e m image, and it is unrolled for only twelve states, three iterations of four subsets. no validation set is used. table one lists the settings. for the simulations the u-net has about ten million weights, and f b s e m net about fifty thousand, some two hundred times fewer. for patients, it is forty eight million against seventy six thousand.

reels.name: Sim results
reels.cap: Six methods are compared on the test simulations, by lesion error, overall error, and how well lesions stand out from the noise.
reels.doc: Pages 5 to 7: Fig. 3 (one simulated test case, MAPEM's suppressed lesion) and Fig. 4 (lesion error and NRMSE averaged over ten test cases), and the simulation verdict.
reels.words: six methods are compared on the test simulations, by lesion error, overall error, and how well lesions stand out from the noise. figure three shows one test case. low-dose o s e m is noisy. m r guided map e m smooths the noise, but the arrow marks a lesion it suppresses, since the m r image does not show it. the u-net and f b s e m net both look close to the reference. figure four averages the test cases. for hot lesions, map e m reads twenty five point seven percent too low, and f b s e m net on pet alone only seven point four. with m r, the u-net does better on lesions, ten percent against seventeen point six. in overall error, the two m r versions come out lowest. for the simulations, the authors note that the pet-only u-net beats f b s e m net.

reels.name: Patients
reels.cap: For patients, the authors gave F B S E M net more kernels and fewer layers, three layers of thirty seven kernels instead of nine layers of sixteen, and pushed the U-Net to the limit of their G P U memory.
reels.doc: Pages 7 and 8: the patient network's shape (kernels and layers drawn), Fig. 6, Table II's regional errors, and Fig. 8's shorter scans.
reels.words: for patients, the authors gave f b s e m net more kernels and fewer layers, three layers of thirty seven kernels instead of nine layers of sixteen, and pushed the u-net to the limit of their g p u memory. figure six compares two minute scans with their thirty minute references. o s e m is noisy. map e m is not fully converged. the u-net and f b s e m net look much alike, and close to the reference. table two gives the error in mean activity for seven brain regions. combining their mean and spread, f b s e m net with m r has the lowest error, three percent, against six point eight for the u-net with m r and five point nine for map e m. the networks were trained only on two minute scans. figure eight tries them on one minute and thirty second scans, thirty and sixty times shorter than the reference. noise takes over o s e m and map e m, while at thirty seconds f b s e m net on pet alone leaves less noise than the u-net.

reels.name: Discussion
reels.cap: The discussion lists what sets F B S E M net apart.
reels.doc: Pages 9 and 10: shared weights against one network per update (drawn as two chains), gradients that skip the projector, the U-Net's weight count, Fig. 9's physiology catch, and the conclusion.
reels.words: the discussion lists what sets f b s e m net apart. b c d net and e m net train a separate network for every update, while f b s e m net shares one across them all, so it has fewer weights and can run for any number of updates. its regularisation strength is learned, and it can start from a uniform image. and in training, the gradients pass only through the regulariser and the fusion, never through the forward and back projections. the u-net trained on patients had about six hundred times more weights than f b s e m net, which can make it fit its training data too closely. figure nine shows a catch. in the thalamus, uptake rose between the two minute and the thirty minute scans. the networks raised the two minute uptake toward the thirty minute value, so they do not only remove noise, they predict physiology the short scan never saw. the conclusion is candid. with these settings, the u-net denoiser and f b s e m net performed comparably, so denoising after reconstruction can potentially do as well as a reconstruction network.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All 12 pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. the background is on pages one and two, the f b s e m algorithm on two and three, the network, data and training on three to five, the simulation results on five to seven, the patient results on seven and eight, and the discussion on nine and ten. the takeaway is that each update can keep the physics in its e m step, and leave only a small regulariser and one fusion weight to learn. here that matched a denoiser hundreds of times larger, which is both the method's strength and the paper's honest caveat.

title: Deep Learning for PET Image Reconstruction

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a review from I triple E Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences, published in twenty twenty one, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the paper is, who wrote it, and the abstract as one picture: counts in, image out, and the two ways a network can sit in between (all of it learned, or only the prior learned beside trusted physics).
reels.words: this video reads a review from i triple e transactions on radiation and plasma medical sciences, published in twenty twenty one, page by page. its title is deep learning for pet image reconstruction. it comes from andrew reader and colleagues at king's college london. reconstruction turns the counts a scanner records into an image of the tracer. the abstract says deep learning can do this in two ways. a direct method learns the whole mapping, physics and noise included, from scratch. a model-based method keeps the trusted model of the physics and the noise, and learns only the parts we are unsure of, such as the regularization. the introduction says what makes it deep. the mapping is a cascade of operators called layers, and their parameters are learned from training examples. networks reached medical image reconstruction from twenty sixteen, and pet specifically from about twenty eighteen.

reels.name: Model
reels.cap: Section two starts with conventional reconstruction.
reels.doc: Pages 2 and 3: the conventional recipe as one picture that grows. An image goes through the system matrix to the mean counts and through Poisson noise to the measured counts; one ML-EM update taken apart on our phantom; then the penalty, and the prior image that later methods will lean on.
reels.words: section two starts with conventional reconstruction. the image is a grid of voxel values, a vector x. the system matrix a says how strongly each voxel feeds each line of response, and a background r adds scatter and randoms, giving the mean counts to expect. the counts actually recorded scatter around that mean, following poisson statistics. maximum likelihood expectation maximization, or m l e m, finds the image that best explains the counts. each update predicts the data from the current image, divides the measured counts by that prediction, projects those ratios back into the image, and multiplies, so voxels that were too dim get brighter. run on noisy data, it fits the noise as well, giving what the paper calls a night sky reconstruction. so a penalty, r of x, is added to the objective, with a weight beta for its strength. a common choice charges for differences between neighbouring voxels, so a smooth image costs little and a speckled one costs a lot. the paper notes that priors like this are handcrafted for convenience, not learned from evidence. one more matters later, a prior image p, which the estimate is penalised for straying from.

reels.name: Synthesis
reels.cap: The other way to regularize builds the image from parts.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: an image built from basis images (our phantom from its four regions), Fig. 1's loop, and the three drawbacks that the rest of the review answers.
reels.words: the other way to regularize builds the image from parts. the image is a weighted sum of basis images, x equals b times z. our phantom is four region images, weighted by their activities. with only positive weights on smooth parts, a speckled night sky cannot be built. with basis images taken from the patient's magnetic resonance, or m r, scan, this is the kernel method. figure one, on page four, draws the conventional loop. the measured data and the model's prediction from the current estimate are compared in an objective function, and an algorithm updates the estimate. the ground truth t sits to one side, and never enters. the section ends with three drawbacks. fitting noisy data gives noisy images. the prior and its strength beta are chosen by hand. and everything assumes the system model and the noise model are right. the paper says deep learning can address all three.

reels.name: Shift
reels.cap: Section three is the turn.
reels.doc: Pages 4 and 5: the turn. Aim at a good target t instead of the noisy data, learn one mapping F from training pairs (Fig. 2), and stop training when the validation loss turns up.
reels.words: section three is the turn. instead of fitting the noisy data, the a i approach aims at a high quality target, t, and learns a mapping, f, with parameters theta, that takes the data to the target. ideally t is the ground truth, or else an image from far more counts. figure two, on page five, shows the training pairs, measured data along the top, and their targets below. training adjusts theta to make the loss small over all n pairs at once, one mapping for every example. a separate validation set, kept out of the fitting, is watched during training. when its loss starts to rise, the network is learning the training examples rather than the task, so training stops. the hope is that the mapping then generalizes to new data from the same domain.

reels.name: Layers
reels.cap: What can F be?
reels.doc: Pages 5 to 8: a fully connected layer (every input wired to each output), a convolution (one small kernel slid over the image; Fig. 4's learned kernels), and a ReLU after a bias (our edge example; Fig. 5).
reels.words: what can f be? the simplest is linear, a matrix times the data. each output voxel is then a weighted sum of every input value, with the weights along one row of the matrix, which is a fully connected layer. at pet sizes that is millions to trillions of weights. filtered backprojection proves that good linear mappings exist, and a learned one would also learn to suppress the noise. a convolution shares one small kernel across the whole image. here the data are just a noisy image, and the kernel slides over it, giving one output pixel at each stop. figure four learns a single kernel to turn noisy images into clean ones. the noisier the input, the wider the learned kernel, which averages more. for a blurred input it learns a sharpening kernel instead. after a convolution comes a nonlinearity, acting on each voxel. the relu sets negative values to zero and keeps the positive ones, and a bias added first moves where that cut falls. in our example, run over the phantom, an edge kernel finds its edges, positive on one side and negative on the other, and after a bias and the relu only the lesion rims are left. figure five, on page eight, does the same with three kernels. each kernel gives its own map, a bias and a relu threshold each one, and a last kernel with three channels sums them into one output.

reels.name: Deep
reels.cap: Stacking layers makes the network deep.
reels.doc: Pages 7 to 12: layers stacked into a network, Fig. 6's low-dose CNN, the universal approximation theorem, encoders and decoders (Fig. 7), a GAN drawn as generator against discriminator, and the U-Net (Fig. 9).
reels.words: stacking layers makes the network deep. even a stack of purely linear layers is not trivial, in the way the fast fourier transform is the same transform as the slow one, split into steps that run far faster. with nonlinearities between the layers, it becomes a convolutional neural network. figure six maps low dose images, with an m r image as an extra input, to a prediction of the full dose image, trained against the real one. the universal approximation theorem says that, with enough layers, such networks can approximate almost any useful mapping. an encoder turns its input into a compact code, the latent space, and a decoder turns a code back into an image. figure seven goes from sinograms to a 3-d image, shrinking space while adding feature maps, down to a bottleneck where noise is unlikely to survive. a decoder fed random codes is a generator. a g a n trains it against a second network that tries to tell its images from real ones, until that discriminator is right only half the time. the u-net, in figure nine, adds skip connections, passing each level's feature maps straight across to the decoder, which adds expressive power.

reels.name: Four ways
reels.cap: Section four sorts the field into ways to use a network.
reels.doc: Pages 12 and 13: the four places a network can go, as one picture of the conventional loop that changes: the whole loop replaced (direct), the image made by a network (synthesis), the prior pulling toward a network's output (analysis), the whole prior learned and the loop unrolled; then Table I.
reels.words: section four sorts the field into ways to use a network. picture the conventional loop, a fit to the data through the physics, and a handcrafted prior. direct reconstruction replaces all of it, mapping the sinogram straight to the image. synthesis keeps the loop, but requires the image to be a network's output. analysis only penalizes the image for straying from a network's output, a softer rule. and unrolled methods learn the entire prior, with the iterations written out as blocks of one long network. table one, on page thirteen, compares them all by how the image, the data mean and the noise are modelled, and what each needs. post-processing a finished image is left out, since it is no longer reconstruction.

reels.name: Direct
reels.cap: Section five looks at the direct methods.
reels.doc: Pages 14 to 16: the direct methods. AUTOMAP (fully connected layers, then a CNN; Fig. 10) and DeepPET (an encoder-decoder; Fig. 11), what each gave on real PET, and the speed.
reels.words: section five looks at the direct methods. so far they have only been shown on small two dimensional slices, one hundred and twenty eight pixels square. automap, from zhu and colleagues in twenty eighteen, was built for m r i, magnetic resonance imaging, and also tried on pet. two fully connected layers learn something like an inverse radon transform, and convolutional layers then clean up the image. for pet its images came out worse than ordinary o s e m, probably because it was trained on m r images pushed through a simple projection, not on pet. figure ten, on the next page, draws it, the sinogram flattened into one long vector, the fully connected layers, and the convolutional layers that give the image. deeppet, from häggström and colleagues, is a convolutional encoder decoder. it reconstructs up to a hundred times faster, but its real brain images still left room for improvement. figure eleven shows its shape. the sinogram is squeezed into a feature rich latent space, which is small in space but deep in features, and then decoded out as an image.

reels.name: Prior
reels.cap: Section six keeps the physics and the noise model, and uses deep learning only for the regularization.
reels.doc: Pages 16 and 17: deep learning only in the prior. Gong's loop of three steps (MAP-EM toward the network's output, refit the code, collect the residual), drawn with our images; Fig. 12's results; the deep image prior (Fig. 13); and the looser analysis form.
reels.words: section six keeps the physics and the noise model, and uses deep learning only for the regularization. gong and colleagues require the image to be the output of a fixed, trained c n n, x equals f of z, and repeat three steps. a map e m step fits the image to the data, while pulling it toward the network's output. then the code z is refit so the network's output matches that image. and a residual, mu, collects what the network has not yet expressed. gong and colleagues report better lesion contrast for the same noise than denoising after reconstruction, since the image must still agree with the raw data. in figure twelve, on page seventeen, the iterative c n n reaches higher lesion contrast at each liver noise level, and both c n n methods cut liver noise by up to a factor of two. their deep image prior version fixes the network's input instead, the patient's own m r image, and trains the network's weights so its output matches the reconstruction. no training data are needed at all. in figure thirteen it shows the lesions more clearly than the kernel method or a c n n penalty. a looser option is analysis, where the image only pays a quadratic penalty for straying from the network's output.

reels.name: Unrolled
reels.cap: Section seven goes further.
reels.doc: Pages 18 to 21: unrolling. Why (physics kept, prior fully learned), the chain of blocks (EM update with the real system model, then a denoiser, its output the next prior), Fig. 14, and how MAPEM-Net, FBSEM-Net and BCD-Net train; FBSEM-Net's results on simulated and real brains (Figs. 16 and 17).
reels.words: section seven goes further. direct methods throw away years of physics, and the methods so far still keep a convenient handcrafted penalty. the aim is a hybrid, the physics we trust with learning where we are unsure, which also keeps the result interpretable, important for clinical pet. unrolling writes n iterations out as n blocks in a row. each block runs map e m updates with the true system model, then a network denoises the result, and that becomes the prior image for the next block. figure fourteen, on page nineteen, frames the three main methods this way. map e m net, from gong and colleagues, uses two map e m updates per block and a different u-net in each, trained so the very last image matches a high count reference, which means sending the error back through every block. f b s e m net, from mehranian and reader, uses one update per block and the same network in every block, and also learns how strongly to fuse the two. figure sixteen tests it on simulated brains with about a hundred times fewer counts than the reference. o s e m is speckled, while f b s e m net, also given the m r image, comes close to the reference. a u-net run after reconstruction, with the same m r image, does nearly as well. on real data, in figure seventeen, two minutes of scan come close to a thirty minute reference. b c d net, brought to pet by lim and colleagues in twenty eighteen, trains each block's denoiser on its own, so it never has to hold the whole chain in memory.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: The summary weighs the groups.
reels.doc: Pages 22 and 23: the summary (training data each group needs, drawn as piles), the missing fair comparison, and the future directions.
reels.words: the summary weighs the groups. direct methods, so far shown in two dimensions, need tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of training slices. the model-based groups train on the order of tens of 3-d images, and keep the physics and noise model we can trust, but run about as slowly as ordinary iterative reconstruction. what is still missing is a fair comparison of them all on the same data. looking ahead, fully bayesian networks could give an uncertainty estimate beside each image. self-supervised learning could make its own targets by degrading the data it has. cycle gans could learn from inputs and targets that are not paired. for now, simple networks run after reconstruction compete well, and the authors point to time of flight backprojected images as a promising starting point.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the paper as a map.
reels.doc: All 25 pages as a map of where things are, then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the paper as a map. conventional reconstruction is on pages two to four, the turn to learning on four and five, single layers on five to eight, deep networks, encoders and gans on seven to twelve, the four ways to use them on twelve and thirteen, direct methods on fourteen to sixteen, learned priors on sixteen and seventeen, unrolled methods on eighteen to twenty two, and the summary and outlook on twenty two and twenty three. the takeaway is that a network does not have to replace reconstruction. the physics and the poisson noise model can stay as they are, and the network can learn just the part nobody can write down well, the prior.

title: Deep learning-based PET image denoising and reconstruction: a review

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a review from Radiological Physics and Technology, published in twenty twenty four, page by page.
reels.doc: Page 1: what the review is, who wrote it, its three families of deep learning drawn as three small pipelines, and why PET needs them (our short scan next to the activity it came from).
reels.words: this video reads a review from radiological physics and technology, published in twenty twenty four, page by page. its title is deep learning based pet image denoising and reconstruction, a review. it is by fumio hashimoto and colleagues at hamamatsu photonics, chiba university and japan's national institutes for quantum science and technology, with andrew reader at king's college london. the abstract says the review first traces how pet images were reconstructed before deep learning. it then sorts deep learning for pet into three groups. post-processing cleans an image after an ordinary reconstruction. direct methods learn the whole map from the measured sinogram to the image. and iterative methods put a network inside a classical reconstruction, so the physics stays. it ends with an outlook. the introduction explains why. pet can follow tracers at picomole amounts, but few counts are measured, so its images are noisy. here is our own phantom, and what a short scan of thirty seven thousand eight hundred counts gives. more tracer would mean more radiation, so the authors call the history of pet imaging a battle against noise.

reels.name: Classical
reels.cap: Section two starts with filtered backprojection, F B P, from the nineteen seventies and eighties.
reels.doc: Pages 2 to 4: filtered backprojection (the ramp filter, our FBP), Fig. 1, ML-EM as its update with each part named, ordered subsets, our ML-EM stopped early and run long, MAP with a smoothing prior and with an MR-guided one (ours).
reels.words: section two starts with filtered backprojection, f b p, from the nineteen seventies and eighties. each projection in the sinogram is filtered, with a ramp filter that boosts high frequencies, and then smeared back across the image. the ramp also boosts the noise, so at low counts f b p is noisy and streaked. on our short scan, the spread in the flat background is eighty one percent of its mean. figure one runs every classical method on the same simulated brain, with normal dose data on top and low dose data below. f b p is fine at normal dose, and noisy at low dose. between the nineteen eighties and nineties came maximum likelihood expectation maximisation, m l e m, which models the data as poisson counts. its update reads simply. each measured count is divided by the count the current image predicts, the ratios are back-projected, and the image is multiplied by them, scaled by each voxel's sensitivity. it beats f b p because it knows the noise is poisson. ordered subsets, o s e m, made it fast by updating from one part of the data at a time. we ran m l e m on our short scan. three iterations leave it blurred, and the small lesion is seventy one percent too dim. after twenty, the lesion is thirteen percent too dim, with forty two percent noise. after two hundred, the noise has grown to one hundred and fifteen percent. noise and edge artefacts grow as iterations go on, page four says, so in practice the iterations are stopped early, or the image is smoothed afterwards. the other answer is maximum a posteriori reconstruction, which adds a prior that favours smooth images, weighted by a number beta. on our scan, a quadratic prior brings the noise down to twenty four percent, but leaves the lesion forty percent too dim. organ edges can come from an m r image, on combined pet and m r scanners, though in our run it barely helps the lesion, because the m r image cannot see it.

reels.name: Overview
reels.cap: Then the review lays out its three families of deep learning, drawn in figure two.
reels.doc: Pages 4 and 5: Fig. 2, the review's three families.
reels.words: then the review lays out its three families of deep learning, drawn in figure two. post-processing puts a network after an ordinary reconstruction. direct reconstruction puts a network where the whole reconstruction was. iterative reconstruction alternates an e m step with a network. the authors note that the first family does not strictly reconstruct anything.

reels.name: Denoise
reels.cap: Section three is about denoising.
reels.doc: Pages 5 to 7: denoising as x_hat = x + n (drawn with our images), the training objective, the designs of Fig. 3, and Fig. 4's supervised results.
reels.words: section three is about denoising. the image we have is the true image plus noise, made worse because reconstruction is ill conditioned, so small errors in the data grow into large ones in the image. a network f, with weights theta, is trained so that its output from the noisy image matches the clean one, by a loss such as the mean squared error. the u-net is the workhorse. it shrinks the image to capture context, grows it back, and passes detail across at each scale. residual learning has the network output only the noise. a perceptual loss compares features from a pretrained network instead of pixels. with pet and c t or pet and m r scanners, the anatomical image can be a second input. and a generative adversarial network, a g a n, adds a second network that tries to tell the output from a real high dose image. figure three draws these designs, the u-net, a network with an anatomical input, the g a n, and two transformers that came later, a vision transformer and the swin transformer. a cycle g a n can even learn without matched pairs of low and high dose images. figure four tries them on whole body scans. the low count image is grainy. the u-net, the g a n and the cycle g a n all clean it, and their line profiles follow the full count one closely.

reels.name: Self sup
reels.cap: Back on page six, large sets of high quality scans are hard to collect, and a trained network can do poorly on tracers or scanners it never saw.
reels.doc: Pages 6 to 8: learning without clean images: Noise2Noise (our split scan), the deep image prior and its conditional version, pre-training, and Fig. 5.
reels.words: back on page six, large sets of high quality scans are hard to collect, and a trained network can do poorly on tracers or scanners it never saw. so methods grew that need no clean images. noise2noise trains on two independent noisy copies of the same scan. we split our scan's counts into two halves. the network maps one half to the other, and since it cannot predict the noise, it learns only what the two halves share, the activity. the deep image prior needs no training set at all. a network starts from a random input, and its weights are fitted to the one noisy image. a network finds smooth structure easier to make than noise, so if the fitting stops early, the output is a cleaner image. conditional versions feed the m r image instead of random input. pre-training on many existing scans makes the deep image prior more robust across tracers and scanners. figure five compares unsupervised methods on amyloid brain scans. against the noisy image, the plain deep image prior helps, and the m r guided versions keep the most detail.

reels.name: Emerging
reels.cap: Deep learning denoising is already sold with commercial scanners, as software cleared by the F D A.
reels.doc: Pages 8 and 9: what is emerging, each drawn as what it does: denoising sold with the scanner (a noisy image in, a clean one out), a transformer's reach (any two places) against a convolution's small window, diffusion (noise turned into an image), federated learning (hospitals keep their scans and share only weights), a total body scanner covering the whole patient; then Fig. 6.
reels.words: deep learning denoising is already sold with commercial scanners, as software cleared by the f d a. transformers, which relate distant parts of an image, sometimes beat convolutional networks. diffusion models are being tried, and federated learning trains across hospitals without the scans leaving them. total body scanners will add more. figure six compares networks on four patients. from the noisy low count images, the swin transformer, called swin i r, comes out best.

reels.name: Direct
reels.cap: Back on page eight, section four turns to direct reconstruction.
reels.doc: Pages 8 to 12: direct reconstruction: the objective (the denoising one with the sinogram as input), Floyd's 1991 network and the ramp filter it learned (ours, as a kernel), AUTOMAP and DeepPET (weights as bars), Figs. 7 to 10 and their limits, and FastPET's histo-image (ours) with Figs. 11 and 12.
reels.words: back on page eight, section four turns to direct reconstruction. the training is the same as for denoising, except the network's input is the measured sinogram y itself. no forward or back projection is used, so the network must learn the whole physics from examples. the first such network was probably floyd's, for spect, in nineteen ninety one. a trainable layer filtered the projections, and a fixed layer back-projected them. the filter it learned resembled a ramp filter. here is ours, written as a kernel that slides along each projection, a spike with a negative dip on each side. it sharpens what back-projection would blur. twenty seven years later, automap used fully connected layers, where every sinogram value feeds every pixel, to learn the transform for m r and pet. deeppet used a convolutional encoder and decoder instead, with about sixty million weights against automap's eight hundred million, so it trains on less data. its bottleneck is eighteen by seventeen by one thousand and twenty four, so almost no spatial layout of the sinogram is left. page ten draws all three. floyd's network has its trainable filtering layer and its fixed backprojection. automap has its dense connections, and deeppet is a funnel of convolutions. figure ten shows deeppet at work. from the sinogram alone it makes an image that, at first glance, looks as good as o s e m. but the review warns that the details can differ, and such networks may invent structures. they are also limited to two dimensional slices by graphics card memory, and need many training sets to learn the backprojection. another route uses time of flight. instead of a sinogram, each detected event is placed at its most likely point along its line, giving an image called a histo-image. here is ours, from our phantom, blurred along each line by the timing. fastpet learns to sharpen it, a method by whiteley and colleagues. figure eleven draws the framework. the histo-image and an attenuation map from the c t go into a network, which outputs the image. because its input is already an image, it can use a u-net, and grows easily to three dimensions. splitting the histo-image by the direction of each line helps further. in figure twelve, the contrast recovered in three tumours is zero point eight six for list-mode drama, a classical method, zero point seven eight for fastpet, and zero point eight zero with the direction information.

reels.name: Iterative
reels.cap: Section five puts the network inside an iterative reconstruction.
reels.doc: Pages 12 to 16: a network inside iterative reconstruction, as a constraint or as a penalty (our picture of the two in a plane of images), Gong's CNN representation (Figs. 13, 14), the DIP reconstruction (Figs. 15, 16), the penalty form (Eqs. 19, 20), FBSEM-Net (Figs. 17, 18), and the rest.
reels.words: section five puts the network inside an iterative reconstruction. there are two ways. picture each image as a point. the data favour points near their best fit, with the likelihood falling off around it. a network can only make some images, drawn as this curve. as a constraint, the answer must lie on the curve, at its best likelihood. as a penalty, the answer is pulled toward the network's output, and slides from the data's best fit to that output as beta grows. the constrained form is equation eighteen, the poisson likelihood, with the image required to be a network's output. the image must then agree with the data as far as the network allows. gong and colleagues solved it with an alternating method, and in figures thirteen and fourteen their iterative c n n looks closest to the high count image, with the best trade between lesion contrast and noise. the deep image prior also works as the constraint, with no training set. in figures fifteen and sixteen, hashimoto and colleagues fit it through the forward projection only, and with the m r image as input, the result is close to the ground truth. the penalty form is equation nineteen, the likelihood plus beta times a penalty r. r is simply the squared distance between the image and the network's output. it is less constraining, since the image only has to stay near the output, not equal it. f b s e m net, which has a video of its own, is in figures seventeen and eighteen, where its version with m r input looks closest to the reference. page sixteen adds kim and colleagues, who fit the network's output locally before using it, and map e m net by gong and colleagues.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: Section six covers dynamic PET, which follows the tracer over time to estimate kinetic rates.
reels.doc: Page 16: dynamic PET, then the conclusion and outlook.
reels.words: section six covers dynamic pet, which follows the tracer over time to estimate kinetic rates. networks have been used to go straight from short frames to images of those rates, and to separate two tracers scanned together. the conclusion looks to the hardware. total body scanners give much less noisy training data. detectors with thirty picosecond timing have even made reconstruction free imaging possible, which also has a video of its own. and deep learning is moving into signal processing in the detectors too.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the review as a map, with the references filling the last seven pages.
reels.doc: Pages 1 to 16 as a map of where things are (the references fill 17 to 23), then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the review as a map, with the references filling the last seven pages. classical reconstruction is on pages one to four, denoising after reconstruction on four to nine, direct reconstruction on eight to twelve, networks inside iterative reconstruction on twelve to sixteen, and dynamic pet and the outlook on sixteen. the takeaway is that a network can clean the image after reconstruction, learn the whole map from data to image, or sit inside a reconstruction that keeps the physics. the review's own work leans to the last, where the data keep the network honest.

title: Diffusion models for medical image reconstruction

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video reads a review from B J R Artificial Intelligence, published in twenty twenty four, page by page.
