reels.doc: Page 1: what the review is, who wrote it, the abstract, and reconstruction as an inverse problem drawn with our phantom: an image goes through the forward model A to noise-free data, noise is added, and reconstruction must find an image that explains the measurement, helped by prior knowledge.
reels.words: this video reads a review from b j r artificial intelligence, published in twenty twenty four, page by page. its title is diffusion models for medical image reconstruction. it is by george webber and andrew reader at king's college london. the abstract says reconstruction needs prior knowledge of what plausible images look like, and that diffusion models, trained only on high quality images, can learn it. they already lead for fast m r i, c t from very few views, and low dose pet. their advantages are the best image modelling so far, robustness when the scanner changes, and a principled measure of uncertainty. the worry is hallucination. on the right of page one, reconstruction is an inverse problem. an image x passes through the forward model a, and noise is added, giving the measurement m, here a sinogram from our phantom. reconstruction goes back, to the image that most likely explains m. when the data are noisy or incomplete, many images explain them, so the best estimate also asks how probable the image is. balancing the two gives the maximum a posteriori estimate.

reels.name: Paradigms
reels.cap: Table one on page two compares three ways to bring in that prior knowledge.
reels.doc: Pages 1 to 3: Table 1's three ways to bring in prior knowledge, each drawn by what goes in and what comes out (a rule about neighbouring voxels; pairs of measurement and image into a network that learns the scanner too; images alone into a network that learns only what images look like, with the scanner model kept apart), why a diffusion model can give the whole posterior, and Table 2's comparison of generative models.
reels.words: table one on page two compares three ways to bring in that prior knowledge. hand-crafted priors are rules, such as neighbouring voxels should be alike. they need no training, but cannot describe what complex medical images look like. supervised learning trains a network on pairs of measurements and images, so the scanner gets learnt along with the images, and the network fails when the scanner or its settings change. unsupervised diffusion models learn from images alone. no measurements go in, so the scanner is never learnt, and its model a is applied separately, at reconstruction. that is why they cope better when the scanner changes. the price is speed, a hundred or more iterations. and once conditioned on the data, a diffusion model gives not one image but many plausible ones, so the uncertainty in each voxel can be measured. among generative models, which learn from images how likely each image is, table two finds diffusion models stable to train, state of the art in image quality, and good at diverse samples, but slow to generate.

reels.name: Noising
reels.cap: Section three explains diffusion models.
reels.doc: Pages 3 and 4: the forward process (noise added step by step: our phantom, with the share of the image left at each step), the backward process, Fig. 1, training a denoiser (Fig. 2), and D D I M's skipping: the same way back from noise to image, crossed in a few long jumps instead of many small steps.
reels.words: section three explains diffusion models. the forward process takes an image and adds random noise in steps, until nothing of the image is left. on our phantom, a quarter of the way along, ninety two percent of the image remains, halfway seventy percent, then thirty eight, then none. the backward process runs the other way, from pure noise, removing a little noise at each step, and ends at a new image that looks like the training images. figure one draws both, noise added going right, and removed by the network going left. the network is trained as in figure two. pick a training image and a random noise level, add that much noise, and train the network to take it out again, over and over, so one network learns every noise level. going back to page three, the way back runs from pure noise to a clean image. a d d p m crosses it in many small steps, each predicting a slightly cleaner image. a d d i m uses the same network, but at each step jumps to its estimate of the clean image and adds back less noise, so it crosses the same way in a few long jumps, and generates ten to fifty times faster.

reels.name: Score
reels.cap: Reconstruction papers usually describe diffusion through the score.
reels.doc: Pages 3, 5 and 6: the score, an arrow towards more probable images, drawn exactly in our plane (the plausible images lie on a curve); the same plane at four noise levels stacked in 3D, with the paths that carry pure noise down to the curve; then Figs. 3 and 4.
reels.words: reconstruction papers usually describe diffusion through the score. think of every image as a point. here, in our own small example, each point of this plane is an image, and the plausible images lie along this curve. the score is an arrow at every point, aimed towards more probable images, so following the arrows leads to the curve. learning the score directly is too hard, so it is learnt on noisy images, at a series of decreasing noise levels. here is our plane again, now at four noise levels stacked by height. at the bottom the images are clean and lie on the curve. going up, more noise spreads them out, until at the top they are just noise. generating an image means starting at the top and following the score down through the levels. every one of our fourteen paths ends on the curve. figure three on page five draws the same idea with brain images. in part a, the arcs are the noisy versions of the brain images at each level, and the score leads inwards to the clean brains. part b makes the noise level continuous, which page three calls the stochastic differential equation view, so the number of steps can change without retraining. figure four on page six shows score arrows on a tiny five by five image. starting from noise, each red arrow says whether a pixel should get lighter or darker, and the patch settles into a clean one.

reels.name: Recon
reels.cap: Back on page three, to reconstruct, the denoising steps are interleaved with steps that pull the image towards agreement with the measured data.
reels.doc: Pages 3, 4 and 6: reconstruction with a diffusion prior, all in our plane. One measurement allows a line of images; at a noisy image the prior's score points to the curve, the likelihood's to the line, and the step taken is their sum (Bayes). Sixty samples land where the line meets the curve, at two places, so their spread shows the uncertainty. D D S drawn as the jump to the clean estimate before the data step. Then Fig. 5.
reels.words: back on page three, to reconstruct, the denoising steps are interleaved with steps that pull the image towards agreement with the measured data. here is our plane, with the plausible images on the curve. one measurement allows a whole line of images. by bayes' law, the score of an image given the measurement is the prior's score, pointing towards the curve, plus the likelihood's score, pointing towards the line. their sum is the step that is taken. the true image is where they cross, but the line crosses the curve twice. we ran sixty reconstructions from pure noise, taking that step over and over. thirty one ended at the truth, and twenty seven at the other crossing. a single answer would hide this. the spread of the samples is the uncertainty that page two promised. the hard part, on page four, is the likelihood's score for a noisy image, because the measurement was made of a clean one. simply scaling the usual score is fast but inaccurate, which is what our example did. diffusion posterior sampling, d p s, is slow but accurate. decomposed diffusion sampling, d d s, first jumps from the noisy image to the network's estimate of the clean one, and then moves that estimate onto the data. figure five sets out the three uses. plain generation from noise, unsupervised reconstruction, where a measurement consistency step joins each denoising step, and supervised reconstruction, where the network is trained on the measured data itself, and loses the robustness.

reels.name: Practical
reels.cap: On practicalities, most researchers use a U-Net.
reels.doc: Pages 4, 5 and 7: the network drawn by what it takes and gives (a noisy image and its timestep in, the added noise out, through a U-Net), run in a loop for generation; training and generation budgets on that picture; then Algorithms 1 and 2.
reels.words: on practicalities, most researchers use a u-net. it takes a noisy image and its timestep, given through a sinusoidal embedding, and gives back the noise that was added, which is the score up to a scale. training runs from a hundred to fifty thousand epochs, most under five thousand, often with the adam optimiser. generating an image runs the network a hundred to four thousand times, with little gained past a thousand. the final noise level should make images indistinguishable from pure noise. algorithm one on page seven is the training loop. pick a random time and make a noisy image, then make the network's prediction match the noise that was added. algorithm two generates. start from noise, estimate the score and remove a little noise, and, when there is a measurement, condition on it at every step. that one line turns generation into reconstruction.

reels.name: Modalities
reels.cap: Each modality brings its own problems.
reels.doc: Pages 7 to 9: each modality's case study, with the paper's numbers as bars: M R I (error 14 vs 1.4 percent, Fig. 6), C T (S S I M 0.49, 0.79, 0.87, Fig. 7), PET (non-negativity drawn on one row of our phantom with noise added; contrast recovery 87 vs 98 percent, Fig. 8; the two kinds of noise side by side), ultrasound (contrast to noise 6.7 vs 18.4 decibels; Fig. 9 and its variance image).
reels.words: each modality brings its own problems. pet data are fully sampled but have high variance poisson noise, while m r i data are undersampled with milder gaussian noise. for m r i, cao and colleagues' h f s s d e focuses on high frequency detail. on data accelerated about six times, it cuts the reconstruction error from fourteen percent with parallel imaging to one point four percent. in figure six, sense, the conventional method, leaves artefacts, and the diffusion method is the closest to the truth. for c t, vazia and colleagues' spectral diffusion posterior sampling handles several energy bins together. in figure seven, the structural similarity is zero point four nine for the unregularised method, zero point seven nine for the previous best, and zero point eight seven with diffusion. for pet, injected dose and patients vary so much that images need a special normalisation before training. pet activity can never be negative. but the gaussian noise of diffusion pushes some voxels below zero, so the constraint has to be added back. singh and colleagues reconstruct full 3d pet, recovering ninety eight percent of lesion contrast against eighty seven percent for supervised methods. in figure eight, the conventional reconstruction and the deep image prior are blurrier than their diffusion method. back on page eight, a common misconception is that pet's poisson noise, the noise in the measured counts, clashes with diffusion's gaussian noise. it does not. the gaussian is only the known distribution the process ends in, a different thing from any noise in the scans. for ultrasound, zhang and colleagues draw many reconstructions and compute their variance. the contrast to noise ratio rises from six point seven decibels with delay and sum to eighteen point four. in figure nine, delay and sum is speckled, the mean of the diffusion samples is cleaner, and their variance is highest at tissue boundaries, where the method is least sure.

reels.name: Directions
reels.cap: Section five lists the open problems.
reels.doc: Pages 9 to 11: research directions. Hallucination drawn in our plane (a prior learnt from other images puts every sample on its own curve, confidently wrong), the fixes, Fig. 10; a hot start drawn as a short path from a conventional image; imperfect training data; 3D drawn as a volume cut into slices (one direction, then two perpendicular ones), Fig. 11; and latent diffusion.
reels.words: section five lists the open problems. publications roughly tripled in a year. the first is hallucination. training images often differ from the image being reconstructed, for example when they come from another scanner. in our plane, suppose the prior learnt this curve instead. every sample now lands on the wrong curve, where it still explains the measurement, but far from the truth. it looks like a real image and it is wrong. fixes include better ways of conditioning on the measurement, and adapting the prior to each case, as steerable conditional diffusion does with a low rank adaptation. figure ten draws it. when prior and measurement agree, the steps converge, and when they clash, the two kinds of step fight each other. speed is the other barrier. a hot start begins from a conventional reconstruction instead of pure noise. a little noise is added, and only the end of the descent is run. one adaptation claims ten to fifty times fewer iterations on knee m r i. another problem is learning a clean prior from training images that are themselves noisy or undersampled. a whole 3d volume is too big for one diffusion model, so most authors train on 2d slices, as in figure eleven, and add a step that keeps neighbouring slices consistent. lee and colleagues also train models across the perpendicular direction, for two to three times the memory and training time. latent diffusion runs in a compressed space, which could also make 3d feasible.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: The outlook is that one prior, learnt from good images from many scanners, could work out of the box.
reels.doc: Pages 11 and 12: opportunities, the clinical evidence so far (99 of 100 cases as squares), the hardest tuning question drawn as three small planes (data leading, balanced, prior leading), and uncertainty as a safeguard.
reels.words: the outlook is that one prior, learnt from good images from many scanners, could work out of the box. clinical evidence is still thin. for breast m r i at acceleration two, radiologists found the images almost indistinguishable from the originals in ninety nine of every hundred cases. the hardest choice is how much to trust the prior against the data. in our plane, balanced, the samples land where the line meets the curve. if the data lead, samples scatter anywhere along the line, a noisy image. if the prior leads, they land anywhere on the curve, a clean image with invented detail, which is much harder for a clinician to spot. uncertainty helps here. running many reconstructions with different starting noise shows where the answer is unsure, just as our sixty samples split between two crossings. the authors sum up that diffusion models have set new standards across modalities, and that speed, mismatched priors and validation are what remain.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the review as a map, with the references after page twelve.
reels.doc: Pages 1 to 12 as a map of where things are (the references fill 12 to 15), then the one-line takeaway.
reels.words: here is the review as a map, with the references after page twelve. the ways to bring in prior knowledge are on pages one to three, diffusion and reconstruction with it on three to six, practicalities on four, five and seven, the modalities on seven to nine, research directions on nine to eleven, and the outlook on eleven and twelve. the takeaway is that a diffusion model learns, at every noise level, which way looks more like a real image, and reconstruction follows those arrows while staying on the measurement. drawing many samples, rather than one, shows where the answer is unsure.

title: wt pet

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: Ghent University's walk through PET puts a standing patient between two flat panels of monolithic detectors, seventy by a hundred and six centimetres, fifty centimetres apart.
reels.words: ghent university's walk through pet puts a standing patient between two flat panels of monolithic detectors, seventy by a hundred and six centimetres, fifty centimetres apart. every line of response runs from one panel to the other. this video goes through the six papers behind it, with the methods: how the system was sized and costed, how the detectors were modelled, how the images were reconstructed, and what the geometry costs in angular sampling.

reels.name: Sizing
reels.cap: The 2023 design paper starts from patients.
reels.words: the 2023 design paper starts from patients. forty random p e t c t scans gave the height from head to thigh, the shoulder width and the body depth, which set the panel size and the fifty centimetre gap, filled with fourteen by twenty monolithic blocks per panel. cost is then estimated from the two dominant components: scintillator volume times a price per cubic centimetre, thirty euros for l s o and ten for b g o, and sipm area at a thousand euros per five by five centimetre module. electronics are left out. applied to each system, that gives about seven hundred thousand euros for a twenty six centimetre scanner, two point eight million for a hundred and six centimetre cylinder, and about eight hundred and thirty thousand for walk through panels in b g o: three point three times less than the long cylinder, and only twenty percent more than the short one. in l y s o it is about one point three million.

reels.name: Throughput
reels.cap: Throughput was estimated, not assumed.
reels.words: throughput was estimated, not assumed. the group timed a full day of patient handling on a conventional scanner, from c t and scout scan to positioning on the bed. acquisition times were then scaled by each design's sensitivity and time of flight resolution. for the panels, the simulated sensitivity of a hundred and fifty two kilo counts per second per megabecquerel uses every line of response, because depth of interaction removes the blur of oblique lines. the estimate: twenty eight patients a day on a short scanner, fifty three to sixty on a long cylinder, and eighty seven walking through the panels. or, keeping the patient count, two thirds less tracer ordered per patient.

reels.name: Block
reels.cap: Each block is a single crystal, five by five centimetres and sixteen millimetres thick, read by an eight by eight array of six millimetre SiPMs.
reels.words: each block is a single crystal, five by five centimetres and sixteen millimetres thick, read by an eight by eight array of six millimetre sipms. the group's measured block resolves depth in six layers. in the system simulations, the detector is not simulated photon by photon. gate reports the exact interaction point, energy weighted when a gamma scatters inside the block, and it is then smeared with a three dimensional gaussian: sigma of zero point five five millimetres across the face and zero point eight five in depth for b g o, the block's measured average. the l y s o papers use one point one four and two point six seven millimetres full width. points pushed outside the crystal are clamped to its edge. a uniform gaussian ignores edges. so the 2025 paper also tried a spatially varying model: one point zero two millimetres in the centre, worsening to one point three five at the edges, and poorer depth resolution in the two layers nearest the sipms.

reels.name: Recon
reels.cap: The simulation studies reconstruct with list mode maximum likelihood expectation maximisation, M L E M, with time of flight for the image studies.
reels.words: the simulation studies reconstruct with list mode maximum likelihood expectation maximisation, m l e m, with time of flight for the image studies. each recorded event defines a line. its system weights are the voxels along that line, multiplied by the time of flight kernel, so the voxels near the timing estimate count most. the update compares the events with the current image projected along each line, and divides by the sensitivity image, which is how the limited panel geometry enters the reconstruction. the codes are in house: q e t i r, in c plus plus, run with no subsets and ten iterations, and later pet recon, written in julia for the g p u. with no regularisation and no resolution model, whatever the geometry does shows up directly in the images.

reels.name: Coverage
reels.cap: The key analysis comes from the 2026 paper.
reels.words: the key analysis comes from the 2026 paper. in the transverse plane, every line of response is a point in the sinogram: its angle and its offset from the centre. a line counts only if it hits both panels. computing that for every line gives this map. the dark bands are the lines running nearly parallel to the panels, which are never recorded, and that missing range of angles is what stretches images perpendicular to the panels. the 2023 b g o simulation measured exactly this with n e m a point sources in a warm background: under two millimetres parallel to the panels, but up to three point three six perpendicular, worst near a panel.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: Time of flight is the main lever against those missing angles.
reels.words: time of flight is the main lever against those missing angles. the arrival time difference between the two panels, times the speed of light and halved, places the event along its line. at three hundred picoseconds for l y s o, that is about four and a half centimetres. for b g o the papers assume a more conservative six hundred picoseconds, using cherenkov light, though the bench block reached three hundred and twenty seven. because lines between two panels run across the gap, the timing kernel lies along exactly the direction the missing angles blur. four and a half centimetres is still coarse next to millimetre voxels, so every paper ends asking for faster timing.

reels.name: Ring
reels.cap: As a reference, Maya Abi Akl and colleagues put the same L Y S O block into a conventional ring: forty blocks around a seventy centimetre bore, seven or fourteen rings long.
reels.words: as a reference, maya abi akl and colleagues put the same l y s o block into a conventional ring: forty blocks around a seventy centimetre bore, seven or fourteen rings long. they ran the n e m a n u two twenty eighteen tests in gate, with the detector's energy resolution, energy window, coincidence window and a paralysable dead time model. with every angle covered, resolution stays under two millimetres in every direction. sensitivity is twenty nine and a hundred and seven kilo counts per second per megabecquerel, and the count rate peaks at seven hundred and sixteen and twelve hundred and thirty five kilo counts per second. this is what the panels are measured against.

reels.name: Sparse
reels.cap: Then the cost cutting.
reels.words: then the cost cutting. the 2025 design makes the panels sparse: sixty centimetres tall, eight rows of blocks with twenty eight millimetre gaps, about half a block. the gaps are not wasted: the panels step vertically by half a module, so the new block positions sit exactly over the old gaps and the axial sensitivity profile smooths out. evaluated with n e m a sensitivity, the image quality phantom and an x cat anthropomorphic phantom, the sparse build is four point six times less sensitive, needs two to three minutes to match thirty seconds on the long panels, and keeps three to three and a half millimetres perpendicular to the panels.

reels.name: Slide through
reels.cap: The 2026 design goes further: narrow strips almost two metres tall, wider at the torso and narrower at the legs, two hundred and twenty four modules in all, about as many as a standard cylinder.
reels.words: the 2026 design goes further: narrow strips almost two metres tall, wider at the torso and narrower at the legs, two hundred and twenty four modules in all, about as many as a standard cylinder. to cover the body, the strips slide sideways together across a seventy four centimetre field.

reels.name: Motions
reels.cap: Which way should the strips move?
reels.words: which way should the strips move? the paper answers with the same sinogram analysis. a static pair of narrow strips records only a sliver of lines. moving them in opposite directions covers many angles, but only near the centre: nothing beyond about ten centimetres, half the strip width, so most of a patient is lost. moving just one strip covers more angles but a smaller field. parallel motion gives the same, truncated range of angles at every offset, so it was chosen. the paper compares it in gate against two references built from the same detectors: the wide static panels and a cylinder. sensitivity comes from a uniform box source the size of the field, image quality from the n e m a phantom and two x cat patients. the torso gets more sensitivity than the cylinder, the legs half as much, and four minutes matches nine on the cylinder for torso noise. but elongation remains, and the conclusion asks for timing better than three hundred picoseconds.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Read in order, the papers make one argument.
reels.words: read in order, the papers make one argument. each step saves detector and money, and each pays in angular sampling, visible in the sinogram and in the perpendicular blur, which the latest paper hopes faster timing will hide. it is a strong cost and throughput case, with its weakness measured honestly by the group itself. and it shows what a closed ring gets for free: every angle, and nothing that has to move. thanks for watching.

title: Why light's speed comes out the same for everyone

reels.name: Maxwell
reels.cap: In eighteen sixty five, James Clerk Maxwell wrote the laws of electricity and magnetism as four equations, and found they allow a wave.
reels.doc: Light as Maxwell's wave in 3D (electric field in one plane, magnetic in the other), its speed from two bench constants, and the aether everyone assumed it moved through.
reels.words: in eighteen sixty five, james clerk maxwell wrote the laws of electricity and magnetism as four equations, and found they allow a wave. an electric field and a magnetic field each keep the other going, and the pair travels. its speed comes out of two numbers measured on a lab bench, one for electric charges and one for magnets. it came to three hundred thousand kilometres per second, the measured speed of light. so light is this wave. but the equations give one speed, and never say what it is measured against. sound travels through air, so physicists assumed light travels through an invisible medium filling space, the aether. and earth, moving through it at thirty kilometres per second, should feel an aether wind.

reels.name: Aether
reels.cap: In eighteen eighty seven, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley went looking for that wind.
reels.words: in eighteen eighty seven, albert michelson and edward morley went looking for that wind. they split one beam of light in two, sent one half along earth's motion and the other across it, along arms eleven metres long, and brought them back together. where the two halves meet, they make light and dark stripes. against an aether wind, the half going along loses the race by a tiny amount, so turning the table should slide the stripes. they expected a shift of zero point four of a stripe. they saw less than zero point zero two. no wind.

reels.name: Patch
reels.cap: Physicists did not give up the aether.
reels.words: physicists did not give up the aether. in eighteen eighty nine george fitzgerald, and then hendrik lorentz, proposed that moving through it squeezes the arm that points along the motion, by just enough to hide the wind. for michelson's table, fifty five nanometres. lorentz also needed a local time for moving observers, shifted by v x over c squared, which he treated as a mathematical trick. joseph larmor and henri poincaré added slow clocks, and by nineteen oh four the full equations were on paper. but to all of them, it was a squeeze by the aether, and the aether stayed.

reels.name: Einstein
reels.cap: Einstein came at it from another side.
reels.words: einstein came at it from another side. at sixteen he imagined riding alongside a beam of light. he would see the wave standing still, a frozen pattern of field, and maxwell's equations allow no such thing. and in maxwell's theory, a magnet pushed into a coil and a coil pushed onto a magnet were explained in two different ways, though they make exactly the same current. only the relative motion seemed to matter. so he took two rules as starting points. one. the laws of physics are the same for everyone moving steadily, so nobody can tell who is at rest, and the aether is not needed. two. light travels at c, however fast its source moves. he did not derive these. he bet on them, because the evidence pointed that way.

reels.name: Puzzle
reels.cap: Here is why the two rules seem to clash.
reels.words: here is why the two rules seem to clash. a flash of light leaves a lamp, and one second later it has travelled three hundred thousand kilometres. divide one by the other, and you get the speed of light, c. now a rocket flies past at half that speed. lorentz's squeeze makes its rulers shorter and its clocks run slow. yet by the two rules, the crew timing the same flash must also get c, at any speed. how can a shorter distance over a longer time still give the same answer? that question has a beautiful answer, and it comes from drawing space and time as one picture.

reels.name: Naive
reels.cap: Try the squeeze and the slow clocks on their own.
reels.words: try the squeeze and the slow clocks on their own. at half the speed of light, the stretch factor, gamma, is one point one five five. length contraction divides the distance by gamma, from three hundred thousand kilometres to two hundred and fifty nine thousand eight hundred and eight. time dilation multiplies the time by gamma, from one second to one point one five five seconds. divide them, and the crew should measure two hundred and twenty five thousand kilometres per second, three quarters of c. not c. in symbols, the crew's distance over time is d over gamma, divided by gamma t. the two gammas pile up underneath, and one over gamma squared is one minus v squared over c squared. so the faster the rocket, the slower light would look. at nine tenths of c, only nineteen hundredths of c. but every experiment says c. something is missing.

reels.name: Simultaneity
reels.cap: Einstein's key step, which he credited to talks with his friend Michele Besso, was to ask what at the same time means for two clocks far apart.
reels.words: einstein's key step, which he credited to talks with his friend michele besso, was to ask what at the same time means for two clocks far apart. the only way to set them is with light. put a clock at each end of the rocket, and fire a flash from the middle. on board, the light goes the same way to both ends, so it reaches them together, and the crew set both clocks to agree. now watch the same thing from the ground. the rocket moves while the light is in flight. the back end runs into its flash early, and the front end runs away from its flash, so it is hit later. two events the crew call simultaneous happen at different times for us. so from the ground, the rocket's front clock is set behind its back clock, by v l over c squared. this is the relativity of simultaneity, and it is exactly the term the naive sum left out.

reels.name: Lorentz
reels.cap: From his two rules and that way of setting clocks, Einstein derived Lorentz's equations, but as facts about space and time, with no aether.
reels.words: from his two rules and that way of setting clocks, einstein derived lorentz's equations, but as facts about space and time, with no aether. gamma carries the contraction and the dilation. minus v delta t is the rocket moving. and minus v delta x over c squared, in the time, is the clock lag we just found. for our flash, the distance becomes one point one five five times three hundred thousand minus a hundred and fifty thousand, which is a hundred and seventy three thousand two hundred and five kilometres. the time becomes one point one five five times one minus a half, which is zero point five seven seven seconds. divide, and you get three hundred thousand kilometres per second. exactly c. notice what happened. the distance and the time both shrank by the same factor, zero point five seven seven. that is not length contraction, which alone would give two hundred and fifty nine thousand eight hundred and eight kilometres. and the time got shorter, not longer. it is the doppler factor, the rocket running away from the light. because top and bottom shrink together, dividing them still gives c.

reels.name: Proof
reels.cap: And it is not luck with the numbers.
reels.words: and it is not luck with the numbers. for light, the distance is always c times the time. put that into the two rules, and the distance becomes gamma times c minus v, times delta t, while the time becomes gamma times one minus v over c, times delta t. divide one by the other. the gammas cancel, the delta t's cancel, and multiplying top and bottom by c leaves c minus v over c minus v. that is just c, for every speed v.

reels.name: Block
reels.cap: Three years later, Hermann Minkowski, who had taught Einstein in Zurich, turned all of this into geometry.
reels.doc: Newton's picture as a stack of space slices (x, y across, time up), the light cone of one flash, a rocket's worldline, and the rocket's own slices of "now" tilting toward the cone while the cone stays put.
reels.words: three years later, hermann minkowski, who had taught einstein in zurich, turned all of this into geometry. start with newton's picture. space is a sheet, and time stacks the sheets up, one per moment. everyone in the universe shares the same sheet as their now. a flash of light spreads out as a growing circle, so in the stack it traces a cone. a rocket moving at half the speed of light traces a slanted line. einstein's change is this. the moving crew slice the same block at a tilt. their sheets of now lean toward the cone, by just as much as their path leans. nothing in the block shrinks or stretches. and the light cone is the one thing every slicing agrees on.

reels.name: Diagram
reels.cap: Flatten the block to one line of space, across, and time going up.
reels.words: flatten the block to one line of space, across, and time going up. light moves one light second per second, so its path is the diagonal. our own grid of places and moments is square. now give the rocket speed. its time axis leans right, its space axis leans up, and its whole grid pinches toward the diagonal. go faster, and it pinches more. but look at the diagonal of the rocket's grid. it stays on the light line, at every speed. that is what an ordinary rotation cannot do. turn a grid like a stick in your hand, and its diagonal swings away from the light line. a rotation keeps circles, and the light line is not on one. a boost is a hyperbolic rotation instead. the rocket's one second and two second marks slide along hyperbolas, the curves where c t squared minus x squared stays fixed. for light that quantity is zero, so the light line maps onto itself. so a boost really is like a polar transform, but with a hyperbolic angle in place of an ordinary one. tensors are the bookkeeping for quantities, like this one, that every grid agrees on, and einstein later needed them for gravity.

reels.name: Shadows
reels.cap: Every rule we used is a shadow of this one tilt.
reels.words: every rule we used is a shadow of this one tilt. follow the hyperbola up to the rocket's one second mark, and slide across to our time axis. it sits at one point one five five seconds. that is time dilation. a rocket one light second long sweeps out this band. our now line cuts it at zero point eight six six light seconds. that is length contraction. the rocket's now line tilts up. the moment the crew call now at their front end is, for us, zero point five seven seven seconds later. that is the relativity of simultaneity. now our flash, one light second away after one second. read it on the rocket's grid. it sits at zero point five seven seven light seconds and zero point five seven seven seconds. still on the diagonal, so still c.

reels.name: Tests
reels.cap: Then came the checks.
reels.words: then came the checks. cosmic rays make muons about fifteen kilometres up, and a muon lives only two point two microseconds, long enough to cross six hundred and sixty metres. at nearly light speed, its clock runs about ten times slow, so it gets ten times further, and we catch them at the ground. g p s satellites move at three point nine kilometres per second. from speed alone, their clocks fall seven microseconds behind each day. left uncorrected, that would put you two kilometres off every day. relativity is built into every phone's map.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: So here is the answer to the puzzle.
reels.words: so here is the answer to the puzzle. motion does not shrink distances and stretch times one by one. it tilts space and time into each other, and the tilt pinches every grid toward the light line, which is the one line that never moves. contraction, dilation and simultaneity are three shadows of that one tilt, and light's speed comes out as c for everyone.

title: How PET image reconstruction works, from back-projection to deep learning and…

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: A PET scanner never sees the image.
reels.words: a pet scanner never sees the image. around the patient sits a ring of detectors, and all it records is pairs of hits, each one a line along which an annihilation happened. reconstruction is the step that turns millions of these lines into a map of where the tracer is. this video walks through the methods in the order they arrived: analytic back-projection, statistical iterative methods, regularised ones, deep learning, and the commercial tools for low-count scans. for each one: how it works, and the problem that made it necessary. every image you will see is reconstructed here, from the same simulated scan.

reels.name: Sinogram
reels.cap: First, how the data are stored.
reels.words: first, how the data are stored. each line of response is fixed by two numbers: its angle and its offset from the centre. follow a single point source: as the angle turns, its offset swings back and forth, tracing a sine wave in angle-offset space. that is why this table of counts is called a sinogram. a whole patient is a stack of overlapping sines. every method below starts from the same model: the expected count on line i is a weighted sum of the activity in every voxel, with weights set by the scanner's geometry and physics, and the counts actually recorded scatter around that expectation with poisson noise.

reels.name: Backproject
reels.cap: The oldest idea is to run the measurement backwards.
reels.words: the oldest idea is to run the measurement backwards. think of it one event at a time. each detected pair gives a line, and the scanner cannot tell where on that line the decay happened, so back-projection adds a little activity along the whole line. thousands of lines pile up, and where they cross most often, the tracer is. a sinogram groups the same lines by angle. take one angle's projection and smear each count back along its line, across the whole image. add a second angle, then more. with all seventy two angles the shape appears, but blurred: every count was spread along its entire line, not just where it came from. back-projecting a single point gives a star whose brightness falls as one over the distance, so every edge and every lesion is smeared into its surroundings.

reels.name: Fbp
reels.cap: Filtered back-projection fixes the blur before it happens.
reels.words: filtered back-projection fixes the blur before it happens. take each projection and multiply its spectrum by a ramp, which boosts high frequencies. the filtered projection grows negative side lobes, and when it is back-projected those negative lobes cancel the smear from neighbouring angles. event by event, it reads like this: each line now carries a bright core with a thin negative band on either side. where lines cross, the cores add up; away from the crossing, the bands cancel each other's tails, and the star shrinks to a point. with all angles, the image comes back sharp. it is fast and linear, and for decades it was the clinical standard. its weakness is noise. cut the counts to a quarter, and the ramp amplifies the statistical noise into streaks; about forty percent of the pixels even come out negative, which no activity can be. f b p assumes the data are exact projections; they are really poisson counts.

reels.name: Mlem
reels.cap: Statistical methods start from the Poisson model instead.
reels.words: statistical methods start from the poisson model instead. m l e m, introduced for pet by shepp and vardi in nineteen eighty two, looks for the image that makes the measured counts most likely, and gets there with one simple update. start from a guess. forward project it, to predict the sinogram it would produce. compare with what was measured, line by line, as a ratio: above one where the guess is too faint, below one where it is too bright. back-project the ratios into image space, and multiply the guess by them. repeat. the image stays positive by construction, the noise model is built in, and the scanner's physics can sit inside the weights. after one iteration it is a smooth blob, after twenty the lesions are sharp.

reels.name: Noise growth
reels.cap: There is a catch.
reels.words: there is a catch. as the iterations go on, lesion contrast climbs and then levels off by about twenty iterations, but background noise keeps rising. the most likely image, given noisy counts, is itself noisy: maximum likelihood ends up fitting the noise. at a quarter of the counts, iteration twenty is already grainy, and by iteration two hundred the noise has more than tripled. so in practice nobody runs to convergence. scanners stop early and smooth with a gaussian filter, trading resolution for noise by hand.

reels.name: Osem
reels.cap: MLEM's other problem was speed: every update needs a full forward and back-projection of all the data.
reels.words: mlem's other problem was speed: every update needs a full forward and back-projection of all the data. hudson and larkin's fix, in nineteen ninety four, was to split the angles into subsets, here twelve subsets of six angles each, and apply the same update using one subset at a time. each pass through all twelve subsets counts as one iteration, and it does roughly as much as twelve m l e m iterations: here one o s e m iteration lands within six percent of ten m l e m ones. they reported an order of magnitude acceleration. o s e m is not guaranteed to converge, and it inherits mlem's noise growth, but it became, and remains, the clinical workhorse.

reels.name: Penalised
reels.cap: The principled fix is to change the question.
reels.words: the principled fix is to change the question. instead of the most likely image, ask for the image that fits the counts well while also being plausible, by subtracting a penalty on roughness, weighted by a strength beta. a popular penalty is the relative difference penalty. small differences between neighbouring voxels are punished, but large ones, real edges, are punished relatively less, so lesions keep their edges. because noise can no longer grow, the algorithm can run all the way to convergence. at a quarter of the counts: plain o s e m is grainy; a gaussian filter cuts the noise but also the contrast; the penalised image keeps the contrast with the noise of the filtered one, and a larger beta smooths further at some cost in contrast. this is what ge's q.clear does, using a convergent algorithm called b s r e m, with beta as the one setting the user chooses.

reels.name: Deep families
reels.cap: Deep learning entered reconstruction in four places, depending on how much of the physics the network is trusted with.
reels.words: deep learning entered reconstruction in four places, depending on how much of the physics the network is trusted with. simplest: reconstruct as usual, then hand a noisy low-count image to a network trained to output what a full-count scan would look like. this is how most commercial tools work. second, inside the loop: unroll a fixed number of iterations, keep the physics and the poisson model in each one, and replace the hand-made penalty with a learned network. third, the deep image prior: the network's output is the image itself, fitted to this patient's own data through the forward model, with no training set at all. and fourth, direct: a network that maps the sinogram straight to an image, learning the whole inverse. going down the list, the network takes over more of the physics, which needs more training data and gives fewer guarantees.

reels.name: Unrolled
reels.cap: Here is what unrolling means.
reels.words: here is what unrolling means. start from the m l e m update. forward project the current image, compare it with the measured counts as a ratio, and back-project the ratio into an updated image. that step is where the poisson model lives: it pulls the image towards whatever makes this patient's counts most likely. now add a second branch. a small convolutional network looks at the same image and proposes a cleaner version of it. the two are blended into the next estimate, and the balance between them is learned as well. that is one block. stack a fixed number of blocks, say ten, and the whole chain becomes one network that goes from measured counts to an image. it is trained end to end on scans that have a full-count reference: the output is compared with the reference, and the error is passed back through every block, projections included. because every block re-checks the image against the counts, the network only has to learn what clean images look like, not the physics, so it can be small and needs far less training data. mehranian and reader's f b s e m net, in twenty twenty, is built this way.

reels.name: Image prior
reels.cap: The deep image prior deserves a closer look, because it needs no training data.
reels.words: the deep image prior deserves a closer look, because it needs no training data. feed a fixed random input into an untrained convolutional network. its output is the image. forward project that image, compare it with this patient's measured counts using the poisson likelihood, and adjust the network's weights, not the image directly. over the iterations the image sharpens. it works because convolutional networks reproduce smooth, structured content much more easily than noise, so stopping at the right point gives a clean image. gong and colleagues applied this to pet in twenty nineteen.

reels.name: Deep compare
reels.cap: So how do they differ in practice?
reels.words: so how do they differ in practice? a post-processing network learns from many pairs of low- and full-count images. it never sees the counts, it runs in moments after the usual reconstruction, and it can only clean what is already in the image. an unrolled network needs fewer training pairs, because it re-checks the counts in every block, but each scan costs several projections, and training through the projector is heavy. the deep image prior needs no training set at all and fits the counts at every step, but it trains a network from scratch for every patient, which is slow, and someone has to decide when to stop. a direct network must learn the physics itself from very many examples, often simulated. nothing checks its output against the measured counts. it is the fastest once trained, but it is also where invented structure is most likely to creep in.

reels.name: Products
reels.cap: Which brings us to the commercial tools.
reels.words: which brings us to the commercial tools. subtlepet, from subtle medical, works after reconstruction. a low-count image goes in, a two point five d u-net processes it, and out comes an image that looks like a full-count scan. it was trained on pairs of quarter-time and full-time scans of the same patients. an independent study of one hundred and ten patients tested it: at half the counts it brought liver noise back to the full-count level, s u v max shifted by about five percent, and the physicians' reports did not change. at a third of the counts, non-interpretable images fell from eighty three to thirteen percent. but it could not restore a small lesion that was absent from the input: a denoiser cannot add information that was never measured. scanner makers now build their own: ge's precision d l, cleared in twenty twenty three, aims to give time-of-flight-like image quality, canon's aice reconstruction followed a similar path, and subtle's newest version claims up to seventy five percent faster scans, a claim from the company, not yet from independent testing.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Putting it all together.
reels.words: putting it all together. filtered back-projection is fast but ignores the noise. m l e m models the poisson counts, but is slow and fits the noise if run long. o s e m made it fast enough for the clinic. penalised likelihood adds a prior and runs to convergence, at the cost of choosing beta. deep learning denoisers are fast and work remarkably well, but cannot add detail that was never measured. unrolled methods and the image prior keep the physics in the loop, while direct networks hand everything to learning and carry the most risk of inventing structure. each step kept the physics of the counts and added a better idea of what a real image looks like.

title: Ultrafast timing enables reconstruction-free positron emission imaging

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video explains a paper published in Nature Photonics in twenty twenty one.
reels.words: this video explains a paper published in nature photonics in twenty twenty one. it comes from simon cherry's group at the university of california, davis, working with hamamatsu photonics. they made the first images of a positron emitting tracer without any tomographic reconstruction.

reels.name: Lines
reels.cap: In PET, a positron annihilates and sends two photons in opposite directions.
reels.doc: One event is a whole line; timing shrinks it to a blob (210 ps, 3.15 cm) and then a spot (32 ps, 4.8 mm).
reels.words: in pet, a positron annihilates and sends two photons in opposite directions. two detectors catch them at almost the same moment. without timing, that pair only says the event was somewhere on the line between the detectors. so a scanner gathers lines from every angle, and an algorithm works out which picture fits all of them. that step needs complete angular coverage, and it amplifies noise. timing the two photons helps. the photon with less distance to go arrives first, and the offset from the middle of the line is the speed of light times the difference in arrival times, divided by two. the best clinical scanners time pairs to two hundred and ten picoseconds, which still leaves the event spread over three point one five centimetres. this paper reached thirty two picoseconds, which narrows it to four point eight millimetres, small enough to place the event directly. the paper simulates three sources between two detectors. without timing, they smear into one streak. with two hundred and ten picoseconds, they are still one blob. with thirty two picoseconds, three separate spots appear, from a single measurement.

reels.name: Detector
reels.cap: Ordinary PET detectors are too slow for this.
reels.doc: The Cerenkov-radiator-integrated MCP-PMT: gamma in, prompt photons, photoelectron, avalanche, a fast pulse out.
reels.words: ordinary pet detectors are too slow for this. their crystals give off light over nanoseconds, and their light sensors add too much jitter. so the authors built a different detector. its window is a plate of lead glass three point two millimetres thick. a photocathode is laid directly on the glass, followed by two microchannel plates and an anode. a gamma ray stopping in the glass frees a fast electron. the electron outruns light in the glass and gives off cherenkov light within a few picoseconds, and those photons reach the photocathode without crossing any optical boundary. each one knocks out an electron, which the microchannel plates multiply about one point eight million times, into a pulse at the anode. the jitter for a single photon is only twenty two picoseconds. here is one of the detectors. the thin glass is the price. each detector catches only twelve point nine percent of the gamma rays reaching it, so both catch their photon for fewer than two percent of pairs.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: Each detector's pulse is recorded in full, fifty billion samples a second.
reels.doc: Two waveforms in, one time difference out: a CNN; 32.9 ps -> 26.4 ps; five positions 25 mm apart.
reels.words: each detector's pulse is recorded in full, fifty billion samples a second. a convolutional neural network takes both waveforms in, and gives out the difference in arrival times. to train it, the authors recorded a source in the middle of the line, and shifted each recorded pair by a delay they chose, so the right answer was known. about a million such events taught the network to read the time from the pulse shapes. with the source at the centre, the arrival differences pile up in a narrow peak. timing each pulse where it crosses a fixed fraction of its height gives a width of thirty two point nine picoseconds. the network narrows it to twenty six point four, or three point nine six millimetres. then the source was moved along the line in steps of twenty five millimetres. every peak moved the same distance, so the timing reads position correctly. across the ten centimetre range, the timing averaged thirty two picoseconds, or four point eight millimetres.

reels.name: Scan
reels.cap: The setup has just two detectors facing each other, with the object between them.
reels.doc: Two detectors, one line: x from where the line is, y from the timing; rows stack into the first image.
reels.words: the setup has just two detectors facing each other, with the object between them. along the line, the timing gives each event's position. across it, the position comes from where the detectors are. at one position, every detected pair becomes a dot on the line, and the dots are counted into one row of the image. then the object steps sideways, and the next row is filled. no rotation and no reconstruction are needed. this is the first such image, straight from the counts. the scan is thirty five millimetres wide. the two empty holes are already visible. sharpness across the line is set by the two millimetre collimator opening, and along the line by the timing.

reels.name: Images
reels.cap: The authors then imaged three test objects, first a small cylinder with two empty holes eight millimetres across.
reels.doc: Three test objects: 8 mm voids, 3 mm rods, an 18.4 cm brain slice from ~20,000 events.
reels.words: the authors then imaged three test objects, first a small cylinder with two empty holes eight millimetres across. both holes stand out clearly. the second object holds rods of different sizes. rods three millimetres across can be told apart. that means a sharpness of about four to five millimetres. the third object is the size of a human head, a slice of brain eighteen point four centimetres across. its detail comes through at about four point eight millimetres. every event lands where it belongs, so few events are needed. ten thousand events already show the brain, twenty thousand show it well, and more adds little.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: These images were slow.
reels.doc: Slow today (24 h, ~1000 MBq) like the first CT (9 days); >1000x sensitivity -> ~1 min; open geometries.
reels.words: these images were slow. the brain image took twenty four hours of scanning, with up to about a thousand megabecquerels of tracer. but the first c t scans took up to nine days, and c t now takes under a second. the authors list the obvious upgrades. they would use a denser and thicker radiator, and tile many detectors into panels. together they could raise the sensitivity more than a thousand times, bringing the brain scan down to about a minute. because no reconstruction needs complete angles, a scanner need not be a closed ring. two panels on either side of a patient would do. and with no reconstruction step, the image could be watched as it builds up.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the whole chain.
reels.doc: The whole chain, inputs to outputs: photon pair, detectors, waveforms, network, time difference, pixel.
reels.words: here is the whole chain. a photon pair reaches two cherenkov detectors, which give two fast waveforms. a network reads the time difference from them, the time difference gives a position, and the event goes straight into its pixel. at thirty two picoseconds that position is good to four point eight millimetres, and the image needs no reconstruction at all.

title: Fast Emitting Nanocomposites for High-Resolution ToF-PET Imaging Based on…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video explains a paper published in Advanced Materials Technologies in twenty twenty four.
reels.words: this video explains a paper published in advanced materials technologies in twenty twenty four. it comes from angelo monguzzi's group at the university of milano bicocca, working with cern. they built a pet scintillator from thin layers of a heavy crystal and a fast plastic, made heavier with tiny grains of hafnium oxide.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: In PET, a positron annihilates and sends two gamma rays in opposite directions.
reels.doc: The arrival difference places the event (210 ps -> 3.15 cm, 10 ps -> 1.5 mm); slow vs fast light; the formula's three terms.
reels.words: in pet, a positron annihilates and sends two gamma rays in opposite directions. two detectors catch them a moment apart. the offset of the event from the middle of the line is the speed of light times the difference in arrival times, divided by two. today's best clinical scanners time the pairs to two hundred and ten picoseconds, which leaves each event smeared over three point one five centimetres. the field is aiming for ten picoseconds, which would pin it down to one point five millimetres. the timing comes from the light that the scintillator gives off. in a slow scintillator, the photons trickle out over a long time. in a fast one, the same number of photons comes out in a short burst. the detector reacts to the first few photons, so the more of them arrive early, the more precisely the moment is fixed. the paper puts this as a formula. the timing spread grows with the square root of the rise time, the square root of the decay time, and shrinks with the square root of the number of photons collected.

reels.name: Tradeoff
reels.cap: Scintillators come in two kinds.
reels.doc: BGO stops the gamma ray and is bright but fades over 300 ns; plastic fades in 1.4 ns but is too light.
reels.words: scintillators come in two kinds. a heavy crystal such as bismuth germanate, called b g o, stops the gamma ray within a few millimetres and gives plenty of light. but that light fades over about three hundred nanoseconds. a plastic scintillator fades in about one point four nanoseconds. but its density is only about one gram per cubic centimetre, so most gamma rays pass straight through it. no single material is both heavy and fast.

reels.name: Layers
reels.cap: The paper's answer is to combine the two.
reels.doc: The heterostructure: the gamma ray stops in BGO, its recoil electron crosses into the fast layer, both glow.
reels.words: the paper's answer is to combine the two. thin layers of b g o alternate with layers of a fast plastic, each one hundred micrometres thick. a gamma ray is absorbed in a b g o layer and knocks out an electron. the electron travels a fraction of a millimetre, crossing into the next plastic layer, and leaves energy along its path in both materials. the energy left in the plastic comes out as a fast flash, while the b g o part glows slowly. the fast flash marks the moment of the event, so the stack keeps the stopping power of b g o and borrows the speed of the plastic. the weak point is the plastic itself. it is so light that the electron leaves only a little of its energy there. so the authors set out to make the fast layer heavier.

reels.name: Composite
reels.cap: The new ingredient is hafnium oxide, grains about eighty five nanometres long, with a density of nine point six eight grams per cubic centimetre.
reels.doc: Hafnium oxide grains (85 nm, 9.68 g/cm3) mixed at 2.5 % wt into polystyrene with POPOP: 1.02 -> 1.5 g/cm3.
reels.words: the new ingredient is hafnium oxide, grains about eighty five nanometres long, with a density of nine point six eight grams per cubic centimetre. the fast layer starts as polystyrene, with a dye called popop that gives the fast light. the authors mix the hafnium oxide grains into it. at two and a half percent by weight, the density rises from one point zero two to one point five grams per cubic centimetre.

reels.name: Yield
reels.cap: The grains also make the film brighter.
reels.doc: Light yield: 3800 ph/MeV without grains, 9500 at 2.5 % wt, against EJ-232 8400 and BGO 10 000; 3 % falls.
reels.words: the grains also make the film brighter. without them, the film gives about three thousand eight hundred photons for each mega electron volt it absorbs. with them, it gives nine thousand five hundred, more than the commercial plastic e j two three two, and close to the ten thousand of b g o. the paper's measurements show the light rising with the amount of hafnium oxide, reaching its best at two and a half percent, then falling back at three percent. so two and a half percent is the recipe.

reels.name: Device
reels.cap: The device is a cube three millimetres on a side, built from alternating layers of B G O and nanocomposite.
reels.doc: The 3 mm cube of 100 um layers; energy share 0.29 -> 0.35; the 440-660 keV, >= 50 keV window keeps 24 %.
reels.words: the device is a cube three millimetres on a side, built from alternating layers of b g o and nanocomposite. simulations show what the grains buy. with plain plastic, the fast layers would take twenty nine percent of the deposited energy. with the nanocomposite, they take thirty five percent. the measured events can be sorted by where their energy went. the useful ones carry between four hundred and forty and six hundred and sixty kilo electron volts in total, with at least fifty kilo electron volts in the nanocomposite. that keeps twenty four percent of all events.

reels.name: Result
reels.cap: Here is the timing test, with pairs of gamma rays from a sodium twenty two source.
reels.doc: Coincidence timing: BGO 244 ps, multilayer 180 ps (26 % better), nanocomposite alone 141 ps.
reels.words: here is the timing test, with pairs of gamma rays from a sodium twenty two source. each histogram's width is the timing spread. bulk b g o gives two hundred and forty four picoseconds. the multilayer gives one hundred and eighty picoseconds, twenty six percent better. the nanocomposite on its own gives one hundred and forty one picoseconds, so the stack gets most of the way from the slow crystal to the fast plastic.

reels.name: Limits
reels.cap: From the measured rise and decay times, the formula predicts ninety four picoseconds for this stack.
reels.doc: Theory 94 ps vs measured 180 ps: beta 0.65 -> 0.2 (light lost at interfaces); the dye slows 1.4 -> 4.1 ns.
reels.words: from the measured rise and decay times, the formula predicts ninety four picoseconds for this stack. the measurement gave one hundred and eighty. the paper traces most of the difference to light lost on its way out. in an ideal build, sixty five of every hundred photons would reach the sensor. in this handmade stack, only about twenty do. the rest are lost at the many interfaces between the layers. the second limit is the decay. the nanocomposite fades over about four point one nanoseconds. the same dye on its own fades in one point four. something in the excited polystyrene slows the dye down, and by the formula that costs about a factor of one and a half in timing.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the whole chain.
reels.doc: The chain, inputs to outputs: gamma ray, BGO layer, recoil electron, nanocomposite, fast flash; what is next.
reels.words: here is the whole chain. a gamma ray stops in a b g o layer, its electron crosses into the nanocomposite, and the nanocomposite gives a fast flash that times the event. the result is one hundred and eighty picoseconds, instead of two hundred and forty four for b g o alone. two things hold it back. light is lost at the handmade interfaces, and the dye slows down inside the polystyrene. the authors plan industrial manufacturing to keep the light, and a denser composite to stop more gamma rays.

title: Laser-driven particle accelerators for cancer therapy: a review of state-of-the-art…

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This video explains a review by Roumani Alabd and Daniel Franklin on laser driven particle accelerators for cancer therapy.
reels.words: this video explains a review by roumani alabd and daniel franklin on laser driven particle accelerators for cancer therapy. today, the proton and ion beams used in therapy come from accelerators the size of a building: linacs, cyclotrons and synchrotrons. a laser plasma accelerator does the accelerating over millimetres instead of tens of metres, by hitting a target with an extremely intense, extremely short laser pulse. by the end, you should have a map of the field: three ways to accelerate, what each one produces, how far each has got, and what still blocks the clinic.

reels.name: Why particles
reels.cap: First, why charged particles at all.
reels.words: first, why charged particles at all. x-ray photons deposit most of their dose near the surface and fade with depth, so the tissue in front of a deep tumour gets more dose than the tumour. protons are different. they lose energy slowly at first, then faster as they slow, and dump most of it in a sharp bragg peak, with no dose beyond it. carbon ions have an even sharper peak, with a small tail from fragments. very high energy electrons give a broad, flat profile that tolerates changes in tissue density. the depth of the peak is set by the energy: sweep a proton beam from sixty to two hundred and fifty mev, and its peak moves from about three to almost forty centimetres. yet about ninety percent of radiotherapy still uses x-rays, and only about two hundred and sixty thousand patients have ever had hadron therapy, because the machines that make these beams are large, specialised and expensive.

reels.name: Accelerators
reels.cap: Conventional machines push particles through radio frequency cavities again and again.
reels.words: conventional machines push particles through radio frequency cavities again and again. a linac lines the cavities up in a row; a cyclotron bends the particles into a spiral so they cross the same gap many times, and makes most of today's therapy protons; a synchrotron ramps its magnets around a fixed ring, and makes the heavier ions. each needs a dedicated building, power and shielding, and switching between ion species is slow. a laser plasma accelerator replaces the cavities with the electric field inside a plasma, of order a teravolt per metre. at that field, ten micrometres is enough for ten mev. the catch is efficiency: the titanium sapphire lasers that drive them turn only zero point one to one percent of their electrical power into light, and need heavy cooling.

reels.name: Overview
reels.cap: All three mechanisms start the same way.
reels.words: all three mechanisms start the same way. a titanium sapphire laser fires pulses tens of femtoseconds to picoseconds long, focused above ten to the eighteen watts per square centimetre, repeating one to ten times a second. fired into a gas, it drives a wakefield that accelerates electrons. into a foil a few micrometres thick, it drives target normal sheath acceleration, mostly of protons. into a foil just nanometres thick, at a thousand times the intensity, radiation pressure acceleration, which can push protons and carbon.

reels.name: LWFA
reels.cap: Wakefield acceleration first.
reels.words: wakefield acceleration first. the plasma is a sea of light electrons and heavy positive ions. as the laser pulse passes, its ponderomotive force shoves the electrons sideways, out of its path. behind the pulse they leave a bubble that holds only ions. that charge separation makes an enormous electric field inside the bubble. an electron caught at the back is pulled forward and toward the axis, surfs the bubble, and gains energy all the way. the pulses last twenty to forty femtoseconds, shorter than the plasma wavelength, so the wake is driven resonantly. wakefields have produced seven point eight gev electrons. therapy needs fifty to two hundred and fifty mev, and four hundred mev beams can reach beyond forty centimetres.

reels.name: TNSA
reels.cap: For protons, the workhorse is target normal sheath acceleration.
reels.words: for protons, the workhorse is target normal sheath acceleration. the laser hits a thin foil five to fifty micrometres thick. its leading edge makes a hot plasma on the front, and the main pulse drives those electrons to nearly the speed of light, straight through the foil and out of the back, where they hang as a thin negative sheath. the field between the sheath and the foil is of order teravolts per metre. it does not pull ions out of the foil itself, but out of a thin layer of moisture and hydrocarbons on the back surface, which is why the beam is mostly protons, launched normal to the surface. the fastest protons leave in a narrow cone; the slow ones spread wide, up to two to three hundred milliradians. t n s a has given up to six times ten to the thirteen protons per pulse, but its maximum energy grows only with the square root of the laser intensity.

reels.name: RPA
reels.cap: Radiation pressure acceleration needs a thousand times more intensity, ten to the twenty one to ten to the twenty three watts per square centimetre.
reels.words: radiation pressure acceleration needs a thousand times more intensity, ten to the twenty one to ten to the twenty three watts per square centimetre. now the pressure of the light itself does the work. the pulse shoves the electrons forward, the charge separation drags the ions after them, and the two layers move as one. in a target up to about one and a half micrometres thick, the laser bores a hole: a front marches into the target and pushes ions ahead of it, like a piston. in a target thinner than the laser wavelength, five to fifty nanometres, the whole foil flies off as a light sail, reaching higher energies at lower flux. circularly polarised light helps, turning the pulse energy into motion rather than heat. two payoffs: the ions leave as a bunch, so they are far more monoenergetic, and their energy grows linearly with intensity, against the square root for t n s a.

reels.name: Compare
reels.cap: Before looking at the beams in detail, here is how the three branches compare.
reels.words: before looking at the beams in detail, here is how the three branches compare. targets: a gas, a micrometre foil, a nanometre foil. intensity: wakefields and sheath acceleration work from about ten to the eighteen watts per square centimetre; radiation pressure needs ten to the twenty one and up. spectrum: wakefield electrons and sheath protons come out with broad energy spreads, while radiation pressure ions come out as a bunch. spread: wakefield electrons a few milliradians, radiation pressure ions about fifty, slow sheath protons up to three hundred. energy against what therapy needs: electrons are already far beyond it, protons have reached the therapeutic range, and carbon is well short. and biology: laser electrons and laser protons have both treated tumours in mice, while radiation pressure carbon has so far irradiated cells in a dish. so each branch wins somewhere. wakefields win on energy and beam spread, for very high energy electrons. sheath acceleration wins on maturity and particle numbers, for protons today. radiation pressure wins on spectrum and scaling, the route to carbon, but it is the furthest from the clinic.

reels.name: Beam time
reels.cap: How do these beams compare with a synchrotron's?
reels.words: how do these beams compare with a synchrotron's? in time, a laser driven bunch lasts femtoseconds to picoseconds; synchrotron bunches last hundreds of picoseconds to nanoseconds. so the peak current reaches kiloamperes, against milliamperes. in angle, slow t n s a protons spread over two to three hundred milliradians, radiation pressure ions about fifty, wakefield electrons one to five, and a conventional beam only microradians. and every shot carries a broad spread of energies and several ion species at once, which a synchrotron never does.

reels.name: Beam yield
reels.cap: Those numbers hide a catch.
reels.words: those numbers hide a catch. one shot may carry ten to the twelve to ten to the thirteen protons, but in one study only about ten to the nine landed within one mev of the eighty five mev cut-off, roughly a thousand times fewer. and a petawatt laser fires about once a second, so the average current is nanoamperes: comparable with the beams clinics already use, not orders of magnitude above them.

reels.name: UHDR
reels.cap: Why care about such short pulses?
reels.words: why care about such short pulses? because of flash. above about forty grays per second, irradiated normal tissue appears to be spared. the leading explanation: the dose arrives so fast that it uses up the oxygen in normal cells before the blood can resupply it, so for a moment they behave like hypoxic tumour cells, which resist radiation. laser sources reach extreme peak dose rates: ten to the seven grays per second in an early proton study, ten to the nine in others, two times ten to the nine for a single four hundred picosecond carbon pulse, and up to ten to the thirteen for electrons. their average dose rates are another matter: zero point two grays per second in that early proton study, about one for a kilohertz electron source, and one to two grays per minute in the first mouse study. the review stresses that relying on flash will need careful control of exactly this pulse structure.

reels.name: Transport
reels.cap: A broad, divergent, mixed beam has to be tamed before it can reach a patient.
reels.words: a broad, divergent, mixed beam has to be tamed before it can reach a patient. first, capture it: pulsed solenoids or permanent magnet quadrupoles grab the spreading particles and make them parallel; one recent system collimated a ten mev proton beam with just two permanent magnets. then select. in a laser driven carbon experiment, a zero point nine tesla dipole sat fifty millimetres from the target. a carbon ion has twice a proton's mass to charge ratio, so at the same energy per nucleon it bends on twice the radius, about one metre against half a metre. a five hundred micrometre slit then passes only the carbon. gantry designs built around capture and energy selection come out two to three times smaller than a conventional proton gantry.

reels.name: SOBP
reels.cap: A broad spectrum also changes how dose is planned.
reels.words: a broad spectrum also changes how dose is planned. one energy gives one narrow bragg peak, far too thin for a tumour. several energies, each with its own weight, add up to a spread out bragg peak, flat across the tumour. a laser shot produces many energies at once, and the broad energy assorted depth dose model is built on exactly this idea. the difficulty is that the spectrum changes from shot to shot, and shaping it reliably is one of the open problems the review highlights.

reels.name: Biology
reels.cap: Do these beams act on cells like conventional ones?
reels.words: do these beams act on cells like conventional ones? so far, mostly yes. the relative biological effectiveness at ten percent survival was one point two for hamster cells at ten to the seven grays per second, and one point four for salivary gland cells at ten to the nine. studies that compared laser and conventional protons directly found no significant difference, consistent with the clinical value of one point one. in living animals, laser driven electrons treated tumours on mouse ears with three and six grays in twenty fifteen, matching a clinical linac. in twenty twenty two, the first in vivo laser proton study delivered four grays in a single shot to three millimetre tumours, matching a cyclotron. a few results hint at something new: ultra high dose rate electrons left one point seven to two point nine times more unrepaired d n a breaks a day later, and a v h e e study saw a larger difference between melanoma and normal cells than x-rays gave.

reels.name: Challenges
reels.cap: The review groups the obstacles into five.
reels.words: the review groups the obstacles into five. beam quality: broad spectra that change from shot to shot. transport: beamlines that stay compact yet keep the beam focused. dose shaping, and the biology of ultra short pulses. dosimetry. and clinical engineering and regulation: lasers stable over many thousands of shots, targets that can be replaced, shielding, and standards that do not yet cover ultra high dose rates. dosimetry deserves a closer look. an ionisation chamber collects the charge freed in its gas, but when a whole dose arrives in picoseconds, much of that charge recombines first, and the reading saturates. film responds almost independently of dose rate, but it is read out afterwards, not in real time. one proposed answer measures heat instead of charge: a small graphite calorimeter recorded one to three grays per pulse from fifteen to forty mev laser protons.

reels.name: Future
reels.cap: What is changing?
reels.words: what is changing? tuning a laser plasma source is a nonlinear search in many dimensions, where adjusting one knob at a time is slow and misses the best settings. a closed loop bayesian optimiser adjusts the laser wavefront and target position, fires, measures, and chooses the next shot. the first such system matched the best manual proton energy using only sixty percent of the laser energy. it needs a fast signal from every shot, and transmitted laser light is one candidate. it also needs targets that survive: cryogenic hydrogen jets, liquid sheets and tape drives now allow sustained multi hertz operation. two dedicated research facilities are planned: lhara in the u k, with protons up to one hundred and twenty seven mev and carbon up to thirty three point four mev per nucleon, and dr laser at e l i in romania, aiming for carbon up to one hundred and ten mev per nucleon, about three centimetres in tissue.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: So where does each branch stand on energy?
