reels.words: so where does each branch stand on energy? electrons are there: therapy needs fifty to two hundred and fifty mev, and wakefields have gone far beyond. protons have reached one hundred and fifty mev, inside the therapeutic range and enough for about fifteen centimetres of water. carbon has reached forty eight mev per nucleon, against the one hundred and twenty to four hundred and thirty needed, which is under a centimetre of range.

reels.name: Field map
reels.cap: Putting the map together.
reels.words: putting the map together. three mechanisms, each feeding one kind of therapy. wakefield electrons, for very high energy electron therapy: the energy is reached and tumours have been treated in mice; what remains is the energy spread and dosimetry at extreme dose rates. sheath protons: inside the therapeutic energy range and through a first in vivo study; what remains is the broad spectrum, the wide spread, and building a uniform spread out bragg peak from it. radiation pressure carbon: still under a centimetre of range, and cells only; it needs a thousand times the intensity and faster repetition. across all three run the same open problems: shot to shot stability, compact transport, dosimetry, and regulation that does not yet cover ultra high dose rates. and the enablers the review points to: closed loop optimisation, targets that survive multi hertz operation, and dedicated facilities. its conclusion is that translation will be driven as much by automation, control and target engineering as by peak energy.

title: The i3M Valencia Detectors for Molecular Imaging Lab

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This video is about one lab: the Detectors for Molecular Imaging Lab at i3M in Valencia, led by Antonio González.
reels.words: this video is about one lab: the detectors for molecular imaging lab at i3m in valencia, led by antonio gonzález. for more than a decade it has built pet from monolithic crystals, single blocks of scintillator instead of arrays of tiny pixels. the thread runs from a breast ring of separate blocks in twenty twelve, through a rodent scanner made of one crystal tube, to a breast ring of curved crystals glued into one. along the way came a spin-off, oncovision, and a preclinical line now sold by bruker.

reels.name: Light
reels.cap: Start with why monolithic crystals are hard.
reels.words: start with why monolithic crystals are hard. here is a block fifty millimetres wide and ten thick, with photodetectors on its bottom face. a gamma ray interacts inside it, and the light spreads into a peak across the pixels. move the interaction, and the peak moves with it, so the centroid gives position. move it toward the sensor and the peak narrows, so the width gives depth. i3m paints the other faces black, so light that hits them is lost rather than bounced back, which keeps that shape intact. the trouble is the edges. near a side face, half the light is missing, so the centroid is dragged toward the middle. plotting the centroid against the true position, positions bunch inward near both edges. this is the edge effect, and every design in this story is, in part, an answer to it.

reels.name: Mammi
reels.cap: The lab's first big monolithic system was MAMMI, a breast scanner built with Oncovision.
reels.words: the lab's first big monolithic system was mammi, a breast scanner built with oncovision. twelve lyso blocks form a ring with a hundred and eighty six millimetre opening. each block is ten millimetres thick and cut as a truncated pyramid, forty millimetres at the front and fifty at the back, so the blocks tile the ring with less dead space. each sits on a position sensitive photomultiplier whose sixty four anodes are reduced to five signals: energy, the centroid in two directions, and the spread of the light, which gives depth. at the centre it resolved one point eight millimetres radially. moving outward, the radial number passes three millimetres beyond sixty, and reaches six at the edge of the field, while tangential and axial stay under three. that is parallax, and the depth that could fix it was measured but not used in these images, because of computing limits at the time.

reels.name: Preclinical
reels.cap: The same blocks went into small animal scanners.
reels.words: the same blocks went into small animal scanners. albira, the first commercial pet built on monolithic crystals, used two rings of eight pyramid blocks on photomultipliers. an independent test measured one point seven two millimetres at the centre and five point three percent sensitivity. its successor, bruker's insert for a seven tesla m r i, moved to silicon photomultipliers and reached zero point six eight millimetres and eleven percent. because depth was now used, the resolution stays near zero point nine millimetres all the way to thirty five millimetres off centre.

reels.name: Tube idea
reels.cap: In twenty eighteen the lab, with Stan Majewski and colleagues, asked a radical question.
reels.words: in twenty eighteen the lab, with stan majewski and colleagues, asked a radical question. a ring of separate blocks has gaps, and every block has two side edges where positions bunch up. what if the whole ring were one crystal, a tube with flat outer facets for the sensors? their evidence was indirect. on bruker's insert, keeping only events in the inner sixty percent of each block, away from the edges, sharpened the fitted rod width from one point four five to one point one nine millimetres. and a simulation gave the tube about thirty percent more sensitivity: five point three against three point seven percent.

reels.name: Tube
reels.cap: By twenty twenty two the tube existed.
reels.words: by twenty twenty two the tube existed. this is the crystal: one piece of lyso with a sixty two millimetre bore, ten flat outer facets, each carrying an eight by eight silicon photomultiplier array. it reached about one point four millimetres radially and one point three axially, with three point eight percent peak sensitivity, measured from sinogram profiles rather than reconstructed images. the readout keeps channel counts low. instead of sixty four signals per facet, the rows are summed and the columns are summed, sixteen signals that still describe the light's shape, including the spread that encodes depth. positions come from the centre of gravity, corrected with a calibration map that also absorbs the depth dependence.

reels.name: Semi mono
reels.cap: In parallel the lab developed a hybrid.
reels.words: in parallel the lab developed a hybrid. the block is cut into twenty two thin slabs, under a millimetre each. which slab was hit comes from a simple centroid, the position along the slab from a small neural network, and depth from the ratio of total energy to the brightest signal. in twenty twenty six this became a preclinical scanner: two rings of fourteen blocks around a hundred and six millimetre bore, every one of its seventeen hundred and ninety two channels read out. one network, trained once on one module, serves all twenty eight. it reached one point six one millimetres at the centre and three point five percent sensitivity.

reels.name: Deep breast
reels.cap: The newest system scales the idea to a breast.
reels.words: the newest system scales the idea to a breast. deepbreast is a ring two hundred millimetres across. the single tube could not simply be scaled up: the authors say lyso cannot be grown to that size. so the ring is fourteen curved crystals, twelve and a half millimetres thick, glued edge to edge with meltmount, whose refractive index of one point seven is close to lyso's one point eight. bent circuit boards carry twelve by twelve silicon photomultipliers around the outside. the glue is the point. take an interaction near a joint. with an air gap, the light would stop at the boundary and the position would bunch up there. with index-matched glue, the light carries on into the neighbouring crystal, so optically the ring behaves as one piece, and the side edges disappear.

reels.name: Positioning
reels.cap: Here is a real coincidence, measured on the ring.
reels.words: here is a real coincidence, measured on the ring. each module's sensors are summed into rows and columns, and the light of one gamma ray spreads across the boundary between modules four and five. so an event is positioned from the rows of all fourteen modules, a hundred and sixty eight signals, plus the columns of the three nearest, fed to two small neural networks, one per coordinate, with depth again from energy over the brightest signal. training on the assembled ring with a rotating collimated fan beam cut calibration from eleven days to three point six.

reels.name: Breast results
reels.cap: Against MAMMI, the gain is flatness.
reels.words: against mammi, the gain is flatness. mammi's radial resolution climbed from one point eight to six millimetres toward the edge. deepbreast starts at one point seven and averages one point nine out to eighty millimetres, within ten percent everywhere. that is not only the glue: mammi's figures ignored depth, and deepbreast uses it. sensitivity is two percent, above mammi's one point six, but far below a pixelated breast ring at eleven. depth is resolved to three point six millimetres, energy to nineteen percent, the count rate peaks at fifteen kilocounts per second, and there is no time of flight yet; the authors estimate about a hundred picoseconds would be needed to matter.

reels.name: Compton
reels.cap: Monolithic crystals still reduce each gamma ray to one point.
reels.words: monolithic crystals still reduce each gamma ray to one point. in lyso, a five hundred and eleven kev photon is about as likely to compton scatter as to be absorbed outright. when it scatters and is then absorbed, the light of both deposits merges, and the estimate lands between them. i3m's plan for this, from twenty eighteen, is two separate layers: a thin scatterer and a thick absorber, far enough apart for time of flight to say which was hit first. in twenty twenty four they built the scatter ring and measured one hundred and ninety two picoseconds. that needs the layers about fifty eight millimetres apart; they are thirty eight and a half. so the timing cannot order the hits, and the ring was repurposed.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: So the arc of this lab: separate blocks with edges and gaps, then a single crystal tube, then, when crystals could not grow large enough, a ring glued into optical continuity.
reels.words: so the arc of this lab: separate blocks with edges and gaps, then a single crystal tube, then, when crystals could not grow large enough, a ring glued into optical continuity. the habits carry through: black paint to keep the light's shape, row and column sums to keep channels low, and lately one trained network for every module. what none of these systems does yet is separate several interactions inside one thick crystal; each event is still a single point.

title: How a PET detector is calibrated, pixelated versus monolithic and semi-monolithic, with…

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: A PET detector does not report where a gamma ray hit.
reels.words: a pet detector does not report where a gamma ray hit. it reports charges and timestamps from its photosensors. calibration is everything that turns those numbers into physics: where the interaction was, how much energy it deposited, when it happened, and, across the whole scanner, how efficiently each line of response counts. the answers look very different for a pixelated block than for a monolithic crystal, and that difference is the subject of this video.

reels.name: Block
reels.cap: The conventional detector is the block, introduced by Casey and Nutt in nineteen eighty six.
reels.words: the conventional detector is the block, introduced by casey and nutt in nineteen eighty six. a grid of small crystals, a slotted light guide, and only four photomultipliers. the slots are cut to different depths so that each crystal shares its light between the tubes in its own proportion. light from a crystal on the left lands mostly in tube a; move right and it shifts toward b. so the ratio of b to the sum marks the crystal, and the decoder only needs thresholds between neighbouring values. that only works if all four tubes have equal gain, so the original system shone a common l e d into them and adjusted each one.

reels.name: Flood setup
reels.cap: Here is what that looks like on the bench.
reels.words: here is what that looks like on the bench. a point source sits in front of the block with no collimator, so it bathes the whole face. a gamma ray stops in one crystal, its light spreads through the guide, the tubes share it, and the event becomes one dot at its anger position. one dot says little, so the source keeps firing. after a few hundred events, clusters appear; after a few thousand, a grid; after tens of thousands, one sharp spot per crystal.

reels.name: Flood
reels.cap: That accumulated picture is the flood map, and it drives the first calibration, crystal identification.
reels.words: that accumulated picture is the flood map, and it drives the first calibration, crystal identification. the source was uncollimated, so no single event came with a known position. yet the map shows one bright spot per crystal, blurred by light statistics. the spots are not evenly spaced; edge crystals are squeezed together by the light guide. software finds the peaks, draws boundaries between them, and stores a lookup table that turns any position into a crystal number. the key point: the crystal pattern itself supplies the labels, so no collimator is needed.

reels.name: Energy why
reels.cap: Why does energy need calibrating at all?
reels.words: why does energy need calibrating at all? a photon that leaves the patient untouched arrives with five hundred and eleven kev. one that scatters in the patient changes direction and loses energy, so the line it implies is wrong. in the spectrum, the clean photons form the photopeak, the scattered ones a broad hump below it. an energy window keeps the peak and rejects much of the hump; deepbreast uses four hundred and eight to six hundred and thirteen kev. but the window is applied to a signal, and each crystal turns energy into signal with its own gain. if this crystal's gain is a quarter too low, its photopeak slides down and most of its good events fall outside the window. a quarter too high, and the peak overshoots while scatter slides in. so every crystal's signal has to be mapped to kev first.

reels.name: Energy how
reels.cap: So how is it done?
reels.words: so how is it done? reuse the same uniform acquisition that made the flood map. the crystal lookup table sends every event to its crystal, and each crystal fills its own spectrum. software finds each photopeak, and computes one factor per crystal, five hundred and eleven over the peak position. applied, the factors pull every peak onto five hundred and eleven. they are stored in a table, one entry per crystal, and used on every event from then on.

reels.name: Drift
reels.cap: Why repeat it?
reels.words: why repeat it? because gains do not stay put. the first block detector already had an l e d to re-tune its four tubes as they drifted. silicon photomultiplier gain depends on temperature, so as the detector warms, its photopeak walks and good events leave the window again. so scanners hold their sensors steady: one preclinical system keeps each detector within half a degree with peltier coolers, another holds its sensors at twenty six plus or minus zero point four degrees. whatever drift remains is caught by recalibrating on a regular basis, as the manufacturer recommends. lutetium based crystals even carry their own source: the natural radioactivity of lutetium one seven six, which one group used for a thirty minute calibration with nothing placed in the scanner.

reels.name: Timing why
reels.cap: Timing next, and again the why first.
reels.words: timing next, and again the why first. the two photons from one annihilation fly in opposite directions and reach their detectors at slightly different times. that difference places the annihilation along the line: every hundred picoseconds is one and a half centimetres. with finite timing resolution the position is a blur, the time of flight kernel. now give one detector a hidden delay of two hundred picoseconds, from a longer cable or a slower channel. the kernel slides three centimetres, and every event on this line lands in the wrong place. across a whole scanner, unequal offsets also blur the timing resolution itself. the first total body scanner, with over half a million crystals, measured five hundred and five picoseconds as a whole against four hundred and twelve averaged line by line, which its authors put down to incomplete timing calibration.

reels.name: Timing how
reels.cap: How are the offsets found?
reels.words: how are the offsets found? place a source whose position is known, here at the centre, so both photons of every pair travel the same distance and every true time difference is zero. for one pair of detectors, histogram the measured differences. the peak sits not at zero but at the difference of their two hidden offsets. every pair gives one such equation, and with many more pairs than detectors, a least squares fit recovers every offset. subtract them, and every clock agrees. the cost is counts: each pair needs enough coincidences to place its peak, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of crystals. some groups first remove the purely electronic skews with a pulsed laser, before any gamma rays are involved.

reels.name: Norm why
reels.cap: Last, normalisation, and again why.
reels.words: last, normalisation, and again why. image a perfectly uniform cylinder. each crystal has its own efficiency, shown here by its shade, so a line between two weak crystals records fewer counts than a line between two strong ones, for exactly the same activity. backproject the counts as if every line were equal, and the uniform cylinder comes out patterned: the efficiencies are printed into the image. divide each line by its own efficiency, and it is flat again.

reels.name: Norm how
reels.cap: How are the efficiencies measured?
reels.words: how are the efficiencies measured? acquire a source that should give every line the same rate, pick one crystal, and add up the counts over its whole fan of lines to the far side. divided by what the source geometry predicts, that sum is the crystal's efficiency. this is the fan sum method. a line's correction is then built from its two crystals' efficiencies and a geometric factor shared by similar lines. why not measure every line directly? count the unknowns. here, twenty four crystals against two hundred and seventy six lines. in a total body scanner, half a million crystals against about a hundred billion lines. at one percent precision each factor needs ten thousand counts, so measuring lines one by one would take about ten to the fifteen counts, while crystal fan sums need a few billion.

reels.name: No peaks
reels.cap: Now replace the pixels with one continuous crystal.
reels.words: now replace the pixels with one continuous crystal. a pixelated flood is a grid of spots. a monolithic flood is smooth: every position is possible, so there are no peaks to find and the flood alone cannot say where any event was. the labels have to be bought, with events of known position from a collimated beam, so that the detector can learn which light pattern belongs to which point in three dimensions.

reels.name: Pencil scan
reels.cap: Here is how the library is recorded.
reels.words: here is how the library is recorded. a small source sits behind a slit between two tungsten blocks, so only a narrow beam reaches the crystal. fire, and a gamma ray stops somewhere along the beam. same x, but a different depth each time, so the light pattern is narrower or wider. that is why every point needs many events, about sixty in the delft measurements. then the motorised stage steps the collimator by one millimetre and fires again. step, fire, record, across the face, row after row, until every point on the grid has its own set of light patterns. for a thirty two millimetre crystal that is over a thousand positions, for one detector.

reels.name: KNN
reels.cap: That scan gives a library.
reels.words: that scan gives a library. every grid point holds many recorded light patterns with a known position. for a new event, compare its pattern with the whole library, pick the k closest, and take their position as the estimate. here, with an idealised light model at one depth, the estimate lands under half a millimetre from the truth. the catch is the cost. the delft group's first version needed a fine grid and hundreds of angles of incidence, because depth changes the pattern.

reels.name: Cheaper
reels.cap: Most of the progress since has been about buying fewer labels.
reels.words: most of the progress since has been about buying fewer labels. the first libraries used a pencil beam at every point and many angles. van dam and colleagues needed reference data from perpendicular beams only, cutting calibration time at least a hundredfold. borghi and colleagues then replaced the points with fan beams, one set along x and one along y, for at least another hundredfold. that brought a two centimetre crystal down to two or three hours. in twenty sixteen they also sped up the search itself, comparing each event only with library entries near a rough first guess, about two hundred times faster, and kept events with up to sixteen of sixty four pixels missing.

reels.name: Fan scan
reels.cap: A fan beam changes what one step buys.
reels.words: a fan beam changes what one step buys. a pencil labels one point per step, so it crawls. open the slit into a line, and each step labels a whole column of the face at once. step it across in x, then turn it ninety degrees and step it in y. each event now knows only one coordinate, which is all the one dimensional nearest neighbour method needs. on the same one millimetre grid, that is sixty four positions instead of one thousand and twenty four.

reels.name: Flood DOI
reels.cap: Depth has its own trick, and it needs no collimator at all.
reels.words: depth has its own trick, and it needs no collimator at all. in a flood, how deep the gamma rays interact is not unknown: it follows the exponential attenuation of the crystal, which a quick simulation gives. meanwhile every event has a measurable light concentration, which is higher the closer it is to the sensor. sort the events by that quantity, and cut the sorted list at the fractions the simulation expects in each depth band. the quarter with the most concentrated light is the quarter nearest the sensor, and so on. borghi and colleagues build the depth lookup this way. the valencia group does the same thing in one fit: the edges of the energy over maximum histogram mark the front and back faces of the crystal.

reels.name: Mono energy time
reels.cap: With position known, the other calibrations change character.
reels.words: with position known, the other calibrations change character. energy no longer has one gain per crystal; it has a map. in this delft detector the photopeak shifts with position, and the map differs by depth, so the correction is a lookup over x, y and z. timing too: the delay to the first detected photon depends on how far the interaction is from each pixel. pixels right under the event fire early and sharply; distant ones late and spread out. they store these distributions per voxel and per pixel, and estimate the time by maximum likelihood, after first removing the electronic skews between dies with a pulsed laser.

reels.name: Semi
reels.cap: Semi-monolithic detectors split the problem.
reels.words: semi-monolithic detectors split the problem. which slab was hit is a discrete label again, so a flood and a lookup table do it, as in a pixelated block. the position along the slab is continuous, so it needs collimated data: a slit stepped in half millimetre steps. valencia's preclinical scanner trains one small network on a single module and uses it unchanged on all twenty eight. energy is equalised in three passes, channel gains, then slab peaks, then a map, and depth comes from the flood fit we just saw. for a whole monolithic ring, deepbreast puts a rotating fan beam inside the assembled scanner, four hundred and fifty steps of point eight degrees and ninety nine axial steps, cutting calibration from eleven days to three point six.

reels.name: Upkeep
reels.cap: So what does all this cost?
reels.words: so what does all this cost? here are acquisition times reported in these papers, on a log scale. thirty minutes of lutetium background built one scanner's position tables. about an hour per million events for the delft timing flood. two to three hours per detector for fan beam position calibration. six hours for deepbreast's normalisation phantom. twelve hours for energy, timing and normalisation together, with one sodium source, on a hemispherical brain scanner. and three point six days for deepbreast's position calibration. none of it is done once: clinical sites repeat detector calibration, timing alignment and normalisation on a regular basis as the manufacturer recommends, and again before any performance study.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Putting it together.
reels.words: putting it together. a pixelated scanner calibrates almost everything from floods and uniform sources, because each crystal is its own label. a semi-monolithic one needs a collimated scan only along the slab, and only once. a monolithic one must buy its position labels with collimated beams, while depth, energy and timing can again come from floods, once position is known. pixels give labels for free; monoliths buy them, and the art is buying fewer.

title: Short: one flash in the middle of a moving ship, drawn as a spacetime picture

reels.name: Diagram
reels.cap: Here is a ship two light seconds long, with a lamp in its middle and a clock at each end.
reels.words: here is a ship two light seconds long, with a lamp in its middle and a clock at each end. a crew rides on board, and first we draw everything in their frame of reference, where the ship is at rest. time runs across the page, and distance runs up it. each moment of the ship is one upright slice, and laying the slices side by side turns its history into a picture. the two ends become lines running across, with their clocks' ticks marked along them. the lamp flashes, and each pulse of light becomes a diagonal line. a speed is distance divided by time, so in this picture a speed is a gradient, distance up over time across. light climbs half a light second in half a second, so its gradient is one, and its line rises at forty five degrees. that gradient is c. both pulses arrive as the clocks read one, on the same upright line, so on board the hits are simultaneous. now redraw the same history for observers standing on the ground, outside the ship's frame, who see the ship move at zero point six c. the old rule simply shears the picture upward. but then the forward pulse climbs at one point six c, steeper than forty five degrees, and the backward pulse moves at zero point four c. light is never measured at any speed but c, so this picture is wrong. the lorentz transformation redraws it differently. it is built to keep every light line at a gradient of one, so light moves at c in this picture too. the forward pulse now climbs one light second in one second, at forty five degrees again. to manage that, it tilts the line through the two hits, so the rear is hit at zero point five seconds, and the front at two seconds. for the ground observers, a moment is an upright slice through this picture. each slice shows the ship one point six light seconds long. at two seconds the slice crosses the rear clock as it reads two point two zero, and the front clock as it reads one point zero zero. so the ground finds the front clock one point two seconds behind. for the crew on board, a moment is the tilted line through equal readings. the events and the readings are the same in both pictures, and only the slicing differs.

title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This is the paper.
reels.doc: Page 1: the paper, the magnet and coil it opens with, the two postulates, the ether made superfluous.
reels.words: this is the paper. on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, by albert einstein, received on the thirtieth of june, nineteen oh five. he was twenty six, and a clerk at the patent office in bern. we follow it page by page, in the english translation of nineteen twenty three. it opens not with light but with a magnet and a coil. push the magnet toward the coil, or the coil toward the magnet, and the same current flows. yet the theory of the day explained the two cases in different ways, and the paper says this asymmetry is not in nature. together with the failed attempts to detect earth's motion through the light medium, this suggests that nothing in physics marks absolute rest. he raises this to a postulate, the principle of relativity, and adds a second, that light always moves at a definite speed c, whatever the motion of the body that emits it. with these two, the luminiferous ether will prove to be superfluous. a footnote adds that he had not seen lorentz's latest paper.

reels.name: Sync
reels.cap: Part one is kinematics, and section one defines simultaneity.
reels.doc: Section 1, pages 2 and 3: time at one place is the watch's hand; time at two places needs a definition, and the paper gives one with a light ray from A to B and back.
reels.words: part one is kinematics, and section one defines simultaneity. when i say a train arrives at seven, i mean that the hand of my watch points to seven as the train arrives. that works for events next to my watch. for events far away, it does not. so put a clock at a, and an identical clock at b. a light ray leaves a at a's time, t a, is reflected at b at b's time, t b, and returns to a at t a prime. einstein defines the two clocks to be in step when the trip out takes as long as the trip back. out equals back is a definition, not a measurement. what experience fixes is the round trip, twice a b over the time on one clock, and that is c.

reels.name: Rod
reels.cap: Section two restates the two principles, and asks how long a moving rod is.
reels.doc: Section 2, pages 4 and 5: the two ways to measure a moving rod, and clocks at its ends that the riders find out of step, because light runs out against the motion and back with it.
reels.words: section two restates the two principles, and asks how long a moving rod is. ride along with it, and you measure its rest length. or mark where its two ends are at one moment of the stationary clocks, and measure between the marks. everyone had assumed the two answers agree. now put clocks at the rod's two ends, set to the stationary time, and let riders on the rod test them with light. going out, the light chases the end that runs away, at c minus v. coming back, the end runs toward it, at c plus v. so the riders find their clocks out of step, though the stationary observers call them in step. we cannot attach any absolute meaning to the concept of simultaneity.

reels.name: Lorentz
reels.cap: Section three sets up two frames, K at rest, and k moving at v, each with its own rods and clocks, set by light as in section one.
reels.doc: Section 3, pages 5 to 9: the frames K and k, k's time from the light test, the sphere of light check, and the transformation itself.
reels.words: section three sets up two frames, k at rest, and k moving at v, each with its own rods and clocks, set by light as in section one. to find k's time, tau, he demands that k's clocks pass the same light test, with the light's trips timed from k at c minus v and c plus v. out comes tau as a times, t minus v over c squared minus v squared, times x prime. then the check. a sphere of light, x squared plus y squared plus z squared equals c squared t squared, becomes, in the moving frame's own coordinates, the same sphere. so the two principles do not contradict each other. a symmetry argument fixes the last unknown, and the transformation reads tau equals beta times, t minus v x over c squared, xi equals beta times, x minus v t, and the two cross directions unchanged. his beta is what we now call gamma.

reels.name: Meaning
reels.cap: Section four reads the equations.
reels.doc: Section 4, pages 9 to 11: a moving sphere is an ellipsoid, a moving clock is slow, a clock taken round a loop comes back behind, and the clock at the equator.
reels.words: section four reads the equations. a sphere moving at v is, seen from the stationary frame, an ellipsoid, shortened along the motion by the root of one minus v squared over c squared. at v equals c, moving bodies would shrink into flat figures. a clock moving with k runs slow, by about half of v squared over c squared, in seconds per second. so a clock carried from a, round a closed path and back to a, arrives behind the one that stayed. this is the seed of the twin paradox. he even predicts that a balance clock at the equator runs slower than one at a pole. earth's spin carries it at four hundred and sixty five metres per second, so it would lose about a tenth of a microsecond a day. general relativity later showed that gravity cancels this, and clocks at sea level all tick together.

reels.name: Velocities
reels.cap: Section five adds velocities.
reels.doc: Section 5, pages 11 and 12: velocities add as (v + w)/(1 + vw/c^2), and nothing adds past c.
reels.words: section five adds velocities. two speeds, v and w, combine to v plus w, over one plus v w over c squared. half of c plus half of c gives zero point eight c, and c plus anything gives c again. the speed of light cannot be raised by adding to it.

reels.name: Part two
reels.cap: Part two, the electrodynamic part, fills the next eleven pages.
reels.doc: Pages 12 to 23 as thumbnails, each section lit as it is named; then the electron's energy and the thanks to Besso on page 23.
reels.words: part two, the electrodynamic part, fills the next eleven pages. section six transforms maxwell's equations, and the magnet and coil puzzle dissolves. electric and magnetic forces are one field, seen from different frames. section seven gives the doppler effect and aberration for any speed, eight the energy and pressure of light, nine moving charges, and ten the electron. for the electron he finds the energy of motion, m c squared times, beta minus one. it grows without limit as v approaches c, so nothing reaches the speed of light. three months later, a three page follow up drew the conclusion, e equals m c squared. the paper ends by thanking his friend and colleague michele besso. it cites no one else at all.

reels.name: Map
reels.cap: So here is the whole paper.
reels.doc: The whole paper as 24 thumbnails, each stretch lit as the voice names what lives there.
reels.words: so here is the whole paper. page one, the two postulates. pages two and three, time defined by light. three to five, simultaneity depends on motion. five to nine, the transformation. nine to eleven, short rods and slow clocks. eleven and twelve, adding velocities. and from twelve on, electrodynamics and the electron. two postulates and a careful definition of time, and the rest follows.

title: Performance Characteristics of the NeuroEXPLORER, a Next-Generation Human Brain PET/CT…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video explains a twenty twenty four paper in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine, by Li and colleagues.
reels.words: this video explains a twenty twenty four paper in the journal of nuclear medicine, by li and colleagues. it measures how well the neuroexplorer performs, a pet scanner built only for the human brain. here it is, with the c t scanner in front, and the ring of pet detectors seen from inside. we will see why the brain needs such a scanner, how its crystals report where in them each photon stopped, and what the measurements and first images show.

reels.name: Need
reels.cap: Many targets in the brain are tiny.
reels.doc: A small nucleus blurred: the share of its activity read falls with the blur; few counts make it noisy too.
reels.words: many targets in the brain are tiny. a nucleus in the thalamus or the midbrain can be just a few millimetres across. a scanner blurs every point, here by four millimetres, and the blurred nucleus reads only sixty two percent of its true activity. sharpen the blur to two millimetres, and it reads ninety two percent. that is why the neuroexplorer aims for a resolution near two millimetres. a small region also collects few counts, so repeated scans of it scatter widely. the best brain scanners until now had too little sensitivity, and no time of flight, to fix that.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: Seen down the bore, the PET ring is twenty detector modules, fifty two point four centimetres across.
reels.doc: The ring end on (its diameter), from the side (its length and six rows), the shoulder cut-outs, the camera.
reels.words: seen down the bore, the pet ring is twenty detector modules, fifty two point four centimetres across. from the side, it is forty nine point five centimetres long, six rows of detector blocks. a head goes in from this end. three blocks are left out on each side of the last row, so the shoulders can slide in, and the brain sits at the middle of the ring, where it is seen best. a camera at the far end watches the face ten to thirty times a second, so the scan can be corrected when the head moves.

reels.name: Parallax
reels.cap: Here is the ring seen end on, with a source at its centre.
reels.doc: End-on ring: an off-centre source's lines enter the crystals at a slant; without depth the line misses it.
reels.words: here is the ring seen end on, with a source at its centre. its photon pairs leave along lines that meet the crystals head on. move the source twenty centimetres off centre. now its lines cross the crystals at a slant. zoom in where one photon arrives. the crystals are twenty millimetres deep and one point five six millimetres wide. this photon enters here, and stops twelve millimetres along its path, six crystals over. a detector that cannot tell depth places the hit at the front of the crystal where it stopped. the same happens at the other end, so the line it draws misses the source by six millimetres. this error is called parallax. the neuroexplorer reads the depth in eight bins, two and a half millimetres each. knowing the bin, it slides the hit back along the line to the crystal face, and the line passes within a millimetre of the source.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: Each crystal has a partner beside it along the scanner's axis.
reels.doc: The U: two crystals joined by an optical bridge, a sensor under each; the light split gives the depth.
reels.words: each crystal has a partner beside it along the scanner's axis. at the far end, an optical bridge joins the two into a u, and a light sensor sits under each crystal. when a photon stops in one crystal, it makes a flash of light. most of the light goes straight down to its own sensor. some goes up, through the bridge, and down to the partner's sensor. the higher the flash, the closer it is to the bridge, and the more light the partner gets. so the split between the two sensors gives the depth, read out in eight bins. the depth helps the timing too. light from a flash high in the crystal takes longer to reach the sensor than light from a low one. ignoring that would blur the timing by about ninety nine picoseconds.

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: A photon pair defines a line through the head.
reels.doc: One line through a head: 236 ps places the annihilation within 3.5 cm; EXPLORER's 430 ps within 6.4 cm.
reels.words: a photon pair defines a line through the head. the two photons reach their detectors at slightly different times, and the neuroexplorer measures that difference to two hundred and thirty six picoseconds. that places the annihilation within about three and a half centimetres along the line. a head is about fifteen centimetres wide, so the line is cut to a short piece of it. explorer, at four hundred and thirty picoseconds, placed it within six point four centimetres.

reels.name: Resolution
reels.cap: To measure resolution, a tiny radioactive point is scanned at one, ten and twenty centimetres from the centre.
reels.doc: Point source at 1, 10 and 20 cm: each image a blur, its width drawn on it (Table 1).
reels.words: to measure resolution, a tiny radioactive point is scanned at one, ten and twenty centimetres from the centre. each image of the point is a blur. across the ring, its width is one point six four millimetres near the centre, two point zero six at ten centimetres, and two point five one at twenty. along the scanner's axis it is a little wider, two point seven three to two point nine three millimetres. these numbers come from filtered back projection, a simple reconstruction. with the scanner's own iterative reconstruction the centre reaches one point four three millimetres, but the authors expect real brain scans to do worse than that.

reels.name: Sensitivity
reels.cap: From the side, a point at the centre of the scanner sends many of its pairs into detector at both ends.
reels.doc: Side view: the pairs a point sends into detector; the measured triangle (Fig. 2); 12 of 100; count rates (Fig. 3).
reels.words: from the side, a point at the centre of the scanner sends many of its pairs into detector at both ends. a point near the end loses most of them through the open side. so the measured sensitivity is a triangle along the scanner, highest in the middle, which is where the brain sits. at the very centre, eleven point eight percent of the decays are recorded, about twelve of every hundred. both photons must also be stopped by the crystals, and many are not. over the whole scanner, that makes forty six counts a second for every kilo becquerel. the rates rise with the activity in the scanner. the useful rate peaks at fifty eight kilo becquerels per millilitre. brain scans run below ten, in the green band, so there is plenty of headroom.

reels.name: Phantoms
reels.cap: A Hoffman phantom is a plastic model of the brain's grey and white matter, filled with tracer.
reels.doc: Hoffman brain phantom (Fig. 5), then the Derenzo rods off centre with and without depth (Fig. 6).
reels.words: a hoffman phantom is a plastic model of the brain's grey and white matter, filled with tracer. in twelve slices, its folds are crisp. beside the matching c t slice, the border between grey and white lines up. a derenzo phantom holds rods in six sizes. here it sits eighty five millimetres off centre, where parallax hurts. without depth, the small rods smear. with depth, rods one point six millimetres wide separate. with thirty iterations, even the one point two millimetre rods show.

reels.name: Human
reels.cap: A healthy volunteer received three hundred and twenty seven mega becquerels of F D G, a glucose tracer.
reels.doc: First human images (Fig. 7): axial slices, MRI comparison with small structures, and the long axial view.
reels.words: a healthy volunteer received three hundred and twenty seven mega becquerels of f d g, a glucose tracer. these slices sum the data from forty to seventy minutes after injection, and the folded grey matter is sharp from the top of the head to the cerebellum. next to matching m r i slices, small structures stand out, like the colliculus in the midbrain, and the caudate and putamen deep in the brain. the ring is forty nine point five centimetres long, so it reaches below the head. the neck is in view, so the carotid arteries can give the tracer's input curve straight from the image, without sampling blood from an artery.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Back to the small nucleus.
reels.doc: Back on the small nucleus: at the measured resolution it reads 97%; then what is not yet shown.
reels.words: back to the small nucleus. blurred by four millimetres it read sixty two percent of its activity. at the measured one point six four millimetres, it reads ninety seven percent. reading the depth in each crystal keeps that sharpness away from the centre, the timing cuts each line to a short piece of the head, and the long ring gathers enough counts to use it. these are first measurements. the resolution comes from a point in air with a simple reconstruction, one volunteer was scanned, and correcting the images for head motion is still being built in.

title: How flow matching models work

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: A generative model has one job.
reels.words: a generative model has one job. you show it examples, like these points, and it learns to turn random noise into new examples of the same kind. flow matching moves every noise point along a smooth path, until the cloud becomes the data. it trains stable diffusion 3 and meta's voicebox, and its loss fits on one line. by the end you will know what the network learns, the loss that trains it, and why sampling takes several steps.

reels.name: Field
reels.cap: The model is a velocity field.
reels.words: the model is a velocity field. a neural network, v theta, takes in a position and a time, and outputs an arrow: which way, and how fast, a point there should move. a point follows its arrow: d x by d t equals v. as time runs from zero to one, the arrows change, and the points they carry trace out paths. on a computer we take small steps. the new position is the old one, plus the step size h times the arrow. that is euler's method, and a hundred such steps carry the noise to the data.

reels.name: Space time
reels.cap: Stack time upwards, and the flow becomes a bundle of threads.
reels.doc: Time stacked upwards: each sample's path is a thread from the noise plane (t = 0) to the data plane (t = 1).
reels.words: stack time upwards, and the flow becomes a bundle of threads. at the bottom, at time zero, the noise. at the top, at time one, the two moons. the threads bend, and some swing a long way round. training has to find this whole bundle, knowing only samples from the bottom and the top.

reels.name: Likelihood
reels.cap: Why not fit the flow the classic way, by maximum likelihood?
reels.doc: Why not maximum likelihood: the change of variables needs the whole path solved, divergence included, every training step; flow matching regresses one arrow per sample.
reels.words: why not fit the flow the classic way, by maximum likelihood? it takes in a data point and outputs its log density: the noise density where its path began, minus the divergence of the field, integrated along the path. so every training step has to run each path backwards, one network call after another, and estimate that divergence on the way. that is slow, and it gets slower as the flow gets more complex. flow matching never runs the flow while training. it fits the arrows directly, with one network call per sample.

reels.name: Pairs
reels.cap: Flow matching starts from one pair: a noise point, x zero, and a data point, x one, drawn independently.
reels.words: flow matching starts from one pair: a noise point, x zero, and a data point, x one, drawn independently. join them with a straight line. the point at time t is a blend: one minus t of x zero, plus t of x one. at time zero it sits on the noise, and at time one, on the data. differentiate with respect to time. the first term gives minus x zero, the second plus x one, so the velocity is x one minus x zero: the same arrow everywhere on the line. do this for many random pairs, and every point on every line comes with a known target arrow.

reels.name: Loss
reels.cap: Training is plain regression.
reels.words: training is plain regression. sample a time, a noise point and a data point. form the blend, x t. the network takes in x t and t, and outputs its arrow there. compare it with the target, x one minus x zero, and square the difference. averaged over a batch, that is the whole loss. so one training step takes in a batch of pairs and outputs a single number, whose gradient nudges the weights, theta. here is a real run, computed for this video: twenty thousand steps on the two moons. notice that the loss levels off at about two point six, far above zero. it cannot reach zero, because the targets contradict each other. that turns out to be the point.

reels.name: Average
reels.cap: Pick one point and one time.
reels.doc: At one point and time, the lines through it disagree; the squared loss is minimised by their mean, which the trained network reproduces. The fan is the pairs whose blend lands within 0.06 of the point.
reels.words: pick one point and one time. many lines pass through it, from different pairs, and each one asks for a different arrow. a squared error is smallest at the average, so the best network outputs the expected velocity of the lines passing through x at time t. the trained network agrees: its arrow lands on the average. and the spread of the arrows around it is the loss floor we just saw. lipman and colleagues proved that this averaged field carries the noise distribution exactly onto the data. and the gradient of the easy per-pair loss equals the gradient of matching that field directly, which we could never compute.

reels.name: Sample
reels.cap: The sampler takes in fresh noise and a number of steps, follows the learned arrows, and outputs samples.
reels.words: the sampler takes in fresh noise and a number of steps, follows the learned arrows, and outputs samples. here are four runs from the same noise, with one, two, four and thirty-two steps. with one step, every point jumps along its first arrow, and they all land in the same place, the average of the data. with more steps, the arrows are read again along the way, and at thirty-two steps the moons come out sharp. at one step, the very first arrow at time zero is the average over every pair, so the paths have to curve away from it later. each bend costs extra steps, and every step is a network call.

reels.name: Reflow
reels.cap: Rectified flow, from Liu and colleagues, straightens the paths.
reels.doc: One round of reflow (rectified flow): pair each noise point with the sample the first network makes from it, train again on those pairs, and the paths straighten; one step then lands on the moons.
reels.words: rectified flow, from liu and colleagues, straightens the paths. run the trained flow, and pair each noise point with the sample it produces. then train again, on those pairs. these new lines no longer cross, so there is nothing to average, and the learned paths come out straight. measured as end-to-end distance over path length, straightness goes from zero point five six to one. now a single step is enough. before reflow, one step lands on the average, zero point four six off the data. after it, one step lands on the moons, zero point zero two off.

reels.name: Recipe
reels.cap: So the whole recipe is three moves.
reels.words: so the whole recipe is three moves. blend a noise point and a data point along a straight line. regress the network's arrow onto that line's direction. then, to generate, follow the arrows from fresh noise. diffusion models fit the same mould, with a curved, noisier path between the two. their network takes the same input, a noisy point and a time, but most output a guess of the noise that was added. the flow matching network takes that input too, and outputs a velocity: which way to go. choosing the straight line is what makes flow matching simple to train, and quick to sample.

title: Roadmap toward the 10 ps time-of-flight PET challenge

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video explains a roadmap published in twenty twenty in Physics in Medicine and Biology.
reels.words: this video explains a roadmap published in twenty twenty in physics in medicine and biology. twenty two authors, led by paul lecoq at cern, each wrote one part of it. together they ask what it would take for a pet scanner to time its photon pairs to ten picoseconds. reaching that means every part of the detector has to get faster. the crystal turns the gamma ray into light. the light sensor turns that light into an electrical pulse. the electronics stamp the pulse with a time. and the image is built from those times. first, though, why that goal would be worth the effort.

reels.name: Flight
reels.cap: When a positron annihilates inside the patient, two photons fly apart along a line.
reels.doc: Two photons from one annihilation; the arrival difference places the event; the TOF blur shrinks to 1.5 mm.
reels.words: when a positron annihilates inside the patient, two photons fly apart along a line. the photon with less distance to go reaches the ring first. at that moment, the other photon still has this much further to fly. that extra distance, the speed of light times the difference in arrival times, is twice the event's offset from the centre of the line. so the time difference alone says where on the line the event happened. a real detector times each pair only so precisely. with a timing blur of five hundred picoseconds, the event could be anywhere in about seven and a half centimetres of the line. today's fastest clinical scanner, at two hundred and fourteen picoseconds, narrows that to three point two centimetres. at ten picoseconds, it shrinks to one and a half millimetres. at that point, each event lands at its own spot on its line. the image simply fills up, one event at a time, with no tomographic reconstruction at all.

reels.name: Gain
reels.cap: Precise timing also cuts the noise in the image.
reels.doc: The paper's SNR gain for a 40 cm patient: 2.3, 3.5 and 16; what the gain buys.
reels.words: precise timing also cuts the noise in the image. the paper gives the gain in signal to noise ratio over a scanner without timing, for a patient forty centimetres across. five hundred picoseconds gives two point three. two hundred and fourteen picoseconds gives three point five. ten picoseconds gives sixteen, a gain as large as making the scanner cover the whole body. compared with today's two hundred and fourteen picoseconds, the noise variance would fall about twenty one times, so the same image needs that many times fewer counts. that can buy a lower dose, a shorter scan, or imaging for much longer after one injection.

reels.name: Status
reels.cap: Today's fastest clinical scanner times its photon pairs to two hundred and fourteen picoseconds.
reels.doc: Where timing stands: 214 ps in a scanner, 98 and 58 ps in the lab, against 10 ps.
reels.words: today's fastest clinical scanner times its photon pairs to two hundred and fourteen picoseconds. in the lab, the best long crystal, twenty millimetres, reaches ninety eight picoseconds, and a short one, three millimetres long, fifty eight. the goal of ten picoseconds is still almost six times beyond the best of these. the roadmap follows the gap down the detector chain. for each part, it asks what limits the timing today, and what could get it to ten picoseconds.

reels.name: Crystal
reels.cap: A gamma ray stopping in a crystal makes tens of thousands of light photons, but they trickle out over tens of nanoseconds.
reels.doc: Slow light: at most ~5 photons per ps at the start; CTR^2 ~ tau_r tau_d / N; depth adds 40 ps in 20 mm.
reels.words: a gamma ray stopping in a crystal makes tens of thousands of light photons, but they trickle out over tens of nanoseconds. only the first few photons set the time. even the brightest and fastest crystals give at most about five photons in the first picosecond, so the paper puts their limit near fifty picoseconds. the paper's rule of thumb links the square of the timing blur to the rise time, times the decay time, divided by the number of photons. standard crystals are already close to the limits on all three. long crystals add another blur. inside the crystal, light travels slower than the gamma ray, so a gamma ray stopping deep and one stopping shallow send their light to the sensor at different times. in a twenty millimetre crystal that spreads the timing by about forty picoseconds, unless the depth is measured and corrected.

reels.name: Prompt
reels.cap: The way past that limit is light that comes out at once.
reels.doc: Prompt light: Cherenkov photons and nanocrystal layers; the paper's map of what a layered crystal needs.
reels.words: the way past that limit is light that comes out at once. ordinary scintillation light trickles in. but the fast electron knocked loose by the gamma ray outruns light in the crystal, and gives off cherenkov light within ten picoseconds. there are only ten to seventeen of these photons per gamma ray. even so, with lead glass built into a fast photomultiplier, cherenkov timing has reached thirty picoseconds. a second idea is a layered crystal. sheets of a heavy crystal stop the gamma ray, and between them are sheets of nanocrystals that glow in well under a nanosecond. the electron set loose by the gamma ray crosses both, so every event gets a burst of fast photons. the paper calculates what such a layered crystal would need. along the bottom is the nanocrystals' light yield, and up the side is the timing jitter of the light sensor. reaching ten picoseconds needs about twelve hundred photons per mega electron volt from the nanocrystals, together with a sensor jitter of ten picoseconds.

reels.name: Sensor
reels.cap: A silicon photomultiplier is a grid of tiny avalanche diodes.
reels.doc: One photon's timing jitter: 70 ps today, 10 ps needed; the paper's SPTR plot; 3D digital SiPMs.
reels.words: a silicon photomultiplier is a grid of tiny avalanche diodes. a photon landing on one sets off an avalanche, but the moment its pulse starts wanders from one photon to the next. in the best sensors today it wanders by seventy picoseconds. for ten picoseconds overall, that has to fall to about ten. the paper measured timing with several commercial sensors. the blur grows steadily with the sensor's jitter, and the best measured sensors sit near seventy picoseconds. a simulated digital sensor, which times every photon, does better than an analog one at the same jitter, and the gain grows toward ten picoseconds. that is why the roadmap backs three dimensional digital sensors. a top layer holds the diodes, and a chip bonded right under it gives every diode its own timer. each photon comes out as a time stamp, and the first few stamps are combined into the best estimate of when the gamma ray arrived.

reels.name: Electronics
reels.cap: The electronics see a rising pulse with noise riding on it.
reels.doc: Jitter = noise / slope on a threshold crossing; J = e_n C_d t_d / Q; 1 mm pixels; 5 ps TDC steps.
reels.words: the electronics see a rising pulse with noise riding on it. they mark the time when it crosses a threshold. noise moves that crossing earlier or later, and a steeper edge moves it less. so the jitter is the noise divided by the slope. for a light sensor, the paper writes the jitter as the amplifier's noise, times the sensor's capacitance, times the pulse duration, divided by its charge. sensor pixels no bigger than one millimetre keep the capacitance small, and then a jitter near one picosecond is within reach. the timer itself must count in steps of five picoseconds or less, and the clock that feeds thousands of channels must be just as steady.

reels.name: Image
reels.cap: With ten picoseconds, building the image becomes simple.
reels.doc: At 10 ps the image is counts per voxel over sensitivity; plates instead of a ring (Fig. 17); calibration.
reels.words: with ten picoseconds, building the image becomes simple. each event already sits at one spot on its line, so the image is just the number of events in each voxel, divided by how sensitive the scanner is at that voxel. no forward and back projection is needed. precise timing also frees the scanner's shape. the paper simulates a breast between two flat plates, with no ring around it. without timing, the image is distorted. with three hundred picoseconds, it is better but still stretched. with ten picoseconds, it looks like the object. the catch is calibration. in a simulated scanner timing to twenty five picoseconds, an offset error of only three picoseconds caused errors of up to twenty one percent.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: Here is the roadmap on one timing scale.
reels.doc: The chain on one timing scale: where each part stands against 10 ps.
reels.words: here is the roadmap on one timing scale. standard crystals stop near fifty picoseconds, so prompt light, from cherenkov emission or nanocrystal layers, has to carry the timing. light sensors must improve from seventy picoseconds to about ten. electronics can already come close, given small sensor pixels. and the image would need almost no reconstruction, only timing calibrated to a few picoseconds. the authors found no law of physics that rules ten picoseconds out. what stands in the way is the gap on each of these rows, and the engineering to close it.

title: Liquid Time-constant Networks

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: Most neural networks react to their input at a fixed pace.
reels.words: most neural networks react to their input at a fixed pace. what if each neuron could change how fast it responds, depending on what it is seeing right now? that is the idea behind liquid time constant networks. in this video: where they come from, why their dynamics stay bounded, how they are solved and trained, and how they compare with other recurrent networks on time series.

reels.name: Background
reels.cap: A classic recurrent network updates its hidden state in fixed steps, one per input.
reels.words: a classic recurrent network updates its hidden state in fixed steps, one per input. a neural o d e instead lets a network f define the rate of change of the state, so the state flows in continuous time and a numerical solver computes it. a more stable variant, the continuous time r n n, adds a leak term, minus x over tau, which pulls the state back to rest with a time constant tau. but tau is one fixed number per neuron, whatever the input.

reels.name: Neuron
reels.cap: The authors start from a simple linear neuron: a leak, plus an input S.
reels.words: the authors start from a simple linear neuron: a leak, plus an input s. then they make s a neural network f times a minus x, where a is a learned bias. this is borrowed from biology. in a non spiking neuron, a synapse drives the membrane towards its reversal potential, and the drive fades as it gets there. substitute s back in and you get equation one. look at what multiplies x: one over tau, plus f. the network f now sits inside the decay rate, so the neuron's effective time constant, tau system, equals tau over one plus tau f. it changes with the input at every moment: the time constant is liquid.

reels.name: Liquid
reels.cap: Here is one simulated neuron.
reels.words: here is one simulated neuron. the input at the top, the state in the middle, and its effective time constant at the bottom, which can never exceed tau. a weak input arrives. the time constant dips a little, and the state rises slowly to a modest level. when the input stops, it relaxes back. now a strong input. the time constant collapses, so the neuron snaps up almost at once, and settles close to a. once the input is gone, the time constant returns to its slow value, and the neuron remembers a little longer. same neuron, same weights: how quickly it reacts is decided by what it sees.

reels.name: Bounded
reels.cap: A time constant that moves with the input could, in principle, run wild.
reels.words: a time constant that moves with the input could, in principle, run wild. the paper proves it can't. theorem one: each neuron's time constant stays between tau over one plus tau w, where w bounds the incoming weights, and tau itself. theorem two: the state stays between zero and the extreme values of a. push an ever growing input into our neuron. the state climbs towards a but never passes it, and the time constant falls to its floor and stops. the outputs cannot explode, however large the input becomes.

reels.name: Solver
reels.cap: Equation one has no closed form solution, so a solver steps it forward in time.
reels.words: equation one has no closed form solution, so a solver steps it forward in time. when f is large the equation is stiff: a plain explicit euler step overshoots, and the error grows with every step. why does that happen, and how do they fix it? look at where x appears in equation one. once on its own, multiplied by the decay rate. that is a linear appearance, like three x. and twice inside f, wrapped in a sigmoid. that is a nonlinear one. a solver step turns the derivative into an update: the new x is the old x, plus a time step times the right hand side. the only question is whether each x on the right uses the old value or the new one. explicit euler uses old values everywhere. it is cheap, but with a large decay rate it overshoots. implicit euler uses new values everywhere. it is stable, but then the new x sits inside a sigmoid, and every step needs an iterative solve. the fused step splits the difference. inside f it uses the old x, so f becomes just a number for this step. the bare x uses the new value. that leaves a linear equation in the new x, which rearranges into a single division. it is the same rule on every step; nothing switches at run time. the new x is a weighted blend of the old x and a, so it cannot overshoot, whatever the step size, and it costs one evaluation of f, just like explicit euler. to train, they unroll the solver and use plain backpropagation through time, rather than the adjoint method popular for neural o d es. it costs more memory, but the backward pass is accurate, because nothing has to be re-integrated in reverse.

reels.name: Expressive
reels.cap: To compare expressive power, the authors feed a circle into randomly weighted networks, project the hidden states onto their first two principal components, and measure the length of the curve that comes out.
reels.words: to compare expressive power, the authors feed a circle into randomly weighted networks, project the hidden states onto their first two principal components, and measure the length of the curve that comes out. a longer, more tangled curve means the network can represent more complex functions. here are the measured lengths, on a log scale, with hard tanh activations. for neural o d es and c t r n ns, the length grows exponentially with depth, from about a hundred to tens or hundreds of thousands. the l t c is already above twelve thousand with a single layer, and grows only gently after that. their theorems give matching lower bounds on this growth. part of the reason is computational depth: the solver takes about eighty one steps per input for an l t c, against four for a c t r n n, so each layer is effectively much deeper.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: On seven real time series tasks, from hand gesture segmentation and room occupancy to traffic, power and ozone prediction, the L T C is compared with an L S T M, a C T R N N, a neural O D E and a continuous time G R U, a
reels.words: on seven real time series tasks, from hand gesture segmentation and room occupancy to traffic, power and ozone prediction, the l t c is compared with an l s t m, a c t r n n, a neural o d e and a continuous time g r u, all with thirty two hidden units. the l t c is best on four of the seven: gesture, occupancy, traffic, where it cuts the error from zero point one seven to about zero point one, and ozone. on the other three it is close behind the winner. on person activity recognition, with the same split as the latent o d e paper, the l t c reaches eighty eight point two percent, against eighty four point six for the best o d e model. and on modelling the physics of a simulated half cheetah robot, predicting its next observation, it has the lowest error of all five models.

reels.name: Outro
reels.cap: The authors are upfront about the limits.
reels.words: the authors are upfront about the limits. like other continuous time models, l t cs suffer from vanishing gradients, so they are not the obvious choice for long term dependencies. they depend on a good solver. and the extra expressivity costs time and memory. their equations resemble dynamic causal models from neuroscience, so they point to causality, and to controlling robots in continuous time, as natural next steps. in one line: a network whose neurons learn not just what to respond to, but how fast. thanks for watching.

title: How scintillators make light

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Almost every PET scanner starts with a scintillator: a material that turns one invisible gamma ray into a flash of visible light.
reels.words: almost every pet scanner starts with a scintillator: a material that turns one invisible gamma ray into a flash of visible light. how it does that depends on what it's made of. the gamma ray itself makes no light. it is absorbed, or compton scatters, and frees one energetic electron. everything after that, the light, how much, and how fast, is the material's response to that one electron. the electron's energy ends up as thousands of lower energy photons, in proportion to the energy deposited, which a photodetector can count. so every scintillator has two jobs. turn that energy into many photons. and emit them below the material's own excitation energy, because otherwise the next atom along would simply absorb them again. there are three families of scintillator, and the clearest way to tell them apart is the trick each one uses for that second job.

reels.name: Inorganic
reels.cap: In an inorganic crystal, such as L S O or sodium iodide, the light comes from the band structure of the whole solid, a wide band gap insulator.
reels.words: in an inorganic crystal, such as l s o or sodium iodide, the light comes from the band structure of the whole solid, a wide band gap insulator. it happens in three stages. first, conversion. the fast electron cascades, ionising atoms and knocking out more electrons, until the carriers can no longer ionise. they cool to the band edges, leaving a dense track of electron hole pairs. that takes about a femtosecond. each pair costs two to three times the band gap, the rest goes into lattice vibrations. so the gap sets a hard ceiling on how much light the material can ever make. second, transport. the carriers wander through the crystal, some pairing up as excitons. some are lost on the way, to defects and traps that the growth process left behind. third, luminescence. the carriers are captured at a luminescence centre, usually an activator dopant such as cerium in l s o, or thallium in sodium iodide, and recombine there, emitting a photon. because the activator's levels sit inside the gap, that photon has less energy than the gap, and the crystal is transparent to its own light. this last stage also sets the decay time, and with it the timing.

reels.name: Centres
reels.cap: Why not just let the electron fall straight back across the gap?
reels.words: why not just let the electron fall straight back across the gap? because that photon would have almost exactly the gap energy, and the next atom would absorb it. in a wide gap insulator it's also slow and mostly dark, which is why pure sodium iodide only scintillates when it's cooled. the usual fix is an activator. cerium, with its five d to four f transition, in l s o, l y s o, lanthanum bromide and gagg. or an s squared ion, thallium or europium, in sodium iodide, caesium iodide and strontium iodide. some hosts need no dopant. in a self-activated crystal, an ion of the lattice is its own centre: bismuth in b g o, the tungstate group in p w o. it absorbs high and emits much lower, a large stokes shift. in a self-trapped exciton, the electron hole pair distorts the lattice around itself, and that relaxation takes energy out before it emits. undoped caesium iodide, and the slow light of barium fluoride. in a few fluorides there's core valence luminescence. a valence electron drops into a hole in a deeper core band, and the photon carries that spacing, which is smaller than the gap. no carriers need to cool or travel, so it's sub nanosecond: the fast light of barium fluoride. and in direct gap semiconductors and perovskites, a free exciton emits only just below the gap. self absorption is a real limit, so they're used thin, or as nanocrystals.

reels.name: Organic
reels.cap: Organic scintillators work completely differently.
reels.words: organic scintillators work completely differently. the light belongs to a single aromatic molecule, not the bulk. its pi electrons have a ladder of singlet states, each split into vibrational sublevels, and a triplet state off to the side. the fast electron kicks pi electrons into the upper singlets. they drop to s one within picoseconds, and s one fluoresces back to the ground state in one to three nanoseconds. it's fast because the transition is allowed, and there's no charge transport stage in the way. and it lands on a vibrationally excited level of the ground state, so the photon is lower in energy than the absorption. that vibrational offset is the organic's way of staying transparent. some excitations cross over to the triplet, which can't easily radiate. but two triplets can annihilate, refilling s one, so the same fluorescence comes out hundreds of nanoseconds late. densely ionising particles make more triplets, which is how pulse shape discrimination tells particles apart. practical plastic scintillators are a chain. a polymer base absorbs the energy and hands it, by forster transfer, to a fluor at about one percent, and a wavelength shifter moves the light to where the photodetector is sensitive. the catch: an organic is made of carbon and hydrogen, so it stops gamma rays poorly, and its yield can't be raised by doping. heavy metals can be loaded in, but only for stopping power.

reels.name: Excimer
reels.cap: The third mechanism belongs to the noble elements, liquid xenon and argon.
reels.words: the third mechanism belongs to the noble elements, liquid xenon and argon. again the gamma ray frees one fast electron, which ionises and excites xenon atoms along its track. an excited atom on its own would emit at one hundred and forty seven nanometres. but every neighbouring atom absorbs exactly that line, so the light would never get out. instead, within picoseconds, the excited atom grabs a neighbour, and forms an excimer: a two atom molecule that only exists while it's excited. it sits in a bound well. the ground state has no well at all. the excimer emits a vacuum ultraviolet photon, at one seventy eight nanometres in xenon. it lands on that unbound ground state, so the two atoms simply fly apart. there's no molecule left to absorb the light, and the liquid is transparent to it. like the organics, it has a singlet and a triplet, giving a prompt and a slow component. liquid xenon is bright, about as bright as sodium iodide, and dense enough to stop five eleven k e v photons. what keeps it out of clinical scanners is engineering: it's cryogenic, its light is vacuum ultraviolet, and it's a liquid. the upside is that it can collect the ionisation charge as well, giving a time projection chamber that locates every interaction in three dimensions.

reels.name: Summary
reels.cap: So, three mechanisms.
reels.words: so, three mechanisms. in an inorganic crystal the light comes from the band structure of the solid, and an activator level inside the gap keeps it from being reabsorbed. in an organic, it comes from one molecule, and a vibrational offset does the job. and in a noble liquid, the emitting molecule is built on the spot by the excitation, used once, and falls apart, because its ground state isn't bound. two other ways of detecting gamma rays aren't scintillation at all. cherenkov light has no excited state behind it, and direct conversion detectors collect charge instead of light. which mechanism a material uses decides how much light it makes, and how fast that light arrives. and for pet, those two numbers are what matter most.

title: Mainly electromagnetism and matter

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This video is a map of the second volume of the Feynman Lectures on Physics, the second year of Richard Feynman's introductory course at Caltech, written up with Robert Leighton and Matthew Sands.
reels.words: this video is a map of the second volume of the feynman lectures on physics, the second year of richard feynman's introductory course at caltech, written up with robert leighton and matthew sands. it has forty two chapters. they fall naturally into seven parts: the language of fields, electrostatics, magnetism, maxwell's equations and waves, relativity, matter, and a final stretch that goes beyond electromagnetism. and almost all of it is organised around four equations, which the book writes down in its very first chapter. by the end you should know what each part is for, the one idea at its heart, and how they hang together.

reels.name: Hook
reels.cap: Feynman opens with a thought experiment.
reels.words: feynman opens with a thought experiment. imagine a force like gravity, but about a billion billion billion billion times stronger, with two kinds of charge that attract and repel. matter is a fine mixture of both, so the forces cancel almost perfectly. now stand at arm's length from someone, and give each of you one percent more electrons than protons. the repulsion would be enough to lift a weight equal to the whole earth. forces this large, this delicately balanced, are what the volume sets out to describe.

reels.name: Language
reels.cap: To say anything about fields you need a language for them, and the first three chapters build it.
reels.words: to say anything about fields you need a language for them, and the first three chapters build it. a vector field gives an arrow at every point in space. its simplest derivative, the gradient, points up the steepest slope of a scalar like temperature. the divergence measures how much field flows out of a tiny box: here, a source. the curl measures how much it circulates around a tiny loop: here, a whirl. two theorems connect the little to the large: gauss's theorem turns flux out of a surface into divergence inside it, and stokes's theorem turns circulation around a loop into curl through it. every law in the rest of the book is written with these.

reels.name: Electrostatics
reels.cap: Electrostatics is the longest part, nine chapters, and it rests on two equations: the divergence of E is the charge density, and the curl of E is zero.
reels.words: electrostatics is the longest part, nine chapters, and it rests on two equations: the divergence of e is the charge density, and the curl of e is zero. around a point charge the field points straight out. wrap it in any closed surface and the flux through it measures the charge inside: that is gauss's law, which handles every symmetric problem. for conductors there are tricks, like the method of images: the field of a charge above a conducting plane is exactly that of the charge and an opposite mirror charge below it. the rest of the part applies the same two equations to the energy stored in fields, to thunderstorms and lightning, and to dielectrics, where molecules stretch into little dipoles.

reels.name: Unity
reels.cap: Chapter twelve is one of the book's quiet gems.
