reels.words: chapter twelve is one of the book's quiet gems. here is the potential around two opposite charges. it satisfies one equation: laplacian of u equals minus a source. but the same equation describes the temperature around heat sources, the shape of a stretched membrane under pressure, neutrons diffusing from a source, ideal fluid flowing past an obstacle, and even how to light a plane evenly. the same equations have the same solutions: solve one problem, and you have solved them all. feynman uses it to argue that a physicist can keep a broad view of nature instead of a narrow one.

reels.name: Magnetism
reels.cap: Magnetism comes next.
reels.words: magnetism comes next. a steady current makes a magnetic field that circulates around it: ampère's law, the curl of b set by the current. then one of the book's best moves. a charge moves alongside a current-carrying wire. in the wire's frame the wire is neutral, and the force on the charge is magnetic. jump into the charge's frame: length contraction changes the spacing of the plus and minus charges differently, the wire is no longer neutral, and the same force is now electric. magnetism is what electricity looks like from a moving frame. finally, induction. push a magnet into a loop, and a current flows: a changing magnetic field makes a circulating electric field. along the way the vector potential appears, which turns out to matter even more in quantum mechanics.

reels.name: Maxwell
reels.cap: Chapter eighteen puts everything together.
reels.words: chapter eighteen puts everything together. the book warns that anything earlier that contradicts this chapter was a special case, true only for fixed charges or steady currents. equation one: the flux of e out of a surface measures the charge inside. two: a changing magnetic field makes a circulating electric field. three: there are no magnetic charges, so b never flows out of anything. four: currents make circulating magnetic fields, and so does a changing electric field. that last term was maxwell's addition, and with it the equations become symmetric enough to support waves. feynman judges that, seen from ten thousand years on, maxwell's discovery of these laws will be the most significant event of the nineteenth century.

reels.name: Waves
reels.cap: Put the four equations together in empty space and something new appears.
reels.words: put the four equations together in empty space and something new appears. a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, whose change makes an electric field, and the pair sustains itself: a wave, e and b at right angles, moving at the speed of light. light is an electromagnetic wave. the next chapters follow the consequences: accelerated charges radiate, circuits and cavities resonate, and waveguides carry fields in shaped patterns. in the middle sits chapter nineteen, a famous lecture on the principle of least action.

reels.name: Relativity
reels.cap: Part five shows that Maxwell's equations were relativistic all along.
reels.words: part five shows that maxwell's equations were relativistic all along. a charge at rest has a field pointing out evenly in every direction. set it moving close to the speed of light, and the field squeezes into a flat disc across the motion, while a magnetic field circles it. in relativistic notation the potentials form one four-vector, and e and b are parts of a single field tensor that mix when you change frames. the part ends with the energy and momentum carried by fields, the puzzle of the electron's electromagnetic mass, and how charges move in electric and magnetic fields.

reels.name: Matter
reels.cap: Part six turns to matter.
reels.words: part six turns to matter. light passing through glass drives the bound electrons into oscillation, and their re-radiated waves add to the original, slowing it: that is where the refractive index comes from, and reflection follows from the same picture. then magnetism. in a paramagnet the atomic magnets point at random. in a ferromagnet they lock together into domains, and an applied field lines them all up. the part also covers the geometry of crystals, tensors for properties that depend on direction, and magnetic resonance.

reels.name: Beyond
reels.cap: The last part goes beyond electromagnetism, using the field ideas already built.
reels.words: the last part goes beyond electromagnetism, using the field ideas already built. elasticity: how a beam bends under load, and how materials stretch and twist. fluids, in two chapters. the first treats ideal flow without viscosity, which john von neumann called the study of dry water. the second adds viscosity, wet water, with wakes and vortices behind obstacles. and the volume closes with curved space. feynman imagines a bug that lives on a surface and can only measure it from inside. by measuring a triangle, it can tell the surface is curved without ever leaving it, a first step toward einstein's gravity.

reels.name: Book map
reels.cap: Here is the whole map.
reels.words: here is the whole map. at the centre, the four equations. part one gives the language. electrostatics is the first two equations with nothing changing in time. magnetism adds steady currents, then induction lets fields change. chapter eighteen assembles all four and finds light. relativity reveals them as one field. matter adds how materials respond. and the last part reuses the same mathematics for solids, fluids and curved space. a good way to read it: the core runs through chapter twenty one; after that, choose the parts that matter to you.

title: The timing cost of bulk optical scattering in monolithic PET scintillators: a joint…

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: Part two.
reels.words: part two. in part one, bulk optical scattering made the depth of interaction in a monolithic pet crystal easier to measure. this paper asks what that costs. same detector as before: a fifty by fifty by ten millimetre slab of l s o, with a black absorbing wrap, read out by an eight by eight array of silicon photomultipliers. scattering releases light the wrap would otherwise absorb, and over the whole crystal the depth bound is lowest at a scattering length of about two millimetres. in time of flight pet, the coincidence time resolution, or c t r, localises each annihilation along its line of response. a faster detector means a shorter segment, and less noise. scattering makes photons take longer paths. so what does the depth gain cost in timing, and in energy resolution?

reels.name: Timing
reels.cap: Every detected photon has an arrival time.
reels.words: every detected photon has an arrival time. their density, f, rises sharply at first, then decays with the forty nanosecond scintillation. timing information sits in that leading edge. released light that arrives early sharpens it. but long scattered paths smear it out. the fisher information on the interaction time grows with the number of photons in the first twenty nanoseconds, and with how steep the leading edge is. the bound treats position, time and energy together, as five unknowns estimated jointly from the same light, in one five by five fisher matrix. its time bound converts to a coincidence time resolution for two identical detectors. the simulated arrival times get a seventy picosecond rise time, and an assumed sensor jitter of eighty or two hundred picoseconds, for the clear crystal and seven scattering lengths, from half a millimetre to one metre.

reels.name: Sweep
reels.cap: Here is the C T R bound over the whole crystal.
reels.words: here is the c t r bound over the whole crystal. with the faster sensor, the clear crystal sits at one hundred and sixty five picoseconds. weak scattering, at eight to sixteen millimetres, actually improves it, to one hundred and fifty three. the released light arrives within the leading edge. it is back to the clear value at four millimetres. below that it rises: one hundred and ninety five picoseconds at the depth optimum of two millimetres, and three hundred and thirty six at half a millimetre. the slower sensor shows the same shape, with a bigger dip, fourteen percent, and it only returns to the clear value at two millimetres. a one metre scattering length, a real monocrystal, behaves like the clear crystal. knowing the position barely helps the timing, and a maximum likelihood estimator gets within about a third of the bound.

reels.name: Energy
reels.cap: Now energy.
reels.words: now energy. if the interaction position were known, scattering would help the energy resolution a little, from three point four to about two point seven percent, because there is more light. but the position has to be estimated from the same light. then the energy bound climbs: from four point seven percent to nine point seven at four millimetres, and twenty point eight at the depth optimum. the reason is the mechanism from part one. scattering encodes depth in the total amount of light. but an unknown energy also scales the total light. the two can't be told apart. run it the other way: with the energy unknown, the depth bound at two millimetres more than triples, to zero point five three one millimetres, and it gets worse the stronger the scattering. and the arrival times don't break the tie. they carry almost no depth information the counts don't already have.

reels.name: Trade
reels.cap: Put the two bounds on one plot: depth against timing, one point per scattering length, from weak scattering at the top left, to strong at the right.
reels.words: put the two bounds on one plot: depth against timing, one point per scattering length, from weak scattering at the top left, to strong at the right. the designs no other point beats on both axes form the pareto front: sixteen, eight, the clear crystal, four, and two millimetres. its knee is at four millimetres. there, the depth bound is thirteen percent better than the clear crystal's, for one picosecond of c t r, which is within the noise. going on to two millimetres buys a little more depth precision, but costs about thirty picoseconds, an eight percent loss in time of flight signal to noise. in the interior the knee sits at two millimetres, and with the slower sensor the clear crystal drops off the front entirely.

reels.name: Index
reels.cap: Across refractive index, the clear crystal loses light as n rises, from about twelve hundred to six hundred photons, and its C T R bound rises with it.
reels.words: across refractive index, the clear crystal loses light as n rises, from about twelve hundred to six hundred photons, and its c t r bound rises with it. at each index's depth optimum, scattering restores the light to about sixteen hundred photons. but the optimum moves to stronger scattering, so its c t r bound pulls further away: twelve percent worse than clear at n of one point six, thirty six percent at two point one five. with the slower sensor, the optimum stays within a few percent of the clear crystal. swap the black wrap for a specular reflector, and the clear crystal collects three thousand photons, with a c t r of one hundred and twenty picoseconds. weak scattering still sharpens the timing. but the depth gain only appears at the strongest scattering, and never beats the absorbing wrap. the wrap and the scattering length act as one design choice.

reels.name: Outro
reels.cap: The usual caveats apply.
reels.words: the usual caveats apply. the rise time and sensor jitters are assumed, so the c t r values are for comparing designs, not absolute predictions. cherenkov light isn't simulated, and the scatterers absorb nothing.

title: High-Sensitivity PET using Optimised Continuous Cylindrical Shell Nanocomposite and…

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This thesis proposes a P E T scanner unlike the ones in hospitals today.
reels.words: this thesis proposes a p e t scanner unlike the ones in hospitals today. instead of tens of thousands of separate crystals, a single continuous shell of scintillator, read out by light sensors on both its inner and outer surfaces. let's see why you would build it, what it takes to make it work, and how well it does in simulation.

reels.name: PET basics
reels.cap: A radioactive tracer in the body emits positrons.
reels.words: a radioactive tracer in the body emits positrons. each one annihilates with an electron and produces two gamma photons of five hundred and eleven kilo electron volts, flying in opposite directions. when a ring of detectors catches both, the source lies somewhere on the line between the two hits, the line of response. millions of such lines are combined into an image. two numbers matter most. sensitivity: what fraction of decays the scanner actually records. and spatial resolution: how sharply it places each source.

reels.name: Conventional
reels.cap: Most scanners use blocks of small, separate crystals.
reels.words: most scanners use blocks of small, separate crystals. a large scanner needs tens of thousands of them, each wrapped so its light stays inside. the wrapping and the gaps between blocks are dead space, where gammas escape. and sharper images need more, smaller crystals, so cost climbs fast. the alternative is monolithic slabs: big single crystals that work out where the gamma hit from the pattern of light. but large, high quality crystals are expensive to grow, and near the edges of a slab the position estimate gets worse.

reels.name: Idea
reels.cap: Wilson takes the monolithic idea to its limit: one continuous cylindrical shell.
reels.words: wilson takes the monolithic idea to its limit: one continuous cylindrical shell. it has no internal boundaries, so no dead space, and no edges anywhere around the ring. small silicon photomultipliers cover both the inner and the outer surface. a shell like this can't be cut from a single crystal. instead it uses two newer materials: nanocomposites, scintillating nanoparticles held in a polymer, and transparent ceramics, made of sintered grains. both are cheaper and far easier to form into shapes. the catch: they scatter the scintillation light, and the nanocomposites are less dense.

reels.name: Locate
reels.cap: First, how does a monolithic detector locate a hit?
reels.words: first, how does a monolithic detector locate a hit? a gamma stops at some point inside the slab and releases a flash of thousands of light photons, spreading in every direction. light sensors on the front and the back count how many land on each pixel. here is what they see. the face nearer the flash gets a tall, narrow spot. the far face gets a low, wide one. so the centre of the spots says where across the slab the hit was, and their widths say how deep. to turn that into numbers, the thesis uses a simple model of the light. from a point source, the photons reaching a pixel fall off with distance r, like light from a bulb, and an exponential term accounts for light lost on the way. the model is fitted to the front and back maps together, by least squares, and the best fit gives the position, the depth, and the number of photons.

reels.name: Thickness
reels.cap: These materials force a design choice: the shell's thickness.
reels.words: these materials force a design choice: the shell's thickness. too thin, and most gammas pass straight through. too thick, and the light scatters and fades before it reaches the sensors, and more gammas bounce around by compton scattering, so the position estimate falls apart. so the thesis defines a score that captures both effects: the fraction of incoming gammas whose hit point can be located within, say, five millimetres. to find the best thickness, simulate a handful of thicknesses, fit a smooth curve through the scores, and take its maximum. for the ceramic glue gag, that is about twenty seven and a half millimetres, where sixty eight percent of gammas are located within five millimetres.

reels.name: Materials
reels.cap: Wilson ran this optimisation for five nanocomposites and four transparent ceramics, each simulated in GATE with full tracking of every light photon.
reels.words: wilson ran this optimisation for five nanocomposites and four transparent ceramics, each simulated in gate with full tracking of every light photon. the ceramics win overall, because they are much denser and stop gammas in less material. the best was the garnet glue gag, cerium doped. the best nanocomposite was lanthanum fluoride in polystyrene, helped by a high nanoparticle loading and a good refractive index match. these two go forward into a full scanner.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: The scanner is sized for the head or for small animals: an inner radius of two hundred and thirty three millimetres, and with glue gag a shell about twenty five millimetres thick.
reels.words: the scanner is sized for the head or for small animals: an inner radius of two hundred and thirty three millimetres, and with glue gag a shell about twenty five millimetres thick. its surfaces carry more than four thousand silicon photomultipliers, every one a grid of one millimetre pixels. a decay sends two gammas into the shell, and each makes its own splash of light on the inner and outer sensors. to reuse the flat slab method, the algorithm cuts the ring into two halves, midway between the two splashes. it then unrolls each half into a flat slab, mapping angle to distance, so both surfaces line up, and fits the same light model to the inner and outer maps. it works. with glue gag, the median distance between the estimated line of response and the true source is about one point three to one point six millimetres, getting only slightly worse as the source moves off centre. lanthanum fluoride, less dense and less bright, gives three to four millimetres. and around eighty percent of glue gag's endpoints land within five millimetres of the truth.

reels.name: Coincidence
reels.cap: In a real scan, decays arrive constantly, and this scintillator glows for about eighty four nanoseconds after each hit.
reels.words: in a real scan, decays arrive constantly, and this scintillator glows for about eighty four nanoseconds after each hit. in one giant detector, flashes overlap in time, so which flashes belong together? conventional coincidence logic, built for separate crystals, doesn't apply. wilson's method goes in steps. first, split the inner and outer surfaces into sixteen sectors, plus a second set shifted by half a sector, so a splash on a boundary in one set sits in the middle of a sector in the other. every ten nanoseconds, the light in each sector is summed, giving thirty two signals. second, deconvolve each signal by the scintillator's measured pulse shape. that undoes the slow glow and leaves one sharp spike at the start of each event, even when the pulses overlapped. third, apply a small threshold in each time step and count the sectors above it. one sector means a single gamma. exactly two means a coincidence, which goes on to the localisation step. more than two is ambiguous, and is set aside. in simulation, both gammas reach the shell in about a third of all decays. the algorithm correctly finds seventeen point four percent of all decays as true coincidences, misses fifteen percent, mostly gammas that left too little light, and adds two percent of false, random pairs. for comparison, a typical whole body scanner records around two percent.

reels.name: Images
reels.cap: The final test puts it all together.
reels.words: the final test puts it all together. three tiny sources sit in the field of view: at the centre, and at half and three quarters of the radius. three seconds of scanning, about twenty seven million decays, are simulated photon by photon. the lines of response go into the open source stir toolkit, after corrections, and are reconstructed with filtered back projection and with the iterative o s e m algorithm. all three sources come out as clean, compact spots. measured as full width at half maximum, the o s e m images resolve them to under four millimetres in almost every direction: from about two point four millimetres along the scanner axis at the centre, to four point four at three quarters of the radius. filtered back projection smears a little more in one direction.

reels.name: Outro
reels.cap: In short: a continuous shell scanner works, at least in simulation.
reels.words: in short: a continuous shell scanner works, at least in simulation. the thickness can be tuned to each material, the lines of response are placed to within about a millimetre and a half, sensitivity is high, and point sources are resolved to about four millimetres or better. the next steps are standard nema performance tests, correcting for positron range to sharpen the images, and working around the huge computing cost of simulating every light photon. but the case is made: cheaper, shapeable scintillators open a very different path to high sensitivity pet. thanks for watching.

title: PRISM: a physics-informed spatiotemporal convolutional network for interaction…

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This video is about PRISM, a manuscript by Ragy Abraham, Daniel Chahine, Mitra Safavi Naeini and Daniel Franklin.
reels.words: this video is about prism, a manuscript by ragy abraham, daniel chahine, mitra safavi naeini and daniel franklin. it asks how to find where a gamma ray hit inside a pet scanner made of one continuous ring of scintillator. the ring is moulded from a nanocomposite, lanthanum fluoride nanoparticles in polystyrene, forty two point nine millimetres thick and two hundred and ninety six long, read out on both its inner and outer surfaces by four thousand seven hundred and eighty eight silicon photomultiplier tiles. this is the open gate model: a source in the bore, scintillation flashes in the ring, and optical photons spraying to both surfaces.

reels.name: Problem
reels.cap: Here is a short piece of the ring seen side on, inner surface below, outer surface above.
reels.words: here is a short piece of the ring seen side on, inner surface below, outer surface above. a five hundred and eleven kev photon can compton scatter and then be absorbed, leaving two flashes. the target is the first point of interaction. each flash sends light toward both surfaces. in this simulation the rayleigh scattering length, six point eight three centimetres, is applied as a removal length, so a scattered photon simply stops. on top of that come three structural problems: the ring has no edge, so angle zero and two pi are neighbours; a coincidence has two photons with no natural order; and the light pattern changes with depth.

reels.name: Unroll
reels.cap: The network's input starts from the photodetector hits.
reels.words: the network's input starts from the photodetector hits. picture the inner surface as a cylinder of pixels, three millimetre virtual pixels, four by four on each tile. cut it along one line and unroll it, and it becomes an image: four hundred and sixteen bins around the ring, eighty four along it. notice the spot on the left edge: it continues on the right, because the cut is arbitrary. the outer surface has more facets, four hundred and ninety six bins, and is resampled to the same four hundred and sixteen.

reels.name: Burst
reels.cap: Time is kept too.
reels.words: time is kept too. the light is binned into frames of ten nanoseconds, on the inner and outer surfaces together. lanthanum fluoride decays with a thirty nanosecond constant, so five frames, fifty nanoseconds, hold about eighty one percent of the light, and each frame is dimmer than the last. stacked up, one burst is a tensor of six channels, five frames, eighty four by four hundred and sixteen pixels. two channels are the raw counts, one is a depth ratio computed from them, and three tell the network where each pixel sits. this is a real simulated event from the paper: two light spots on each surface, one per gamma ray, and mostly empty pixels.

reels.name: Depth ratio
reels.cap: The depth channel uses the same idea as dual ended readout.
reels.words: the depth channel uses the same idea as dual ended readout. take an interaction near the inner surface: the pixel right below it sees much more light than the pixel above. move it outward and the balance tips. the normalised difference d runs from plus one, inner dominant, to minus one, outer dominant, and it does not depend on how bright the event was. this curve is computed with a simple solid angle and removal model. in the real material, scattering and the facet geometry blur it, so the paper treats d as a noisy hint rather than a measurement.

reels.name: Circular
reels.cap: Ordinary networks treat the image's edges as real edges.
reels.words: ordinary networks treat the image's edges as real edges. a three by three filter at the left border would see zeros, a wall that does not exist in the ring. prism uses circular padding: before every convolution the far right column is copied in on the left, and the other way round, so the filter sees the spot whole. the same issue hits the output. a raw angle jumps from two pi back to zero, so the network predicts sine and cosine of the angle instead, which are smooth all the way round.

reels.name: Network
reels.cap: The network itself is a three dimensional residual encoder, convolving across frames, axial position and angle at once.
reels.words: the network itself is a three dimensional residual encoder, convolving across frames, axial position and angle at once. six input channels become sixteen, then thirty two, sixty four, one twenty eight and two fifty six, while the map shrinks from eighty four by four sixteen to six by twenty six. two attention steps sit near the end: a block attention module, and a gate that weights each time frame. the last layer makes two heat maps, one per gamma ray, and a small perceptron turns eight numbers into the two points. in total, three point six four million parameters. how do coordinates come out of a heat map? each map is six by twenty six cells. taking the brightest cell would snap the answer to fourteen degree steps. soft arg max instead takes a softmax and averages each coordinate under it, which lands between cells. it reads off frame, axial position, and sine and cosine of the angle, eight numbers for two points. there is no radial axis, so depth has to be smuggled through those eight numbers, a limit the authors point out themselves.

reels.name: Perm
reels.cap: Now the training objective.
reels.words: now the training objective. in a coincidence the two gamma rays leave from one annihilation, and nothing in the light says which one is first. suppose the network finds both points but calls them the other way round. scored as labelled, that is a huge error. prism's loss takes the smaller of the two pairings, so a correct answer is never punished for its order. a loss that insists on the order pushes an unsure network toward the middle of the pair, near the scanner axis. on top, hard example mining doubles the weight of the six worst events in each batch of thirty two.

reels.name: Geometry
reels.cap: Two more terms use the geometry.
reels.words: two more terms use the geometry. the ring only exists between two hundred and thirty five and two hundred and seventy eight millimetres from the axis. a rectified penalty is zero inside and grows outside, and the same holds for the axial ends. the polar term measures the error in cylindrical parts, weighting the tangential error by one point five, because the tangential position of each end of a line of response is what sets resolution across the image. together: the mined pairing loss, plus half the polar term, plus a fifth of the boundary term.

reels.name: Results
reels.cap: The training data came from Open GATE: eight point five nine million decays from a uniform cylinder gave seven hundred and thirty five thousand bursts, and nine thousand one hundred and twenty true coincidences in the he
reels.words: the training data came from open gate: eight point five nine million decays from a uniform cylinder gave seven hundred and thirty five thousand bursts, and nine thousand one hundred and twenty true coincidences in the held out test set. the split is by decay, so no event leaks between sets. on those events, generic three d networks miss by twenty five to thirty one millimetres. petnet, the same backbone without the loss and padding, gets twenty two point eight five. prism gets a median of eight point two six millimetres, with the same three point six four million parameters, so the gain comes from those two changes taken together, not from size.

reels.name: Components
reels.cap: These are the paper's residuals split into cylindrical parts.
reels.words: these are the paper's residuals split into cylindrical parts. the radial, or depth, error is largest, with a median of three point four millimetres and a long tail toward predictions that are too shallow. tangential, two point zero, axial, one point seven six. combining both ends of a line of response, the line shifts by about two point four millimetres at the centre. for perspective, simply putting every point on the inner surface would give a radial median of four point nine one, because most gammas stop near the inner face. along the axis, the error is flat in the middle and climbs toward the ends, where the light pattern is cut off by the black end faces.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: Where are the errors?
reels.words: where are the errors? this map of the mean error over the ring's cross section is even all the way round, with no seam at angle zero, as circular padding should give. what changes is depth: the outer rim is bright. split the shell into four layers, and the median error climbs from four point seven millimetres in the innermost quarter, which holds sixty nine percent of the interactions, to twenty six point seven in the outermost. the predicted depths are squeezed inward: they rarely reach the outer half of the shell. keeping only events predicted in the inner half brings the median to six point six seven millimetres, a software choice between sensitivity and resolution.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: The authors are clear about the limits.
reels.words: the authors are clear about the limits. the photodetectors are ideal, random coincidences are not modelled, and it is all simulation. in a separate point source study, images built from prism's end points reached three point two to three point five millimetres, against about two point four with the true points. next, they want to drop single point regression. when the light could come from two places, a regressor lands in between, in empty space. a dense three d probability map could keep both. so, in a thick, scattering, seamless ring, building the geometry into the network cut the median error about threefold, to eight point two six millimetres.

title: Two reviews of PET detector design, read together

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This video is about two reviews of PET detector design.
reels.words: this video is about two reviews of pet detector design. the first, by konstantinou, lecoq, benlloch and gonzalez, introduces metascintillators. the second, by gonzalez montoro and colleagues from stanford, valencia, seattle and bruker, reviews monolithic crystals. a pet detector has three jobs. it must stop the five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt photon, tell when it arrived, and tell where. metascintillators chase the when, without giving up the stopping. monolithic crystals chase the where, in three dimensions, with no gaps. by the end you should have both arguments, the numbers they rest on, and the open problems each review names, including where the two meet.

reels.name: TOF gain
reels.cap: Why does timing matter so much?
reels.words: why does timing matter so much? both photons of an annihilation travel along one line. if the detectors measure the difference in their arrival times, the emission point is pinned to a stretch of that line. its length is the speed of light times the time difference, over two. fewer possible positions along the line means less noise in the image. at two hundred and fourteen picoseconds, the timing of the siemens biograph vision, the stretch is about three centimetres, and in a twenty centimetre head the gain is about two and a half. at ten picoseconds it shrinks to one and a half millimetres, close to the positron range, and the gain grows to about eleven and a half. the review rounds these to about three and twelve. that ten picosecond goal is what metascintillators are built for.

reels.name: Trade off
reels.cap: Timing depends on how many photons appear in the first instants after the gamma interacts.
reels.words: timing depends on how many photons appear in the first instants after the gamma interacts. l y s o is dense, so it stops five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt photons well. it rises in seventy four picoseconds and gives thirty two thousand photons per mega electron volt, but they come out over a forty nanosecond decay. a plastic like e j two three two decays in one point four nanoseconds, so although it gives only eight thousand four hundred photons, more of them arrive early. with the review's own pulse model, the first two hundred picoseconds hold about one hundred and forty photons for the plastic, against about fifty for l y s o. but the plastic is light, and the gamma mostly passes straight through. barium fluoride sits in between, with a fast component under a nanosecond but lower density. the review calls this trade-off unbreakable with conventional scintillators.

reels.name: Meta idea
reels.cap: The metascintillator idea starts from the recoil electron.
reels.words: the metascintillator idea starts from the recoil electron. when the gamma interacts, it frees an electron that travels and loses energy along its track, up to about half a millimetre. nothing confines that electron to one material. so stack thin slabs of a dense host and a fast emitter, each thinner than that range. the electron crosses several slabs, and part of its energy lands in the fast emitter. each event shares the energy differently. a first metapixel, built by turtos and colleagues, stacked eight pairs of quarter millimetre plastic and fifth of a millimetre b g o, three point six millimetres in all. events purely in b g o timed at one hundred and twenty picoseconds, while events with most of their energy in the plastic reached forty. it was the first proof of energy sharing.

reels.name: Sharing
reels.cap: How much fast emitter is enough?
reels.words: how much fast emitter is enough? the authors simulated slabs from fifty to three hundred micrometres in gate, with b g o, l y s o and barium fluoride as hosts. for each event they recorded the energy left in the plastic. the distribution is skewed: most events leave little, a tail leaves a lot. they count an event as useful above eighty kilo electron volts, about fifteen percent of the gamma, or about seven hundred fast photons. across all designs, the more plastic, the more energy it catches, but the lower the density, and so the stopping power. each colour is one host, falling roughly exponentially. two hundred micrometres of l y s o with one hundred of plastic keeps the density above five grams per cubic centimetre, and still puts about fifty kilo electron volts in the plastic on average.

reels.name: Pulse
reels.cap: The light from a shared event is the sum of two pulses: the fast emitter's, scaled by the energy it caught, and the host's, scaled by the rest.
reels.words: the light from a shared event is the sum of two pulses: the fast emitter's, scaled by the energy it caught, and the host's, scaled by the rest. with nothing in the plastic, this is plain l y s o. put eighty kilo electron volts in the plastic, and the first two hundred picoseconds already hold a quarter more photons. with the whole gamma in the plastic, the early light is about two and a half times larger. so each event carries its own timing quality, set by how much energy it shared.

reels.name: Bound
reels.cap: How good can such a detector be?
reels.words: how good can such a detector be? the review answers with a cramer rao lower bound on timing. plastic lowers the density, so to stop as many gammas as a twenty millimetre l y s o pixel, the metascintillator pixel grows to twenty seven millimetres. the bound counts how many photons are detected early, and how much their paths spread their arrival times. for an event entirely in l y s o it is one hundred and sixty nine picoseconds. for an event entirely in the plastic, forty one. weighting the bound by the sharing distribution gives a spread of timings, one per event, with a weighted mean of one hundred and thirty one point four picoseconds: about thirty better than an l y s o pixel of the same stopping power. the fast events in the tail could even serve as priors in reconstruction.

reels.name: Beyond
reels.cap: The same thinking extends to light transport, and to faster ingredients.
reels.words: the same thinking extends to light transport, and to faster ingredients. inside a dense crystal, light that hits the exit face beyond the critical angle is reflected back: up to ninety percent of it in b g o. a photonic crystal slab on that face, a pattern at the scale of the wavelength, diffracts some of it out. on real crystals it improved timing by up to fifty seven percent, and light yield by up to one hundred and forty four percent. cadmium selenide nanoplatelets emit within about twenty picoseconds, thanks to quantum confinement, but they absorb their own light and need organic ligands. cherenkov light comes within about ten picoseconds. it gives only tens of photons, but times some events very well.

reels.name: Mono idea
reels.cap: Now the second review, on position.
reels.words: now the second review, on position. a pixelated array is a grid of small crystals separated by reflector. light stays in the pixel it was made in, so the position is simply which pixel fired, good to about half the pitch. the reflector gaps can be as thin as seventy micrometres, but depth is lost unless extra layers or sensors are added. a monolithic crystal is one continuous block, here fifty by fifty by fifteen millimetres. the light spreads over many silicon photomultipliers, and the shape of that spread is the measurement. its centre gives the position across the face. with no gaps inside the block, more gammas are stopped: in one simulation of a small animal scanner, sensitivity at the centre rose from seventeen to twenty one percent.

reels.name: Depth
reels.cap: The same light also gives depth.
reels.words: the same light also gives depth. an interaction close to the sensors makes a narrow, peaked spot. far from them, the same light spreads wide and flat. a simple estimator is the total energy e over the peak signal i, which grows with the distance from the sensors. the light models predict it grows linearly or quadratically, depending on the crystal's shape and the finish of its walls. with it, depth resolutions below three millimetres have been reported for crystals up to twenty millimetres thick. knowing the depth removes the parallax error that blurs the edges of a ring scanner's field of view.

reels.name: Positioning
reels.cap: The difficulty is near the edges, where the crystal wall cuts the light off.
reels.words: the difficulty is near the edges, where the crystal wall cuts the light off. in the centre, the centre of gravity of the signals finds the event exactly. move the event toward the wall, and the centre of gravity lags behind, pulled toward the middle: an event four millimetres from the wall reads almost ten. raising each signal to a power before averaging, here squared, weights the peak more, and the same event reads six. this compression at the edges is the classic weakness of monolithic crystals, and it is what the more elaborate algorithms are for.

reels.name: Algorithms
reels.cap: The review sorts positioning into three families.
reels.words: the review sorts positioning into three families. the first uses the shape of the light directly: centre of gravity, raising to a power, and e over i for depth. they need no calibration, but suffer at the walls. the second is statistical: least squares, chi squared, nearest neighbours and maximum likelihood compare each event with reference light distributions. the references come from a collimated beam stepped across the whole face, which is slow. nearest neighbour methods match the others with two hundred times fewer reference events. the third is machine learning: neural networks, and gradient tree boosting, which needs under an hour of calibration per block and positions almost uniformly over the volume. the question the review leaves open is how to calibrate more than a thousand monolithic modules, and keep them calibrated day to day.

reels.name: Thickness
reels.cap: Thickness sets the main trade-off inside monolithic designs.
reels.words: thickness sets the main trade-off inside monolithic designs. on fifty by fifty millimetre l y s o blocks read by sixteen by sixteen silicon photomultipliers, the measured resolution away from the edges was zero point six eight millimetres at ten millimetres thick, zero point nine at fifteen, and one point two nine at twenty. meanwhile the fraction of gammas stopped, from the attenuation of l y s o, rises from about fifty six to eighty one percent. the review notes that clinical scanners need at least two centimetres, and that many monolithic studies use thinner crystals, trading sensitivity away.

reels.name: Mono timing
reels.cap: Timing is where the two reviews meet.
reels.words: timing is where the two reviews meet. in a pixel, nearly all the light reaches one sensor. in a monolithic block the same light is spread over many, so each sees only a few photons, and its first photon is late and noisy. the fix is to combine many timestamps, weighted by their energy, and to calibrate every channel for time walk and skew. a fifty by fifty by fifteen millimetre l y s o block with analogue sensors reached five hundred and fifty picoseconds over the whole block, four hundred and forty at its centre. digital sensors on a twenty two millimetre block reached two hundred and fourteen, and a maximum likelihood method on a ten millimetre block, one hundred and fifty seven. below one hundred picoseconds is the goal the review sets. and it is where the metascintillator review leaves its own question open: which readout suits a metascintillator, pixelated or monolithic.

reels.name: Gaps
reels.cap: Here is the map with its gaps.
reels.words: here is the map with its gaps. for metascintillators, energy sharing is demonstrated and the timing bound is promising, but it is simulated: the review asks for system-level measurements, a choice of readout, and reconstruction that uses each event's own timing. for monolithic crystals, millimetre positions and depth are shown, with no gaps inside the block. but most gammas scatter before they are absorbed, sixty eight percent in l s o, and a single light centroid loses the separate interactions. calibration does not yet scale to a full scanner, and timing must fall below one hundred picoseconds. the two open questions point at each other: a composite block read out as a monolith, where each event's position and timing quality must both be estimated from its light. a per-event lower bound, like the one the metascintillator review uses for timing, is a natural way to ask how well that can be done.

title: The open-field mouse brain PET programme

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: Most PET scans of mice are done under anaesthesia, which changes how the brain works and rules out studying behaviour.
reels.words: most pet scans of mice are done under anaesthesia, which changes how the brain works and rules out studying behaviour. this programme is led by andre kyme and steven meikle in sydney. it is building a brain pet scanner for a mouse that is awake and free to move. here is what that takes, piece by piece: the detectors, how they are calibrated, how the images are reconstructed, and a hard limit that the physics sets.

reels.name: Concept
reels.cap: The design surrounds an open field with four box shaped detector panels.
reels.words: the design surrounds an open field with four box shaped detector panels. because the mouse keeps moving, its head is tracked, and every line of response is placed back into the brain's own frame of reference during reconstruction. the aim is brain pet and behaviour, recorded at the same time. a mouse brain is tiny, so the detector needs very fine crystals. gammas hit the flat panels of a box at steep angles, so it also needs depth of interaction. and all of this has to stay affordable to read out.

reels.name: Motion
reels.cap: Each decay is recorded in the scanner's frame.
reels.words: each decay is recorded in the scanner's frame. here the same spot in the brain emits twice: once with the mouse here, and once after it has moved and turned. in the scanner's frame the two lines of response pass through different places, so an image made from them blurs. the fix: track the head's position and orientation at every moment, and move each line of response by the inverse of that pose, into the mouse's own frame. there, both lines cross at the same point in the brain, and the image is sharp again. the catch, which comes back later, is that the scanner's sensitivity also has to be recomputed for every pose.

reels.name: Detector
reels.cap: The detector blocks are arrays of twenty three by twenty three L Y S O crystals, each less than eight tenths of a millimetre wide and twenty millimetres long.
reels.words: the detector blocks are arrays of twenty three by twenty three l y s o crystals, each less than eight tenths of a millimetre wide and twenty millimetres long. each block is read at both ends, by silicon photomultipliers on the front and the back. the light from an interaction splits between the two ends. a hit near the front sends more light to the front, one near the back sends more to the back, so the fraction reaching each end measures depth. reading both ends would normally double the electronics. instead, custom boards combine the seventy two sensor signals of a block into just eight channels, nine to one, feeding a low cost commercial chip. the 2025 paper reports ten and a half percent energy resolution and two point three millimetre depth resolution, at the price of slower timing, one point three nanoseconds.

reels.name: Calibration
reels.cap: Every crystal needs its depth signal calibrated.
reels.words: every crystal needs its depth signal calibrated. the usual way is a collimated beam through a slit in lead, stepped to known depths one at a time, which is slow for thousands of crystals. their 2026 paper skips that. put an ordinary sodium twenty two source on the front face. its gammas travel along the crystals, and how many stop at each depth follows a known exponential, so one uncollimated exposure already contains every depth, in known proportions. two calibrations built on this, one physics based and one a small neural network, matched the collimated gold standard to within about half a millimetre. a full four by four panel was then calibrated from a single exposure, reaching two millimetre depth resolution.

reels.name: Virtual
reels.cap: Depth information has a cost in reconstruction.
reels.words: depth information has a cost in reconstruction. every pair of crystals, at every pair of depth bins, is its own line of response. for this scanner that is about seven point three billion lines, and a system matrix of around eight terabytes. motion compensation makes it worse, because the sensitivity has to be recomputed as the animal moves. the 2024 fix is a virtual cylinder: a ring of small imaginary detectors inside the field of view. each real line of response is assigned to the virtual pair it passes through, so many real lines collapse into one. with zero point four seven millimetre virtual detectors and six depth bins, that removes eighty six percent of the lines, with transaxial images almost identical to the full geometry and sub millimetre resolution across the field.

reels.name: Scatter
reels.cap: With crystals this fine, a gamma often Compton scatters in one crystal and is absorbed in another.
reels.words: with crystals this fine, a gamma often compton scatters in one crystal and is absorbed in another. to draw the right line of response, the system must pick the crystal hit first. if scattering were mostly forward, the energies would usually give it away. but in their simulation of the real detector, scattering into a neighbouring crystal is almost evenly split: fifty four percent forward, forty six percent backward, not the seventy percent forward a naive klein nishina reading suggests. a neural network still does well: it finds the right crystal for ninety percent of single crystal events and eighty two percent of scattered ones, and positions events better than classic anger logic. but the authors name the ceiling: with forward and backward scatter close to one to one, energies and light patterns alone can't pick the first crystal with certainty.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: Put together, the programme shows dual ended depth encoding at a fraction of the usual channel count, a calibration that needs no collimator, reconstruction that stays tractable with depth bins and motion, and a clear st
reels.words: put together, the programme shows dual ended depth encoding at a fraction of the usual channel count, a calibration that needs no collimator, reconstruction that stays tractable with depth bins and motion, and a clear statement of what energies alone can't tell you about scatter. that last point leaves an open question: whether adding arrival times can do what energies can't, and put scattered interactions in the right order. the work is funded by the australian research council, with collaborators at u c davis. thanks for watching.

title: The Prism-PET programme

reels.name: Opening
reels.cap: This is the Prism-PET programme from Amir Goldan's group at Weill Cornell Medicine.
reels.words: this is the prism-pet programme from amir goldan's group at weill cornell medicine. its idea fits in one picture: long crystals, read from one end, with a row of tiny glass prisms on the other end that send each crystal's light into its neighbour. that small trick gives a single ended detector a sense of depth. here is why that matters, how it works, and how far the group has taken it.

reels.name: Parallax
reels.cap: PET crystals are long, around twenty millimetres, so they can stop five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gammas.
reels.words: pet crystals are long, around twenty millimetres, so they can stop five hundred and eleven kilo electron volt gammas. a gamma arriving at an angle may travel into the crystal and stop deep inside. if the detector can't tell how deep, it places the event at the crystal's face, and the line of response shifts. this is parallax error, and it gets worse towards the edge of the field of view, and in compact scanners like brain pet. measuring the depth of interaction, or d o i, removes the error. the usual way is a second photodetector on the far end of every crystal, which roughly doubles the electronics. prism-pet gets depth from one end.

reels.name: Light guide
reels.cap: Start with the common single ended design.
reels.words: start with the common single ended design. thin crystals sit on an array of silicon photomultipliers, several crystals per sensor, and a flat glass light guide sits on top. light from a crystal enters the glass and spreads to many neighbours. the amount of light that gets shared depends on depth, so it can encode d o i. but the sharing is isotropic: the light ends up as weak signals spread over many sensors, where dark counts swamp them. and crystals at the edges and corners have fewer neighbours to share with, so they come out worse.

reels.name: Prism idea
reels.cap: Prism-PET replaces the flat glass with an array of small right triangle prisms.
reels.words: prism-pet replaces the flat glass with an array of small right triangle prisms. in this side view each prism covers two crystals, but the prisms are offset by one crystal from the sensors underneath, so the two crystals under a prism always sit on different sensors. follow the light. a gamma stops in a crystal and light goes both ways. light heading down reaches this crystal's own sensor. light heading up enters the prism, turns a hundred and eighty degrees, and comes down the neighbouring crystal onto a different sensor. how the light splits depends on depth. an interaction near the sensors sends most light straight down. one near the prism shares much more with the neighbour. so the ratio of the brightest sensor to the total, called w, tracks depth. the key difference from glass is that the sharing is deterministic: each crystal lights a fixed pattern of its own sensor and its nearest neighbours, so the signals stay strong. separate centre, edge and corner prism designs keep the pattern working at the borders, and the fixed patterns let up to nine crystals share one sensor and still be told apart.

reels.name: Module
reels.cap: The first module paper, in twenty twenty, used sixteen by sixteen arrays of one point four millimetre L Y S O crystals, twenty millimetres long, four crystals to each sensor.
reels.words: the first module paper, in twenty twenty, used sixteen by sixteen arrays of one point four millimetre l y s o crystals, twenty millimetres long, four crystals to each sensor. against the same module with a flat glass guide, the prisms made depth resolution twice as sharp, from five millimetres to two and a half, improved energy resolution from thirteen to nine percent, and kept crystals cleanly separated right out to the corners. a year later, they replaced the simple ratio with a small convolutional neural network. depth resolution dropped to one point eight four millimetres averaged over the array, with the biggest gains at the edges and corners, where the ratio struggles. that is the best single ended depth resolution reported at twenty millimetres. one caveat: inter crystal scatter events, about forty percent of the photopeak, were cut first.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: In twenty twenty three the group built a prototype brain scanner: forty modules in a single ring, arranged as a decagon that hugs the head.
reels.words: in twenty twenty three the group built a prototype brain scanner: forty modules in a single ring, arranged as a decagon that hugs the head. it reached two point eight five millimetre depth resolution and two hundred and seventy one picosecond timing, and one point two millimetre intrinsic spatial resolution. reconstructed images reached one point five three millimetres, and in a derenzo phantom, one millimetre rods were resolved, which the authors claim is the highest resolution reported for a human brain pet scanner. the price is sensitivity: one point two percent, from a ring only two and a half centimetres long.

reels.name: Tapered
reels.cap: Light sharing also gives a second clock.
reels.words: light sharing also gives a second clock. light from an interaction heading down reaches the crystal's own sensor first. light going up through the prism arrives at the neighbour later. the difference in arrival times depends on depth: an optical time of flight. the catch is light leaking at the crystal to sensor interface, which scrambles these timestamps. the fix: taper each crystal from one point five millimetres down to one point two at the readout end, so it sits entirely inside the sensor's active area. tapering cut the time of flight depth resolution from almost fourteen millimetres to five point four, the first experimental demonstration of this kind of depth encoding in a module. it also improved the energy based depth, the energy resolution and the timing, while costing almost nothing in sensitivity. combining time and light reached two point two five millimetres for centre crystals.

reels.name: Scatter
reels.cap: Thin crystals have a cost.
reels.words: thin crystals have a cost. a gamma often compton scatters in one crystal and finishes in another. at one point four millimetres, only thirty seven percent of photopeak events stay in a single crystal, and the scanner simply throws the rest away. but the prisms make recovery possible. because each crystal lights a fixed pattern, the readout of a scattered event is just the sum of known patterns, which can be decomposed. in simulation, a neural network trained on these patterns found the first crystal in eighty three percent of photopeak events, and in about two thirds of the scattered ones, cutting events assigned to the wrong line of response from sixty four to forty seven percent. it is not yet shown on real data.

reels.name: Outlook
reels.cap: The group is now at Weill Cornell, where Prism-PET is the main brain project: a compact, portable, upright scanner, with motion compensation and attenuation correction without C T.
reels.words: the group is now at weill cornell, where prism-pet is the main brain project: a compact, portable, upright scanner, with motion compensation and attenuation correction without c t. in late twenty twenty four it won a six point two million dollar grant from the national institute on aging, aimed at early diagnosis of alzheimer's disease. and other groups are taking the design up. the lesson for detector design: you can get depth from a single readout face by shaping where the light goes. prism-pet does it deterministically, with geometry at the far end. the alternative is to shape it statistically, inside the crystal itself, by engineering how it scatters light. thanks for watching.

title: First Human Imaging Studies with the EXPLORER Total-Body PET Scanner

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: This video explains a twenty nineteen paper in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine, by Badawi and colleagues.
reels.words: this video explains a twenty nineteen paper in the journal of nuclear medicine, by badawi and colleagues. it reports the first human scans on explorer, the first total-body pet scanner. a typical pet scanner sees a slice of the body only about twenty two centimetres long. to image a whole person, the bed steps them through it, one slice of body at a time. explorer is one hundred and ninety four centimetres long. it covers almost every adult body in a single acquisition. we will see where its forty-fold gain comes from, what the gain can buy, and how far four volunteers support each claim.

reels.name: Acceptance
reels.cap: Look at the scanner from the side.
reels.doc: Side view of the scanner: the pairs a point emits, and the share whose both ends land on detector.
reels.words: look at the scanner from the side. the detector ring is these two lines. a positron annihilation in the body sends out two photons back to back, in a random direction. the pair is only counted if both photons hit detector. most of them leave through the open ends. at the centre of a twenty two centimetre scanner, only twenty seven percent are caught. make the scanner one hundred and ninety four centimetres long, and almost every direction is caught. explorer only accepts pairs tilted up to fifty seven degrees, so the centre catches eighty four percent. that is three times more. now move the point towards the end of the short scanner. its share falls, and it reaches zero once the point leaves the ring. most of the body is out of view most of the time.

reels.name: Coverage
reels.cap: Plot that share along the whole body.
reels.doc: Sensitivity along the body: one bed's triangle, shared over 17 beds, against EXPLORER's plateau.
reels.words: plot that share along the whole body. for one bed position of the short scanner it is a triangle, peaking at zero point two seven in the middle of the ring. stepping half a ring at a time over a hundred and eighty centimetres takes seventeen bed positions, so each point is in view for only one seventeenth of the scan. averaged over the scan, the share is zero point zero one six. explorer sees every point for the whole scan, and from a wider angle. its average is zero point seven. that is forty three times more, from geometry alone. the paper's own simulations, with time of flight, put the gain at up to forty.

reels.name: Scanner
reels.cap: Here is EXPLORER from the side.
reels.doc: The hardware as built: eight units seen side on, the ring seen down the bore, then one detector block. Each length is drawn where the camera sees it at true length (side on for the units, face on for the ring).
reels.words: here is explorer from the side. it is built from eight units, each twenty four centimetres long, with gaps of only two and a half millimetres between them. looking down the bore, the ring is seventy eight point six centimetres across. each unit is tiled with detector blocks. a block is a seven by six array of l y s o crystals, two point seven six millimetres wide and eighteen point one millimetres deep, read out by four silicon photomultipliers.

reels.name: Specs
reels.cap: When an annihilation sends its two photons into the ring, the two detectors they strike define a line through the point where it happened.
reels.doc: Timing, energy and spatial resolution, each drawn as the thing it blurs; the reconstruction named.
reels.words: when an annihilation sends its two photons into the ring, the two detectors they strike define a line through the point where it happened. the two photons' arrival times differ by up to a few nanoseconds, and explorer measures that difference to four hundred and thirty picoseconds. that places the annihilation within about six point four centimetres along the line. the energy resolution is eleven point seven percent, and only photons between four hundred and thirty and six hundred and forty five kilo electron volts are kept. the images are reconstructed with list mode o s e m, using the time of flight and a model of the detector blur. near the centre the spatial resolution is two point nine millimetres.

reels.name: Budget
reels.cap: Every claim in the paper spends the same budget.
reels.doc: The count budget on a log ruler: factors add as lengths, so the gain is a length that can be spent.
reels.words: every claim in the paper spends the same budget. the counts in an image grow with the sensitivity, the activity injected, the scan time, and how much of the tracer has not yet decayed. on a log scale, factors add as lengths. start from a short scanner's twenty minute scan. explorer's sensitivity adds a length of forty three. keep everything else the same, and that buys a better image.

reels.name: Images
reels.cap: The first volunteer was scanned for twenty minutes, with voxels of one by one by one and a half millimetres.
reels.doc: Better and faster: the first volunteer's 20 min images (Fig. 2), then the same scan cut short (Fig. 3).
reels.words: the first volunteer was scanned for twenty minutes, with voxels of one by one by one and a half millimetres. the images show the walls of the carotid artery and the end plates of the vertebrae, without the usual noise. then the same data were cut shorter and shorter, halving the counts at each step, down to eighteen point seven five seconds, sixty four times fewer. the noise grows as the counts fall. the authors judged the images diagnostic at thirty seven and a half seconds, and arguably even at eighteen. a short scanner given the same scan time for the whole body would collect about forty times fewer counts.

reels.name: Activity
reels.cap: Fluorine eighteen halves every hundred and ten minutes.
reels.doc: Later and lower dose, on one log activity axis: the decay curve, the scans and the injected activities.
reels.words: fluorine eighteen halves every hundred and ten minutes. the second volunteer was injected with two hundred and fifty six mega becquerels, and scanned again at one, three, eight and ten hours. by ten hours only five point seven mega becquerels were left, and the images still looked diagnostic. that is the activity an injection of eight point three mega becquerels leaves after the usual hour. its dose would be about zero point one six millisieverts. a standard injection is about two hundred and ninety mega becquerels. two volunteers were given about thirty and about ten percent of it. at twenty five mega becquerels, a ten minute scan still gave good images, though that volunteer weighed only forty three and a half kilograms.

reels.name: Dynamic
reels.cap: The second volunteer was also scanned from the moment of injection.
reels.doc: One-second frames of the whole body: the bolus path and the time-activity curves it leaves. Illustrative.
reels.words: the second volunteer was also scanned from the moment of injection. the data were cut into one second frames, each showing the whole body. the bolus reaches the heart, passes through the lungs, comes back to the heart, and leaves down the aorta into the arteries. one second frames are fine enough to see the bolus arrive later and spread out between the left ventricle and the descending aorta. and because every organ is in view at once, each one gets its own curve, measured against the blood in the same frames. that is what kinetic modelling of the whole body needs. these are the paper's own frames, one per second. at fifteen seconds the tracer is still in the veins of the leg and in the heart. by twenty nine seconds it has reached the arteries of the whole body. the measured curves show the same order: the left ventricle peaks first, and the descending aorta a moment later.

reels.name: Takeaway
reels.cap: So the paper spends one budget five ways.
reels.doc: Back on the count budget: each claim's evidence pulsed on its spend, then how strong the evidence is.
reels.words: so the paper spends one budget five ways. a twenty minute scan gave the sharpest images, a scan sixty four times shorter was arguably still diagnostic, ten hours after injection still worked, so did twenty five mega becquerels, and one second frames followed the tracer through the whole body. but the support is four volunteers, judged by eye, with no controlled comparison against a conventional scanner. the authors call it qualitative, and leave the numbers to future trials. every claim spends the same forty-fold gain, and it comes from geometry. each point in the body is seen from a wider angle, and it is seen for the whole scan.

title: The Ziv-Zakai and Bhattacharyya bounds for the monolithic slab, a sequel to slab_crlb

reels.name: Intro
reels.cap: In the first video, the Cramer Rao bound told us how well the light pins down one interaction in the monolithic slab: fifty by fifty by ten millimetres of L S O, read by eight by eight silicon photomultipliers.
reels.words: in the first video, the cramer rao bound told us how well the light pins down one interaction in the monolithic slab: fifty by fifty by ten millimetres of l s o, read by eight by eight silicon photomultipliers. but in the study's gate runs, about four in ten photopeak events leave their energy at more than one site. the gamma compton scatters, and the scattered photon is absorbed somewhere else. each site makes its own pool of light, and the pools simply add on the photomultipliers. so from this pattern, can we tell two sites from one, and how far apart must they be? the bhattacharyya bound and the ziv zakai bound can. both are computed here, for the same slab.

reels.name: Model
reels.cap: Here are the pools, from above.
reels.doc: The light model computed here, as input -> box -> output, its assumptions, its pools, and superposition.
reels.words: here are the pools, from above. a site near the readout makes a tight pool, one near the entrance a broad one. with scattering, the total changes with depth too. for two sites, the mean count on each photomultiplier is the first site's pool plus the second's, each weighted by its share of the energy. that superposition is assumed, as in the plan for paper three.

reels.name: Clouds
reels.cap: Take one photomultiplier, and two places the site could be.
reels.doc: One photomultiplier, two sites: the best guess is wrong only where the count histograms overlap. Two photomultipliers: each event is a dot, each site a cloud of dots, the best test a boundary between the clouds, and its mistakes the dots on the wrong side. Everything after this measures how much two clouds overlap.
reels.words: take one photomultiplier, and two places the site could be. from site a it expects about four photons, from site b about nine. each event's count scatters around those means. the best guess picks whichever site makes the count more likely. so it can only be wrong where the two histograms overlap. half that shared area is its error rate: about one event in six. add a second photomultiplier, and each event becomes a dot: its two counts. events from site a land in one cloud, events from site b in another. the best test is a boundary between the clouds. dots on the wrong side of it are its mistakes. move the sites apart, and the clouds part and the mistakes vanish. bring them together, and the mistakes multiply. so every question in this video is one question: how much do two clouds overlap?

reels.name: Distance
reels.cap: Counting overlapping dots is slow, so Bhattacharyya measures the overlap with geometry.
reels.doc: Bhattacharyya's idea as geometry: Poisson clouds are stretched along bright channels; square-rooting the counts makes every cloud round and the same size, so the overlap depends only on the distance d between centres. BC = exp(-d^2/2) turns d into a score, which fences in the error of every test (64 channels: Space, Sum).
reels.words: counting overlapping dots is slow, so bhattacharyya measures the overlap with geometry. first, look at the clouds' shapes. a bright photomultiplier scatters more than a dim one, so each cloud is stretched along its bright direction. now take the square root of every count. every cloud turns round, and all of them the same size, however bright the photomultiplier. so the overlap now depends on one thing: the distance d between the centres. bhattacharyya turns it into a score, e to the minus d squared over two. it is one when the clouds sit on top of each other, and falls towards zero as they part. and that score fences in the error of every possible test: none can do better than the bottom of this band, and the best is never worse than the top. the true error, dashed, lies inside it.

reels.name: Space
reels.cap: So how do sixty four counts become one cloud?
reels.doc: Where the 64 counts live: the light model maps a site to 64 means, one point in a space with an axis per photomultiplier; in square-root units each event scatters round it by 1/2 on every axis. Single 511 keV sites (x across the slab, every depth; y = 0.4) trace a curved sheet, drawn on the three PCA axes that keep most of its spread; one event is a tiny cloud on it. At 5 keV the sheet shrinks by sqrt(5/511) towards zero and the cloud does not.
reels.words: so how do sixty four counts become one cloud? the light model takes in a site and an energy, and gives out sixty four mean counts. sixty four numbers are one point, in a space with one axis per photomultiplier. each event's counts land near that point, and in square-root units they scatter by the same half a count along every one of the sixty four axes. so the noise is a round cloud, as with two photomultipliers, only in sixty four dimensions. at five kilo electron volts every count is a hundredth as large. the sheet shrinks towards zero, so zoom in: the cloud has kept its size, and now covers much of the sheet. that is the threshold, in the real sixty four count space.

reels.name: Sum
reels.cap: Why a plain sum?
reels.doc: The Bhattacharyya distance between two single sites 2 mm apart across (27 keV, where it is about 1) as 64 terms, one per photomultiplier, that add; independent channels make the overlaps multiply, so the distances add; correlated Gaussian noise would use the covariance instead.
reels.words: why a plain sum? each photomultiplier counts its own photons. so the overlap in sixty four dimensions is the product of sixty four single overlaps, and their distances add. the cloud picture extends to any number of axes. if the noise were correlated, say by crosstalk, the clouds would be tilted ellipsoids, and the distance would use the covariance: one eighth, delta mu, sigma inverse, delta mu. here sigma is diagonal, and it comes back to the sum.

reels.name: Jacobian
reels.cap: Near one site, the light model is nearly a straight line.
reels.doc: Near one site the light model is linear: the 64 x 4 Jacobian takes a nudge (dx, dy, dz, dE) to the change in every mean count. Its columns, as maps; divided by the noise they are arrows in the 64-axis space, and the Fisher matrix of the first video is their dot products. Nearly perpendicular arrows: the bounds barely couple.
reels.words: near one site, the light model is nearly a straight line. a small nudge in position or energy goes in, the jacobian, sixty four rows by four columns, gives out the change in every count. nudge the site across, and light moves from one side of the pool to the other. the same along y, turned. nudge it deeper, and the pool broadens: its centre dims and its rim brightens. add energy, and every count grows in proportion: the pool itself.

reels.name: Path
reels.cap: Now let the site slide across the crystal, and follow its cloud in square-root space.
reels.doc: The Ziv-Zakai idea as geometry (illustrative, two photomultipliers): as the site slides, its cloud's centre traces a path. The CRLB reads only how fast the centre moves near the truth. The ZZB asks, for every shift h, how often sites h apart are confused, and adds up h times that confusion, so a far rival on a fold counts. Fewer photons shrink the path while the clouds keep their size: the threshold.
reels.words: now let the site slide across the crystal, and follow its cloud in square-root space. from one edge, through the middle, to the other edge, its centre traces a path. the cramer rao bound looks only at the path near the true site: how far the centre moves for a small step. if it quickly outruns its cloud, small errors are rare: the error is the cloud's size over that speed. but this path folds back. a site on the far side makes almost the same pattern, and its cloud overlaps ours. looking only nearby cannot see it. the ziv zakai bound checks every rival. for each shift h, it asks how often the best test confuses two sites h apart. near shifts are confused often, then hardly ever, until the fold brings a bump far out. each confusion costs an error of h, so the bound adds up h times the confusion over every shift. the far bump costs the most, and it is exactly what the cramer rao bound never looks at. with fewer photons the whole path shrinks, but the clouds keep their size. at low energy, every rival sits inside the cloud, the confusion stays high at every shift, and the error leaves the cramer rao line. that is the threshold.

reels.name: Threshold
reels.cap: Now the real slab, in numbers: the error across the slab, against the energy a site leaves.
reels.doc: Transverse error of one site against the energy it leaves (clear crystal; y, z, E known; prior |x| <= 12 mm): the CRLB, the ZZB with the exact and the Bhattacharyya-bounded P_min, the posterior mean and ML on simulated events.
reels.words: now the real slab, in numbers: the error across the slab, against the energy a site leaves. the cramer rao line: a quarter of the light, twice the error. the prior caps everything at the spread of possible positions. the ziv zakai bound, checking every rival, sits on that line while the path is long. dashed, the same bound built from bhattacharyya's distance alone: a little looser, but with no counting at all. so for one site, the cramer rao bound is a safe guide for all but the faintest deposits. the real trouble is a second site.

reels.name: One or two
reels.cap: Two sites across the slab, at five millimetres depth, each with half the energy.
reels.doc: Two sites (equal split, across the slab at one depth) against the single 511 keV site most like them; as they part, the patterns differ, but only as the separation squared.
reels.words: two sites across the slab, at five millimetres depth, each with half the energy. beside them, the single site whose pattern looks most like theirs, found by searching every position and depth.

reels.name: Off surface
reels.cap: Zoom in on the sheet of single sites, near the middle of the slab.
reels.doc: Two sites (4 mm apart across, equal split) as a point just off the sheet of single 511 keV sites, drawn in the sheet's own frame around the best single site (two directions along it, one straight off towards the two-site pattern; all lengths true, in square-root counts). The naive single site at the energy-weighted centre is further away; sliding along the sheet (a deeper site) leaves only the perpendicular part.
reels.words: zoom in on the sheet of single sites, near the middle of the slab. now two sites four millimetres apart, half the energy each. their light adds, and the sum is not on the sheet: it floats just off it, with its own round cloud.

reels.name: Close sites
reels.cap: On the photomultipliers, here is what sets two sites apart from the centre site: the light spread along the line joining them.
reels.doc: What is left when a single site has done its best (residual maps), why it vanishes up close (expand about the energy-weighted centre: the first order cancels, leaving 1/2 w1 w2 d^2 mu''), and the computed D_B against the separation (slope ~ 4) and against the split.
reels.words: on the photomultipliers, here is what sets two sites apart from the centre site: the light spread along the line joining them. the best single site copies part of that by sitting deeper, and this is what is left: the part no single site can make. why does it vanish up close? write the two sites about their energy-weighted centre c, the first a share of d to one side, the second to the other. expand each pool about c. the first-order shifts are weighted so they cancel exactly: the centre site copies them. what is left is the second order: half w one w two d squared, times the pool's curvature. the split matters too. the leftover scales roughly as w one w two, squared, so an uneven split, one site with most of the energy, is far harder to tell from one.

reels.name: Separation
reels.cap: Now sweep the separation, in the clear crystal.
reels.doc: P_min bracket (and the exact P_min) against separation, across and in depth, clear crystal; delta* at 10 %; the CRLB on the separation, centre unknown, against the line sigma = delta.
reels.words: now sweep the separation, in the clear crystal. for sites across the slab, the band is the bhattacharyya bracket on the best test's error, and the dots are the exact error, by monte carlo, inside it as they must be. sites one above the other in depth part a little sooner.

reels.name: Scattering
reels.cap: An uneven split needs more.
reels.doc: delta* (exact P_min = 10 %, equal split) for each scattering length, across and in depth; at equal light; and the effect of an uneven split.
reels.words: an uneven split needs more. and paper three's guess, that scattering hurts separability, holds here only at equal light.

reels.name: Outro
reels.cap: To sum up.
reels.words: to sum up. bhattacharyya: square-root two light patterns, and measure the gap between them; that distance fences in the error of any test. ziv zakai: slide along the path of patterns and check every rival, near and far. it agrees with the cramer rao bound while the path is long next to the clouds, and catches the threshold when it is not. and for two sites in the clear slab, about four millimetres is the least separation at which any method can tell them from one. the caveats are on screen: a model, known splits, and bounds that compare designs, not predicted resolutions.

title: The Fourier transform in one minute

reels.name: Sum
reels.cap: Any signal can be built from pure tones.
reels.words: any signal can be built from pure tones. take one sine at one hertz, a weaker one at three, and a weaker one still at five. add them up, and you get something close to a square wave. the fourier transform runs this backwards: given the sum, which tones are in it?

reels.name: Coil
reels.cap: Start with our three hertz tone, drawn against time.
reels.doc: The wrap made literal: the graph of g bends around the time axis (each point keeps its height as its distance from the axis; time becomes angle, 1 turn/s), then the camera looks down the axis and sees Wind's drawing.
reels.words: start with our three hertz tone, drawn against time. now wrap it around the time axis, like a ribbon around a rod. each point keeps its height, now as its distance from the rod, and time turns into angle: here, one full turn per second. now look straight down the rod. the wave has become a looping drawing around a centre, and how fast it turns, the trial frequency, is ours to choose.

reels.name: Wind
reels.cap: Here is that drawing, at one turn per second.
reels.words: here is that drawing, at one turn per second. mark its centre of mass, and plot how far it sits from the middle as we dial the trial frequency. for most frequencies the loops spread evenly and the centre stays near the middle. but at exactly three hertz, every peak lands on the same side, and the centre jumps out. keep turning, and it falls back again.

reels.name: Mix
reels.cap: Now mix two tones: two hertz, and a weaker one at four.
reels.doc: Two tones superimposed: one winding, two peaks, each as tall as its tone is strong (0.5 and 0.3).
reels.words: now mix two tones: two hertz, and a weaker one at four. wind the mix around the circle the same way. sweep the trial frequency. at two hertz the stronger tone lines up, and the centre jumps out. past it, the centre settles again, until four hertz, where the weaker tone lines up, and it jumps out less. so every tone in the mix gets its own peak, as tall as that tone is strong.

reels.name: Spectrum
reels.cap: That is the whole transform.
reels.words: that is the whole transform. the exponential is the winding, and the integral is the centre of mass, one for every frequency. feed it our square wave, and out come three spikes: one, three and five hertz, each as strong as the tone that made it.
